MetaphysisNonossifying fibromaWell-circumscribed lytic lesionSpontaneous resolution
DiaphysisOsteoid osteomaSmall round lucency with sclerotic margins, central nidusSpontaneous involution over years
DiaphysisEwing sarcoma MalignantMoth-eaten lysis with onion-skin periosteal layerst(11;22); lung metastases drive mortality
Scenario bank
  1. 13 year old with a firm painless mass above the knee for 3 weeks; x-ray shows a metaphyseal bony spur whose cortex is continuous with the adjacent bone. Without intervention → Benign growth until physeal closure → Osteochondroma — then static through adulthood, observation alone
  2. Adolescent with a hard painless nodule near the knee; the spur points away from the joint and its medullary cavity is continuous with the bone → Osteochondroma → The most common benign bone tumour — cortical continuity is diagnostic
  3. Adolescent boy with nocturnal thigh pain unrelated to activity and relieved by ibuprofen; film shows a small round lucency with sclerotic margins → Osteoid osteoma → Diaphyseal, with a central nidus
  4. Untreated osteoid osteoma over the following years → Spontaneous involution → Which is why NSAIDs and serial films are reasonable
  5. Why an osteoid osteoma hurts at night and answers to ibuprofen → Prostaglandin production by the nidus → NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins, so the response is near-diagnostic
  6. 15 year old with weeks of progressive knee pain and a palpable mass; metaphyseal film shows mixed lucency and density with a sunburst periosteal reaction → Osteosarcoma → The commonest primary bone malignancy of childhood, at the metaphysis
  7. 12 year old with progressive night pain, fever and a mid-shaft femoral lesion; film shows a moth-eaten lytic lesion with onion-skin periosteal layers → Ewing sarcoma → Diaphyseal, and systemic features suggest metastatic disease
  8. The genetic lesion underlying Ewing sarcoma → A t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 translocation → Producing a fusion transcription factor; small round blue cells
  9. Child with a pathological fracture through a well-defined lucency with a thin sclerotic margin in the proximal humeral metaphysis, no periosteal reaction → Unicameral bone cyst → Medullary expansion thins the cortex; resolves at skeletal maturity
  10. 28 year old with knee pain and an eccentric expansile lytic epiphyseal lesion with a soap-bubble appearance → Giant cell tumour of bone → Epiphyseal and after skeletal maturity; RANKL-driven
  11. 16 year old with constant knee pain and a well-circumscribed epiphyseal lucency with a thin sclerotic rim that crosses the physis → Chondroblastoma → Epiphyseal but skeletally immature — the age separates it from giant cell tumour
Gates and red flags Growth after physeal closure in an osteochondroma is the counselling point — it suggests chondrosarcoma · Night pain that wakes from sleep with systemic features points at malignancy or Ewing, not a benign lesion · Periosteal reaction separates the aggressive from the indolent: sunburst and onion-skin are ominous, absent reaction is reassuring · Age splits the epiphyseal pair — chondroblastoma before skeletal maturity, giant cell tumour after · A painless hard mass with no systemic features and cortical continuity needs observation, not biopsy
Pearls Location first — epiphysis, metaphysis or diaphysis narrows the list before the film is read · Cortical and medullary continuity is what makes an osteochondroma diagnosable on a single plain film · Osteoid osteoma's NSAID response is mechanistic: the nidus makes prostaglandins · Giant cell tumour is benign but behaves badly, and denosumab works because the stroma overexpresses RANKL · Ewing is the diaphyseal small round blue cell tumour; osteosarcoma is the metaphyseal osteoid-producing one
Pairs with Part I Benign Limb Pain in a Child, which owns the well child with limb pain and the osteoid osteoma discrimination. Part I The Post-Traumatic Limb Mass carries myositis ossificans. Store the discriminator as a question: where in the bone, and what is the periosteum doing?
Transferable rule When the options are natural courses rather than diagnoses, name the lesion first and then recall what it does — each wrong option is a different tumour's behaviour, offered to whoever never named one.
Class-vs-memberRight family of bone lesion, wrong member's natural history.
Salient decoyMalignant transformation is real at ~1% and reads as the cautious answer.

Scheuermann Kyphosis

MSK · rigid vs flexible kyphosis · the correction test decides everything

The decision point

A teenager presents with progressive thoracic kyphosis. The question gives you one exam move: does the curve correct when the patient lies prone or on hyperextension? A curve that corrects is postural roundback; a curve that does not correct is structural. When the kyphosis is rigid and the lateral spine film shows anterior wedging ≥5° in ≥3 consecutive vertebrae, the diagnosis is Scheuermann disease. Schmorl nodes (disc herniation through the endplate) support the diagnosis but are not required.

Pattern-matching “teenager with kyphosis” to postural roundback without running the correction test is the miss. The fix is a single exam finding: ask “does it correct?” before naming the disease.

Defining criteria Scheuermann radiographic criteria — anterior wedging ≥5° in ≥3 consecutive thoracic vertebrae · Correction test — rigid kyphosis does not correct with prone positioning or active extension; flexible kyphosis does · Schmorl nodes — disc herniation through the vertebral endplate; supportive but not required
Thoracic kyphosis — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Scheuermann diseaseAdolescent M, progressive rigid kyphosis, painDoes not correct prone; ≥5° wedging in ≥3 vertebrae—
Postural kyphosisAdolescent, round-shouldered, flexibleCorrects with prone positioningRigid on exam
Ankylosing spondylitisYoung adult M, sacroiliac pain, morning stiffness >30 minSacroiliitis on imaging; bamboo spine is lateNo SI symptoms, adolescent
Compression fractureOsteoporosis or trauma; acute focal painHeight loss at one level, not three consecutiveThree-level wedging, no trauma
Vertebral tumorNight pain, weight loss, neurologic findingsPain that wakes from sleep; focal lytic/blastic lesionNo red flags, multilevel pattern
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo M, progressive thoracic roundback that does not correct when prone, lateral film shows 5-degree anterior wedging at T7 through T9 with Schmorl nodes → Scheuermann disease → observation or bracing if skeletally immature
  2. 15 yo F, round-shouldered posture that fully corrects when she lies prone and when she actively extends, no pain, normal films → Postural kyphosis → postural exercises and reassurance
  3. 14 yo M with Scheuermann disease, Cobb angle 55 degrees, 2 years of growth remaining, compliant with exercises but curve progressing → Thoracolumbosacral orthosis → bracing for progressive curves in skeletally immature patients
  4. 17 yo M with Scheuermann disease, Cobb angle 80 degrees, refractory pain, skeletal maturity reached → Posterior spinal fusion → surgery for severe curves or refractory symptoms at skeletal maturity
  5. 16 yo M with rigid thoracic kyphosis on exam, the most appropriate initial imaging → Standing lateral thoracic spine radiograph → plain film first for structural kyphosis
  6. Why Schmorl nodes form in Scheuermann disease → Disc material herniates through a weakened cartilaginous endplate into the vertebral body
Pearls The correction test is the fastest discriminator in spinal deformity: prone or hyperextension separates structural from postural in one move · Scheuermann treatment — Cobb-angle-driven: <50° and asymptomatic → observe; 50–75° with growth remaining → brace; >75° or refractory pain → surgery · Schmorl nodes are disc herniations through the endplate — they look dramatic on imaging but are the mechanism, not the emergency · Postural kyphosis has no structural vertebral changes; films are normal or show smooth, correctable curvature
Pairs with Scoliosis screening — shared complaint: adolescent spinal deformity; discriminator: coronal vs sagittal plane.
Transferable rule One exam maneuver — does the curve correct with positioning — separates structural from postural kyphosis, and the radiographic criteria exist to confirm Scheuermann, not to diagnose it; the bedside test comes first.
Unchecked attributePostural kyphosis tempts because it is the most common cause of adolescent roundback, but the correction test was not checked.
True-fact-wrong-slotAS causes spinal deformity in young males, but presents with sacroiliac involvement, not isolated thoracic wedging.

Musculoskeletal & Rheumatology

The Acute Hot Joint (adult)

Aspirate before you treat

Source vignette Pt — adult with an acute hot, swollen, erythematous joint, severe pain on passive range of motion, and fever; history of obesity, hypertension and diabetes · Imaging — radiograph shows joint space narrowing · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned empiric antibiotics, anti-inflammatory therapy and arthrocentesis
The decision point

An acute hot, swollen, erythematous joint with severe pain on passive range of motion and fever gets aspirated — and the reason is stronger than "this looks septic." Nothing on exam can exclude infection, gout and septic arthritis overlap completely, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage in days. Aspiration is diagnostic and therapeutic.

The comorbidities point the opposite way from how they read. Obesity, hypertension, and diabetes feel like "metabolic → gout" — but diabetes is a septic arthritis risk factor, and joint space narrowing on x-ray means preexisting joint disease, another one.

Synovial fluid analysisWBC & PMN interpretation
Synovial fluidWBCPMNInterpretation
Non-inflammatory (OA)200–2,000 ⚠︎<25%Degenerative
Inflammatory (gout, RA)2,000–50,000 ⚠︎>50%Crystal or autoimmune
Septic>50,000, often >100k>75%Drain + IV antibiotics
Crystals Gout — negatively birefringent needles (monosodium urate). Pseudogout — positively birefringent rhomboids (CPPD), with chondrocalcinosis on x-ray. Serum uric acid is useless acutely — often normal during a flare (urate shifts into the joint) and elevated in many who never flare.
Management ladder — the acute hot joint
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Arthrocentesis — cell count + differential, Gram stain, culture, crystalsAlways, for any acute hot joint
2Empiric IV antibiotics after cultures drawn — vancomycin ± ceftriaxone/cefepimePurulent fluid or >50,000 WBC; do not wait for culture
3Joint drainage — serial aspiration, arthroscopic, or open washoutConfirmed septic arthritis
Scenario bank
  1. 47 yo F, hot knee, aspirate 68,000 WBC, 85% PMN, no crystals → Septic arthritis → vancomycin + drainage
  2. 55 yo M, acute first-MTP pain after a steak dinner, aspirate 12,000 WBC, negatively birefringent needles → Gout → NSAID or colchicine
  3. 72 yo F, hot knee, x-ray shows chondrocalcinosis, positively birefringent rhomboids → Pseudogout
  4. 47 yo F, aspirate shows crystals AND 60,000 WBC → Treat as septic → crystals do not exclude coexisting infection
  5. 68 yo M with a knee prosthesis, aspirate 3,000 WBC, 70% PMN → Prosthetic joint infection → the 50,000 threshold does not apply — the prosthetic gate is ~3,000/µL with >70% PMN (guideline-verified)
  6. 24 yo F, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustular rash → Disseminated gonococcal → NAAT + cultures
  7. 47 yo F with cellulitis overlying the knee → Arthrocentesis straight through the cellulitis → it seeds the joint; go image-guided or through clean skin
  8. 60 yo M with sickle cell, hot joint → Add Salmonella to coverage
Trap autopsy Naproxen — skipped tier; treats an unestablished diagnosis and delays drainage. Serum uric acid — wrong parameter; neither rules in nor out. Intra-articular corticosteroid — actively contraindicated into a possibly infected joint. MRI — redundant; the x-ray is done and there's no trauma.
Pairs with Part I Septic Arthritis of the Hip, Transient Synovitis Mirror twin (pediatric), and Septic Bursitis — the extraarticular mimic, where preserved joint motion moves the needle from joint to bursa. Note the asymmetry: tier 1 has no fork in adults — every acute hot joint aspirates. The pediatric twin is the only place the answer diverges, and it diverges on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid.
Transferable rule When a test is both diagnostic and therapeutic and the disease it excludes is time-destructive, it precedes every treatment option — even one that would be right for the more likely diagnosis. You don't aspirate because it's probably septic; you aspirate because you can't prove it isn't.

Acute Low Back Pain with No Red Flags

A wall of negatives is permission to do less

Source vignette Pt — adult with acute low back pain under 4 to 6 weeks after a clear mechanical trigger; neurologic examination completely normal, and the history systematically negative for red flags · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned imaging, specialist referral, opioids and conservative care
The decision point

Acute (<4–6 weeks) back pain with a clear mechanical trigger and a completely normal neurologic exam, in a stem that spends its sentences deleting red flags. Nothing licenses imaging or escalation → NSAIDs + stay active.

Stem findings → options ruled out
Stem lineWhat it kills
"no fever, chills"Osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess
"no constipation or urinary incontinence"Cauda equina
"no tenderness over the spine" (paraspinal only)Fracture, malignancy, infection
"DTRs normal, strength intact, sensation normal"Radiculopathy with objective deficit
"began 1 day after moving furniture"Supplies the mechanical cause
Management ladder — acute low back pain
TierInterventionEscalate when
1NSAIDs + stay active (avoid bed rest); ± heat, ± short muscle relaxantNo improvement at 4–6 weeks, or a red flag appears
2Physical therapy; MRI if radicular symptoms persistRadicular symptoms ≥6 weeks
3Epidural steroid injectionFailed conservative therapy
4Surgical referralProgressive deficit, cauda equina, refractory pain
Trap autopsy Bed rest — actively harmful; bed rest delays recovery. A reversed-teaching item: the old advice is now the wrong answer. CT lumbosacral spine — wrong twice: no indication at 1 week, and wrong modality (MRI images disc and nerve root). Epidural injection — skipped tier, needs ≥4–6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone — systemic steroids do not improve outcomes in acute sciatica.
Why the no-imaging rule exists Early imaging leads to more surgery without better outcomes. Asymptomatic disc bulges and degenerative change are near-universal by middle age, so a scan mostly generates incidental findings that invite intervention. Also: ~90% of acute low back pain and ~90% of sciatica resolve within 6 weeks.
Scenario bank
  1. 47 yo F, same pain now at 8 weeks with persistent L5 symptoms, normal strength → MRI, PT, consider epidural
  2. 47 yo F, new urinary retention and saddle anesthesia → Emergent MRI + decompression
  3. 47 yo F, new foot drop → Urgent MRI → this is a progressive deficit
  4. 62 yo F with prior breast cancer, pain worse at night, unrelieved by rest → MRI for metastasis
  5. 34 yo M, 3 months, better with activity, worse with rest, morning stiffness >30 min → Inflammatory back pain → SI joint imaging, HLA-B27
  6. 68 yo M, leg pain walking, relieved leaning forward → Spinal stenosis
  7. 28 yo M who injects drugs, back pain with fever and focal spinal tenderness → MRI + blood cultures
  8. 72 yo F on chronic prednisone, pain after a minor fall → X-ray for compression fracture
  9. 47 yo F with CKD and prior GI bleed and acute mechanical low back pain → Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID → same tier, a different agent
Pairs with Part I Low Back Pain Red Flags and Inflammatory Back Pain & Spondyloarthritis. This is the third member of the family and the one with no red flags. Store the discriminator as a question: "Any red flag, and is the neuro exam normal?"
Transferable rule When a stem spends most of its sentences on what the patient doesn't have, it is building a case for doing less. A dense list of pertinent negatives is permission for conservative management.
Skipped tierClass-vs-member

Transient Synovitis: Management

Ask what remains unanswered after the completed study

Source vignette Pt — child, 1 day of hip pain and a limp, upper respiratory infection 10 days ago; appears well, vitals normal, no trauma and no bony tenderness, range of motion limited by pain · Labs — pending at the time of the question · Imaging — ultrasonography shows a small effusion · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned radiography, antibiotics, observation alone and analgesia
The decision point

In this source case, the ultrasound has shown a small effusion, and the child appears well with no trauma and no bony tenderness. The available facts support symptom treatment with ibuprofen. Before adding another imaging study, identify a remaining question that would change management; a completed ultrasound does not exclude every indication for another modality.

Laboratory results are pending in this source case. The supplied clinical picture supports the keyed next step while those results are unavailable. This does not make pending laboratory results irrelevant in every limping child; interpret them with the course and examination when available.

The stem ledgerdone / normal / elapsed — and what each entry rules out
LedgerEntryKills
DoneUltrasonography → small effusionNo additional imaging question is identified by the supplied case; another modality requires its own indication.
Normal"appears well," vitals normal, no tenderness, no traumaSupports the symptomatic-treatment choice in this case; reassess if concerning findings emerge.
Elapsed1 day of pain; URI 10 days ago—
BotheredLimping, ROM limited by painPure observation
Kocher, with what you have Fever >38.5 no · non-weight-bearing no (he walks with a limp) · ESR >40 pending · WBC >12,000 pending. Two known criteria negative; even if both pending values returned positive that's 2/4 — below the aspiration threshold. Kocher is clinic-ledger — not stated in the bank explanation for either this or the septic-arthritis stem.
Management ladder — the limping child after workup
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Rest + NSAIDs, activity as toleratedFever develops · refuses to bear weight · no improvement in 24–48 h ⚠︎
2CBC, ESR, CRP + re-examine → score Kocher≥3 criteria or deterioration
3ArthrocentesisKocher 3–4/4, or effusion with toxicity
4Surgical drainage + IV antibioticsPurulent fluid, >50,000 WBC
Exit ramps & stop criteria Fever → septic pathway · refuses to bear weight → Kocher climbs · point tenderness over bone → osteomyelitis → MRI · not resolving past 1–2 weeks ⚠︎ → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → X-ray · age 10–16 → SCFE → frog-leg lateral · night pain, bruising, weight loss → CBC with smear.
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, post-URI limp, T 39.2, refuses to bear weight, ESR 78 → Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → Kocher 3 of 4
  2. 4 yo M, well-appearing, point tenderness over the femoral metaphysis → Osteomyelitis → MRI
  3. 6 yo M, insidious limp over 6 weeks, normal labs → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → X-ray becomes correct when the timeline is chronic
  4. 13 yo M, 95th %ile height, 3 weeks of thigh pain, ↓ internal rotation → Slipped capital femoral epiphysis → frog-leg lateral of both hips
  5. 4 yo M, limp with night pain waking him, bruising → CBC with smear
  6. 2 yo M, limp after unwitnessed fall, tibial tenderness → Toddler's fracture → tibia X-ray
  7. 4 yo M on ibuprofen, still limping at 3 weeks → Re-image; synovitis should have resolved
  8. 4 yo M, aspirate 80,000 WBC, PMN-predominant → Septic arthritis → drainage + IV antibiotics
Warning about the common mnemonic "Post-viral limp = ibuprofen, not imaging" is an outcome, not a discriminator — and it fails on bank item 1, where a post-viral limp with fever is septic arthritis. Store the question instead: "Is he toxic, and has the joint already been imaged?"
Pairs with Part I Transient Synovitis Mirror twin and Septic Arthritis of the Hip. Part I settles which disease; this settles what to do.
Transferable rule Before ordering another test, identify the unresolved question it would answer and how the result would change the next step. Do not repeat a question the completed study already answered.
Redundant workupMirror twin

Congenital Muscular Torticollis and Plagiocephaly

Tilt toward the mass, chin away · UWorld · the ear tells you which flat head

Source vignette Pt — 2 mo F, right occipital flattening with the right ear pushed forward, head tilted left with the chin turned right, firm non-transilluminating mass in the left sternocleidomastoid, breech delivery · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital muscular torticollis, a lymphatic malformation, craniosynostosis, clavicular fracture and a posterior fossa tumor
The decision point

Torticollis has a direction, and the direction is the diagnosis. The sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side, so a shortened left muscle pulls the left ear toward the left shoulder and swings the chin right — exactly the geometry described, with the mass in the left sternocleidomastoid. The flat head is downstream: she can only look one way, so she lies on one spot.

The etiology is in the delivery note. Breech presentation means intrauterine crowding, the same mechanism that produces developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot. The non-transilluminating mass is the sentence written to stop you answering the neck lump instead of the syndrome.

Defining criteria Congenital muscular torticollis — head tilts toward the tight sternocleidomastoid, chin rotates away from it · Positional plagiocephaly — flat occiput with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced anteriorly, a parallelogram skull · Lambdoid craniosynostosis — flat occiput with the ipsilateral ear displaced posteriorly, a trapezoid skull with a palpable ridge
The infant with a neck mass or flat head — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Congenital muscular torticollisIntrauterine crowding — breech, twins, oligohydramniosTilt toward, chin away, firm non-transilluminating sternocleidomastoid mass
Positional plagiocephalySupine sleep, car seats, limited neck rotationIpsilateral ear pushed forward; parallelogram
CraniosynostosisPremature suture closureIpsilateral ear pushed backward, palpable ridge, no neck mass
Cystic hygromaCongenital lymphatic malformation, aneuploidy associationFluctuant and transilluminates, posterior triangle
Clavicle fractureShoulder dystociaCrepitus and arm pseudoparalysis, not a neck tilt
Posterior fossa tumor Can't missAcquired tilt in an older childCranial nerve palsies and papilledema, no neck mass
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo F, right occipital flattening with the right ear pushed forward, tilts left with chin right, firm left sternocleidomastoid mass, breech delivery → Congenital muscular torticollis → repositioning, tummy time and physical therapy
  2. 3 mo F, flat right occiput with the right ear anterior, full neck range of motion, sleeps supine → Positional plagiocephaly → repositioning and tummy time
  3. 4 mo M, flat right occiput with the right ear displaced posteriorly, a palpable ridge, no neck mass → Craniosynostosis → head CT and craniofacial referral
  4. Newborn F with a soft, fluctuant posterior-triangle neck mass that transilluminates → Cystic hygroma → karyotype and imaging
  5. Newborn after shoulder dystocia, not moving the right arm, with crepitus over the clavicle → Clavicle fracture → reassurance and gentle immobilization
  6. 8 yo M with a new head tilt, morning vomiting, papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy → Posterior fossa tumor → MRI of the brain
  7. 3 wk M with a painless firm neck mass who tilts toward it, delivered breech → Congenital muscular torticollis
  8. 2 mo F with congenital muscular torticollis, what else must be screened for → Hip ultrasound → developmental dysplasia of the hip is the association
  9. 2 mo F with torticollis and a positive Ortolani and Barlow maneuver → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → Pavlik harness
  10. 6 mo F with congenital muscular torticollis and no improvement after 3 months of stretching → Refer to pediatric orthopedics
Crowding is a package deal Breech, oligohydramnios and multiple gestation produce congenital muscular torticollis, developmental dysplasia of the hip, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot together. Find one and examine for the rest — the stem's explicit note that the hips are stable is the examiner confirming they know this.
Pearls Cystic hygroma is soft, fluctuant and transilluminates; the torticollis mass is firm and does not · Missed or delayed treatment leads to permanent craniofacial asymmetry · Treatment is positioning, tummy time, passive stretching and physical therapy, with helmets reserved for severe or refractory plagiocephaly · An acquired head tilt in an older child with any neurologic sign is a posterior fossa tumour until imaged
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence shares the constraint physiology — absent amniotic fluid produces clubfeet and flat facies by the same mechanism that produces torticollis in a breech infant.
Transferable rule When a stem asks for the underlying cause, the answer explains every finding rather than the most alarming one, so count the findings your choice leaves orphaned and reject any option that leaves one behind.
Salient decoyBirth trauma sells the clavicle fracture, which affects the arm rather than the neck.
Mirror twinCraniosynostosis is the other flat-head diagnosis, separated only by which way the ear points.
True-fact-wrong-slotA posterior fossa tumour causes acquired tilt with cranial nerve findings, not a neonatal neck mass.

Pediatrics 5 topics + 6 board-style

Growth, development and the general-paediatric board questions that belong to no single organ. Everything else paediatric is filed under its organ system and reachable from the Pediatrics shelf — age is a filter here, not a category.

Growth & Developmental Milestones

Derive, don't memorize

The decision point

Growth: birth weight is regained by 10–14 days, doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 1 year, quadruples by 2. When numbers match a milestone rule and the exam is normal, the answer is the reassurance option and every distractor is an unnecessary intervention.

The four developmental laws
  • Motor descends the body — 2 mo lifts head · 4 mo head steady + forearms · 6 mo rolls / props on hands · 9 mo sits alone · 12 mo pulls to stand and cruises
  • Grasp moves pinky-side → thumb-side — 4 mo midline · 6 mo whole-hand reach · 9 mo raking · 12 mo pincer
  • Language: vowels → consonants → meaning — 4 mo "ooo" · 6 mo raspberries/squeals · 9 mo "mamama" · 12 mo "mama" meaning mama
  • Social: everyone → someone — 2 mo social smile at anyone · 6 mo familiar faces · 9 mo stranger and separation anxiety · 12 mo social games, object permanence
Age anchors
AgeImageHook
2 moThe Greeter — lifts head, tracks you, smiles, coosTWO eyes track, TWO lips smile
4 moThe Sphinx — head steady on forearms, hands to midline and mouthFOUR = everything to the FORE
6 moThe Roller — rolls, sits propped, mouths toys, laughsSIX: Sits, Squeals, raSpberries
9 moThe Anxious Sitter — sits alone, rakes, babbles, cries at strangersNINE = "No! Not you!"
12 moThe Little Person — cruises, pinches a Cheerio, first wordONE year = ONE word, ONE-finger pinch
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, birth weight 3.2 kg, now 6.6 kg, normal exam → Normal growth — weight doubles by 4 to 6 months → reassurance
  2. 12 mo M whose weight has tripled since birth → Normal growth → reassurance
  3. 10 day M who has not yet regained his birth weight → Normal weight loss — birth weight is regained by 10 to 14 days → reassurance
  4. 2 mo M who lifts his head and smiles socially → Age-appropriate development
  5. 9 mo M who cannot sit without support → Gross motor delay → developmental evaluation
  6. 6 mo M who does not babble and does not respond to sound → Audiology evaluation
  7. 18-month-old with a 12 to 15 word vocabulary understood mainly by family, frequent jargon, single words without phrases, who scribbles, follows a one-step command without gesture and shows stranger anxiety, but pulls to stand and only cruises → Gross motor delay → walking easily is expected by 18 months
  8. 18-month-old with isolated gross motor delay and otherwise normal development → Refer for early intervention services → under age 3 the referral is the pathway
  9. Why an 18-month-old’s language is normal although strangers understand few of his words → Speech is expected to be intelligible mainly to family at this age, with jargon normal → intelligibility milestones come later
Red flags — worth more points than the milestones No social smile by 3 mo · no babbling by 9 mo · no words by 15 mo · not walking by 18 mo · hand preference before 12 months (suggests hemiparesis) · loss of any acquired milestone at any age — regression is always pathologic (Rett, autistic regression, metabolic disease, leukodystrophy).
Primitive reflexes must leave before the skill arrives Palmar grasp gone 3–6 mo (enables voluntary grasp) · Moro by 6 mo · rooting by 4 mo · ATNR by 4–6 mo · parachute appears 6–8 mo and stays for life · Babinski normal until 12–24 mo. Persistence beyond these windows = UMN lesion / cerebral palsy. Note: the CDC 2022 revision moved milestones from the 50th to the 75th percentile — that's why "sits without support" now sits at 9 months where older sources say 6.
The 18-month set, and the ages that neighbour it Walks easily and climbs — the gross motor item, and the one this stem fails · Scribbles — fine motor · At least 3 words beyond mama and dada, with frequent jargon — language; intelligibility to strangers is not expected yet · Follows a one-step command without gesture — cognitive · Two-word phrases belong to 24 months and 75% intelligible speech to age 3, so a stem citing either against an 18-month-old is testing whether you know the age rather than the child · Stranger anxiety is normal from 6 to 9 months to about age 2 and argues for intact social development rather than against it
Pairs with Part I Toddler Food Refusal owns the case where growth falters because of how the child eats rather than how much.

Maternal Carryover in Newborn Labs

separate maternal carryover from the baby's own disease · board question · Is the infant voiding, growing and normal on exam — and does the mother's chart explain the number?

Source vignette Pt — 23 h old, well, 2 voids, 3% weight loss; mother on hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease · Labs — creatinine 4.2 · Q — the most likely explanation; options spanned maternal creatinine crossing the placenta, hypoxic-ischemic renal injury and prerenal azotemia
The decision point

Creatinine crosses the placenta freely, so a value drawn at 23 hours is a two-patient result — and this mother has end-stage renal disease on regular hemodialysis. The infant's own ledger says the kidneys are working: two voids (the floor is one void per day of life), 3% weight loss (expected is under 10%), normotensive, no edema, no dysmorphism. With no red flag and a maternal source sitting in the history, the number needs no renal explanation of its own.

Defining criteria Neonatal creatinine at birth — equals the mother's value; it falls over the first 2 postnatal weeks to a nadir set by the infant's muscle mass · Urine output floor — at least one void per day of life · Expected weight loss — under 10% of birth weight in the first days · Red flags that make it the baby's kidney — oliguria, edema, or hypertension; any of the three earns a renal ultrasound and a trended creatinine, especially with nephrotoxic drugs or perinatal hypoxia
Pertinent positives & negatives Mother with ESRD on hemodialysis — her creatinine is high and it crosses the placenta; this is the explanation · Two voids at 23 hours — meets the one-void-per-day-of-life floor; excludes renal agenesis and argues against oliguric injury · 3% weight loss — within expected; excludes dehydration and breastfeeding failure as the cause of the number · Apgars 8 and 9 — excludes perinatal asphyxia, and with it hypoxic-ischemic renal injury · Examination otherwise unremarkable — normotensive, no edema, no Potter facies or limb deformity; no red flag, so no imaging is indicated · Total bilirubin 4.3 at 23 hours — normal for age; the jaundice explains why a panel exists, not why the creatinine is high · Intraamniotic infection with ampicillin and cefotaxime — the reason chemistries were drawn at all; neither drug is nephrotoxic, which removes a named risk factor ⚠︎ · Maternal SLE — inert for the creatinine, but it is the setup for the transplacental antibody diseases the same axis generates ⚠︎
An abnormal newborn laboratory value — the differential
ExplanationIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Maternal renal failure (carryover)Creatinine crosses the placenta; the day-1 value is the mother's and falls over 2 weeksA well infant with normal output and a mother with renal disease— (the answer)
Bilateral renal agenesis Can't missOligohydramnios sequence; pulmonary hypoplasiaNo or minimal urine output, respiratory distress, Potter facies and limb deformitiesVoided twice; no distress; normal exam
Hypoxic-ischemic renal injuryPerinatal asphyxia injures the tubules; creatinine rises abnormally over daysLow Apgars and an abnormal neurologic examApgars 8 and 9; exam normal
Dehydration (prerenal)Inadequate intake while feeding is established; prerenal azotemiaWeight loss ≥10% with reduced voids3% loss; two voids
Breastfeeding jaundiceInadequate intake early; explains hyperbilirubinemia, and only reaches creatinine through dehydrationIt answers the bilirubin, not the creatinineBilirubin normal for age; no dehydration
Tier fingerprint done — chemistry and bilirubin drawn as part of the sepsis workup · normal — urine output, weight, blood pressure, examination · elapsed — 23 hours, which is exactly when a maternal value has not yet cleared.
Management ladder — newborn maternal carryover
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Well infant, output and exam normal, maternal source in the chart: document voids and repeat the creatinine in 24–48 hours ⚠︎Oliguria (fewer voids than days of life), edema, hypertension, or a creatinine that fails to fall
2Any red flag, or a risk factor (nephrotoxic drug, perinatal hypoxia): renal ultrasound and trend the creatinine; review the medication listAnuria, a rising creatinine, or electrolyte or fluid derangement
3Nephrology involvement; renal replacement therapy for refractory derangement ⚠︎—
Numbers that gate & exit ramps the one-void-per-day-of-life floor, the 10% weight-loss limit, and the 2-week normalization window — all in-context. · no void by 24 hours with respiratory distress → obstructive uropathy or agenesis, image now · maternal anti-Ro/SSA with fetal or neonatal bradycardia → congenital heart block ⚠︎ · maternal Graves → transplacental TSI and neonatal thyrotoxicosis ⚠︎ · maternal ITP → transplacental antiplatelet IgG and neonatal thrombocytopenia ⚠︎.
Decision spine What was actually asked? — The creatinine — not the jaundice that brought her in · Is the baby making urine? — Two voids at 23 hours → the floor is met · Is she dry? — 3% loss → no · Was there an insult? — Apgars 8 and 9 → no · Does the mother's chart contain the number? — ESRD on hemodialysis → yes, and creatinine crosses the placenta
Scenario bank
  1. 23-hour-old, well, 2 voids, 3% weight loss, creatinine 4.2, mother on hemodialysis for ESRD → Maternal creatinine carryover → maternal creatinine crosses the placenta; Repeat the value rather than image
  2. Day 4, creatinine still 4.2, one void in 24 hours, mother on hemodialysis → Renal ultrasound and a trended creatinine → The value should have been falling
  3. Day 1, no void in 26 hours, respiratory distress, flat facies and limb deformities → Bilateral renal agenesis → Potter sequence from oligohydramnios
  4. Term infant, Apgars 2 and 4, encephalopathic at 4 hours, creatinine rising on day 2 with oliguria → Therapeutic hypothermia → with supportive renal care; Hypoxic-ischemic injury
  5. Day 5, breastfeeding, 12% weight loss, one void in 24 hours, sodium 152, sunken fontanelle → Supervised feeding with supplementation and rehydration → Breastfeeding failure with prerenal azotemia
  6. Day 3, mother with immune thrombocytopenia, infant platelets 40,000, well with no bleeding → Observe with serial platelet counts → Transplacental antiplatelet IgG
  7. Day 5, mother with Graves disease, infant tachycardic and irritable with a goiter → Methimazole with a beta-blocker → Transplacental thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
  8. Mother with systemic lupus erythematosus; fetal heart rate 55 at 22 weeks, persisting after birth → Maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibody transfer → transplacental passage; Congenital complete heart block
  9. 23-hour-old, well, creatinine 4.2 explained by maternal ESRD; which intervention is inappropriate → Initiate neonatal renal replacement therapy → The number is not the infant's
  10. Day 1 creatinine 4.2 from maternal ESRD; which test establishes the infant's own renal function → Repeat serum creatinine in 1-2 weeks → The nadir reflects infant muscle mass
Decoy note The delivery paragraph is the whole trap: infection, arrest of labor, cesarean — three details that are compatible with the right answer and suggestive of the wrong one, disarmed by the Apgars two sentences later. The jaundice is a second decoy of a different kind — it is the reason the panel was drawn, so it feels like the thing to explain, and the question deliberately asks about a different value in the same panel. Maternal SLE is inert for the creatinine but not for the topic: it is the entry point to the antibody-mediated members of this same family.
Pearls Day-one creatinine is the mother's; it falls to the infant's own nadir over two weeks, and normal urine output proves the kidneys work. · Creatinine, IgG antibodies, and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin all cross the placenta, so all three can produce a "neonatal" finding that is really maternal — IgM and TSH do not. · Normal urine output is the cheapest renal function test in a newborn: at least one void per day of life, so two voids on day one is normal and none by 24 hours is not. · Up to 10% weight loss in the first days is expected; beyond that, look for feeding failure with hypernatremia and prerenal azotemia. · Ampicillin and cefotaxime are the non-nephrotoxic sepsis pair; when gentamicin is in the stem instead, a rising creatinine acquires a named risk factor ⚠︎. · The maternal antibody diseases run on one sentence of history each: anti-Ro/SSA → congenital heart block; Graves → neonatal thyrotoxicosis; ITP → neonatal thrombocytopenia; all transient as maternal IgG clears ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence owns the obstructed, oliguric end of this differential — the infant whose creatinine really is his own. Store the discriminator as a question: is the baby making urine, and does the mother's chart contain the number? Candidate twin — confirm: a brief on maternal-antibody neonatal disease (anti-Ro, TSI, antiplatelet) does not exist yet; this brief wants it.
Transferable rule A newborn's laboratory value in the first days belongs to two patients — read the maternal history as part of the panel before attributing anything to the infant, and when a number and a ledger disagree, the ledger of output, growth and examination decides.
Salient decoyHypoxic-ischemic renal injury — Apgars 8 and 9 with a normal examination; asphyxia leaves a mark the stem does not have
True-fact-wrong-slotDehydration — 3% weight loss and two voids; the stem's own numbers exclude it
Salient decoyBreastfeeding jaundice — It answers the bilirubin; the question asked about the creatinine, and it reaches creatinine only through a dehydration that is absent
Treat-the-numberBilateral renal agenesis — Agenesis produces no or minimal urine; she voided twice, breathes normally, and has no Potter features

Maternal Hormone Effects in the Newborn

what is physiologic and what is not · board question · Is the infant well, and is the finding inside the first two weeks?

Source vignette Pt — 5 do F, white mucoid vaginal discharge streaked with blood, afebrile, feeding and voiding well, otherwise normal examination · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned maternal hormone withdrawal, candidal vaginitis and a vaginal foreign body
The decision point

In utero, maternal estrogen crosses the placenta and proliferates the fetal endometrium. At delivery that supply stops: maternal progesterone is withdrawn and estrogen's trophic effect is lost, the endometrium sloughs, and the newborn has light vaginal bleeding — typically within the first 2 weeks and lasting under five days. The white mucoid component is physiologic leukorrhea, the same hormone acting on the same tissue, and it travels with labial swelling and breast hypertrophy as the other estrogen effects. This infant is afebrile, painless, feeding and voiding normally, five days old, with an otherwise unremarkable examination. That is the whole answer, and the management is reassurance.

Defining criteria Neonatal withdrawal bleeding — light vaginal bleeding in the first 2 weeks of life, self-limited (<5 days), from withdrawal of maternal progesterone and loss of maternal estrogen's trophic effect on a proliferated endometrium · The other maternal estrogen effects — physiologic leukorrhea (thin, white discharge), labial swelling, breast hypertrophy ± galactorrhea · Diagnosis and management — clinical diagnosis; observation with parental reassurance; resolves on its own within days
Pertinent positives & negatives White mucoid discharge with blood streaks on day 5 — leukorrhea plus withdrawal bleeding, both maternal estrogen effects, both inside the two-week window · Afebrile, painless, feeding and voiding adequately — a well infant; infection and foreign body bring pain, odor, purulence, or systemic signs · Mother treated for an STI early in pregnancy and subsequently tested negative — a documented test of cure, which closes the vertical-transmission branch rather than opening it · Forceps-assisted delivery — instrumentation is a planted trauma cue; it does not produce vaginal bleeding five days later · A 9-year-old sister at home — the household-contact cue for group A Streptococcus, named in the source precisely because it is a plausible route · Age 5 days — far too young for a vaginal foreign body, which requires toilet-training age or self-exploration · Remainder of the examination unremarkable — no mucosal erythema (candida), no purulence (streptococcal), no odor (foreign body) · Exclusively breastfed with normal output — nothing systemic; this is a well-baby finding presenting to an emergency department
Maternal hormone effects in the newborn — physiologic or not
CauseIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Maternal hormone withdrawalTransplacental estrogen proliferates the endometrium; delivery removes it and the lining sloughsLight bleeding with leukorrhea in the first 2 weeks of a well newborn, often with labial swelling or breast hypertrophy— (the answer)
Candidal vaginitisYeast overgrowth; in a prepubertal child essentially requires recent antibiotics or immunosuppressionThick, adherent white discharge with an erythematous mucosa; bleeding is not typicalDischarge is mucoid, mucosa is normal, no antibiotic or immunosuppression history
Chlamydia trachomatis (vertical)Passage through an infected birth canalConjunctivitis or afebrile pneumonia — not vaginal dischargeWrong syndrome entirely; and the mother's post-treatment test was negative
Group A streptococcal vaginitisTransmitted from a colonized household contact, such as an older siblingMucosal erythema with purulent — not bloody — discharge; uncommonDischarge is bloody and mucoid; mucosa normal; child well
Vaginal foreign bodyToilet paper is commonest; needs toilet-training age or self-explorationFoul-smelling discharge with pain in an older childA 5-day-old cannot place one; no odor, no pain
Trauma or sexual abuse Can't miss ⚠︎Any genital bleeding without a physiologic explanationBleeding outside the newborn window, an inconsistent history, or other injuriesClassic timing, classic appearance, well infant — but this is the row that must be consciously excluded, not forgotten
Management, in one line Management is one sentence: the diagnosis is clinical, nothing is cultured or imaged, and the intervention is education and reassurance while it resolves over days.
Decision spine How old is she? — Day 5 → inside the two-week maternal-hormone window · Is she well? — Afebrile, painless, feeding and voiding → yes · Is the discharge purulent or malodorous, or the mucosa inflamed? — No · Are the other estrogen effects present or plausible? — Leukorrhea is here; look for labial swelling and breast hypertrophy · Can I name a disqualifying criterion? — If not, reassurance is the answer — and the planted cues are not criteria
Scenario bank
  1. 5-day-old with white mucoid vaginal discharge streaked with blood, afebrile, feeding and voiding well, otherwise normal examination → Maternal hormone withdrawal → Physiologic and self-limited
  2. A well-appearing 5-day-old girl has white mucoid vaginal discharge streaked with blood; her parents ask for testing. → Reassurance and observation → It resolves within days
  3. 3-week-old with bilateral breast enlargement and a drop of milky fluid, no redness, feeding well → Physiologic breast hypertrophy → with galactorrhea; Another maternal estrogen effect
  4. 2-week-old with a red, warm, tender breast bud, temperature 38.5 C and irritability → Culture and intravenous antibiotics → Neonatal mastitis
  5. Newborn whose vaginal bleeding has continued 8 days and is increasing at day 10 of life → Evaluate further rather than reassure → Outside the self-limited window
  6. 4-year-old with foul-smelling bloody vaginal discharge and no systemic symptoms → Examination for a vaginal foreign body → Toilet paper is the commonest
  7. 6-year-old with vaginal discharge and a positive gonorrhea nucleic acid amplification test → Report for suspected sexual abuse → and initiate an evaluation; Never a reassurance branch
  8. The physiologic basis of vaginal bleeding in a newborn → Progesterone withdrawal after delivery → maternal estrogen proliferates the fetal endometrium in utero, and withdrawal after delivery causes sloughing; All the estrogen effects share one cause
  9. 7-day-old with purulent conjunctivitis who at 6 weeks has an afebrile staccato cough with tachypnea; mother untreated in pregnancy → Vertical Chlamydia trachomatis transmission → Eyes and lungs, never the vagina
  10. Well 5-day-old with classic withdrawal bleeding; which evaluation is unnecessary → Vaginal culture with pelvic ultrasonography → The diagnosis is clinical
Decoy note This stem plants one cue per distractor, and reading them as a set is the fastest way through it: the word white for candida, the maternal STI for chlamydia, streaks of blood for a foreign body, the 9-year-old sister for streptococcus, and the forceps delivery for trauma. Every one is answered by the same two facts — the age and the wellness. The maternal history in particular is a trap that runs backwards: "a shot and a pill" then "subsequently tested negative" is a documented test of cure, so the sentence that looks like it opens the infectious branch is the sentence that closes it.
Pearls Light vaginal bleeding with white discharge in a well newborn's first two weeks is maternal hormone withdrawal, and it needs only reassurance. · Maternal estrogen crosses the placenta and does four things to a newborn — withdrawal bleeding, leukorrhea, labial swelling, and breast hypertrophy with or without galactorrhea. All are physiologic, and all resolve. · The window is the criterion: bleeding in the first 2 weeks lasting under 5 days is physiologic, and anything outside that is not. · A newborn cannot place a vaginal foreign body; that diagnosis needs toilet-training age or self-exploration, plus odor and pain. · Neonatal breast hypertrophy is bilateral and painless; a red, warm, tender breast bud with fever is mastitis and earns culture and antibiotics ⚠︎. · Vertical chlamydia shows up in the eyes and the lungs — conjunctivitis in the first weeks, afebrile pneumonia at 4 to 12 weeks ⚠︎ — never as vaginal discharge. · Prepubertal genital bleeding or a sexually transmitted organism outside the newborn period is an abuse evaluation until proven otherwise ⚠︎ — the one branch of this differential that is never reassurance.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Benign Neonatal Rashes is the same concept in a different organ — sort the newborn finding into physiologic, removable, or pathologic, and reassure only after the sort. That brief owns the skin; this one owns the genital and breast findings. Store the discriminator as a question: is the baby well, and is the finding inside its window?
Transferable rule Reassurance is a diagnosis with criteria, not an absence of one. Name the disqualifying finding — fever, pain, odor, purulence, systemic illness, or a finding outside its stated window — before you reject the benign answer, because a stem that plants one cue per distractor is testing whether you can leave all of them alone.
Class-vs-memberCandidal vaginitis — Candidal vaginitis is thick and adherent with an erythematous mucosa and does not bleed; in a prepubertal child it essentially requires recent antibiotics or immunosuppression
True-fact-wrong-slotChlamydia trachomatis — Vertical chlamydia causes conjunctivitis or pneumonia, not vaginal discharge — and her post-treatment test was negative
Unchecked attributeVaginal foreign body — It requires a child old enough to toilet-train or self-explore; a 5-day-old cannot, and there is neither odor nor pain
Salient decoyGroup A streptococcal vaginitis — Vaginal streptococcal infection is uncommon and produces mucosal erythema with purulent, not bloody, discharge

Aneuploidy: Reading the Newborn

Which trisomy, from the hands, the midline and the cry · UWorld · the feature map

Source vignette Pt — newborn girl delivered for fetal growth restriction to a 40-year-old woman; prenatal ultrasound showed a ventricular septal defect, further testing declined · Exam — weight and head circumference below the 5th percentile, hypertonia, clenched fists with the second digit overlapping the third and the fifth overlapping the fourth · Q — which additional finding is most likely; options spanned cat-like cry, cutis aplasia, micrognathia, microphthalmia, transverse palmar crease and webbed neck
The decision point

The hands close the question. Clenched fists with overlapping fingers plus hypertonia, growth restriction, microcephaly and a VSD is trisomy 18, and the expected companion finding is micrognathia — alongside a prominent occiput, low-set pointed ears and rocker-bottom feet. Advanced maternal age is the risk factor, through meiotic nondisjunction.

Every wrong option belongs to a different aneuploidy, so this is a feature-map question, not a reasoning one. Cutis aplasia and microphthalmia are trisomy 13. A transverse palmar crease is trisomy 21, which is also hypotonic — the opposite tone to this infant. A cat-like cry is cri-du-chat, a webbed neck is Turner. Learn them as a grid rather than one at a time.

Defining criteria Trisomy 18 hand — clenched fist, index over third and fifth over fourth, with hypertonia · Trisomy 13 midline — cutis aplasia, microphthalmia, holoprosencephaly, omphalocele · Trisomy 21 tone — hypotonia with a transverse palmar crease · Combined first-trimester screen for trisomy 18 — low PAPP-A, low hCG, enlarged nuchal translucency · Confirmation — full karyotype; FISH alone misses mosaicism
Aneuploidy — the feature mapone signature finding each
SyndromeSignature findingSupporting featuresWhat it means
Trisomy 18 (Edwards)Clenched fists, overlapping fingers; hypertoniaGrowth restriction, microcephaly with prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set pointed ears, rocker-bottom feetVSD or PDA in over half; 95% die in the first year
Trisomy 13 (Patau)Cutis aplasia, microphthalmiaHoloprosencephaly, omphalocele — midline defectsAlso highly lethal in infancy
Trisomy 21 (Down)Transverse palmar crease; hypotoniaUp-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spotsCardiac defects and intestinal atresia
Cri-du-chat (5p deletion)Cat-like cryMicrocephaly with protruding metopic suture, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, hypotoniaIntellectual disability, short stature
Turner (45,X)Webbed neckLow hairline, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, short statureCoarctation and gonadal dysgenesis
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn with fetal growth restriction, microcephaly, a ventricular septal defect, hypertonia and clenched fists with the second digit overlapping the third → Trisomy 18 → Edwards syndrome — overlapping fingers are the hand sign
  2. Which additional finding is expected in a newborn with growth restriction, microcephaly, VSD and overlapping fingers → Micrognathia → With prominent occiput, low-set pointed ears and rocker-bottom feet
  3. Newborn with cutis aplasia of the scalp, microphthalmia, an omphalocele and holoprosencephaly → Trisomy 13 → Patau — the midline-defect trisomy
  4. Infant with a high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly with a protruding metopic suture, hypertelorism and a flat nasal bridge → Cri-du-chat syndrome → 5p deletion — the cry is the name
  5. Newborn girl with a webbed neck, low posterior hairline, broad chest with widely spaced nipples and cubitus valgus → Turner syndrome → 45,X — and coarctation, so check the femoral pulses
  6. Hypotonic newborn with up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots and a transverse palmar crease → Trisomy 21 → Down syndrome — hypotonia, not the hypertonia of trisomy 18
  7. Why advanced maternal age raises the risk of trisomy 18 → Meiotic nondisjunction in oogenesis → Homologous chromosomes fail to separate, giving a disomic gamete
  8. Suspected trisomy 18 in a newborn with dysmorphic features; confirming it → Full karyotype → FISH can suggest it but misses mosaicism
  9. Trisomy 18 confirmed in a liveborn infant with a large VSD; the framework for care → Multidisciplinary supportive and palliative care → About 50% die within 2 weeks and 95% within the first year
  10. First-trimester screen showing low PAPP-A, low hCG and an enlarged nuchal translucency → Diagnostic karyotype by chorionic villus sampling → A positive screen always needs a diagnostic test
Gates and caveats Tone separates 18 from 21 — hypertonia with clenched fists versus hypotonia with an open hand · A positive screen is never a diagnosis — cell-free fetal DNA is a screen, however sensitive; karyotype confirms · Cell-free DNA needs 10 weeks or the fetal fraction is too low · Mosaicism — only a full karyotype across multiple cells finds it · Trisomy 18 GI burden — Meckel diverticulum, malrotation and omphalocele in over three quarters, so the abdomen is not incidental
Pearls The hand is the fastest discriminator in the newborn nursery: overlapping fingers for 18, single transverse crease for 21 · Trisomy 13 is the midline trisomy — scalp, eye, forebrain, abdominal wall · Advanced maternal age drives meiotic nondisjunction, which is sporadic and not inherited · Mosaic trisomy arises after fertilisation and so carries no recurrence risk from the parents · Prominent occiput plus micrognathia is the trisomy 18 profile in one line
Pairs with Part I Teratogenic Exposures, which owns the acquired dysmorphology this must be separated from. Store the discriminator as a question: what are the hands doing, and is the tone up or down? Part I Multiple Anomalies in a Newborn is the twin for the non-aneuploid malformation syndromes — CHARGE, VACTERL and Fanconi anaemia — which share coloboma, cleft palate and cryptorchidism with the trisomies and are separated by head size and by the nares.
Transferable rule When every option is a finding from a different syndrome, the question is a lookup, not a deduction — find the one feature you are certain maps to the stem and let it carry the answer.
Class-vs-memberRight family of aneuploidy, wrong trisomy's signature finding.
Unchecked attributeTone is stated in the stem and ignored: hypertonia rules out trisomy 21.

Multiple Anomalies in a Newborn

the rarest component names the syndrome, never the commonest · UWorld · choanal atresia and coloboma are the two that decide

Source vignette Pt — newborn M, 1 hour old, 37 weeks, spontaneous vaginal delivery, scant prenatal care; growth parameters 25th–50th percentile · Course — turned blue during skin-to-skin, pinked up with stimulation and crying · Vitals — temperature 36.8 °C, pulse 150, respirations 48; saturation 97% while crying, falling to 80% when the crying stops · Exam — a 5-French catheter will not pass through either naris; ears short and wide with no earlobes; a lesion of the right eye shown; cleft palate; a loud harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border; testes not palpable; skin and extremities normal · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CHARGE syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, Fanconi anaemia, trisomy 13 and the VACTERL association
The decision point

The stem hands you six anomalies and five syndromes, and most of the six are shared. A heart defect belongs to every option on the list. Cleft palate belongs to three of them, cryptorchidism to three, dysmorphic ears to four. Counting anomalies therefore cannot separate anything. What separates is the finding that appears on the fewest lists: choanal atresia, which among these five belongs to CHARGE alone, and coloboma, which belongs to CHARGE and trisomy 13 and to no one else. Take the intersection and only CHARGE survives — and the stem then closes trisomy 13 with a percentile, because head circumference is 25th–50th and trisomy 13 is microcephalic.

Seven seconds and wrong is a single-cue read: a newborn with anomalies across several organ systems plus a heart defect looks like an association, and VACTERL is the association most students have a ready slot for. The fix is not more syndromes. It is to stop counting the anomalies and start hunting for the one that appears on the fewest lists — a malformation syndrome is named by its rarest component.

Defining criteria — CHARGE, letter by letter C — Coloboma — a gap in an eye structure, here the finding photographed · H — Heart defect — commonly tetralogy of Fallot or a ventricular septal defect; here the harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border · A — Atresia choanae — a 5-French catheter will not pass either naris · R — Retardation of growth and development — postnatal, so it cannot yet be seen at an hour of life · G — Genitourinary anomalies — cryptorchidism here; the testes are not palpable · E — Ear abnormalities — short, wide, lobeless ears, and hearing loss · Gene — CHD7, which regulates gene expression during fetal development; testing confirms the clinical diagnosis
The newborn with multiple anomalies — which syndromeevery one of them carries a heart defect, so the heart decides nothing
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
CHARGE syndromeColoboma, heart defect, choanal atresia, growth and developmental delay, genitourinary and ear anomalies; often cleft lip or palate, hypotonia, anosmia; CHD7Choanal atresia or coloboma in a newborn who also has a heart defectNot excluded — this is the answer
Trisomy 13 (Patau) Can't missHoloprosencephaly, microcephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, cutis aplasia of the scalp, coloboma, cryptorchidism, heart defectMicrocephaly with midline scalp defects and polydactylyHead circumference 25th–50th percentile, and choanal atresia is not a trisomy 13 feature
22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge)Conotruncal heart defect, thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcaemia, cleft palate, dysmorphic earsHypocalcaemic seizure with an absent thymic shadowNeither coloboma nor choanal atresia belongs to it, and the thymic and calcium signature is absent
VACTERL associationVertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defect, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, renal anomalies, limb defectsImperforate anus or a radial ray defect alongside the heart defectNo vertebral, anal, oesophageal, renal or limb finding — and it has no eye or nasal component at all
Fanconi anaemiaAbsent or hypoplastic thumbs, café-au-lait macules and abnormal pigmentation, short stature, renal and ear anomalies, heart defect, marrow failure laterAbnormal thumbs with abnormal skin pigmentationSkin and extremities are stated to be normal; coloboma and choanal atresia are not its features
What to do about it The airway first — bilateral choanal atresia in an obligate nasal breather is an airway emergency; an oral airway holds it until surgical repair, and the giveaway pair is desaturation with feeding and pinking with crying · Then the screen — echocardiogram and renal ultrasonography in every infant with CHARGE, plus audiology · Then confirm — CHD7 testing, although the diagnosis is usually made clinically in the newborn period · Then the long view — lifelong multispecialty care, because growth, puberty and development are all affected
Decision spine — solve the stem in 10 seconds

1. Does a catheter pass through both nares? — no is choanal atresia, and among these five it is CHARGE's alone. 2. Is there a coloboma? — CHARGE or trisomy 13, and nobody else. 3. Is the head small? — microcephaly moves it to trisomy 13; a normal head circumference moves it away. 4. Are the thumbs and the skin normal? — normal thumbs with normal pigmentation exclude Fanconi anaemia. 5. Is there a vertebral, anal, oesophageal, renal or limb anomaly? — their absence excludes VACTERL. 6. Which finding sits on the fewest lists? — that one names the syndrome.

Scenario bank
  1. 1-hour-old M, cyanosis at rest that clears with crying, no catheter passes either naris, coloboma, short lobeless ears, cleft palate, a harsh holosystolic murmur, undescended testes, normal head circumference → CHARGE syndrome → the eye and the nose name it
  2. Newborn whose desaturation recurs whenever he stops crying, with bilateral choanal atresia confirmed at the bedside → Place an oral airway → it does what crying was doing, until surgical repair
  3. Newborn in whom CHARGE syndrome has been diagnosed clinically → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasonography → the two organ systems the acronym names but the examination cannot see
  4. Confirming the diagnosis in a newborn with coloboma, choanal atresia and a ventricular septal defect → CHD7 gene testing → genetic confirmation of a clinical diagnosis
  5. Newborn with cleft lip and palate, coloboma, postaxial polydactyly, punched-out scalp defects, cryptorchidism and a head circumference below the 3rd percentile → Trisomy 13 → microcephaly and midline defects, with nares that are patent
  6. Newborn with hypoplastic thumbs, café-au-lait macules, short stature, a horseshoe kidney and a ventricular septal defect → Fanconi anaemia → thumbs and pigmentation together
  7. Newborn with imperforate anus, hemivertebrae, an absent radius and a ventricular septal defect, who cannot be fed because a catheter coils in the upper oesophagus → VACTERL association → no eye or nasal component in this one
  8. Newborn with an interrupted aortic arch and a seizure on day 2, ionised calcium low, no thymic shadow on the chest film → 22q11.2 deletion syndrome → parathyroid and thymic failure together
  9. Why bilateral choanal atresia declares itself in the delivery room while unilateral disease often waits for a first upper respiratory infection → Bilateral obstruction leaves no route but the mouth → feeding is when it fails; the obligate nasal breather opens it only by crying
Pearls Cleft lip or palate, hypotonia and anosmia are common in CHARGE but do not name it — the eye and the nose do · Choanal atresia can be isolated, but finding it obliges a search for the rest of the acronym · Trisomy 13 and CHARGE share coloboma, cleft palate, cryptorchidism and a heart defect; microcephaly and choanal atresia are the two that separate them · VACTERL and CHARGE overlap only in the cardiac and renal letters, which is exactly why neither of those letters can be used to choose · They re-ask this by holding the heart defect constant and swapping the single uncommon anomaly: the thumbs for Fanconi, the anus for VACTERL, the thymus for 22q11.2, the head size for trisomy 13 · CHD7 — the gene, and a useful hook, since the letters of the syndrome and the gene both start with CH
Pairs with Part I Aneuploidy: Reading the Newborn is the twin that runs the same feature-map reasoning for the trisomies, which is where this brief hands off once microcephaly appears. 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome owns the option in depth. Cyanosis in the Newborn owns the bedside catheter test and the crying manoeuvre. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia owns the VACTERL workup. Store the discriminator as a question: which of these anomalies is on the fewest lists?
Transferable rule In a newborn with anomalies in several systems, do not count the anomalies — find the one that appears on the fewest syndrome lists and let it name the diagnosis. The shared findings tell you that a syndrome exists; they never tell you which one.
Class-vs-memberVACTERL is the ready slot for “anomalies in several systems”, but every one of its six components is absent here.
Unchecked attributeTrisomy 13 matches four of the stem's findings and is excluded by two it does not have — the head circumference was given and not read.
Salient decoyThe cleft palate is present in CHARGE, trisomy 13 and 22q11.2, so it cannot discriminate anything.
Salient decoyThe harsh holosystolic murmur is the most striking finding and the least useful one; all five options carry a heart defect.
6 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Pediatrics

Shock in Children

The category is the mechanism, not the appearance · Aquifer · perfusion before pressure

Source vignette Pt — 4 yo F, fever to 40 C, petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds, no response to three fluid boluses; no blood pressure reported · Q — the category of shock; options spanned distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic and obstructive
The decision point

Fever, a petechial rash and shock in a preschooler is septic shock, and septic shock is by definition distributive: inflammatory mediators produce vasodilation and capillary leak, so blood is maldistributed rather than absent, inadequate or obstructed.

The trap is that she does not look vasodilated. Capillary refill of 4 seconds is cold shock, which is how children usually present — they compensate by vasoconstricting and running the heart rate up, so the bedside picture mimics hypovolemia. Note also what the stem withholds: there is no blood pressure, because in children hypotension is a late, pre-arrest finding.

Defining criteria Distributive shock — vasodilation and capillary leak with maldistributed flow despite normal or high cardiac output · Shock in a child — a perfusion diagnosis: mental status, capillary refill above 2 seconds, weak pulses, urine output under 1 mL/kg/h · Hypotension — not required, and marks decompensation when present · Fluid-refractory shock — persistent after 40 to 60 mL/kg, the trigger to start a vasoactive infusion
The four categories of shock — what to look for
CategoryMechanismThe NBME tell
DistributiveVasodilation and capillary leakFever with a source, urticaria, or a spinal injury; wide pulse pressure when warm
HypovolemicVolume loss — gastrointestinal, hemorrhage, burns, ketoacidosisA stated route of loss, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes
CardiogenicPump failure — myocarditis, arrhythmia, congenital lesionGallop, hepatomegaly, crackles; worsens with fluid
ObstructiveMechanical block — tamponade, tension pneumothorax, ductal-dependent lesionDistended neck veins with clear or asymmetric lungs, muffled sounds
Anaphylactic distributive subtypeIgE-mediated vasodilationUrticaria, angioedema, wheeze within minutes of exposure
Neurogenic distributive subtypeLoss of sympathetic tone above T6Hypotension with bradycardia, warm dry skin
Management ladder — pediatric septic shock
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Recognise, obtain access, balanced crystalloid 10 to 20 mL/kg per bolus up to 40 to 60 mL/kg in the first hour, reassessing after eachShock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, or rales or hepatomegaly appear, which stops the fluid
2Start a vasoactive infusion — epinephrine or norepinephrineCatecholamine-resistant shock
3Hydrocortisone for catecholamine-resistant shock or suspected adrenal insufficiencyNo response; consider extracorporeal support
ParallelAntimicrobials within 1 hour for septic shock, cultures first only if they cause no substantial delay—
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo F with fever to 40 C, a petechial rash, obtundation, capillary refill 4 seconds and no response to three fluid boluses → Distributive shock → septic shock, cold phenotype
  2. 4 yo F in septic shock still hypoperfused after 60 mL/kg of isotonic fluid → Start a vasoactive infusion → fluid-refractory septic shock
  3. 4 yo F with septic shock whose blood cultures are pending → Give antimicrobials within 1 hour → cultures first only if they cause no delay
  4. 9 mo M with 5 days of vomiting and diarrhea, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds and tachycardia → Give a 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus → hypovolemic shock
  5. 8 yo M with viral myocarditis, a gallop, hepatomegaly, crackles and capillary refill 4 seconds → Give small 5 to 10 mL/kg fluid aliquots with an inotrope → cardiogenic shock
  6. 16 yo M with a penetrating chest wound, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds and hypotension → Pericardiocentesis → obstructive shock from tamponade
  7. 5 yo F with meningococcemia who remains shocked on an epinephrine infusion → Give hydrocortisone → Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal insufficiency
  8. 16 yo M with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension minutes after eating peanuts → Anaphylactic shock → a distributive subtype
  9. 17 yo M after a cervical spine injury, hypotensive with bradycardia and warm dry skin → Neurogenic shock → also a distributive subtype
Where the reflex inverts Where intensive care is not available and the child has sepsis without hypotension, bolus fluid is recommended against — a strong, high-certainty recommendation that reverses the usual instinct. And adolescence is never itself a reason to admit: the same hospitalisation thresholds apply as for adults.
Pearls Hypotension is a late sign in children; they defend pressure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then decompensate abruptly · Children get cold shock, adults get warm shock — the vasoconstricted child is still distributive · Anaphylactic and neurogenic shock are distributive subtypes, so the category wins unless the subtype's trigger is in the stem · Neurogenic shock is the one hypotension with bradycardia; everything else in shock is tachycardic · Fever plus petechiae plus toxicity is meningococcemia until excluded; petechiae in a well child point instead at immune thrombocytopenia
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis owns the CSF grid and meningococcal disease, so this brief stops at recognition and resuscitation. Store the discriminator as a question: is perfusion abnormal? If yes, resuscitate before you investigate.
Transferable rule Shock is classified by mechanism rather than appearance, and the exam builds its distractors from the appearance, so ask what is wrong with the circulation instead of what the skin looks like.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluid refractoriness in sepsis reflects leak and vasodilation, not pump failure.
Class-vs-memberAnaphylaxis is the right class with the wrong member — no exposure, no urticaria.

Specific Learning Disorder

Behavior confined to school · UWorld · read the child's private interview

Source vignette Pt — 9 yo M, irritable and fighting at school since third grade began, with school refusal; privately reports classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly; behavior normal at home · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned specific learning disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, social anxiety disorder and oppositional defiant disorder
The decision point

The mother's history is the chief complaint; the child's private disclosure is the diagnosis. She describes irritability, a fight and school refusal; he says his classmates call him a baby because he counts on his fingers and reads slowly. Every behavioral option explains the noise, and only one explains the noise and the failing grades.

Two structural signals seal it. Onset is anchored to an academic transition — third grade, where learning to read becomes reading to learn — and the symptoms are confined to school, with normal behavior at home.

Defining criteria Specific learning disorder — achievement below intellectual potential in reading, writing or math for at least 6 months despite support · ADHD — symptoms in at least 2 settings with onset before age 12, so school-only behavior excludes it · Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder — severe outbursts at least 3 times weekly for at least 12 months with persistently irritable mood between them · Oppositional defiant disorder — a pattern of defiance, argumentativeness and vindictiveness toward authority for at least 6 months · Social anxiety disorder — fear of scrutiny across situations, and not diagnosed when better explained by another disorder
The school-age child with behavior change — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Specific learning disorderBehavior downstream of an academic skill deficitThe child names the deficit himself when interviewed privately
ADHDInattention and hyperactivity carried everywhereSchool and home both complain
Disruptive mood dysregulationChronic angry mood between frequent outburstsOutbursts three times weekly for a year; explains no academic decline
Oppositional defiant disorderDefiance toward authorityArgumentative and vindictive, not avoidant
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny generallyFear of eating, speaking or performing anywhere, not only where a weakness shows
Absence seizuresBrief lapses many times dailyStaring spells provoked by hyperventilation
Hearing or vision impairmentSensory barrier misread as inattentionSits close, turns the head, mishears
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, irritable and fighting only at school since third grade began, reads slowly and counts on fingers, normal behavior at home → Specific learning disorder → educational testing
  2. 9 yo M with suspected specific learning disorder, initial evaluation → Educational testing plus hearing and vision screening → rule out psychiatric and medical causes
  3. 8 yo M, inattentive and disruptive at school and at home, loses things, since age 5 → Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
  4. 10 yo M, argumentative and vindictive with all adults for a year, grades normal → Oppositional defiant disorder
  5. 9 yo F, severe temper outbursts 4 times weekly for 18 months, persistently angry between outbursts → Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder
  6. 12 yo F, fear of speaking or eating in front of others in every setting, blushing and trembling → Social anxiety disorder
  7. 7 yo F, brief staring spells many times daily, declining grades, provoked by hyperventilation → Absence seizures → electroencephalogram
  8. 8 yo M, declining grades, turns his head to listen, frequently says what → Hearing impairment → audiology evaluation
  9. 13 yo M refuses to attend school, stomachaches on school mornings that resolve on weekends → School refusal
Behavior is a symptom, not a diagnosis Before naming a behavioral disorder in a school-age child, ask what the child is avoiding. Learning disorder, hearing or vision loss, absence seizures, bullying and abuse all present as acting out.
Pearls Count the settings — behavior in one setting means something about that setting, in two or more it is a disorder the child carries · Symptoms starting at a school transition point to an academic-demand mismatch rather than a primary mood disorder · Early intervention improves self-esteem and social skills as well as grades · Social anxiety is explicitly not diagnosed when the avoidance is better explained by another disorder
Pairs with Candidate twin — confirm. This brief wants a partner on ADHD diagnosis and stimulant management, which the page does not yet carry.
Transferable rule In a pediatric behavior stem the parent's history is the chief complaint and the child's private disclosure is the diagnosis, so when a stem bothers to write that the child was interviewed privately, that sentence is the answer.
Class-vs-memberSocial anxiety is a real disorder whose own criterion excludes it when another disorder explains the avoidance.
Mirror twinOppositional defiant disorder is the defiant version of the same complaint; he is avoidant.

Infant Feeding at Six Months

The answer is an age gate · Aquifer · iron first, then variety

Source vignette Pt — 6 mo F, term, taking breast milk, formula and iron-fortified cereal, weight 75th and length 60th percentile, normal examination · Q — the most appropriate next feeding step; options spanned pureed vegetables and fruit, finger foods, whole milk and continued exclusive breastfeeding
The decision point

Nothing is wrong with this infant, so the question is sequence. At 6 months she has crossed the gate for complementary foods, and she has crossed it correctly — iron-fortified cereal is already in the diet, which is the first complementary food because iron is the limiting nutrient once fetal stores deplete at 4 to 6 months.

Having started with an iron source, the next move is variety: pureed vegetables and fruit, one new single-ingredient food at a time. Every other option is the right intervention at the wrong age — finger foods belong at 8 to 9 months, whole milk at 12 months, and exclusive breastfeeding through 6 months and not beyond.

Defining criteria Readiness for complementary foods — sits with support, good head control, loss of the extrusion reflex, interest in food, converging at about 6 months · Pincer grasp — thumb-to-fingertip pickup emerging at 8 to 9 months, the gate for finger foods · Complementary feeding — begins at about 6 months because breast milk alone no longer meets iron and zinc requirements · Single-food introduction — one new single-ingredient food, then 3 to 5 days before the next
Management ladder — infant feeding by age
TierInterventionAdvance when
0 to 6 moExclusive breast milk or formula; vitamin D 400 IU daily from the first days if breastfed or partially breastfed; iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 months if breastfedAbout 6 months and readiness signs present
About 6 moIron-rich foods first — iron-fortified cereal, pureed meats — then pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every 3 to 5 daysSits independently and pincer grasp emerges at 8 to 9 months
8 to 9 moSoft finger foods, lumpier textures, self-feeding, cup introductionTurns 12 months
12 moWhole cow's milk limited to about 16 to 24 oz daily, table foods, off the bottleAge 2, then switch to reduced-fat milk
De-escalateStop supplemental iron once iron-rich complementary foods are established—
Scenario bank
