  1. 6 mo F, term, taking breast milk, formula and iron-fortified cereal, weight 75th and length 60th percentile, normal exam → Begin pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every few days → complementary feeding at 6 months
  2. 9 mo M, sits independently, brings food to his mouth, pincer grasp emerging, tolerating purees → Offer soft finger foods → self-feeding readiness
  3. 12 mo F, healthy, tracking the 50th percentile, still taking formula → Whole cow's milk, about 16 to 24 oz daily → move from bottle to cup
  4. 14 mo M, pale and irritable, drinks 40 oz of whole milk daily and eats little else, hemoglobin 8.2 with MCV 68 → Limit milk under 24 oz daily and start oral iron → iron deficiency from excess cow's milk
  5. 6 mo F whose parents ask about giving fruit juice → Give no fruit juice before 12 months → offer water in a cup with meals
  6. 4 mo M, exclusively breastfed, term, already receiving vitamin D, no complementary foods started → Oral iron 1 mg/kg daily → until iron-rich complementary foods are established
  7. 3-day-old F, exclusively breastfed, term, uncomplicated delivery → Vitamin D 400 IU daily → continue through the first year
  8. 5 mo M with severe eczema and known egg allergy → Introduce peanut-containing food early, after evaluation → between 4 and 6 months
  9. 8 mo F whose grandmother asks which foods to hold until the first birthday → Honey → infant botulism risk before 12 months
Nothing before 12 months Whole cow's milk (iron deficiency from low content, occult blood loss and impaired absorption), honey (infant botulism) and fruit juice. After 12 months cap milk at 16 to 24 oz daily or you manufacture iron deficiency. And delaying allergens is obsolete — severe eczema or egg allergy means introducing peanut at 4 to 6 months after evaluation.
Pearls Iron first, then variety — iron and zinc are the nutrients breast milk stops covering at 6 months · Vitamin D 400 IU daily for breastfed and partially breastfed infants from the first days through the first year · Iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 months for breastfed infants, stopped once iron-rich foods are in · Whole milk from 12 to 24 months, then reduced-fat, because fat is required for myelination in the second year
Pairs with Part I Growth & Developmental Milestones owns the velocity rules and milestone anchors; this brief supplies the feeding ladder. Store the discriminator as a question: is the growth curve normal, or is it crossing lines? Part I Infant Stool Complaints: Dyschezia, FPIAP & Secondary Lactase Deficiency owns what cow's-milk protein does to the stool before the 12-month gate.
Transferable rule When every option is a reasonable intervention and the patient is well, the question is not what but when, so read the age first and eliminate anything whose gate has not opened yet.
Class-vs-memberFinger foods and whole milk are right interventions at the wrong age.
True-fact-wrong-slotExclusive breastfeeding is recommended through 6 months and not beyond.

Sexual Maturity Rating

One contour or two · Aquifer · the phrase appears in exactly one stage

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo F, breast tissue extending beyond the areola without a separate contour, pubic hair curled and spread partially across the pubis · Q — the sexual maturity rating; options spanned Tanner stages 2 through 5
The decision point

Breast and pubic hair are staged separately, and both land on 3 here, so a single number is safe. The phrase carrying the whole question is without a separate contour: breast tissue extending beyond the areola while still sharing one smooth contour is stage 3, and the moment the areola and papilla rise as a second mound above the breast it becomes stage 4.

The pubic hair corroborates. Curled puts her past stage 2, which is straight and sparse, and partially across the pubis keeps her below stage 4, which is adult-quality hair across the pubis sparing the medial thighs.

Defining criteria Sexual maturity rating — breast and pubic hair staged and reported separately; a single number is correct only when the two agree · The breast 3 versus 4 gate — one contour is 3, a secondary mound is 4 · Discordant stages — a finding rather than a rounding problem; pubic hair well ahead of breast suggests an adrenal androgen source
The five stages and the phrase that decides each
StageBreastPubic hairThe NBME tell
1Papilla elevation only, prepubertalNone or vellus onlyNothing palpable beyond the nipple
2Breast bud, small mound under a widening areolaSparse and straight, lightly pigmentedBud, and straight
3Tissue extends beyond the areola, single contourDarker, coarser, curled, sparse over the pubisNo separation of contours
4Areola and papilla form a secondary moundAdult quality across the pubis, sparing the medial thighsSecond mound
5Mature; areola recedes, papilla projects aloneAdult quantity, spreads to the medial thighsAreola back in contour, hair on the thighs
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F, breast tissue extends beyond the areola without a separate contour, pubic hair curled and spread partially across the pubis → Stage 3 → normal for age
  2. 13 yo F, areola and papilla form a secondary mound above the breast contour, adult-type pubic hair sparing the medial thighs → Stage 4 → menarche typically occurs here
  3. 10 yo F, small mound of breast beneath a widened areola, a few straight lightly pigmented hairs along the labia → Stage 2 → thelarche, normal onset
  4. At which sexual maturity rating does menarche typically occur in girls → SMR 4 → peak height velocity precedes it at SMR 2 to 3
  5. 6 yo F with breast budding and pubic hair, height crossing percentiles upward, bone age advanced to 9 years → Measure LH — with GnRH stimulation if basal LH is not diagnostic → central precocious puberty
  6. 7 yo F with isolated breast development, no pubic hair, normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age → Reassurance and observation → premature thelarche
  7. 14 yo M with no testicular enlargement, height at the 3rd percentile, father entered puberty late → Obtain a bone age → constitutional delay of growth and puberty
  8. 13 yo F with no breast development, short stature, a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples → Obtain a karyotype → Turner syndrome
  9. 13 yo M with tender 2 cm subareolar breast tissue bilaterally, SMR 3, otherwise normal → Reassurance — it resolves within 1 to 2 years → pubertal gynecomastia
The timing gates Precocious puberty is secondary sexual characteristics before 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Delayed puberty is no breast development by 13 or no testicular enlargement by 14. Staging is descriptive until the stage is wrong for the age, and then it becomes a workup.
Pearls Thelarche is the first sign in girls; testicular enlargement of at least 4 mL is the first sign in boys · Girls reach peak height velocity at SMR 2 to 3, boys at SMR 4, which is why a girl who has menstruated has little growth left · Menarche occurs at SMR 4, roughly 2 to 3 years after thelarche and about 6 months after peak height velocity · Isolated breast development with normal growth velocity and bone age is premature thelarche and is observed · Pubertal gynecomastia is normal at SMR 3 to 4, coincides with peak height velocity, and needs reassurance rather than imaging
Pairs with Part I Growth & Developmental Milestones for the velocity framework. This brief wants a partner on precocious versus delayed puberty, where the discriminator is whether bone age is ahead of, matching, or behind chronological age. Part I Precocious Puberty is the partner this brief asked for — the discriminator is whether the stage is merely being described or is wrong for the age.
Transferable rule When the options are the levels of a named scale the stem is quoting one definition verbatim, so find the phrase that appears in exactly one level and stop.
Mirror twinStage 4 is the adjacent stage defined by the one feature the stem explicitly negates.
True-fact-wrong-slotEnlarged areolas appear in the stage 2 description but stage 2 hair is straight.
Class-vs-memberStage 5 requires the areola to recede and hair to reach the thighs.

Faltering Weight

The parameter pattern names the cause · Aquifer · weight, then length, then head

Source vignette Pt — 15 mo M, weight 2nd percentile, length 30th, head circumference 40th, active and eating well, normal examination · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned inadequate caloric intake, cystic fibrosis and congenital heart disease
The decision point

The three growth parameters are the question. Weight at the 2nd percentile with length at the 30th and head circumference at the 40th is an isolated weight deficit with linear and brain growth preserved, and that pattern is inadequate caloric intake — malnutrition consumes the parameters in order, sparing the brain until deprivation is prolonged and severe.

Inadequate intake is the commonest cause of faltering growth, and the commonest reason intake is inadequate is behavioral and psychosocial. Up to 80% of growth failure has no organic disorder behind it. The history seals it: he is active, keeps up with peers, eats well at daycare, has never been hospitalized, and examines normally.

Defining criteria Faltering weight — weight below the 2nd percentile, or crossing two or more major percentile lines downward · Weight alone depressed — inadequate caloric intake, malabsorption, or increased demand · Weight and length depressed together — endocrine or constitutional, with length affected as much or more · All three depressed from the outset — genetic, congenital infection, or intrauterine insult
Faltering weight — the etiologies
EtiologyIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Psychosocial, inadequate intakeUp to 80% of cases; food insecurity, feeding technique, neglect, caregiver depressionWeight down, length and head preserved; catch-up growth when fed
Cystic fibrosisMalabsorption plus chronic lung diseaseSteatorrhea and recurrent respiratory infection, abnormal newborn screen
Congenital heart diseaseIncreased caloric demand, failure with feedsSweating and tachypnea with feeding, murmur, hepatomegaly
Metabolic diseaseEpisodic decompensation with catabolic stressHypoglycemia, acidosis, regression, prior admissions
Renal tubular acidosis or CKDAcidosis and solute loss impair growthPolyuria and polydipsia with length also affected
EndocrineGrowth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidismShort with preserved or excess weight, the inverse pattern
Scenario bank
  1. 15 mo M with weight at the 2nd percentile, length at the 30th and head circumference at the 40th, active and eating well, with a normal examination → Inadequate caloric intake from psychosocial causes → the commonest etiology of faltering weight
  2. 15 mo M with isolated low weight, preserved length and head circumference, and a normal examination, initial evaluation → Detailed diet history and observed feeding → laboratory testing is low-yield here
  3. 4 yo F with height at the 3rd percentile and weight at the 40th percentile, with a normal examination → An endocrine cause — growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism → length affected more than weight
  4. 8 mo M with weight, length and head circumference all below the 2nd percentile since birth, microcephalic and dysmorphic → Genetic or intrauterine cause → symmetric growth restriction
  5. 6 mo F with poor weight gain, bulky greasy stools and two admissions for pneumonia → Sweat chloride testing → cystic fibrosis
  6. 3 mo M with poor weight gain, sweating and tachypnea during feeds and a harsh murmur → Echocardiography → congenital heart disease
  7. 14 mo F with poor weight gain, polyuria, polydipsia and length also at the 3rd percentile → Serum electrolytes with a venous blood gas → renal tubular acidosis
  8. 15 mo M with psychosocial faltering weight who is gaining well after caloric supplementation and family support → Continue outpatient management with close follow-up → catch-up growth confirms the diagnosis
  9. 15 mo M with low weight and length, short parents, and a normal growth velocity along his own curve → Familial short stature → this is not faltering growth
Extensive testing is the wrong reflex In a well-appearing child with a normal history and examination, broad laboratory and genetic testing has a very low yield. The evaluation is a diet history, observed feeding, and attention to the social determinants, and catch-up growth on adequate calories is both the treatment and the confirmation.
Pearls Plot all three parameters before naming a cause; the relationship between them is the diagnostic instrument · Head circumference is defended last, so a fallen head circumference means prolonged severe deprivation or a non-nutritional diagnosis · Familial short stature and constitutional delay are not faltering growth; the child tracks a low but steady curve · Endocrine causes give the inverse pattern — short with preserved or excess weight
Pairs with Part II Prematurity Follow-Up and Corrected Age is the direct mirror: there the parameters are proportionate and the answer is normal; here they are disproportionate and the answer is pathologic. Store the discriminator as a question: are the three parameters together or apart? Part I Toddler Food Refusal owns the case where the refusal pattern, not the calorie ledger, is the finding.
Transferable rule When a stem gives several growth parameters the pattern among them is the diagnostic instrument, and when a differential contains one common unglamorous cause alongside several rare organic ones, the rare disease has to earn its place with a symptom, a sign or an admission.
True-fact-wrong-slotCongenital heart disease limits feeding-related activity; he keeps up with peers.
Class-vs-memberRenal causes impair linear growth too, and his length is preserved.

Prematurity Follow-Up and Corrected Age

Correct the age, then read the chart · Aquifer · a percentile is a position, not a pathology

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo F, former 26-week preterm infant, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles; height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile · Q — the most likely assessment; options spanned normal growth and development for corrected age, global developmental delay and failure to thrive
The decision point

Do the arithmetic first. Born at 26 weeks she was 14 weeks early, so at 18 months chronological her corrected age is about 14 and a half months, and every milestone must be judged against that. Walking has just arrived on time, 10 words is ahead of the three to five expected at 15 months, and following a call, imitating and scribbling are age-appropriate.

The growth line is a percentile-literacy question. All three parameters sit together at the 15th percentile — proportionate, symmetric and comfortably normal. Faltering growth requires a parameter below about the 2nd percentile or a downward crossing of two major lines, and she has neither.

Defining criteria Corrected age — chronological age minus the weeks born before 40 weeks · How long to correct — through 24 months for growth and development; newer data support 36 months in extremely and very preterm children · What is never corrected — immunizations, given at chronological age regardless of gestational age or birth weight; the one weight rule is the birth hepatitis B dose at 2 kg or more, and it is a weight threshold rather than an age correction · Normal percentile range — the 15th percentile is normal; faltering growth needs under about the 2nd percentile or a crossing of two major lines
Assessing the former preterm infant — the differential
AssessmentIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Normal for corrected agePreterm child meeting milestones and tracking a normal percentile once correctedCorrected-age milestones met, parameters proportionate above the 2nd percentile
Global developmental delaySignificant delay in two or more domains at corrected ageNot walking or no words at 18 months corrected, often with a falling head circumference
Isolated growth falteringWeight crosses percentiles downward with intact developmentWeight disproportionately low with length and head preserved
Failure to thriveInadequate calories, malabsorption or increased demandParameter below the 2nd percentile or crossing two major lines
Constitutional smallnessSmall but healthy child on a low-normal curveNormal growth velocity along their own percentile
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, just walking, 10 words, imitates and scribbles, with height, weight and head circumference all at the 15th percentile corrected → Normal growth and development for corrected age → corrected age about 14 and a half months
  2. Former 26-week premature infant now 12 months chronological, how to plot her growth → Plot at corrected age until 24 months → chronological plotting overstates the deficit
  3. 6 mo old former 28-week premature infant due for routine immunizations → Immunize at chronological age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  4. 18 mo F, former 26-week preemie, not sitting, no words, head circumference below the 2nd percentile → Refer for developmental evaluation and early intervention → delay across multiple domains at corrected age
  5. Former 26-week premature infant at neonatal intensive care unit discharge, required screening → Retinopathy of prematurity screening — plus a hearing screen → screening driven by gestational age and birth weight
  6. 18 mo former premature infant with all growth parameters at the 15th percentile and tracking steadily → Continue routine surveillance → the 15th percentile is normal
  7. 15 mo M, former 30-week preemie, weight at the 2nd percentile with length at the 25th and head circumference at the 30th, corrected → Inadequate caloric intake → not explained by prematurity
  8. Why growth and development in a preterm child are assessed at corrected rather than chronological age → She has had fewer weeks of growth and brain development → uncorrected assessment falsely labels delay
  9. 24 mo former 26-week premature infant with normal growth and development → Stop correcting for prematurity → plot chronologically from here
  10. 6 wk old former 31-week infant, medically stable and gaining weight, parents asking about the 2-month vaccines → Give them at 2 months of chronologic age on the standard schedule → prematurity is never corrected for vaccines
  11. Why medically stable preterm infants are vaccinated on time rather than deferred → They are at high risk from vaccine-preventable disease and mount an adequate antibody response → immature is not immunocompromised
  12. Preterm infant weighing 1.8 kg at 12 h of life, mother hepatitis B surface antigen negative, due for the birth dose → Delay until the weight reaches 2 kg → the only weight-gated vaccine
  13. 1 wk old girl born at 29 weeks, birth weight 1.51 kg, tolerating feeds, normal vital signs, nondysmorphic, soft anterior fontanelle, moving all four limbs → Screening head ultrasound → all preterm infants under 32 weeks, at age 1 to 2 weeks
  14. Why prematurity under 32 weeks is the threshold for intraventricular haemorrhage screening → The germinal matrix involutes by 32 weeks → before then its thin-walled vessels rupture with swings in cerebral perfusion
What the scary numbers actually mean Former 26-week premature is the correction factor, not the problem. Mild bronchopulmonary dysplasia with normal head ultrasounds reads as a list of morbidities and is a list of reassurances — normal cranial imaging removes the intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular leukomalacia that drive adverse neurodevelopmental outcome at this gestational age.
Pearls Head circumference is the parameter that predicts neurodevelopment, so preserved head growth in a former preemie is the most reassuring single measurement · A percentile is a position, not a pathology; the concerning patterns are crossing lines downward and disproportion between parameters · Retinopathy of prematurity and hearing screening are gestational-age-driven obligations regardless of how well the infant looks · A preterm infant is more vulnerable to vaccine-preventable disease, not less, which is why the schedule is never delayed
Pairs with Part II Faltering Weight is the mirror. Store the discriminator as a question: are the three parameters together or apart? Together and steady is normal; apart with weight lowest is inadequate calories. Part I Cerebral Palsy and the MRI Pattern owns what the imaging names when the delay does not resolve with corrected age.
Transferable rule When a stem hands you a gestational age the first move is arithmetic rather than interpretation, and when an option set includes the claim that assessment is impossible, treat that as almost always wrong.
Uniform-answer doubtDeclining to assess is not caution; correction exists to make the assessment possible.
Treat-the-numberThe 15th percentile sounds low only against an unexamined assumption that normal means the 50th.
Class-vs-memberGlobal delay is the right framework judged against the wrong age.

Cardiovascular 15 topics + 2 board-style

This system is where "treat the number" lives. Almost every miss here comes from medicating an abnormal lab instead of the outcome named in the question.

Heart Failure: Reducing Hospitalization

Ranking interventions by outcome

The decision point

The question isn't "what's abnormal?" — it's "what drives this outcome?" Uncontrolled hypertension is the direct mechanical driver of decompensation: ↑ afterload → ↑ LV wall stress → remodeling → pump failure → admission. Lipids matter for ischemic events over years; BP matters for decompensations over months. Time horizon is the whole question.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhy it fails
500 mg sodium diet"More of what's working"Impractical and not evidence-based; aggressive restriction may worsen outcomes
Potassium-rich dietAnchors on the K⁺ valueK⁺ 3.8 is normal — nothing to supplement
Blood pressure controlLooks boring—
Cholesterol / triglyceride controlThe values are abnormalReduces ischemic risk over years, not HF admissions over months
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo M with HFrEF, BP 168/96; which intervention most reduces hospitalization → Blood pressure control
  2. 68 yo M with HFrEF; the question asks what reduces mortality → Guideline-directed therapy — ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
  3. 68 yo M with established HFrEF and LDL 150, no clinical ASCVD → Statin per ASCVD risk assessment → statins are neither contraindicated in HF nor beneficial for HF outcomes; the indication is atherosclerotic risk
  4. 68 yo M with HFrEF who has been advised to follow a 500 mg sodium diet → Recommend 2–3 g of sodium daily → the 500 mg target is impractical and not evidence-based
  5. 68 yo M with HFrEF on an ACE inhibitor, potassium 5.8 → Stop the potassium-rich diet and recheck
  6. 68 yo M with HFpEF and uncontrolled hypertension → Blood pressure control → the primary lever in HFpEF
The statins-in-HF footnote CORONA and GISSI-HF tested rosuvastatin specifically in established heart failure and showed no mortality or hospitalization benefit. Once ventricular remodeling is the disease, lipids are a bystander. Pair with the mortality list: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i reduce mortality — diuretics only reduce symptoms and hospitalizations.
Transferable rule When NBME gives multiple abnormal values, the answer is the one mechanistically linked to the outcome in the stem, not the most abnormal number. Match time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon.
Treat-the-number

Statins & the 10-Year ASCVD Risk Assessment

Trump cards → calculator → enhancers

The decision point

Order of operations. Four statin-benefit groups get a statin with no calculation: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥190, diabetes age 40–75, and — only for the rest — 10-year risk ≥7.5%. The Pooled Cohort Equations apply to ages 40–75 without ASCVD; they aren't even validated under 40.

Defining criteria Statin-benefit groups, no calculation — clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥190, diabetes age 40–75 · Calculator, everyone else — 10-year risk ≥7.5% (PCE validated only for ages 40–75) · CAC tiebreaker — 0 → statin may be withheld (unless diabetic or smoker); ≥100 → statin
10-year ASCVD risk categories → actionPooled Cohort Equations output
10-yr riskCategoryAction
<5%LowLifestyle only
5–<7.5%BorderlineLifestyle; statin if risk enhancers
7.5–<20%IntermediateModerate-intensity statin
≥20%HighHigh-intensity statin
Tiebreakers Risk enhancers push borderline/intermediate toward treatment: family history of premature ASCVD, LDL ≥160, CKD, metabolic syndrome, preeclampsia or early menopause, inflammatory disease (RA, psoriasis, lupus, HIV), South Asian ancestry, TG ≥175, elevated ApoB / Lp(a) / hsCRP · CAC score is for genuinely uncertain intermediate-risk decisions: 0 → statin may be withheld (unless diabetic or smoker); ≥100 → statin, full stop.
Scenario bank
  1. 52 yo M, LDL 210, no known ASCVD → High-intensity statin without calculating risk
  2. 58 yo M with type 2 diabetes, LDL 120, no ASCVD → Moderate-intensity statin — diabetes 40–75 is a benefit group
  3. 34 yo M, LDL 150, smoker, asking for his 10-year risk → Lifestyle therapy; defer the calculator → the Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under age 40
  4. 55 yo M, 10-year risk 9%, low HDL → Moderate-intensity statin after a risk discussion
  5. 60 yo M with a prior myocardial infarction → High-intensity statin — clinical ASCVD needs no calculation
  6. 55 yo M with low HDL requesting medication to raise it → No pharmacotherapy → no HDL-raising drug has reduced events; treat LDL and total risk instead
Why HDL is bait Low HDL predicts risk but raising it pharmacologically has never reduced events. Niacin (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) — no benefit on top of statin, plus harm. CETP inhibitors raised HDL up to 130% with no benefit; torcetrapib increased mortality. Fibrates (FIELD, ACCORD-Lipid) — no consistent mortality benefit. HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target. And when the stem says "prevent cardiovascular mortality," only statins have reproducible mortality data (4S, HPS, JUPITER).
Treat-the-numberTrump-card inversion

Anginal Equivalents & Stress Test Selection

The trigger localizes better than the location

The decision point

Score the three angina criteria and ignore your instinct about location: (1) provoked by exertion, (2) relieved by rest, (3) typical substernal location. 3/3 = typical, 2/3 = atypical, <2 = nonanginal. "Epigastric burning" is a textbook anginal equivalent — and not relieved by antacids kills the GI story outright.

Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M, substernal pressure on exertion relieved by rest, interpretable ECG, able to exercise → Typical angina → exercise ECG
  2. 58 yo M with epigastric burning on exertion, relieved by rest, not by antacids → Angina pectoris → exertional, rest-relieved epigastric burning is an anginal equivalent; evaluate for ischemia
  3. 58 yo M with left bundle branch block who needs ischemia testing → Pharmacologic stress with imaging
  4. 58 yo M with severe asthma requiring pharmacologic stress testing → Dobutamine → avoid adenosine and regadenoson
  5. 58 yo M with high pretest probability and ongoing symptoms → Coronary angiography
  6. How the 2021 AHA/ACC guideline asks chest pain to be described → Cardiac, possible cardiac, or noncardiac
Guideline currency — the terminology was retired The 2021 AHA/ACC Chest Pain Guideline discourages "typical / atypical / nonanginal." The problem: "atypical" was meant to signal angina without classic features, but clinicians were reading it as "not cardiac" — the opposite of its purpose. The preferred descriptors are now cardiac · possible cardiac · noncardiac:
  • Cardiac — central, retrosternal, squeezing, pressure, exertional
  • Possible cardiac — stabbing, tearing, ripping, burning ← where epigastric burning lands
  • Noncardiac — pleuritic, positional, fleeting
Question banks still key "atypical angina" for a 2-of-3 presentation, so know both vocabularies: score the three criteria for the exam, describe by probability in clinic. Note the shift does not change management — "possible cardiac" still gets risk-stratified and tested.
Angina classification — legacy vs 2021 terminology
Historical termCriteria met2021 equivalent
Typical anginaAll 3 — retrosternal, exertional, relieved by rest/nitroglycerinCardiac
Atypical angina2 of 3Possible cardiac
Nonanginal chest pain1 or 0Noncardiac
Stress test selection
SituationTest
Can exercise + interpretable ECGExercise ECG
Uninterpretable ECG (LVH with strain, digoxin, resting ST depression, WPW)Stress imaging (echo or nuclear)
LBBB or paced rhythmVasodilator nuclear — avoid dobutamine (false-positive septal defects)
Cannot exerciseDobutamine echo or vasodilator nuclear
Severe asthma / COPDDobutamine — vasodilators cause bronchospasm
High pretest probability, or high-risk stress findingsCoronary angiography
High-risk stress findings → cath ST depression ≥2 mm at low workload · ST elevation · hypotension with exercise · ventricular arrhythmia · large or multiple perfusion defects · drop in EF.
The risk factor hidden in the PMH SLE causes accelerated atherosclerosis — lupus mortality is famously bimodal (early from disease activity and infection, late from cardiovascular disease). Chronic prednisone compounds it; antiphospholipid antibodies add thrombosis. Framingham and the PCE underestimate risk in SLE. Stems strip the traditional risk factors so the only one available is in the past medical history.
Transferable rule In chest or epigastric symptom stems, the trigger and the reliever localize disease better than the location does. Exertion + rest-relief = cardiac, wherever the patient points. Meals + antacids = GI. Position/breathing = pleural or pericardial. Reproducible on palpation = musculoskeletal.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

Two gates, both must open

The decision point

Prophylaxis requires a high-risk cardiac condition AND a high-risk procedure. MVP with regurgitation, bicuspid valve, rheumatic valve disease, and HCM all came off the list in 2007 — and NBME has been recycling "MVP + dental visit → nothing" ever since.

Gate 1 — high-risk cardiac conditions (the whole list)
  • Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
  • Prior infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired with residual defect near prosthetic material; or fully repaired with prosthetic material for the first 6 months
  • Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy
Gate 2 — high-risk procedures
  • Dental work with gingival manipulation or mucosal perforation
  • Respiratory procedures breaching mucosa; procedures on infected skin or tissue
  • Not routine GI/GU procedures — that indication died in 2007 too
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis
  2. 45 yo M with a prosthetic aortic valve, due for a dental extraction → Amoxicillin 2 g one hour before
  3. 45 yo M with prior infective endocarditis and penicillin allergy, dental cleaning → Cephalexin, azithromycin or doxycycline
  4. 45 yo M with a prosthetic valve undergoing screening colonoscopy → No prophylaxis → GI and GU procedures are no longer covered
  5. 45 yo M with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, due for dental work → Prophylaxis is indicated
  6. 45 yo M with a bicuspid aortic valve, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis → bicuspid aortic valve was removed from the list in 2007
If both gates open Amoxicillin 2 g PO 30–60 min before → penicillin-allergic: macrolide or doxycycline → can't take oral: cefazolin/ceftriaxone IV. Clindamycin is out (C. difficile risk) — the newest edit and prime distractor material.
Transferable rule When a stem lavishes detail on a patient-specific factor that only matters if the intervention is indicated (an allergy, a dose adjustment), treat it as a prompt to verify the indication — not as confirmation of it.
Trump-card inversion

Secondary Hypertension

Hyperaldosteronism, FMD, and the renin fork

The decision point

Young patient + hypertension + hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function = mineralocorticoid excess. Then renin splits the two look-alikes: primary hyperaldosteronism has suppressed renin; renal artery stenosis has high renin.

Secondary hypertension — clue → diagnosis → first test
Clue in the stemDiagnosisFirst test
Hypokalemia + alkalosisPrimary hyperaldosteronismAldosterone-to-renin ratio
Young woman, abdominal bruitFibromuscular dysplasia "string of beads," media of the arteryDuplex / CTA renal arteries
Episodic HTN + headache + sweatingPheochromocytomaPlasma / urine metanephrines
Snoring, obese, daytime sleepinessObstructive sleep apneaPolysomnography
↓ femoral pulses, rib notchingCoarctationEcho / CT
Striae, moon facies, hyperglycemiaCushing syndromeLow-dose dexamethasone / 24-h cortisol
Mechanism chains they test link by link Aldosterone → ENaC upregulation in the collecting duct → Na⁺ reabsorption → electronegative lumen → K⁺ and H⁺ secretion → hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone escape (ANP + pressure natriuresis) means sodium plateaus and there is no edema — a normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis. For renovascular disease, read the verb: "initiated by" → renin; "directly mediates vasoconstriction" → angiotensin II; "causes the hypokalemia" → aldosterone.
Scenario bank
  1. 32 yo F, BP 172/104, potassium 2.9, metabolic alkalosis, normal creatinine → Primary hyperaldosteronism → aldosterone-to-renin ratio
  2. 32 yo F with hypertension, an abdominal bruit and elevated renin → Fibromuscular dysplasia → CT angiography
  3. 38 yo M with episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations and sweating → Pheochromocytoma → plasma free metanephrines
  4. 16 yo M with hypertension, diminished femoral pulses and rib notching → Coarctation of the aorta
  5. 48 yo M, obese, snoring with daytime sleepiness and resistant hypertension → Obstructive sleep apnea → polysomnography
  6. 42 yo F with hypertension, striae, moon facies and hyperglycemia → Cushing syndrome → overnight dexamethasone suppression test
  7. 29 yo M with BP 168/102, potassium 2.8, metabolic alkalosis and normal creatinine → Aldosterone-to-renin ratio → suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease
  8. 44 yo F with primary hyperaldosteronism confirmed biochemically and a unilateral adrenal nodule on CT, planning surgery → Adrenal venous sampling → bilateral hyperplasia is more common than adenoma, so lateralize before resecting
  9. Older man with peripheral vascular disease, severe hypertension and bilateral renal artery stenosis → An ACE inhibitor → the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to hold GFR, so blocking it causes AKI
  10. Hypertension from renal artery stenosis → Angiotensin II → renin initiates the cascade; aldosterone causes the hypokalemia
Choice architecture When both a disease and its cause appear as options (hyperaldosteronism vs. adrenal adenoma), the evidence level picks the winner. Labs proving physiology → name the syndrome. Imaging or pathology proving anatomy → name the lesion. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is more common than adenoma, and adrenal venous sampling precedes surgery.
ACE inhibitors in renal artery stenosis Bilateral RAS + ACE-I → AKI, because the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR. Flash pulmonary edema with severe HTN in an elderly vasculopath is the bilateral-RAS stem.
Pairs with Part I Hypertension: Workup & Drug Choice — once the secondary hunt is negative, that brief picks the agent by comorbidity. Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes owns the case where the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern.

DVT & Pulmonary Embolism

Pretest probability governs the test

The decision point

Pretest probability picks the branch, and stability picks the test. High probability → skip D-dimer and image. D-dimer only earns its keep as a rule-out in low-probability patients — it's elevated in infection, malignancy, pregnancy, and post-op states, so it can never rule anything in.

Defining criteria Anticoagulation duration — provoked DVT 3 months; unprovoked ≥3–6 months · D-dimer role — rule-out in low pretest probability only; never rules in · IVC filter — only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails
VTE testing by pretest probability
SituationNext step
Low pretest probability (PE)D-dimer; negative excludes. Low + PERC negative → no testing at all
High probability, or obvious DVT with PE symptomsCT pulmonary angiography
CTA contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy, pregnancy)V/Q scan
Hemodynamically unstableBedside echo (RV strain) ± empiric anticoagulation — treat first
Unilateral leg swelling, moderate/high probabilityDuplex ultrasound
The swollen leg differential
ConditionThe tell
DVTStasis/hypercoagulable risk, diffuse swelling, calf tenderness, low-grade temp
CellulitisFever, sharply demarcated spreading erythema, skin break or tinea
Ruptured Baker cystSudden calf pain with knee OA/RA; "pseudo-DVT," crescent bruise at the malleolus
Superficial thrombophlebitisPalpable tender cord along a superficial vein
Chronic venous insufficiencyHemosiderin staining, worse standing, bilateral-ish
LymphedemaPainless, non-pitting, dorsal foot, Stemmer sign
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo F, unilateral leg swelling with a high Wells score → Compression ultrasound → skip the D-dimer
  2. 34 yo F with pleuritic chest pain and low pretest probability → D-dimer to rule out
  3. 62 yo F with suspected PE and creatinine 3.2 → V/Q scan
  4. 62 yo F with suspected PE, hypotensive with right ventricular strain → Thrombolysis
  5. 62 yo F with a warm erythematous calf, fever, and no swelling gradient → Cellulitis
  6. 62 yo F with sudden calf pain and ecchymosis below the malleolus → Ruptured Baker cyst
Pearls ECG in PE is usually just sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 is trivia and neither confirms nor excludes · treatment: DOAC or heparin bridge; thrombolytics only if hypotensive/massive · provoked DVT 3 months, unprovoked ≥3–6 months · IVC filter only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails · the named emergencies: phlegmasia and PE · smokers ≥35 cannot use estrogen-containing OCPs (WHO category 4).
Test-overrides-findings

Innocent vs Pathologic Murmurs

Pediatric murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo

The decision point

Innocent murmurs are turbulent flow through a structurally normal heart: grade 1–2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, and softer with standing or Valsalva. The rule that decides these stems runs in one direction: any single pathologic feature — grade ≥3, holosystolic or diastolic timing, harsh quality, persistence upright, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, or symptoms — buys ECG and echocardiography. And the reversal is its own diagnosis: a murmur that gets louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise.

Defining criteria Benign profile — grade 1–2, early/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, decreases with standing/Valsalva, normal vitals, S1/S2, and growth · Evaluation gate — any single pathologic feature → ECG + echocardiography · The reversal — intensity that increases with standing/Valsalva = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
Benign vs pathologic murmurs — the screening exam
AxisBenignPathologic
HistoryAsymptomatic, normal growthInfants: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance
MurmurEarly/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1–2, decreases uprightHolosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade ≥3, persists upright
Other findingsNormal vitals, normal S1 & S2, symmetric pulsesCentral cyanosis, loud/fixed/single S2, weak femoral pulses, hepatomegaly
ManagementReassuranceECG & echocardiography
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing → Still murmur → reassurance
  2. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography before sports
  3. 6 yo F, continuous infraclavicular hum that disappears with neck rotation → Venous hum → reassurance
  4. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well → ECG and echocardiography → one pathologic feature is enough
  5. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back → Aortic coarctation → collateral flow murmur
  6. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 → Pulmonic flow murmur → innocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer
  7. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur under the right clavicle that fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine → Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veins → venous hum, and why it is usually right-sided
  8. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture → Patent ductus arteriosus → echocardiography
  9. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses → Coarctation with intercostal collateral flow → echocardiography and four-extremity pressures
  10. 6-week-old with a large VSD and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload → Left atrium → left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return
  11. 6 do M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% → A large ventricular septal defect → soft because a wide defect creates little turbulence
  12. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses → Peripheral pulmonary stenosis → resolves by 6 to 12 months
  13. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum below the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down → Venous hum → the one benign murmur that increases upright
  14. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left → The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical → more turbulent flow into the superior vena cava
  15. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms → Echocardiography → peripheral pulmonary stenosis should have resolved by 12 months
  16. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses → Reassurance → the full benign profile is present
  17. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat → Hold sports pending ECG and echo → louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
The three innocent murmurs Still murmur — vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine · Pulmonic flow murmur — systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla · Venous hum — continuous, supra/infraclavicular, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with neck rotation or compression and when supine.
The continuous murmur A continuous murmur in a child has three owners and the location separates them: Right infraclavicular and positional — venous hum, benign, fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine · Left infraclavicular and fixed — patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture · Over the back with weak femoral pulses — coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension · A normally split S2 is not filler — a fixed split is the atrial septal defect tell, so a stem that says S2 moves with respiration is retiring that option on purpose.
Pairs with Part I Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease (the pathologic column's cyanosis and single S2 live there) and Right-Sided Murmurs: Pulmonic Stenosis & Tricuspid Regurgitation — the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Store the discriminator: "what does standing do to it?"
The four benign murmurs Still murmur — younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence · Pulmonic flow murmur — childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety · Venous hum — continuous, supra- or infraclavicular, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with ipsilateral head rotation · Peripheral pulmonary stenosis — the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; resolves by 6 to 12 months · Every benign murmur has an expiry date — outliving the window is itself a pathologic feature · Intensity is not size — a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens
Transferable rule Screening rules run on single disqualifiers: reassurance requires the entire benign profile, but one pathologic feature — on exam, in the vitals, or in the history — is sufficient to buy the workup.
Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle, but the side and the positional change were never checked — a ductus does not care which way the head turns.
Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect survives only if the split S2 goes unread; the stem states that it moves with respiration, which is the opposite of the fixed split ASD requires.
Mirror twinHCM is the dangerous twin of the innocent murmur — the discriminator is the direction the murmur moves on standing.
Uniform-answer doubt"Reassurance" feels too easy on a murmur stem — accept it only after naming the full benign profile.

Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease

Timing of cyanosis + presence of a murmur sort the lesions

The decision point

Two axes sort every cyanotic lesion: when the cyanosis appears (birth vs infancy vs intermittent spells) and whether a murmur is present. The most-tested mechanism is the tet spell: TOF's outflow obstruction is partly dynamic, so crying or dehydration deepens the right-to-left shunt, and squatting or knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance to reverse it. The most-tested trap: TOF's murmur comes from the narrowed RVOT, not the VSD — the VSD is too large to generate one.

Defining criteria The tetralogy — narrowed RV outflow tract, large VSD, overriding aorta, concentric RV hypertrophy · Tet spell mechanics — dynamic RVOT obstruction or dropped SVR → more right-to-left shunt; squatting/knee-chest raises SVR and aborts it · Ductal dependence — HLHS survives on the PDA and ASD; the shunts must stay open
Cyanotic lesions — mechanism → tell
LesionMechanismThe NBME tell
TAPVRtotal anomalous pulmonary venous returnpulmonary veins drain to the right heartcyanosis at birth, no murmur (± soft pulmonic flow)
Truncus arteriosussingle shared arterial trunk over a VSDcyanosis in infancy, holosystolic VSD murmur
Tricuspid atresiano RA→RV path; shunt-dependent through ASD + VSD/PDAcyanosis at birth, VSD and/or PDA murmur
Tetralogy of FallotRVOT narrowing forces right-to-left flow across a large VSDsystolic LUSB murmur from the RVOT; spells relieved by squatting
Ebstein anomalyapically displaced tricuspid valve, atrialized RVTR murmur, widely split S1, "sail sound"; severe = birth cyanosis
HLHShypoplastic left heart syndromeunderdeveloped LV, absent mitral/aortic valves; PDA-dependentcyanosis at birth, no murmur
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo M with tetralogy of Fallot, deeply cyanotic while crying, improves in the knee-chest position; the mechanism of relief → Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shunting
  2. Newborn, cyanotic at birth with no murmur; imaging shows the pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium → Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
  3. Newborn cyanotic at birth, no murmur, severely underdeveloped left ventricle on echocardiogram → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → the PDA and ASD are the only route to the systemic circulation
  4. The harsh left-upper-sternal-border systolic murmur of tetralogy of Fallot arises from → Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tract → the VSD is too large to murmur
  5. Infant with cyanosis and a holosystolic murmur; echo shows a single great vessel overriding a VSD → Truncus arteriosus
  6. Infant with a tricuspid regurgitation murmur, widely split S1, and an early systolic "sail sound" → Ebstein anomaly → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
  7. Newborn with Down syndrome, fixed split S2, grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, mild cyanosis with feeds → Complete atrioventricular canal defect → echocardiography
  8. 4 mo M with episodes of deep cyanosis while crying that resolve when held knees to chest, and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border → Tetralogy of Fallot → RVOT obstruction drives right-to-left flow across the VSD
Pearls Silent cyanosis (no murmur) = TAPVR or HLHS — flow through an ASD or a large PDA is too low-velocity to murmur · severe RVOT narrowing = cyanosis at birth; milder narrowing = intermittent spells in infancy · Ebstein's spectrum runs from birth cyanosis (tiny RV, severe TR) to adult right-heart failure · truncus is the one whose cyanosis characteristically arrives in infancy, not at birth.
Pairs with Part I Innocent vs Pathologic Murmurs — central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 sit in that brief's pathologic column and land here. Store the discriminator: "cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur?" Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn runs the sort that has to finish before this lesion catalog opens.
Transferable rule Congenital heart stems are sorted on two axes before any anatomy is recalled — the clock (birth / infancy / episodic) and the murmur (present, absent, and which structure actually makes it).
True-fact-wrong-slotThe VSD is real anatomy in TOF — offered as the murmur's source, where the RVOT is the answer.
Treat-the-numberA spell's oxygen saturation invites "give oxygen" — the shunt is anatomic; SVR, not FiO₂, is the lever.

Right-Sided Murmurs: Pulmonic Stenosis & Tricuspid Regurgitation

Inspiration augments the right side · click and S2 decide

The decision point

Right-sided murmurs intensify with increased venous return — inspiration, leg raise, hepatic compression. Within the right side, the accessory sounds decide: pulmonic stenosis is an ejection click followed by a crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace with widened splitting of S2, usually congenital and often silent until adult dyspnea; tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic at the left lower sternal border with the right-heart-failure exam — distended jugulars, pulsatile tender hepatomegaly, ascites, edema, RV heave.

Defining criteria Right-sided rule — murmur intensifies with inspiration, leg raise, or hepatic compression · Pulmonic stenosis — ejection click → crescendo–decrescendo murmur, left 2nd interspace, widened S2 splitting · Tricuspid regurgitation — holosystolic at the LLSB + right-heart-failure signs · Severe congenital PS — percutaneous balloon valvulotomy preferred
Systolic murmur look-alikes — what the S2 and click decide
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Pulmonic stenosiscongenital, isolated; rarely carcinoid or rheumaticejection click + widened, respiration-varying S2 split
Atrial septal defect↑ right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valvewide, FIXED S2 split; no click
Bicuspid aortic valve → ASpremature calcification, presents in the 40s–50sright 2nd interspace; narrowed or paradoxical S2 split
Functional flow murmurhigh-output states — anemia, feverno click, normal S2; treat the cause
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathydynamic LV outflow obstructionleft mid-sternal border; louder with standing/Valsalva
Tricuspid regurgitationusually functional, from RV dilationholosystolic LLSB, ↑ with inspiration; no click
Scenario bank
  1. 18 yo F, ejection click then a crescendo–decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace, widely split S2 that varies with respiration → Pulmonic valve stenosis → echocardiography
  2. 20 yo M, midsystolic murmur with a wide and fixed S2 split → Atrial septal defect
  3. 22 yo F with severe symptomatic congenital pulmonic stenosis → Percutaneous balloon valvulotomy
  4. 64 yo M, distended jugular veins, pulsatile tender hepatomegaly, holosystolic LLSB murmur louder on inspiration → Tricuspid regurgitation
  5. 20 yo F with menorrhagia, hemoglobin 8, soft midsystolic murmur, normal S2, no click → Functional flow murmur → treat the anemia
  6. 52 yo M, systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace with paradoxical S2 splitting → Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve → the most common congenital defect found in adults
Pearls Inspiration is the free maneuver in every murmur stem — right-sided murmurs grow, left-sided don't · pulsatile liver + v waves in the JVP belong to TR · pulmonic stenosis is the murmur that hides until adulthood, then presents as exertional dyspnea · carcinoid is the rare acquired cause of PS.
Pairs with Part I Innocent vs Pathologic Murmurs — the innocent pulmonic flow murmur is this brief's benign twin; the ejection click and the S2 split are what separate them. Store the discriminator: "is there a click, and what is the S2 doing?"
Transferable rule Systolic murmurs are separated by their company, not their sound: the accessory findings — click, S2 behavior, response to inspiration or standing — carry the diagnosis, and the murmur itself is nearly interchangeable.
True-fact-wrong-slotTR also augments with inspiration — offered against PS, where the click and split decide.
Mirror twinThe anemia flow murmur is the benign twin — normal S2 and no click are its exoneration.

Hypertension: Workup & Drug Choice

Baseline labs · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it

Source vignette Pt — 48 yo M, hypertension confirmed over 3 visits, gout on allopurinol · Labs — ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy · Q — the most appropriate initial antihypertensive; options spanned losartan, hydrochlorothiazide and stopping the allopurinol
The decision point

Confirmed hypertension gets a fixed baseline panel — and the panel's job is to find end-organ injury and the comorbidity that picks the drug. Injury on the initial workup (LVH on ECG) means start treatment now; further characterization (echo, stress testing) never delays the first agent. With no comorbidity, four classes are interchangeable first-line. With one, the stem is a matching exercise — and the most-tested match is gout → losartan (mildly uricosuric) with thiazides avoided (they raise urate).

Defining criteria Initial workup — electrolytes, creatinine, urinalysis/albumin, fasting glucose or A1c, lipids, TSH, ECG (echo optional) · Treatment gate — confirmed hypertension + end-organ injury → start drug therapy at that visit · First-line, no comorbidity — ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide, dihydropyridine CCB · Two-drug gate — BP ≥10–20 mm Hg above goal
Antihypertensive choice by comorbidity
ComorbidityPreferred agents
Coronary diseaseAngina: β-blocker, CCB · post-MI: ACE inhibitor/ARB + β-blocker
HFrEFACE inhibitor/ARB, β-blocker, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist, dihydropyridine CCB
Atrial fibrillation/flutterβ-blocker, nondihydropyridine CCB
Chronic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB
GoutLosartan, other ARB, CCB — avoid diuretics
OsteoporosisThiazide diuretic
Migraineβ-blocker, CCB
Calcium kidney stonesThiazide diuretic
Scenario bank
  1. 48 yo M, hypertension confirmed on 3 visits, LVH on ECG, gout on allopurinol → Losartan → mildly uricosuric; thiazides raise urate
  2. 62 yo F, hypertension and osteoporosis → Thiazide diuretic → reduces urinary calcium loss and treats both
  3. 60 yo M, hypertension with CKD and albuminuria → ACE inhibitor
  4. 45 yo F, hypertension and frequent migraines → Β-blocker → one drug, both diagnoses
  5. 58 yo M, hypertension and recurrent calcium stones → Thiazide diuretic → loop diuretics increase urinary calcium; thiazides reduce it
  6. 55 yo M, newly confirmed hypertension with LVH on ECG, no ischemic symptoms → Start an antihypertensive now → end-organ injury is the treatment gate
Pearls Stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the LVH — and invites a flare · LVH regresses on ARB/ACEi therapy · β-blocker + nondihydropyridine CCB is the rate-control pairing for AF that also happens to treat the pressure · the same thiazide that is wrong in gout is doubly right in osteoporosis and calcium stones — the comorbidity flips the drug's sign.
Pairs with Part I Secondary Hypertension — that brief decides whether to hunt a cause; this one decides which drug, once the hunt is negative or not indicated. Store the discriminator: "resistant, young, or hypokalemic?"
Transferable rule Drug-choice stems are matching exercises where each agent has a signed value per comorbidity — the same drug is the answer in one stem and the avoided option in the next, so store the pairings, never a favorite drug.
Treat-the-numberThe uric acid level baits "discontinue allopurinol" — a move that lowers nothing that matters.
Sequencing trapEcho or stress testing offered before the first antihypertensive — characterization never delays treatment.

Cyanosis in the Newborn

lung, heart, or airway — sorted before any lesion is named · board question · Is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

Source vignette Pt — 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen · Imaging — ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned respiratory distress syndrome, d-transposition of the great arteries and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
The decision point

Three bedside facts close this before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe — grunting, flaring, retracting — and cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen, which cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. And the two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease, and a 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

When the examination is instead a list of normals — no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor — the sort has already excluded lung and heart, and the remaining finding is temporal. What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it, is then the whole question: cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern — cyanosis worsened by crying — is a tet spell.

Defining criteria Oxygen responsiveness — saturation rises substantially with supplemental oxygen in alveolar disease; it does not in d-transposition, because most systemic flow bypasses the pulmonary vasculature · Preductal vs. postductal — the right upper extremity is preductal and the lower extremities postductal; a higher preductal saturation means right-to-left ductal shunting · Ductal closure clock — the ductus arteriosus begins to constrict as early as 12 hours after birth, so ductal-dependent lesions declare after that, not at minutes · RDS risk — inversely related to gestational age, highest at ≤28 weeks; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce but do not eliminate it · Bilateral choanal atresia — incomplete canalization of the posterior nasal passage; cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, with noisy breathing (stertor), symptomatic shortly after birth · Why crying relieves it — neonates are obligate nasal breathers; hypoxia and hypercapnia trigger crying, which opens the oral airway and temporarily bypasses the obstruction · The bedside test — inability to pass a catheter through the nares into the oropharynx, confirmed by CT or nasal endoscopy · The stability gate — a cyanotic newborn whose hypoxemia does not correct on oxygen gets echocardiography, and prostaglandin E1 is added when the infant is hemodynamically unstable, because instability is what raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting, flaring, retractions — work of breathing; this is lung disease, and it excludes the two structural cardiac options, which give tachypnea without distress · 65% → 92% on oxygen — the alveoli can be recruited; excludes d-transposition outright · Right upper and left lower extremity both 65% — no ductal gradient; argues against persistent pulmonary hypertension and against a coarctation presentation · Cyanosis at minutes of life — too early for ductal closure, which begins at about 12 hours; coarctation cannot yet have declared · 32 weeks, 1.7 kg — the base rate for surfactant deficiency; RDS incidence is inversely related to gestational age · Ground-glass with air bronchograms and low lung volumes — RDS; transient tachypnea gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures, and pulmonary hypertension a clear or oligemic film · Grade 1/6 systolic murmur — soft and non-specific, consistent with a physiologically open duct rather than a structural lesion · A dose of antenatal glucocorticoids — lowers the risk, so it feels exculpatory; it never excludes the diagnosis · PPROM with intrapartum penicillin — sets up group B streptococcal pneumonia, whose film is indistinguishable from RDS — and which is not on this option list ⚠︎ · Acrocyanosis — peripheral cyanosis of hands, feet, and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes is a normal finding in the first 24–48 hours of life; central cyanosis (mucous membranes blue) requires workup
Cyanosis in the newborn — sorting by physiology
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency; alveolar collapse minutes to hours after birthDistress plus oxygen responsiveness plus ground-glass with air bronchograms in a preterm infant— (the answer)
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid; term or late pretermMild distress and cyanosis; perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissuresSevere distress; the film is ground-glass, not streaky
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missHigh pulmonary vascular resistance; right-to-left ductal shuntPreductal saturation above postductal; film often normal, poorly oxygen-responsiveEqual limb saturations; oxygen worked; the film is abnormal
d-Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyCyanosis without retractions, and oxygen does not helpGrunting and retractions; 65% to 92% on oxygen

Cyanosis with a normal examination — sorting by trigger
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bilateral choanal atresiaPosterior nasal passage fails to canalize; the obligate nasal breather obstructs whenever his mouth closesWorse with feeding, better with crying; stertor; catheter will not pass— (the answer)
Tetralogy of FallotRight ventricular outflow obstruction; a spell when systemic resistance fallsCyanosis worse with crying and agitation — the inverted trigger — plus a murmur ⚠︎Crying makes him pink; there is no murmur
Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyConstant cyanosis unchanged by feeding or crying, unimproved by oxygenThe cyanosis comes and goes with what he is doing
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresiaAspiration through a fistula or from a blind pouchCoughing and choking with feeds, respiratory distress, a tube that coilsHe fed well without coughing; lungs are clear
LaryngomalaciaSupraglottic collapse on inspirationInspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommonNo stridor at all
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid after deliveryTachypnea with flaring, retractions and grunting in the first hoursNo respiratory distress of any kind
Management, in one line Management is one sentence, because this stem asked only for the sort: RDS is supported with CPAP, reserving mechanical ventilation and exogenous surfactant for severe or failing cases; the heart branch would instead be a prostaglandin infusion to hold the duct open, and the pulmonary-hypertension branch inhaled nitric oxide ⚠︎. Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: the first move is an oral airway with orogastric feeding to bypass the obstruction, and definitive treatment is surgical repair.
Decision spine Is he working to breathe? — Grunting, flaring, retracting → lung, not heart · Does oxygen help? — 65% to 92% → not a fixed right-to-left shunt, so not transposition · Do the limbs differ? — No → nothing is shunting across the duct · How old is he? — Thirty minutes → the duct is still open; ductal-dependent lesions have not declared · What does the film show? — Ground-glass with air bronchograms in a 32-weeker → surfactant deficiency · If every examination finding is normal — the trigger is the finding: worse with feeding and better with crying is nasal obstruction; worse with crying is a tet spell; unchanged by either is a fixed shunt.
FigureApproach to neonatal cyanosisshow

Redrawn rather than reproduced. The one deliberate change from the usual published version: echocardiography and prostaglandin are shown as separate steps with the stability gate between them, because bundling them is what makes the sequencing question hard.

Scenario bank
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; prostaglandin is added only if the infant is unstable
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying; the bedside maneuver that supports the diagnosis → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old F, pulse oximetry 99% right hand and 91% right foot, well appearing, no cyanosis, femoral and brachial pulses 2+ → Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn → inhaled nitric oxide if severe
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, HR 120, RR 50, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
Decoy note The dose of antenatal glucocorticoids is the most effective bait here: it is genuinely protective, so it reads as if RDS has been treated away, when it only lowers the risk. The grade 1/6 murmur is the second — soft, non-specific, and in a 30-minute-old almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM with intrapartum penicillin points at group B streptococcal pneumonia, whose film is indistinguishable from RDS; the exam removed that ambiguity by leaving it off the option list, but a real stem would not ⚠︎. This stem is built almost entirely out of negatives: six normal findings, each of which retires one option, and exactly one positive — the timing. Readers who answer in half a minute are answering from the word "cyanosis" and the word "newborn," which together select a cardiac lesion and nothing else. "Primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery" and "voided and passed meconium" are inert; their only function is to establish that the baby is well, which is itself the precondition for the whole sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic, therapeutic, and occasionally harmful — it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt, treats RDS, and constricts the duct a ductal-dependent lesion needs ⚠︎. · A lesion that depends on the duct declares when the duct closes, from about 12 hours onward; cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition, or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying — collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis; that is why shunt physiology can be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers, so nasal obstruction gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern belongs to the tet spell — cyanosis worsening with crying and agitation, relieved by knee-to-chest positioning ⚠︎; one complaint, opposite triggers. · The bedside test is free: pass a catheter through each naris; imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE: coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities; unilateral disease often hides until childhood as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea is not distress — fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions and clear lungs points at the heart, while work of breathing points at the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is transposition's signature, and the absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Part II Neonatal Respiratory Distress owns the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes and Part I Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease owns the lesion catalog once the sort points at the heart; Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia owns the newborn clock — which diagnosis belongs at which hour — and carries choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours bucket. This brief is the seam between all three. Store the discriminator as a question: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Part I Multiple Anomalies in a Newborn picks up where the catheter test ends: choanal atresia found, which syndrome owns it.
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before you name a disease — the bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response, and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which catalog you are even allowed to open. When the sort returns nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the finding — and a trigger that runs the wrong way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeA respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress and buys CPAP, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs — the rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries — Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension — That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn — TTN is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta — The duct does not begin to constrict until about 12 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot — Its trigger is inverted — tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink — and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia — Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia — It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon

Kawasaki Disease

Medium-vessel vasculitis · a 10-day clock

The decision point

Fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 criteria. IVIG must be given within 10 days of fever onset — this is an act-now answer, not a work-up answer. Sterile pyuria is a feature, not a distractor: KD causes urethritis, giving urinary WBCs with no bacteria.

Defining criteria Diagnosis — fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5 CRASH criteria · Treatment window — IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset · IVIG resistance — fever persisting 36 h after IVIG → second dose · Echo surveillance — at diagnosis, 2 weeks, and 6–8 weeks
CRASH and Burn
  • Conjunctivitis — bilateral, nonexudative, limbal sparing
  • Rash — polymorphous, perineal accentuation with desquamation
  • Adenopathy — cervical ≥1.5 cm, usually unilateral (the least common criterion)
  • Strawberry tongue / cracked red lips — no ulcers, no exudate
  • Hands and feet — erythema and edema acutely, periungual desquamation in week 2–3
  • Burn — fever ≥5 days
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, fever 6 days, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, hand edema, cervical node 1.8 cm → Kawasaki disease → IVIG plus aspirin
  2. 4 yo M, fever 5 days with only 3 criteria but coronary changes on echocardiography → IVIG and aspirin now → incomplete Kawasaki disease is treated on the coronary finding
  3. 4 yo M with Kawasaki disease presenting on day 12 of fever → Give IVIG even beyond day 10 → treat while inflammation persists
  4. 4 yo M with fever, a sandpaper rash, exudative pharyngitis and a positive rapid strep → Scarlet fever → penicillin
  5. 4 yo M with fever, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a descending rash → Measles
  6. 4 yo M with Kawasaki disease and sterile pyuria on urinalysis → Continue IVIG and aspirin as planned → sterile pyuria is KD urethritis, a feature of the disease, not a second diagnosis
  7. 4 yo M with fever, shock, rash and multiorgan involvement weeks after COVID-19 → MIS-C
Treatment and the two facts they always test IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~20–25% to ~3–5% · high-dose aspirin acutely, then low-dose — Kawasaki is the exception to the never-give-children-aspirin rule · echocardiogram at diagnosis, 2 weeks, 6–8 weeks · IVIG-resistant (fever persists 36 h) → second dose ± steroids ± infliximab · live vaccines (MMR, varicella) must be deferred 11 months after IVIG.
Kawasaki mimics & their discriminators
MimicThe discriminator
AdenovirusExudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis — KD's is nonexudative
Scarlet feverSandpaper rash, Pastia lines, no conjunctivitis; responds to penicillin
SJS / TENMucosal erosions and ulcers, target lesions, drug exposure
Staph scalded skinNikolsky positive, perioral crusting
Toxic shock syndromeHypotension + multiorgan failure; desquamation later
MeaslesKoplik spots, cough/coryza, cephalocaudal rash, unvaccinated
MIS-CPost-COVID, older children, prominent GI symptoms and shock
Incomplete KD Fever ≥5 days with only 2–3 criteria, especially in infants <6 months — who have the highest aneurysm risk and the most atypical presentations. Use CRP/ESR + supplemental labs + echo, and treat if supportive.
Transferable rule When a candidate diagnosis explains only a subset of the findings, it is wrong. UTI explains two lines of this stem; Kawasaki explains all of them. Ask which findings your diagnosis leaves orphaned.

Acute Rheumatic Fever

The causal chain beats the vivid detail

The decision point

Sore throat 2 weeks ago → migratory large-joint arthritis → new holosystolic apical murmur + fever. That's 2 major Jones criteria on a strep foundation. A travel or camping detail is a setting, not a mechanism — no tick bite, no rash, and the 2–4 week latency belongs to the pharyngitis.

Jones criteria — 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus evidence of strep
  • Major (JONES): Joints (migratory polyarthritis) · O carditis · Nodules (subcutaneous) · Erythema marginatum · Sydenham chorea
  • Minor: fever, arthralgia, ↑ESR/CRP, prolonged PR
Pearls Type II hypersensitivity via molecular mimicry against M protein · Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells on pathology · acute attack hits the mitral valve as regurgitation; decades later it returns as mitral stenosis · treatment = penicillin + aspirin, then monthly benzathine penicillin for years · treating the pharyngitis prevents ARF but not PSGN.
Scenario bank
