Pulmonary

Neonatal Respiratory Distress

Fluid in the fissures · Aquifer · four stem facts settle it before pathophysiology

Source vignette Pt — 1 h old term M, cesarean delivery at 40 weeks without labor, birth weight 4200 g, RR 80, saturation 88% on room air correcting to 98% with supplemental oxygen · Imaging — fluid in the interlobar fissures · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned transient tachypnea of the newborn, respiratory distress syndrome and group B streptococcal pneumonia
The decision point

Fluid in the interlobar fissures is retained fetal lung fluid — water where it should not be, in a term baby whose lungs are structurally normal — and it appears in no competing diagnosis. Add 88% correcting to 98% on supplemental oxygen, which tells you the problem is alveolar fluid rather than a shunt, and this is transient tachypnea of the newborn.

The mechanism sits in the delivery note. Cesarean without labor is the classic setup, because labor's catecholamine surge is what flips the alveolar epithelium from secreting fluid to absorbing it. Macrosomia at 4200 g rides along as a second risk factor.

Defining criteria Neonatal tachypnea — respiratory rate above 60 per minute · Transient tachypnea — retained fetal lung fluid, onset within the first 2 hours, resolving within 24 to 72 hours · Beyond 72 hours — the diagnosis was wrong; look again
The newborn in respiratory distress — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Transient tachypneaTerm or late preterm, cesarean without labor, macrosomia, maternal diabetes or asthmaFluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking; resolves in 24 to 72 h
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency, worsening over 48 to 72 hLow lung volumes, diffuse ground-glass with air bronchograms
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, fetal distressCoarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation
Group B strep pneumoniaRupture 18 h or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxisFilm mimics RDS exactly; temperature instability, neutropenia
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera crush the developing lungScaphoid abdomen, shifted heart sounds, bowel gas in the chest; the film shows intrathoracic bowel loops with a displaced cardiac silhouette. Ventilate with limited pressures — the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missFailed transition, often after asphyxia or aspirationPre- to post-ductal saturation gap above 10%, poorly oxygen-responsive
Scenario bank
  1. 1 h old term M, cesarean at 40 wk without labor, birth weight 4200 g, RR 80, saturation 88% on room air correcting to 98% with oxygen, fluid in the interlobar fissures → Transient tachypnea of the newborn → supportive care; resolves within 72 hours
  2. 29 wk preterm M, grunting and retracting at 2 h, low lung volumes with diffuse ground-glass opacity and air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant and CPAP
  3. 41 wk newborn delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation → Meconium aspiration syndrome → watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension
  4. Term newborn with severe distress at delivery, a scaphoid abdomen, heart sounds displaced to the right and bowel gas in the left hemithorax → Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach → congenital diaphragmatic hernia; bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest
  5. Intubated infant with congenital diaphragmatic hernia whose saturations fall, right hand 92% and foot 78%, suprasystemic pulmonary pressures on echocardiography → Inhaled nitric oxide → the cyanosis is pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung, not a closing duct
  6. Term newborn with distress, rupture of membranes 24 h before delivery, maternal fever 38.5 C, no intrapartum prophylaxis and temperature instability → Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis
  7. 1 h old term infant with suspected transient tachypnea and a respiratory rate of 80 → Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen → feeding at this respiratory rate risks aspiration
  8. Term newborn with preductal saturation 88% and postductal saturation 76%, minimal improvement on 100% oxygen and a nearly clear chest x-ray → Obtain an echocardiogram → persistent pulmonary hypertension versus cyanotic heart disease
  9. 29 wk preterm on CPAP for respiratory distress syndrome with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions → Intubate and give surfactant → CPAP has failed
  10. Term infant labelled transient tachypnea of the newborn, still tachypneic at 96 hours of life → Re-evaluate for another diagnosis → TTN resolves within 72 hours by definition
  11. 36 wk F, infant of a mother with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, central cyanosis, grunting and retracting, saturation 64% improving to 82% on oxygen with equal pre- and postductal readings, bilateral ground-glass opacities → Surfactant → respiratory distress syndrome in a late preterm infant of a diabetic mother
  12. Term neonate with severe cyanosis unresponsive to 100% oxygen, no retractions, comfortable tachypnea and a structurally normal chest radiograph → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → suspected cyanotic congenital heart disease pending echocardiography
  13. How poorly controlled maternal diabetes raises the risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome → Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonises cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation → phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production is suppressed
Two exit ramps Do not bag-mask a suspected diaphragmatic hernia — you inflate bowel inside the chest; intubate and decompress with a nasogastric tube. And maternal diabetes cuts both ways: it raises the risk of transient tachypnea and simultaneously delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe.
Pearls Labor is what dries the lungs — the catecholamine surge switches alveolar epithelium from secretion to absorption · Transient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description; beyond 72 hours the label is wrong · A saturation gap above 10% between the right hand and a foot means right-to-left ductal shunting · Hypoxemia that corrects on modest oxygen is alveolar disease; hypoxemia that does not is a shunt · The hyperoxia test is still commonly keyed on exams but has largely been abandoned clinically · Displaced heart sounds have three owners and the abdomen tells you which — scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on the side of the defect is a diaphragmatic hernia, a distended hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant is a tension pneumothorax needing needle decompression, and a well infant with the heart on the right and no distress is dextrocardia · The lungs stay small after the hernia is repaired — viscera occupied the thorax during lung development, so hypoplasia with vascular remodeling, and the pulmonary hypertension that follows, outlast the defect
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence. Shared complaint is a newborn in respiratory distress in the first hours; what flips is whether the lungs are structurally normal. Store the discriminator as a question: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that were never built? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn is the seam upstream of this brief — work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart before the film narrows the parenchymal causes. Part I Mechanisms of Hypoxemia supplies the physiology underneath the oxygen response used here.
Transferable rule Four stem facts decide neonatal respiratory distress before any pathophysiology — gestational age, whether labor occurred, when the distress began, and what the film shows — and then the oxygen response separates lung disease from shunt.
Class-vs-memberRespiratory distress syndrome is the right category of neonatal lung disease but a preterm member.
True-fact-wrong-slotGroup B strep needs risk factors the stem never supplies.
Class-vs-memberProstaglandin is the right class of answer for a cyanotic newborn, but a diaphragmatic hernia's cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not from a closing duct.
True-fact-wrong-slotDiaphragmatic hernia presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen, not at an hour with fissural fluid.

Gastroenterology & Hepatology 14 topics + 3 board-style

Pregnancy is a setting, not a diagnosis — and gestational age is the assassin that fires three times.

Liver Disease in Pregnancy

Trimester decides everything

The decision point

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy, intrahepatic cholestasis, and preeclampsia/HELLP are all third-trimester diseases. A patient at 14 weeks with elevated transaminases, obesity, and diabetes has a metabolic liver disease that has nothing to do with being pregnant.

Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash → Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy → ursodeoxycholic acid
  2. 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases → Acute fatty liver of pregnancy → urgent delivery
  3. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 → HELLP syndrome → delivery
  4. 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases → Hyperemesis gravidarum
  5. 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases → Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease — the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeks
  6. 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal → Placental alkaline phosphatase — physiologic → reassurance
  7. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid → Delivery at 36 to 37 weeks → intrahepatic cholestasis carries stillbirth risk
  8. 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine → Emergent delivery → acute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by delivering
  9. 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms → Reassurance → the placenta makes alkaline phosphatase
The lab detail most people misread Alkaline phosphatase is supposed to be elevated in pregnancy — the placenta makes its own isoenzyme, and levels run 2–4× normal. But AST, ALT, and bilirubin do NOT rise physiologically. Elevation of those is always pathologic.
Liver labs in normal pregnancy
Rises physiologicallyFalls physiologicallyShould stay normal
Alkaline phosphatase (placental), WBC (to ~15,000), ESR, fibrinogen and factors VII/VIII/X, total T4 and TBG, cholesterol, GFRHemoglobin (dilutional), platelets (mild gestational), creatinine and BUN, PaCO₂, TSH in the first trimesterAST, ALT, bilirubin
Liver disease in pregnancy — by trimester
ConditionTimingThe tellManagement
Hyperemesis gravidarum1stVomiting, ketonuria, >5% weight lossSupportive
Intrahepatic cholestasis2nd–3rdPruritus of palms and soles, worse at night; ↑bile acids, ↑bilirubin; stillbirth riskUrsodeoxycholic acid; deliver 36–37 wk
Preeclampsia / HELLP Emergency>20 wkHTN + proteinuria; Hemolysis, Elevated LFTs, Low Platelets, RUQ pain, schistocytesDelivery
Acute fatty liver Emergency3rdHypoglycemia, ↑ammonia, coagulopathy, ↑Cr, encephalopathy; LCHAD deficiency linkEmergent delivery
AFLP vs. HELLP Hypoglycemia + coagulopathy + high ammonia + renal failure = AFLP. Hemolysis + thrombocytopenia + more hypertension = HELLP. Both are treated by delivering. Cholecystectomy in pregnancy is safest in the second trimester.
Transferable rule Trimester is to obstetric stems what duration is to pediatric joint stems — check that the timing permits the pregnancy-specific disease before reaching for it.
Salient decoy

MASLD / Metabolic Fatty Liver

Formerly NAFLD · a diagnosis of exclusion

The decision point

Metabolic syndrome (obesity, T2DM, hypertension, dyslipidemia) + transaminase elevation with AST/ALT ratio <1 + hyperechoic liver on ultrasound. Alcohol gives the opposite ratio: AST:ALT ≥2 ("t-oAST").

  • Most common chronic liver disease in the US; progression is steatosis → MASH → fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC, and HCC can occur without cirrhosis
  • Exclude first: alcohol, hepatitis B/C, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and drugs (steroids, amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen)
  • Stage fibrosis with FIB-4 or transient elastography
  • Treatment: 7–10% weight loss reverses steatohepatitis; bariatric surgery if BMI ≥35; GLP-1 agonists; resmetirom for MASH with fibrosis
Scenario bank
  1. 48 yo M, BMI 34, type 2 diabetes, ALT 70, AST 45, hyperechoic liver → MASLD
  2. 48 yo M with AST 180 and ALT 70 and a history of heavy drinking → Alcohol-associated liver disease → AST:ALT of 2 or more
  3. 48 yo M with MASLD asking what most improves liver histology → 7 To 10% weight loss
  4. 48 yo M with MASLD and a high FIB-4 score → Assess fibrosis with elastography
  5. 48 yo M with MASLD and LDL 160 → Statins are safe and indicated
  6. 32 yo M with fatty liver, low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease
Pearls Significant alcohol intake threshold: >21 drinks/week (men), >14 (women) · gallstones in pregnancy are common (progesterone → gallbladder stasis) and usually incidental without wall thickening, fever, or pain · young patient with steatosis + tremor + Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease.

Cholestasis & the LFT Patterns

Classify → localize → then test for causes

The decision point

Classify the pattern before testing for causes. Alk phos ↑↑ with normal AST/ALT and a direct hyperbilirubinemia is cholestasis — and abdominal ultrasound answers the one question that branches everything downstream: are the ducts dilated? Intrahepatic vs. extrahepatic decides whether the next test is an antibody or a cross-sectional image.

Step 1.5, which stems love to test separately: confirm the alk phos is hepatic with a GGT (or 5′-nucleotidase). Alkaline phosphatase also comes from bone, placenta, and intestine.

LFT patternshepatocellular vs cholestatic
PatternLabsCausesTargeted tests
HepatocellularAST/ALT ↑↑, alk phos normal or mildViral hepatitis, MASLD, alcohol (AST:ALT ≥2), autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson, α1-antitrypsin, drugsASMA / anti-LKM1, iron studies, ceruloplasmin
CholestaticAlk phos ↑↑ + direct bilirubin ↑PBC, PSC, choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head cancer, stricture, drugs, infiltrative diseaseUltrasound first, then AMA or MRCP/CT
Isolated hyperbilirubinemiaBilirubin ↑ aloneIndirect: Gilbert, hemolysis, Crigler-Najjar · Direct: Dubin-Johnson, RotorFractionate, smear, reticulocytes
Alk phos ↑ with normal GGT—Not liver at all — bone (Paget, metastases, vitamin D deficiency, healing fracture, growing child) or placentaBone-specific workup
After the ultrasound
  • Ducts NOT dilated → intrahepatic → AMA (antimitochondrial antibody) for PBC; MRCP and biopsy if suspicion persists
  • Ducts dilated → extrahepatic → MRCP (biliary tree) or CT (pancreatic mass) → ERCP only when intervention is needed
Primary biliary cholangitis vs primary sclerosing cholangitis
PBCPSC
PatientMiddle-aged womenYoung men
AntibodyAMAp-ANCA
AssociationSjögren, Hashimoto, RA, celiacUlcerative colitis (~70–80%)
Imaging / pathSmall intrahepatic ducts; florid duct lesion, granulomas"Beads on a string" on MRCP; onion-skin fibrosis
ClinicalPruritus + fatigue, xanthelasma, hyperlipidemiaFatigue, jaundice; ↑ cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer
TreatmentUrsodeoxycholic acidNo effective medical therapy → transplant
Scenario bank
  1. Ultrasound shows a dilated CBD and a pancreatic head mass → CT abdomen → pancreatic adenocarcinoma
  2. Normal ducts + AMA positive in a woman with pruritus → Primary biliary cholangitis → ursodiol
  3. Young man with ulcerative colitis and a cholestatic pattern → MRCP → beads on a string → PSC
  4. Alk phos elevated with a normal GGT → Bone source or pregnancy → not liver disease at all
  5. Charcot triad (fever + RUQ pain + jaundice) → Ascending cholangitis → urgent ERCP
  6. Painless jaundice + weight loss + palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) → Pancreatic head malignancy → not stones
  7. Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia appearing with fasting or illness, all else normal → Gilbert syndrome → reassurance
  8. Cholestatic pattern after amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, OCPs, or chlorpromazine → Stop the drug, then monitor
  9. Cholestasis + hilar lymphadenopathy + hypercalcemia → Sarcoidosis
Trap autopsy ASMA and iron studies — right idea (autoimmune and metabolic liver disease), wrong pattern: both cause hepatocellular injury. ERCP — correct modality, wrong rung: invasive, carries post-ERCP pancreatitis risk, and you don't yet know whether there is anything to intervene on. Repeat LFTs in 3 months — appropriate only when a reversible cause has been identified and removed; here the alk phos is 7× normal with no cause found.
Transferable rule The LFT panel is a triage instrument, not a list of abnormal values. Diagnostic tests are pattern-specific — ordering an autoimmune hepatitis antibody in a cholestatic patient is testing for the wrong disease category entirely.
Sequencing trap

Zenker Diverticulum

Regurgitation of undigested food in an old man · UWorld · the swallow study comes before any scope or tube

Source vignette Pt — 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck on swallowing, weight stable · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Zenker diverticulum, achalasia and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
The decision point

The stem gives an elderly man with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and a gurgling sound in the neck. That cluster is Zenker — a pulsion pouch through the weak posterior hypopharyngeal wall because the cricopharyngeus fails to relax. The question the exam scores is not the diagnosis but the sequence: barium esophagram first, because a blind endoscope or nasogastric tube can enter the pouch and perforate it.

The miss is usually a reflex: dysphagia → endoscopy. Ask what the endoscope could hit before you order it. Once the pouch is shown, treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy (with or without diverticulectomy); the tested complication is aspiration pneumonia.

Dysphagia in an adult — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Zenker diverticulumElderly man; cricopharyngeal dysfunction; food pools in a posterior pharyngeal pouchRegurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, neck gurgling; esophagram before scope
AchalasiaLoss of myenteric inhibitory neurons; middle age; dysphagia to solids and liquids from the startBird's beak on esophagram; manometry confirms absent peristalsis and a non-relaxing LES
Esophageal cancer Can't missSmoker or drinker (SCC) or long-standing reflux (adenocarcinoma); progressive solid then liquid dysphagiaWeight loss with progressive solid-food dysphagia; endoscopy with biopsy
Schatzki ring / peptic strictureDistal mucosal ring or reflux scar; intermittent solid-food dysphagiaEpisodic impaction with meat or bread, no weight loss; dilation
Oropharyngeal (neurologic) dysphagiaStroke, Parkinson disease, myasthenia; trouble initiating the swallowCoughing or choking at the start of the swallow, nasal regurgitation; videofluoroscopy and speech therapy
Scenario bank
  1. 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck when he swallows, weight stable → Zenker diverticulum → barium esophagram
  2. 79 yo M with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and a gurgling neck; the most appropriate initial study → Barium esophagram → a blind scope or tube risks perforating the pouch
  3. 81 yo M with suspected Zenker diverticulum and poor oral intake; the intervention to avoid → Blind nasogastric tube placement → the tube enters the pouch and perforates it
  4. 72 yo M whose esophagram shows a posterior pharyngoesophageal outpouching above the cricopharyngeus → Cricopharyngeal myotomy with or without diverticulectomy → the pouch is the symptom, the non-relaxing muscle is the cause
  5. 76 yo M with known Zenker diverticulum, 3 days of fever, productive cough and a right lower lobe infiltrate → Aspiration pneumonia → pooled contents aspirate at night
  6. 46 yo F, dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, 5 kg weight loss, esophagram with a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird's beak → Achalasia → manometry, then pneumatic dilation or myotomy
  7. 63 yo M, 40 pack-years and daily alcohol, 3 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia now with liquids, 8 kg weight loss → Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma → endoscopy with biopsy
Why the sequence matters Regurgitated undigested food means the food never reached the stomach — the pouch or a non-emptying esophagus is holding it. Undigested regurgitation plus a neck finding is the pouch; undigested regurgitation plus dysphagia to liquids from day one is achalasia. Either way the first study is the esophagram; endoscopy leads only when the stem carries an alarm feature for cancer (weight loss, smoking, progressive solid dysphagia) and no neck finding.
Pearls Zenker is a false (pulsion) diverticulum — mucosa and submucosa herniate through the posterior wall between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the cricopharyngeus · the mechanism tested is cricopharyngeal motor dysfunction, diminished relaxation, not a structural weakness alone · halitosis comes from food decaying in the pouch · the complication tested is aspiration pneumonia · treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy, with diverticulectomy for larger pouches
Pairs with This brief wants a partner on achalasia and the esophageal dysphagia differential (not yet written). Store the discriminator as a question: is the regurgitated food undigested, and is the finding in the neck or in the chest?
Transferable rule When the diagnosis implies a blind pouch or a cavity the instrument cannot see, image it before you instrument it — the esophagram before the endoscope in Zenker is the same rule as the ultrasound before the needle in a hip effusion.
Sequencing trapUpper endoscopy is the right modality one step early — the blind scope can perforate the pouch the esophagram would have shown.
Salient decoyWeight loss and age pull toward cancer, but undigested regurgitation with a neck gurgle is the pouch, and the esophagram settles both.
Class-vs-memberManometry is the right family of test for a motility cause, but it answers achalasia, not a pharyngeal pouch.

Infant Stool Complaints: Dyschezia, FPIAP & Secondary Lactase Deficiency

The well-appearing child decides the tier · UWorld · reassure, eliminate, or work up

Source vignette Pt — 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times daily then passes a soft yellow stool, normal examination · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned reassurance and parental education, a glycerin suppository and switching to an extensively hydrolyzed formula
The decision point

Three benign stool complaints share one exam shape — a thriving, well-appearing infant or child whose parents are alarmed — and the answer is set by the stool and the timing, not by the alarm. Straining and screaming for minutes, then a normal soft stool, under 9 months, is infant dyschezia → reassurance only. Painless blood-streaked stools in a well infant under 6 months is food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis → eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet, or an extensively hydrolyzed formula. Watery diarrhea and bloating after dairy is reintroduced following gastroenteritis is secondary lactase deficiency → temporary lactose avoidance, no workup.

The two mimics that change the tier are both ill-appearing: FPIES (profuse vomiting and lethargy 1–4 h after the trigger, non-IgE) needs fluids, and IgE-mediated allergy (urticaria, wheeze, anaphylaxis within minutes) needs epinephrine. The miss is treating the parents' distress as a finding: a formula change, a suppository, or a stool workup for a thriving infant is the wrong rung.

Defining criteria Infant dyschezia — under 9 months, strains and cries for minutes, then passes a normal soft stool, thriving; hard stool means constipation instead · Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis — well-appearing infant under 6 months, painless blood-streaked stools, insidious onset; non-IgE · Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome — under 12 months, profuse vomiting with diarrhea, dehydration and lethargy within hours (1–4 h) of the trigger, ill-appearing; non-IgE · IgE-mediated food allergy — urticaria, vomiting, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension within minutes (under 1 h), any age · Osmotic diarrhea — stops with fasting, raised stool osmotic gap, acidic stool pH
The well-appearing infant with a stool complaint — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Infant dyscheziaUnder 9 months; cannot coordinate a Valsalva with pelvic-floor relaxation; resolves spontaneouslyScreams and strains, then a normal soft stool; reassurance, nothing else
Functional constipationInfrequent, hard or pellet stools, often at a diet transitionHard stool — the one word that converts dyschezia into constipation
FPIAPUnder 6 months, breastfed or formula-fed; cow's milk or soy protein; resolves by about 1 yearPainless blood streaks in a well infant; eliminate cow's milk and soy, no scope
FPIESUnder 12 months; non-IgE; classic triggers include cow's milk and soyProfuse vomiting, lethargy, dehydration 1–4 h after feeding, ill-appearing; fluids, not epinephrine
IgE-mediated food allergyAny age; minutes after exposure; may progress to anaphylaxisUrticaria or wheeze within an hour; epinephrine, strict avoidance, allergist
Secondary lactase deficiencyBrush-border lactase lost after gastroenteritis or with IBD; osmotic diarrheaDiarrhea and bloating when dairy is reintroduced after a resolving gastroenteritis; no fever, no vomiting
Necrotizing enterocolitis Can't miss PreemiePreterm infant on enteral feeds; bacterial invasion of an ischemic bowel wallDistension, bloody stools, pneumatosis intestinalis in a preemie — never a well-infant diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times a day, then passes a soft yellow stool, normal exam → Reassurance and parental education → infant dyschezia resolves by about 9 months
  2. 5 mo F, passed meconium on day 1, now hard pellet stools every 3 days with straining since starting solids, thriving → Functional constipation → dietary change, then an osmotic laxative
  3. 6 wk F, exclusively breastfed, thriving, blood-streaked soft stools for a week, comfortable and well → Eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet → food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis
  4. 3 mo M on cow's milk formula, well-appearing, gaining weight, blood streaks and mucus in soft stools → Extensively hydrolyzed formula → soy cross-reacts, so it is not the substitute
  5. 2 mo F, breastfed, with food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; the recommendation to avoid → Stop breastfeeding and start a soy-based formula → soy protein triggers the same reaction and breastfeeding need not stop
  6. 7 mo M, 2 hours after his first cow's-milk formula, repetitive profuse vomiting, pale, limp and lethargic, no urticaria or wheeze → Intravenous fluid resuscitation → food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome is non-IgE, so epinephrine does nothing
  7. 9 mo F, hives and wheezing within 15 minutes of her first scrambled egg → Intramuscular epinephrine → IgE-mediated food allergy, strict avoidance and allergist referral
  8. 6 yo M, viral gastroenteritis 10 days ago that was improving, now watery diarrhea and bloating since milk was reintroduced, afebrile, no vomiting → Temporary lactose avoidance, then reintroduce → secondary lactase deficiency needs no workup
  9. 5 yo F, diarrhea after a resolving gastroenteritis that stops when she fasts, acidic stool pH, raised stool osmotic gap → Transient loss of brush-border lactase → colonic bacteria ferment the unabsorbed lactose
  10. 5-day-old born at 32 weeks, bilious and coffee-grounds emesis, distended tender abdomen, pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray → Blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with bowel rest → necrotizing enterocolitis
Where the rule breaks The whole ladder rests on well-appearing and thriving. Lethargy, dehydration, or profuse vomiting is FPIES; urticaria or wheeze is IgE-mediated; a preterm infant with distension and bloody stools is necrotizing enterocolitis; a child with fever, vomiting, or weight loss after gastroenteritis is no longer the classic lactase vignette and earns a workup. Formula changes, rectal stimulation, and laxatives are the named wrong answers for dyschezia — hard stool is the only word that makes a laxative right.
Pearls Dyschezia is a coordination failure — raised intra-abdominal pressure without pelvic-floor relaxation, and inadequate abdominal tone for an effective Valsalva · FPIAP is non-IgE and self-limited; maternal elimination of cow's milk and soy, resolution by about 1 year · FPIES is the ill-appearing non-IgE twin: delayed hours, no urticaria, treated with fluids · IgE-mediated disease is the only one that gets epinephrine · secondary lactase deficiency is osmotic — stops with fasting, acidic stool, no fever — and IBD is the other cause of brush-border loss
Pairs with Part II Infant Feeding at Six Months owns the cow's-milk age gate; this brief owns what cow's-milk protein does to the stool before that gate opens. Part I Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia carries the necrotizing enterocolitis item — the ill preemie that a bloody stool must never be called proctocolitis. Store the discriminator as a question: is the infant well-appearing, and is the stool soft? Part I Constipation in a Child owns the toddler end of the same complaint, where the withholding cycle rather than the protein is the disease.
Transferable rule When the patient is thriving and the parents are frightened, the tier is set by the finding, not by the fear — read the stool, the timing after the trigger, and the child's appearance, and reassure or eliminate before you ever test.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance feels like doing nothing, but for dyschezia every active option is a named wrong answer.
Class-vs-memberSoy formula is the right idea (remove the trigger) with a member that cross-reacts.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpinephrine treats food allergy — the IgE kind; FPIES vomiting hours later is non-IgE and needs fluids.
Sequencing trapA stool workup is the tier above dietary change in a well child whose diarrhea followed dairy.

Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Puberty starts the scope, the polyps set the colectomy · UWorld · APC, hundreds of adenomas, cancer by 40

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, asymptomatic, father has familial adenomatous polyposis · Labs — APC testing positive · Q — the most appropriate screening step; options spanned annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting now, colonoscopy at age 40 and prophylactic colectomy now
The decision point

An APC mutation (autosomal dominant) means hundreds to thousands of adenomas and colon cancer in nearly 100% by age 40. The exam scores two gates. First, screening: annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy from age 10–12 (puberty) — not the first-degree-relative rule, not average-risk screening. Second, the operation: prophylactic proctocolectomy is planned for the teens to early 20s, but is indicated at any age for bleeding, large (over 1 cm) or innumerable polyps, or high-grade dysplasia.

The miss is usually a parameter — the right rung with the wrong number (colonoscopy at 40, or at 10 years before the relative's cancer). Those are the rules for sporadic family history; a known APC carrier is a different pathway. The other tested move is the one after colectomy: upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas, which the colectomy does nothing about.

Defining criteria Familial adenomatous polyposis — autosomal dominant APC mutation, hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas, colon cancer in nearly 100% before age 40 · Screening gate — annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting at puberty, age 10–12 · Colectomy gate — prophylactic proctocolectomy in the teens to early 20s, or at any age with GI bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps, or high-grade dysplasia · Upper tract — upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas · Gardner syndrome — FAP plus osteomas and desmoid tumors · Turcot syndrome — FAP plus CNS tumors
Management ladder — familial adenomatous polyposis
TierInterventionEscalate when
0APC genetic testing of at-risk children of an affected parentMutation found, or testing unavailable → screen as affected
1Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy from age 10–12Polyposis develops → plan surgery; any colectomy trigger → operate now
2Prophylactic proctocolectomy (or colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis), usually teens to early 20sImmediately, at any age: GI bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps, high-grade dysplasia
3Upper endoscopy surveillance for duodenal and ampullary adenomas, continued after colectomyRetained rectum after ileorectal anastomosis keeps its own endoscopic surveillance
Hereditary colon cancer syndromes — the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Familial adenomatous polyposisAPC, autosomal dominant; adenomas carpet the colon from adolescenceHundreds of polyps; scope from puberty, colectomy in the teens to 20s
Gardner syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors
Turcot syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus CNS tumors
Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)Mismatch-repair mutation; few polyps, early right-sided cancer; endometrial and other cancers in the familyEarly colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree
Peutz-Jeghers syndromeHamartomatous polyps that intussuscept or bleedMucocutaneous pigmentation of lips and buccal mucosa
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M whose father has familial adenomatous polyposis; APC testing positive; asymptomatic → Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting now → the screening gate opens at puberty, age 10–12
  2. 10 yo F whose mother has FAP; the child has never been tested → APC genetic testing → a positive result starts annual endoscopic screening
  3. 14 yo M with FAP, colonoscopy shows a few small adenomas under 1 cm, no dysplasia, no bleeding → Continue annual colonoscopy and plan colectomy for the late teens to early 20s → no immediate trigger is present
  4. 17 yo F with FAP, colonoscopy shows innumerable polyps, several over 1 cm, one with high-grade dysplasia → Total proctocolectomy → a colectomy trigger is met at any age
  5. 19 yo M with FAP under annual surveillance, now with rectal bleeding and iron deficiency → Colectomy now → bleeding is an any-age indication
  6. 23 yo F, total proctocolectomy for FAP 2 years ago, asymptomatic → Upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas → colectomy does not remove upper-tract risk
  7. 28 yo M with hundreds of colonic adenomas, a mandibular osteoma, and a firm abdominal-wall desmoid tumor → Gardner syndrome → FAP pathway, same colectomy rules
  8. 36 yo F with right-sided colon cancer, 12 polyps on colonoscopy, a mother with endometrial cancer at 45 and a brother with colon cancer at 42 → Lynch syndrome → mismatch-repair testing of the tumor
Where the rule breaks The numbers here belong to a known APC carrier. A first-degree relative with sporadic colon cancer follows a different rule (earlier than average-risk screening, but not annual scoping from puberty), and a Lynch pedigree — few polyps, endometrial cancer in the family — follows a third. Match the pathway before you match the number. Colectomy timing is a plan, not a wait: any of bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps, or high-grade dysplasia converts "teens to early 20s" into "now."
Pearls APC is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two risk and is tested rather than presumed · screening starts at puberty because adenomas appear in adolescence and cancer follows within decades · Gardner adds osteomas and desmoids, Turcot adds CNS tumors — both are FAP for management purposes · the colectomy fixes the colon and nothing else: duodenal and ampullary adenomas need their own endoscopy · Lynch is the polyp-poor counterpart with a mismatch-repair mechanism and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree
Pairs with Part I Postmenopausal Bleeding names Lynch syndrome among the endometrial cancer risk factors — the same pedigree seen from the gynecologic side. This brief wants a partner on Lynch syndrome and colorectal cancer screening intervals (not yet written). Store the discriminator as a question: how many polyps, and is there an APC mutation?
Transferable rule Hereditary cancer questions are pathway questions — identify the syndrome first, because every number (start age, interval, operation) belongs to a pathway, and the sporadic family-history numbers are the planted wrong parameters.
Wrong parameter"Colonoscopy at 40" is the right intervention with the sporadic family-history number; an APC carrier is scoped annually from puberty.
Sequencing trapPolypectomy of the largest lesions is a rung below what innumerable polyps or dysplasia already licenses.
Uniform-answer doubt"No further surveillance" after colectomy feels earned, but the duodenum was never operated on.

Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

Macules on the lips, polyps in the gut · UWorld · the exam finding that redirects the workup

Source vignette Pt — 13-year-old girl, 2 months of fatigue worse after walking to class; menarche at 12, regular 28-day cycles, menses 6–7 days with cramping; well-balanced diet, no medications · Exam — pale conjunctivae; a few brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa; abdomen soft, no organomegaly · Labs — haemoglobin 8.4, MCV 70, platelets and leukocytes normal · Q — the best next step; options spanned ACTH stimulation, bone marrow evaluation, iron with oral contraception, lead level and upper and lower endoscopy
The decision point

Everything before the mouth reads as ordinary adolescent iron deficiency: a 13-year-old, six-day menses, microcytic anaemia. Then brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa appear, and they are not part of that story. They are the mucocutaneous marker of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and the anaemia becomes occult bleeding from hamartomatous polyps rather than menstrual loss. The next step is upper and lower endoscopy.

This is a stem where the answer lives in one clause of the physical examination and every earlier sentence points the other way. The distractor that fits the demographic — iron and an oral contraceptive — treats the anaemia and leaves the syndrome undiagnosed.

Defining criteria Peutz-Jeghers — autosomal dominant, tumour-suppressor mutation, with mucocutaneous pigmented macules and two or more gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps · Macule distribution — lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles · Polyp complications — obstruction or intussusception, anaemia from bleeding, rectal prolapse · Cancer risk — gastrointestinal, breast and genital tract · Surveillance — annual haemoglobin plus upper and lower endoscopy
Pigmentation plus anaemia — the differentialwhere the pigment is decides
DiagnosisThe pigmentThe anaemiaWhat to do
Peutz-JeghersDiscrete brown macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms and solesMicrocytic, from occult polyp bleedingUpper and lower endoscopy; genetic testing
Primary adrenal insufficiencyDiffuse hyperpigmentation, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areasUsually normocytic if presentACTH stimulation test
Lead poisoningBlue gingival line at the tooth marginMicrocytic with basophilic stipplingBlood lead level
Menstrual iron deficiencyNoneMicrocytic, from heavy or prolonged mensesIron; hormonal control if bleeding is heavy
Marrow failure or malignancyNoneUsually normocytic, with other cytopeniasBone marrow evaluation
Scenario bank
  1. 13 year old with fatigue, pale conjunctivae, haemoglobin 8.4 with MCV 70, and brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa → Upper and lower endoscopy → Peutz-Jeghers — the macules convert an iron-deficiency workup into a polyposis one
  2. Adolescent with hyperpigmented macules on lips, buccal mucosa and palms, and recurrent abdominal pain from intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Hamartomatous polyps, autosomal dominant
  3. How Peutz-Jeghers polyps produce a microcytic anaemia → Chronic occult blood loss from the polyps → Iron deficiency, not marrow failure — the MCV is the clue
  4. Established Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; the ongoing surveillance → Annual haemoglobin with periodic upper and lower endoscopy → Plus awareness of breast and genital tract risk
  5. Adolescent with fatigue, generalised hyperpigmentation worst over elbows and knees, anorexia and weight loss → Primary adrenal insufficiency → Diffuse pigmentation in sun- and pressure-exposed areas, not discrete macules
  6. Child with microcytic anaemia and a blue line along the gingival margin → Lead poisoning → Gingival lead lines, not mucosal macules
  7. Adolescent girl with microcytic anaemia, regular 6-day menses and oral pigmented macules; which management is inadequate → Iron and oral contraception alone → It treats the anaemia and ignores the syndrome causing it
Gates Microcytic anaemia in an adolescent girl is not automatically menstrual — look at the mouth, the palms and the family history before settling · Intussusception in an older child is a lead point until proven otherwise, and a hamartoma is one · Cancer risk extends beyond the gut to breast and genital tract, so surveillance is lifelong · A normal platelet and leukocyte count argues against marrow failure
Pearls The macules can fade in adulthood while the polyp risk does not — a negative skin examination in a parent does not exclude the family history · Hamartomatous, not adenomatous, which is why the cancer risk is broader than colon alone · MCV separates the bleeding causes from the marrow causes before any imaging · Perioral pigmentation plus intussusception in a child is the classic paired presentation
Pairs with Part I Familial Adenomatous Polyposis, which owns the adenomatous syndromes and their colectomy timing; this brief owns the hamartomatous one. Store the discriminator as a question: where exactly is the pigment, and what is the MCV?
Transferable rule When a stem builds an ordinary explanation and then adds one finding that does not belong to it, that finding is the question — the preceding sentences were the distractor.
Salient decoyAdolescent girl plus menses plus microcytic anaemia reads as iron deficiency before the mouth is examined.
Class-vs-memberRight category of mucocutaneous pigmentation, wrong distribution.

Toddler Food Refusal

the refusal pattern names the cause · board question · Is he refusing a texture, a food group, or eating altogether — and is he atopic?

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo, stuck on pureed textures, eczema, weight fallen from the 25th to the 5th percentile · Labs — swallow study normal · Q — the most appropriate test; options spanned endoscopy with esophageal biopsy, tissue transglutaminase antibody and allergy skin testing
The decision point

He is not anorexic and he is not avoiding a food group — he is stuck on a texture. Advancing from purees to solids normally happens between 6 and 12 months, and failure to make that transition is the toddler's way of reporting dysphagia he cannot describe. The stem then removes the competing explanations one at a time: the swallow study is normal, so the problem is below the pharynx; development is normal, so this is not a behavioral or autism-spectrum feeding disorder; the stools are soft and daily with a benign abdomen, so it is not celiac disease or an intraabdominal process. What remains is inflammation of the esophagus, and the supporting clue is the one that reads like background history — eczema, because atopy accompanies most eosinophilic esophagitis. The diagnosis is histologic, so the test that establishes it is endoscopy with esophageal biopsy.

Defining criteria Eosinophilic esophagitis — endoscopy with esophageal biopsy showing ≥15 eosinophils per high-power field, with alternative diagnoses such as achalasia and infection excluded · The texture milestone — advancement from purees to solids normally occurs between 6 and 12 months; failure to advance is itself the abnormal finding · What a normal swallow study buys — it excludes oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration, moving the lesion below the pharynx
Pertinent positives & negatives Prefers purees, refuses all solid meat, fruit and vegetables — a texture-based refusal, not a food-group avoidance; this is the toddler presentation of esophageal disease · History of eczema — atopy, present in most patients with eosinophilic esophagitis, and the detail that converts suspicion into a likely diagnosis · Weight from the 25th to the 5th percentile with height at the 30th — a caloric deficit; weight crosses percentiles before height does · Normal swallow study — a spent move; oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration are already excluded, so no further swallow-imaging option survives · Development otherwise normal — argues against a developmental or behavioral feeding disorder · Daily soft stools, no diarrhea or vomiting, soft nondistended abdomen — celiac disease typically brings diarrhea or constipation with pain and distension, and none is present · Moist mucous membranes, normal vital signs — chronic and compensated, not acute; this is a diagnostic question, not a resuscitation one · Refusal of every solid rather than of bread and pasta — the distinction that separates an esophageal problem from a gluten one
The toddler who stops advancing his diet — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Eosinophilic esophagitisTh2 response to food antigen; comorbid atopy; age-shifting presentationFailure to advance past purees in an atopic toddler; ≥15 eosinophils per hpf on biopsy— (the answer)
Celiac diseaseGluten-driven enteropathy; poor weight gain with malabsorptionDiarrhea or constipation with pain and distension; avoidance of gluten-rich foods specificallySoft daily stools, benign abdomen, refusal of all solids
Oropharyngeal dysphagiaNeuromuscular disease or incoordination; aspiration riskCoughing and choking with feeds; abnormal video swallow studyThe swallow study is normal
Anatomic obstruction (stricture, ring, vascular ring ⚠︎)Fixed narrowing; solids worse than liquidsAbrupt onset or a caustic/reflux history; a lesion on esophagram or endoscopyNo such history; endoscopy would show it, which is why the scope is still the answer
Developmental or behavioral feeding disorderSensory aversion, autism spectrum, learned avoidanceDevelopmental delay or a normal endoscopy with feeding therapy as the answerDevelopment is normal for age
Systemic causes of poor gain (hyperthyroidism, intraabdominal mass)Raised demand or anorexia from diseaseIncreased appetite with tachycardia and goiter, or anorexia with a palpable massHe refuses food and has a normal examination
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: dietary elimination is first-line, with proton pump inhibitors and swallowed topical glucocorticoids as pharmacologic options and feeding therapy for the maladaptive eating that follows (all in-context).
Decision spine Is he refusing food, or is he not hungry? — Refusing → a mechanical or inflammatory problem, not a metabolic one · What exactly does he refuse? — Every solid, tolerates purees → a texture problem · Is the swallow normal? — Yes → the lesion is below the pharynx · Is he atopic? — Eczema → eosinophilic esophagitis · What establishes it? — Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy — the diagnosis is a cell count, not a serology
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo stuck on purees with eczema, weight from the 25th to the 5th percentile, and a normal swallow study → Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy → 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field is diagnostic
  2. 2 yo with biopsy-confirmed eosinophilic esophagitis; first-line treatment → Dietary elimination → Pharmacologic therapy is the next tier
  3. 16 yo with known eosinophilic esophagitis, a meat bolus impacted for 3 hours, now drooling → Urgent endoscopy → Adolescent presentation of the same disease
  4. 8 yo, atopic, months of abdominal pain and vomiting; esophageal biopsies show 25 eosinophils per high-power field → Eosinophilic esophagitis → The school-age presentation
  5. 3 yo with poor weight gain, chronic diarrhea, a distended abdomen, and avoidance of bread and pasta → Tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA level → Celiac disease
  6. 14 mo with coughing and choking during feeds and two prior pneumonias → Video swallow study → Oropharyngeal dysfunction with aspiration
  7. Toddler with suspected eosinophilic esophagitis; which test will not establish the diagnosis → Allergy skin testing → It diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy rather than this
  8. 2 yo with poor weight gain, normal development, no atopy, a normal swallow study, and normal endoscopy with normal biopsies → Feeding therapy for a behavioral feeding disorder → The scope has excluded the organ
  9. The immunologic basis of eosinophilic esophagitis → A Th2-mediated response to food antigen → Comorbid atopy is the clinical correlate
  10. Child with confirmed eosinophilic esophagitis; why allergy testing may still be performed → To guide dietary elimination given frequent concomitant IgE sensitivities → After the diagnosis, never instead of it
Decoy note "Has always been a picky eater" invites a behavioral reading and is the reason the stem bothers to say development is normal. The stool sentence is a planted negative doing real work: soft daily stools with no diarrhea or vomiting is what kills celiac disease and gastroenteritis. The eczema is the opposite of a decoy — it is the supporting evidence most readers skim past, because it arrives in the past-medical-history slot where decorative details usually live.
Pearls A toddler stuck on purees with eczema and falling weight has eosinophilic esophagitis; endoscopic biopsy showing fifteen or more eosinophils proves it. · The shape of the refusal localizes the problem: a texture refusal points at the esophagus, a food-group refusal at celiac disease or an IgE allergy, and a poor appetite with normal eating at systemic or metabolic disease. · Eosinophilic esophagitis shifts its presentation with age — toddlers refuse solids, school-age children have abdominal pain and vomiting, adolescents get dysphagia and food impaction. · Atopy accompanies most cases, so eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis or a known food allergy in a feeding-refusal stem is a clue rather than background. · The diagnosis is a cell count on biopsy, not a serology or a skin test; allergy testing guides the elimination diet only after the scope has settled the question. · Dietary elimination is first-line, with a proton pump inhibitor or a swallowed topical glucocorticoid as pharmacologic options, and feeding therapy for the avoidance the illness taught.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Faltering Weight owns the general approach to poor weight gain and the growth-curve reading; this brief takes over once the child is refusing rather than simply not growing. Store the discriminator as a question: is he refusing food, and if so, is he refusing a texture or a food group? Candidate twin — confirm: a celiac disease brief does not exist yet, and it would own the serology-and-biopsy pathway this brief only points at.
Transferable rule When a complaint has a shape, the shape is the finding — in feeding problems, refusal of a texture, refusal of a food group, and loss of appetite are three different diseases wearing one growth curve, so name the shape before you choose a test.
Salient decoyTissue transglutaminase antibody — Celiac brings diarrhea or constipation with pain and distension, and its children avoid gluten-rich foods — not every solid; this child's stools and abdomen are normal
True-fact-wrong-slotAbdominal ultrasonography — A mass causes anorexia, not a preference for purees, and the abdomen is soft, nontender and nondistended
True-fact-wrong-slotThyroid function tests — Hyperthyroidism raises appetite and adds tachycardia and goiter — the appetite runs in the opposite direction from this stem
Sequencing trapAllergy skin testing — It diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy, which presents acutely with urticaria and angioedema; even in confirmed disease it only guides the diet, and the priority is establishing the diagnosis

Right Lower Quadrant Pain

appendix, ileocecum, or neither · board question · Is there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo, migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, sibling with the same illness · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Campylobacter infection, acute appendicitis and Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection
The decision point

Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis are shared by both live answers, so none of them decides anything. Two findings do, and appendicitis can explain neither: twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours, and a brother with the same illness. What owns both is infectious ileocecitis — the pseudoappendicitis of organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, which reads as the appendicitis script, is in fact explained by the same answer: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.

Defining criteria Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) — right lower quadrant pain from acute ileocecitis caused by organisms with an ileocecal predilection, specifically Yersinia enterocolitica and Campylobacter jejuni · The discriminating symptom — profuse watery or mucoid diarrhea, which acute appendicitis is not classically associated with · The imaging tell — ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with sparing of the appendix · When Campylobacter earns antibiotics — duration beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fevers, or a patient who is pregnant, immunocompromised, or elderly
Pertinent positives & negatives Twelve mucus-containing stools in 24 hours — profuse mucoid diarrhea; the single finding appendicitis cannot produce · A brother with the same illness, now improving — a shared exposure; appendicitis has no contacts, and the sibling's course also fits a self-limited enteritis · Migratory periumbilical → right lower quadrant pain — the appendicitis script, and simultaneously explained by jejunal-then-ileocecal spread of Campylobacter · Right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or rigidity — no peritonitis; this argues against an advanced or perforated appendix without excluding an early one · Fever 38.8 °C with WBC 13,700 and 80% neutrophils — inflammation shared by both diagnoses; decides nothing on its own · Mucus in the stool — argues against norovirus, whose stools are watery without mucus · No hematochezia in the patient, with fever above 38.5 °C — argues against E. coli O157:H7, which usually brings hematochezia within 1–3 days and rarely high fever · Age 17 — diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age, which is most of why that option is a throwaway
Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Infectious ileocecitis — Campylobacter, YersiniaUndercooked poultry or a sick contact; ileocecal predilection; fever with mucoid or bloody diarrheaProfuse mucoid diarrhea with right lower quadrant pain; imaging spares the appendix— (the answer)
Acute appendicitisLuminal obstruction; migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, vomitingLittle or no diarrhea, progressive localized peritonitis, no sick contactsTwelve mucoid stools and an affected sibling
E. coli O157:H7Shiga toxin colitis; undercooked beef or a point-source outbreakHematochezia within 1–3 days and fever above 38.5 °C is rareThe patient has no bloody stools and a temperature of 38.8 °C
NorovirusCommon-source outbreak; prominent vomitingWatery stools without mucus, normal white blood cell countMucoid stools with a neutrophilic leukocytosis
Cecal diverticulitisRight-sided diverticular inflammationRight lower quadrant pain and fever in an adult; mild or no diarrheaExceedingly rare at 17; profuse mucoid diarrhea
Crohn ileitis ⚠︎Chronic transmural ileal inflammationWeeks to months of pain, weight loss, perianal diseaseThree days of illness with a sick contact
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: Campylobacter is treated supportively, since it is usually self-limited within seven days, with antibiotics reserved for the severe or high-risk cases listed above, and surgery is not required in infectious ileocecitis (all in-context).
Decision spine Is there diarrhea, and how much? — Twelve mucoid stools → appendicitis does not do this · Is there a sick contact? — A brother with the same illness → an infectious exposure, not a luminal obstruction · Are there peritoneal signs? — No rebound, no rigidity → not a surgical abdomen at this moment · What is the stool like? — Mucoid, with or without blood → invasive bacterial rather than viral · Which organisms live at the ileocecum? — Campylobacter and Yersinia — and that is the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo with migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness → Campylobacter infection → Infectious ileocecitis
  2. A hemodynamically stable 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness has had 3 days of symptoms without bloody stools. → Supportive care with stool studies → Usually self-limited within 7 days
  3. A 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness now presents on day 9 with bloody stools and fever to 39.5 °C. → Start antimicrobial therapy → A high-risk criterion is met
  4. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and vomiting but no diarrhea, with rebound tenderness → Surgical consultation for appendectomy → The classic script without the stool
  5. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain and diarrhea in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after examination → Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen → Ileocecal inflammation with a spared appendix
  6. 16 yo with months of right lower quadrant pain, weight loss and a perianal fistula → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation → Crohn ileitis
  7. 6 yo with severe crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools, temperature 37.6 C, after a family cookout → Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection → Hematochezia early, high fever rare
  8. That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld → Empiric antibiotics → Risk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome
  9. Three weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barre syndrome → The classic post-infectious sequela
  10. Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis → The second named sequela
Decoy note The brother is the most instructive detail in the stem, because it works in two directions at once: his existence supports an infectious cause, while his bloody stools invite the reader to assign Shiga toxin E. coli to a patient who has no blood in his own stool. A finding described in a contact is evidence about the exposure, not about this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is the second trap and is subtler still — it is not inert, it is genuinely explained by the right answer, which is why it feels like confirmation of the wrong one.
Pearls Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools and does not come with a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia does both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea is what an appendix cannot do, and a sick contact is what an appendix cannot have; either one alone should stop the surgical reflex. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and therefore mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may seed the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, which is exactly why the pain migrates like appendicitis. · The two tested sequelae of Campylobacter are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis. · Antibiotics are for illness beyond seven days, bloody stools, high fevers, or pregnancy, immunocompromise, or advanced age; otherwise the treatment is supportive. · The opposite instinct applies to Shiga toxin E. coli, where antibiotics are withheld ⚠︎ — so "invasive bacterial diarrhea" is not one management rule but two.

Store the discriminator as a question: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness? This brief also pairs with the microangiopathy brief authored earlier in this batch, which owns the anemia-with-thrombocytopenia end of the same organism's story; add the reverse link when both are on the page.
Transferable rule When a stem hands you a textbook script, deliberately hunt for the finding the script cannot explain — a symptom the disease does not produce, or an exposure it cannot have — because examiners build distractors out of complete scripts and build answers out of the leftovers.
Salient decoyAcute appendicitis — Appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea, and it cannot explain a sibling with the same illness; there are no peritoneal signs
True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 — Hematochezia appears in the patient within 1–3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs; the blood belongs to the brother, not to this patient
Class-vs-memberNorovirus — Norovirus gives watery stools without mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting
Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis — It is exceedingly rare in children and adolescents, and it does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea

Constipation in a Child

clear the alarm signs, then soften before you instrument · board question · Is growth normal and the examination benign, and is there stool in the rectum?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, nontender abdomen, anal fissure · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned an oral osmotic laxative, a rectal enema and abdominal radiography
The decision point

The stem hands you the mechanism in its chronology: stools were daily and soft until toilet training began, and the pain came before the hardness got worse. That is the withholding cycle — one painful stool teaches the child to hold, holding lets the rectum desiccate the next stool, and the next one hurts more. The anal fissure is the cycle's signature and its accelerant. Everything the examination doesn't show is doing equal work: growth on the 75th percentile with a nontender abdomen and a normal perineum clears the alarm-sign screen, which is what licenses treating rather than investigating. The move is the one that breaks the cycle at its only modifiable point — an oral osmotic laxative to make the next stool painless.

Defining criteria Alarm signs — delayed passage of meconium, fever or vomiting, ribbon stools, poor growth, severe abdominal distension, and abnormal examination findings such as a displaced anus or a tuft at the gluteal cleft · Cow's-milk limit — under 24 oz per day; this child's 24 oz is at the limit, not above it · Complications that are not alarm signs — anal fissure, hemorrhoids, enuresis and urinary tract infections; each argues for the functional diagnosis rather than against it
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset coincides with toilet training — the commonest trigger, alongside solid-food and cow's-milk introduction and school entry; it dates the problem to a behavior rather than an anatomy · Previously daily soft stools — normal baseline function excludes a congenital motility defect, which would have declared earlier · Cries and screams with defecation — pain is the engine of withholding, and it is the symptom the laxative is aimed at · Growth tracking at the 75th percentile — clears the growth alarm sign and effectively removes Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism and celiac disease · Anal fissure — a complication of hard stools, and the reason a rectal enema is the wrong instrument here · Abdomen firm and mildly distended but nontender — stool load without obstruction; severe distension would be the alarm sign, and this is not it · 24 oz of milk, refuses fruit — the diet is a contributor to modify, not a cause to eliminate · Urinates in the toilet without difficulty — the problem is stool-specific, which argues against a neurologic cause affecting both
Constipation in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Functional constipationToddler at a transition — toilet training, school entry, cow's milk; painful stool leads to withholding, which hardens the next stoolNormal growth and examination, onset tied to a transition, anal fissure as a complication— (the answer)
Hirschsprung disease Can't missAganglionic distal segment; usually declares in the neonatal periodDelayed meconium beyond 48 hours ⚠︎, ribbon stools, distension, poor growth; anal fissures are uncommonPassed meconium normally, thriving, fissure present
Congenital hypothyroidismSlowed transit with systemic featuresPoor linear growth, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle ⚠︎Height and weight both on the 75th percentile
Tethered cord or spinal dysraphismOccult dysraphism impairing sacral outflowSacral dimple, hair tuft or displaced anus, with urinary symptoms and lower-limb findingsNormal perineal examination; urinates without difficulty
Celiac diseaseGluten enteropathy; constipation is a recognised presentation ⚠︎Falling weight percentile, distension with irritability, iron deficiencyGrowth tracking, well nourished
Excessive cow's-milk intakeFat and protein without fiber; slow transit and satiety that crowds out fiberMilk volume well above 24 oz per day, often with iron deficiency24 oz is within the recommended range
Classify first — constipation in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Any alarm sign?"Height and weight have been tracking along the 75th percentiles… remainder of the examination is unremarkable"No — treat rather than investigate; the film and the manometry both die here
Impacted or not?"abdomen is firm, mildly distended, and nontender"; no stool ball describedNot impacted — maintenance therapy without a disimpaction step
Is the rectum safe to instrument?"An anal fissure is present"The rectal route causes further trauma; if disimpaction were needed, go oral

Tier fingerprint done — nothing has been tried, so no failure has been earned · normal — growth, perineum, abdominal tenderness and urinary function, all of them eliminations · bothered — the child cries with every stool, which licenses treating today rather than counselling and waiting.
Management ladder — constipation in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Oral osmotic laxative such as polyethylene glycol, plus increased dietary fiber and water, cow's milk kept under 24 oz per day, and age-appropriate toileting guidance — sitting after meals with the feet supported ⚠︎A stool ball on examination or overflow soiling means disimpaction is needed first
2Disimpaction — high-dose oral polyethylene glycol, or an enema; enemas are limited when an anal fissure is present because they cause further rectal trauma. Follow with long-term maintenance so the dilated rectum can return to normal sizeFailure to clear, or vomiting and severe pain suggesting obstruction, earns an abdominal x-ray
3Constipation persisting despite standard therapy — anorectal manometry; suction rectal biopsy is the confirmatory test for Hirschsprung disease ⚠︎Manometry abnormal or alarm signs emerging means paediatric gastroenterology and an anatomic workup
MaintenanceContinue the laxative for months rather than days ⚠︎ — the goal is a painless stool often enough that the child unlearns withholdingRelapse on weaning means resuming and re-addressing the behavioural side
Numbers that gate & exit ramps cow's milk under 24 oz per day and the alarm-sign list are in-context; the 48-hour meconium threshold, the duration of maintenance therapy and toileting-posture advice are ⚠︎. · delayed meconium with ribbon stools and poor growth → Hirschsprung disease, manometry then rectal biopsy ⚠︎ · sacral dimple, hair tuft or a displaced anus → spinal imaging for occult dysraphism · vomiting or severe distension with pain → abdominal x-ray, because severe impaction mimics obstruction · overflow soiling in an older child → impaction with encopresis, so disimpact before maintenance and tell the parents the soiling is not deliberate · milk intake well above 24 oz with pallor → reduce milk and check for iron deficiency ⚠︎.
Decision spine Any alarm sign? — Growth normal, examination benign, meconium normal → no, so the investigation options are dead · Is there an impaction? — Nontender abdomen with no stool ball → no, so disimpaction is not the tier being tested · Is the rectum instrumentable? — There is a fissure → no rectal route even if one were needed · Is the diet outside limits? — 24 oz of milk is at the ceiling rather than over it → modify rather than withdraw · What breaks the cycle? — Make the next stool painless → an oral osmotic laxative
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, a nontender abdomen and an anal fissure → Initiate an oral osmotic laxative → Functional constipation
  2. 6 yo M with involuntary soiling of his underwear and a palpable suprapubic stool mass, without an anal fissure → Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy → Impaction with overflow incontinence
  3. 4 yo F with fecal impaction requiring disimpaction who has a painful anal fissure on examination → High-dose oral polyethylene glycol → Enemas cause further rectal trauma
  4. 2 yo M with constipation and pallor who drinks 40 oz of cow's milk daily and eats little else → Reduce cow's milk intake and start a laxative → Milk volume above the recommended limit
  5. 3 yo F with constipation, daytime urinary incontinence and a tuft of hair over the sacrum → Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine → Occult spinal dysraphism
  6. 5 yo M whose constipation persists after 3 months of adequate laxative and dietary therapy, with normal growth and examination → Anorectal manometry → Refractory to standard therapy
  7. Newborn who first passed meconium at 60 hours, now with ribbon-like stools, abdominal distension and poor weight gain → Hirschsprung disease → Manometry, then rectal biopsy
  8. 8-month-old with constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large anterior fontanelle → Congenital hypothyroidism → Check the TSH
  9. Why one painful bowel movement can produce weeks of worsening constipation in a toddler → Withholding desiccates stool in the rectum→ so the next defecation hurts more, which reinforces withholding; The cycle is the disease
  10. 3 yo M with functional constipation who drinks 24 oz of cow's milk daily; which management is inappropriate → Discontinuing cow's milk entirely → It removes calcium and vitamin D without benefit
  11. 15-month-old with constipation since infancy refractory to dietary changes, thin caliber stools, distended abdomen, explosive stool and gas on rectal exam → Contrast enema → Hirschsprung disease
Decoy note Two details invite over-reading in opposite directions. Refusing to eat fruit and the milk volume together read like a dietary indictment, but the stem quietly places the milk at the limit rather than above it, so the diet is a contributor to adjust rather than the answer. And a firm, mildly distended abdomen sounds ominous until you notice the two qualifiers the alarm-sign list actually uses: severe distension, and tenderness. Neither is here. The anal fissure is the most misread finding of all — it is not evidence of an alternative diagnosis, it is the expected complication of the diagnosis you already have, and its only management consequence is to close the rectal route.
Pearls A growing child with painful hard stools and a normal examination gets an oral osmotic laxative, not a rectal procedure or an image. · Constipation in children is a behavioural cycle with a mechanical consequence; the laxative exists to make the next stool painless so the child stops holding, which is why it runs for months rather than days ⚠︎. · The three transitions that generate it are solid food and cow's milk, toilet training, and school entry — a stem that names one is telling you the diagnosis. · An anal fissure is a complication of constipation rather than a competing diagnosis, and it is the reason to disimpact by mouth rather than by rectum. · Hirschsprung disease declares with delayed meconium and poor growth, and fissures are uncommon in it; normal growth with a fissure is functional disease. · Growth is the alarm sign that does the most work — a child tracking a percentile has essentially excluded hypothyroidism, celiac disease and Hirschsprung disease before you order anything. · Enuresis and urinary tract infections are complications of constipation, so a wet child with hard stools gets the bowel treated first.

Part I Infant Stool Complaints: Dyschezia, FPIAP & Secondary Lactase Deficiency owns the infant end of the same complaint, and Part II Tethered Cord and Closed Spinal Dysraphism owns the exit ramp this brief's perineal examination is screening for. Store the discriminator as a question: is growth normal, and is there stool in the rectum?
Transferable rule When a common condition has a benign screening profile, the examination's normals are the permission to treat, and the alarm-sign list is the only thing that converts treatment into investigation. A complication of the diagnosis is evidence for it rather than against it — but it can still change which instrument you are allowed to use. --- Batch 5, brief 01 · 2026-09-10.
Unchecked attributeDiscontinue milk — 24 oz is within the recommended 16 to 24 oz range; withdrawal costs calcium and vitamin D and buys nothing
Sequencing trapObtain abdominal radiograph — The film is for severe impaction that mimics obstruction, with pain and vomiting; this abdomen is nontender and benign
Salient decoyAdminister rectal enema — There is no impaction to disimpact, and the anal fissure makes the rectal route actively harmful here
Sequencing trapObtain anorectal manometry — Reserved for constipation that persists despite standard therapy; no therapy has been tried and no alarm sign is present

Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome

Stereotyped episodes, well in between · UWorld · the pattern is the diagnosis

Source vignette Pt — 9-year-old girl, 8 months of nausea, vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain for several days each month; episodes begin early morning, recur 10–15 times daily for 2 days, nonbloody and nonbilious; more frequent at the start of the school year; two admissions for intravenous hydration · Between episodes — active, eating well, growth at the 25th percentile and unchanged · Exam — well hydrated, erosive maxillary caries, soft nontender abdomen, normal neurologic examination · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned bulimia, chronic pancreatitis, cyclic vomiting, factitious disorder imposed on another, reflux and inflammatory bowel disease
The decision point

Three features together make this cyclic vomiting syndrome: episodes that are stereotyped, self-limited over 1 to 2 days, and complete wellness between them with normal growth. Stress at the start of term is the trigger; most patients have a personal or family history of migraine. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so the well-between-episodes pattern does the work.

The erosive caries are worth naming because they cut the other way from how they feel. They are evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrent, not evidence of purging — there is no bingeing, no restriction and no preoccupation with shape.

Defining criteria Stereotyped episodes — the same acute nausea, abdominal pain, headache and vomiting each time · Duration — self-limited over 1 to 2 days · Interval — often regular, around 2 to 4 weeks, and asymptomatic between · Association — personal or family history of migraine · Triggers — infection or stress
Recurrent vomiting in a child — the differentialwhat happens between the episodes
DiagnosisBetween episodesKey discriminatorWhat to do
Cyclic vomiting syndromeEntirely well, growing normallyStereotyped, self-limited, regular intervals; migraine historyRehydration and antiemetics; triptans may abort
Bulimia nervosaPreoccupied with shape and weightBingeing with compensatory behaviourPsychiatric assessment
Chronic pancreatitisPoor growth, diarrhoeaEpigastric tenderness on examinationPancreatic imaging and enzyme studies
Inflammatory bowel diseaseWeight loss, fever, ongoing symptomsDiarrhoea with abdominal tendernessInflammatory markers and endoscopy
Gastroesophageal refluxOngoing low-grade symptomsRegurgitation and substernal pain, not episodic burstsTrial of acid suppression
Factitious disorder imposed on anotherInconsistent history, symptoms unwitnessedNo objective corroboration of the illnessCareful documentation; child protection
Scenario bank
  1. 9 year old with 8 months of stereotyped vomiting episodes lasting 2 days, 10-15 times daily, entirely well between them, normal growth, erosive maxillary caries → Cyclic vomiting syndrome → A diagnosis of exclusion with predictable intervals
  2. The historical association that supports cyclic vomiting syndrome → Personal or family history of migraine → Triggers are often infection or stress
  3. Child with established cyclic vomiting syndrome presenting mid-episode, dehydrated → Intravenous rehydration with an antiemetic → Abortive triptans may shorten the episode
  4. Adolescent with self-induced vomiting after binge eating, preoccupied with body shape, normal weight → Bulimia nervosa → Bingeing and compensatory behaviour, not stereotyped episodes
  5. Child with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, poor growth and epigastric tenderness → Chronic pancreatitis → Growth failure and tenderness, unlike the well-between-episodes pattern
  6. What the erosive dental caries in a child with recurrent vomiting indicates → Evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrent → It supports the history rather than implying purging
Gates Bilious vomiting, weight loss, fever or an abnormal neurologic examination takes this off the cyclic list and onto an urgent one · Growth must be normal — faltering growth means keep looking · Laboratory work and imaging are usually done during an acute episode to exclude the urgent causes, not between them · Most children outgrow it during adolescence
