Pearls The interval is the finding — regular, predictable, and symptom-free between · Dental erosion documents recurrent acid exposure without saying who caused it · Migraine history is the single most useful piece of the history · Diagnosis of exclusion means the workup is aimed at what would be dangerous, not at confirming the label
Pairs with Part I Headache in a Child: What Earns Imaging, which owns the migraine end of the same biology. Store the discriminator as a question: how is the child between the episodes?
Transferable rule For episodic illness, the diagnostic information is in the interval, not the episode — ask what the patient is like when it is not happening.
Salient decoyDental erosion in an adolescent girl suggests purging to anyone who stops reading there.
Unchecked attributeNormal growth is stated and excludes the chronic inflammatory and malabsorptive options.

Neonatal Jaundice

Timing, direct fraction and Coombs · NBME peds · which mechanism, and does it need light

Source vignette Pt — 4-day-old term M, uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, Apgars 10 and 10, breast-feeding without difficulty, eight wet diapers daily, alert and afebrile · Labs — total bilirubin 11 mg/dL · Q — the most likely underlying cause; options spanned cholestasis, enterohepatic circulation, conjugation-enzyme activity, albumin binding and ligandin
The decision point

Physiologic jaundice is a conjugation problem. The newborn breaks down fetal haemoglobin quickly while hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase is still immature, so unconjugated bilirubin accumulates faster than it can be cleared. A well infant, feeding and voiding normally, jaundiced on day 4 at 11 mg/dL, is the ordinary version of this.

Every wrong option on that list is a real mechanism stated in the wrong direction or the wrong compartment. Ligandin is low at birth, not high. Enterohepatic circulation is increased in the newborn, not decreased. Cholestasis produces a direct hyperbilirubinaemia, which this infant does not have. Albumin displacement is real but needs a displacing drug. Name the direction before you pick the mechanism.

Defining criteria Physiologic — begins after 24 hours, peaks around day 3 to 5, predominantly indirect, resolving by 1 to 2 weeks · Pathologic — jaundice within the first 24 hours, any raised direct fraction, or persistence beyond 2 weeks · Jaundice threshold — clinically apparent above about 5 mg/dL · Physiologic ceiling — peak around 14 to 15 mg/dL, indirect over 90% · Exchange range — generally above 20 mg/dL; kernicterus risk rises at 25 to 30 mg/dL
Neonatal jaundice — the mechanismstiming and the direct fraction separate them
CauseWhenKey discriminatorWhat to do
PhysiologicAfter 24 h, peak day 3–5Well infant, feeding and voiding normally; indirectNothing but time
Suboptimal-intake (breast-feeding) jaundiceDay 3–5Weight loss and few wet diapers; increased enterohepatic reabsorptionFeed more often, lactation support
Breast-milk jaundiceDay 7 onward, can persist weeksThriving infant, indirect, gaining wellContinue breast-feeding
ABO or Rh haemolytic diseaseOften within 24 hCoombs positive; mother O or Rh-negativePhototherapy; exchange above threshold
G6PD deficiency Can't missVariable, can be abruptIndirect with anaemia, often an oxidant triggerRemove trigger; phototherapy
Biliary atresia Can't missBeyond 2 weeksRaised direct fraction, acholic stoolsUrgent evaluation; Kasai before about 60 days
Crigler-Najjar / GilbertPersistent indirectThe same enzyme, absent or reduced rather than immatureDepends on type
Scenario bank
  1. 4 day old M, term, breast-feeding well with eight wet diapers, alert and afebrile, total bilirubin 11 mg/dL → Immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity → Physiologic jaundice — conjugation lags the fetal haemoglobin load
  2. 2 day old F, jaundice to the chest, total bilirubin 19 with direct 0.6, Coombs positive, infant blood group B and mother group O → Phototherapy → ABO incompatibility — below the exchange range
  3. Day 4, exclusively breast-fed, 11% below birth weight, three wet diapers, indirect hyperbilirubinaemia → Suboptimal-intake jaundice → Also called breast-feeding jaundice — too little milk, not the milk itself
  4. Thriving 3 week old, exclusively breast-fed, gaining well, persistent indirect hyperbilirubinaemia, normal direct fraction → Breast-milk jaundice → Late, well-grown, indirect — continue feeding
  5. 6 week old with jaundice, acholic stools and a direct bilirubin of 5 mg/dL → Biliary atresia → A direct fraction is never physiologic
  6. Why dehydration in the first week worsens an indirect hyperbilirubinaemia → Increased enterohepatic reabsorption → Slow gut transit lets intestinal bilirubin return to the circulation
  7. Term newborn jaundiced at 14 hours of life; establishing whether this is pathologic → Total and direct bilirubin with a Coombs test → Onset inside 24 hours is pathologic until proven otherwise
  8. Well term newborn with suboptimal-intake jaundice on day 4; which management is inappropriate → Stopping breast-feeding → Feed more often, not less — milk intake drives bilirubin out
  9. Which mechanism makes a sulfonamide dangerous in a jaundiced newborn → Displacement of bilirubin from albumin → Free bilirubin crosses into the basal ganglia
Exit ramps and gates Under 24 hours — never physiologic; send bilirubin with a direct fraction and a Coombs · Any direct fraction — stop thinking physiologic and start thinking obstruction or infection · Beyond 2 weeks — check the direct fraction and the stool colour before reassuring · Phototherapy versus exchange — light first; exchange is for the severe range or for signs of encephalopathy, not for a number close to threshold · Feeding — jaundice almost never earns stopping breast-feeding; more milk moves bilirubin out through the gut
Pearls The newborn gut reabsorbs bilirubin, so anything that slows transit raises the indirect fraction · Suboptimal-intake versus breast-milk jaundice — the first is a hungry infant losing weight in the first week, the second a thriving one still jaundiced in the second · Ligandin and glucuronosyltransferase are both low at birth; an option offering either as increased is inverted · Sulfonamides and ceftriaxone displace bilirubin from albumin, which is why they are avoided in jaundiced newborns · A direct fraction is the single finding that converts a routine newborn jaundice into an urgent one
Pairs with Part II The Sick Jaundiced Neonate with a Positive Screen, which owns the unwell infant with a metabolic cause; this brief owns the well one. Part I Cholestasis & the LFT Patterns carries the direct-fraction workup. Store the discriminator as a question: is the infant well, and is any of it direct?
Transferable rule When every option names a real mechanism, the question is usually direction, not identity — check which way each one moves in this patient before choosing between them.
Unchecked attributeLigandin and enterohepatic circulation are both real, and both stated backwards.
Sequencing trapExchange transfusion offered when the level is high but still in the phototherapy range.
Class-vs-memberCholestasis is the right category of liver problem but the wrong bilirubin fraction.

The Distended Newborn Abdomen

Bilious emesis, bloody stool · UWorld · the film tells you which one

Source vignette Pt — 7-day-old term F with truncus arteriosus in the NICU awaiting repair, poor feeding and abdominal distension; T 35 C, BP 60/30, pulse 180, respirations 65, saturation 82% · Exam — lethargic and cyanotic, moderate distension, absent bowel sounds, bright red blood in stool; nasogastric tube returns bilious fluid · Imaging — abdominal x-ray · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned NEC, malrotation with volvulus, intussusception, milk protein proctocolitis and C difficile colitis
The decision point

Three findings arrive together and only one diagnosis takes all three: temperature instability, abdominal distension with bloody stools, and pneumatosis intestinalis on the film. That is necrotising enterocolitis. The trap is the risk factor — NEC is filed under prematurity, and this infant is term. But cyanotic congenital heart disease and hypotension reduce mesenteric oxygen delivery, and ischaemic bowel is ischaemic bowel however it got that way.

Volvulus is the option that fits the bilious return, and it is the one to rule out deliberately rather than by feel. It gives abrupt vomiting in a previously well infant, with proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen. NEC gives air in the bowel wall and gas still visible in the large bowel. Read the gas pattern before you commit.

Defining criteria Pneumatosis intestinalis — air within the bowel wall; highly specific for NEC · Pneumoperitoneum — free air under the diaphragm; means perforation and an operation · NEC risk factors — prematurity, very low birth weight under 1.5 kg, enteral feeding, and in term infants cyanotic heart disease or hypotension · Volvulus film — proximal gaseous distension with a gasless distal abdomen · Intussusception age — 6 months to 3 years
The distended newborn abdomen — the differentialtiming, the stool, and the gas pattern
DiagnosisThe pictureKey discriminatorWhat to do
Necrotising enterocolitis EmergencyLethargy and temperature instability, distension, feeding intolerance, bloody stoolsPneumatosis intestinalis; gas still present distallyNPO, decompression, broad-spectrum antibiotics now
Malrotation with midgut volvulus EmergencyPreviously well, then abrupt bilious vomiting and painProximal gas, gasless distal abdomen; corkscrew on upper GI seriesUpper GI series if stable; laparotomy if not
Duodenal atresiaBilious vomiting from the first feeds, polyhydramnios, trisomy 21Double bubble, present from birth rather than abruptAbdominal film, then surgical bypass
IntussusceptionColicky pain, currant-jelly stool, right upper quadrant massAge 6 months to 3 years; target sign on ultrasoundAir-contrast enema
Milk protein-induced proctocolitisBlood-streaked stools at 2 to 8 weeksThe infant is well — thriving, undistended, normal vitalsMaternal dairy elimination or hydrolysed formula
Clostridioides difficile colitisDistension with watery, sometimes bloody stoolNeonates are colonised but lack the toxin receptorsNot a neonatal diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 7 day old term F with truncus arteriosus awaiting repair, temperature 35 C, lethargy, distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds, bilious nasogastric return and bright red blood per rectum → Necrotizing enterocolitis → Cyanotic heart disease is a term-infant risk factor — mesenteric hypoperfusion
  2. Distended, bloody-stooled neonate; the film finding that settles it → Pneumatosis intestinalis → Air within the bowel wall — specific for NEC; portal venous gas may accompany it
  3. Neonate with pneumatosis, distension and bloody stools, haemodynamically stable → Bowel rest, decompression and broad-spectrum antibiotics → Antibiotics immediately — septic shock is the lethal endpoint
  4. Neonate with NEC whose film now shows free air beneath the diaphragm → Laparotomy → Pneumoperitoneum means perforation
  5. 3 day old, well until now, abrupt bilious vomiting, abdominal pain and shock; film shows proximal gas and a gasless distal abdomen → Malrotation with midgut volvulus → Abrupt, previously well, and the mesenteric root twists around the superior mesenteric artery
  6. Stable infant with suspected malrotation; confirming the anatomy → Upper gastrointestinal contrast series → Outlines the duodenojejunal junction and any corkscrew
  7. Newborn with bilious emesis from the first feeds, polyhydramnios in utero, trisomy 21 features, no distal gas on film → Duodenal atresia → Present from birth rather than abrupt — failure of recanalisation
  8. 9 month old with intermittent colicky pain, currant-jelly stool and a right upper quadrant mass → Intussusception → Age 6 months to 3 years, target sign on ultrasound
  9. Thriving 5 week old, exclusively breast-fed, blood-streaked stools, no distension and normal vitals → Milk protein-induced proctocolitis → A well infant — the whole point is that nothing else is wrong
  10. Neonate with abdominal distension and bloody stools; which diagnosis should not be entertained → Clostridioides difficile colitis → Neonates are colonised but lack the toxin receptors
Exit ramps Free air — stop investigating and operate · Unstable with bilious vomiting — laparotomy without waiting for contrast · Term infant with NEC — look for the perfusion insult: cyanotic heart disease, hypotension, sepsis · Late NEC sequelae — strictures and short-bowel syndrome · Bilious emesis in a newborn is malrotation until an upper GI series says otherwise
Pearls Pneumatosis — gas made by bacteria that have invaded the wall, which is why it is specific · Bilious means the obstruction is distal to the ampulla, so it moves the level, not the urgency · NEC and volvulus both give a distended, bilious, unwell neonate; the gas pattern separates them · The well infant with blood in the stool is almost never surgical — distension and instability are what make it so · Prematurity is the commonest NEC risk factor, not a required one
Pairs with Part I Infant Stool Complaints: Dyschezia, FPIAP & Secondary Lactase Deficiency, which owns the well infant with blood in the stool; this brief owns the sick one. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia carries obstruction above the pylorus. Store the discriminator as a question: is the infant well, and what is the gas doing?
Transferable rule In a distended neonate the stool and the vital signs tell you how sick, but the gas pattern tells you which disease — air in the wall, air where bowel should be, or no air at all.
Unchecked attributeNEC filed under prematurity, so a term infant is ruled out without checking perfusion.
Salient decoyBilious nasogastric return pulls toward volvulus before the film is read.
Class-vs-memberRight category of neonatal bowel emergency, wrong member of it.

Occult GI Bleeding in a Child

Scope both ends, then think small bowel · UWorld · age decides the next study

Source vignette Pt — 10-year-old boy, 2 months of exertional fatigue and exercise intolerance; no melaena, hematochezia or abdominal pain; no medications · Exam — mucosal pallor, no lymphadenopathy, soft nontender abdomen, stool positive for occult blood · Labs — haemoglobin 9.4, MCV 74, platelets 380,000, leukocytes 7,500; ESR and coagulation normal; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies unremarkable · Q — which study most likely reveals the diagnosis; options spanned CT angiography, faecal calprotectin, faecal DNA, technetium 99m pertechnetate scan and tissue transglutaminase antibodies
The decision point

Iron deficiency anaemia with a positive occult blood test and no visible bleeding is occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Both ends have already been scoped and are clean, which moves the search to the small bowel — the segment neither scope reaches. In a child the commonest small-bowel bleeding lesion is a Meckel diverticulum, and the study that finds it is a technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, which images the ectopic gastric mucosa rather than the bleeding itself.

Age changes the answer at this exact fork. An adult with the same negative workup gets capsule endoscopy, because the adult small-bowel causes are angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers. Same algorithm, different branch.

Defining criteria Occult GI bleeding — positive faecal occult blood and/or iron deficiency anaemia without visible bleeding · First step regardless of age — upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Child, source not found — technetium 99m pertechnetate scan for Meckel · Adult, source not found — capsule endoscopy, then CT or MR enterography · Meckel — failed closure of the vitelline duct, with ectopic gastric mucosa that ulcerates adjacent bowel
Occult bleeding with clean scopes — what each study answersthe negative workup is the starting point
StudyWhat it detectsWho it is forWhy not here
Tc 99m pertechnetate scanEctopic gastric mucosaChild with small-bowel bleeding— (the answer)
Capsule endoscopyAngiodysplasia, neoplasia, ulcersAdult with small-bowel bleedingRight idea, wrong age branch
CT angiographyBrisk active bleedingHaemodynamic instability with visible bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to see
Faecal calprotectinIntestinal inflammationSuspected inflammatory bowel diseaseNo pain, diarrhoea or weight loss; scopes and biopsies clean
Tissue transglutaminaseCeliac diseaseMalabsorptive iron deficiencyCeliac does not cause occult blood
Faecal DNA testingColorectal neoplasiaAverage-risk adults over 45Not a paediatric test
Scenario bank
  1. 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, haemoglobin 9.4 with MCV 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel scan — it images ectopic gastric mucosa
  2. How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding → Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid → Ulcerating adjacent small bowel
  3. Child with iron deficiency anaemia and a positive faecal occult blood test; the first step → Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Localise before reaching for small-bowel studies
  4. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Capsule endoscopy → Angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers — the adult small-bowel causes
  5. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 → Meckel diverticulum → Failed closure of the vitelline duct
  6. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help → CT angiography → It needs brisk active bleeding to see anything
  7. Child with microcytic anaemia, chronic diarrhoea and a negative faecal occult blood test → Celiac disease → Malabsorption, not blood loss — the occult blood is negative
Gates Visible bleeding changes everything — hematemesis, melaena or hematochezia with instability goes to CT angiography, not a Meckel scan · Scope first — small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy · Meckel is classically under 2 but presents into adolescence, so age does not exclude it · Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden
Pearls The Meckel scan finds gastric mucosa, not blood — which is why it works on a lesion that is not actively bleeding · Occult means invisible, and invisible means too slow for angiography · Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT is the split · The small bowel is defined here by what the two scopes cannot reach · Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise
Pairs with Part I The Distended Newborn Abdomen, which owns the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Part I Microcytic Anemia: Iron First carries the iron-versus-thalassaemia fork that precedes this workup. Store the discriminator as a question: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
Transferable rule When an algorithm branches on age, the branch point is usually the question — the same negative workup sends a child and an adult to different tests.
Class-vs-memberRight idea of small-bowel imaging, wrong modality for the age.
Sequencing trapReaching for a small-bowel study before the two scopes are done.
Salient decoyMicrocytic anaemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT excludes.
3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Gastroenterology & Hepatology

The Sick Jaundiced Neonate with a Positive Screen

The screen names the panel, the presentation names the disease · handoff · conjugated, big liver, reducing sugar

Source vignette Pt — neonate after ten days of milk feeds, now febrile with hepatomegaly; newborn screen reported positive by telephone · Labs — conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; a non-glucose reducing substance in the urine · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned stopping lactose-containing feeds, continuing feeds pending confirmatory testing, and admission for intravenous antibiotics
The decision point

The phone call is the decoy and the urine is the decider. Every option is on the newborn screen, so a positive screen eliminates nothing. What separates them is that this infant has conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, a large liver, and a non-glucose reducing sugar in the urine after ten days of milk feeds. That triad is galactose-1-phosphate accumulating in a GALT-deficient liver: classic galactosemia.

The fever is not incidental. Galactosemia predisposes to Escherichia coli sepsis, and a febrile 10-day-old is septic until cultured — the sepsis workup runs in parallel with the metabolic answer, never after it.

Defining criteria Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia — direct bilirubin above 1.0 mg/dL ⚠, or above 20% of total; never physiologic and never breast-milk jaundice · Urine reducing substances — positive with dipstick glucose negative means a non-glucose reducing sugar, so galactose or fructose; requires recent intake of that sugar to be positive ⚠ · Classic galactosemia — galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency, confirmed by red cell GALT enzyme activity ⚠, which reads falsely normal after transfusion
The screen-positive neonate - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Classic galactosemiaAutosomal recessive GALT deficiency, symptoms within days of milk feedsConjugated jaundice with hepatomegaly and urine reducing substances in a milk-fed neonate
Hereditary fructose intoleranceAldolase B deficiency, identical hepatic picture with hypoglycemiaOnset with fruit, juice or sucrose at weaning, months old rather than days
Biliary atresia Can't missObstructive cholestasis, Kasai before about 60 daysDirect hyperbilirubinemia in a well infant with acholic stools, reducing substances negative
Maple syrup urine diseaseBranched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, day 4 to 7 ⚠Encephalopathy without hepatomegaly or cholestasis, sweet-smelling urine, ketosis
Cystic fibrosisScreened by immunoreactive trypsinogenMeconium ileus or quiet cholestasis, not fever with vomiting and urinary sugar
Sickle cell or neonatal hyperthyroidismScreen-positive with no hepatic pictureNo cholestasis, no hepatomegaly, no urinary sugar; sickle is silent at 10 days because of HbF
Glycogen storage disease type IHepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hypertriglyceridemiaHypoglycemia within hours of fasting; no galactose trigger, no cataracts
Scenario bank
  1. 3-day-old, asymptomatic, breastfeeding well, newborn screen positive for galactosemia → Stop breastfeeding and start soy-based formula pending confirmation → presumptive galactosemia
  2. 8-day-old with jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting after breastfeeds and positive urine reducing substances → Stop breast milk and start soy-based formula → classic galactosemia
  3. 12-day-old with galactosemia on soy formula, temperature 38.8 C, lethargic → Blood, urine and CSF cultures, then IV ampicillin and gentamicin → Escherichia coli sepsis; every febrile neonate gets a lumbar puncture
  4. 10-day-old with jaundice, hepatomegaly, positive urine reducing substances and a newborn screen positive for galactosemia → Red cell GALT enzyme activity → classic galactosemia
  5. 3-week-old with galactosemia and bilateral cataracts on examination → Galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase → osmotic lens injury
  6. 6-week-old, well and growing, bilateral cataracts only, no hepatomegaly, positive urine reducing substances → Galactokinase deficiency → lactose-free diet
  7. 9-month-old with vomiting, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly and jaundice since juice and fruit were introduced, positive urine reducing substances → Hereditary fructose intolerance → remove fructose, sucrose and sorbitol
  8. 4-week-old, well and feeding well, direct bilirubin 5, acholic stools, urine reducing substances negative → Abdominal ultrasound and HIDA scan → biliary atresia, with Kasai before about 60 days
  9. 5-day-old with poor feeding, lethargy, seizures and urine that smells like maple syrup, newborn screen positive → Protein-free feeds with intravenous dextrose → maple syrup urine disease
  10. 2-week-old with confirmed galactosemia whose parents ask what to feed → Breast milk → soy-based formula is the substitute
  11. 3-month-old with massive hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycemia after a 4-hour fast, lactic acidosis, hypertriglyceridemia, doll-like facies → Glycogen storage disease type I → frequent cornstarch feeds
  12. 10-day-old with vomiting after starting formula, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, urine positive for reducing substances → Classic galactosemia → eliminate galactose and lactose from diet
Exam vs clinic ledger The exam keys 60 days as the Kasai window, and that is the number to pick. The evidence underneath it is not a cliff — native-liver survival falls continuously with age at operation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found operating at 30 days or earlier still beat 31–60 days. Read 60 days as the keyed threshold, not as a deadline with room to spare.
Two things happen at once Stop all lactose and galactose immediately — breast milk and standard formula give way to soy-based formula — without waiting for confirmation, because the injury is ongoing. In parallel, send blood and urine cultures and start empiric neonatal antibiotics ⚠ for Escherichia coli. Confirm afterwards with red cell GALT activity. A negative urine reducing substance test in an infant who has stopped feeding excludes nothing ⚠, because the test needs recent galactose intake.
Pearls Classic galactosemia is GALT deficiency affecting liver, kidney, brain and lens with a predisposition to Escherichia coli sepsis; galactokinase deficiency gives cataracts alone · Reducing substances positive with dipstick glucose negative means galactose or fructose, because glucose is itself a reducing sugar, so read both tests · Cataracts in both galactose disorders come from galactitol via aldose reductase, the same enzyme that makes sorbitol in the diabetic lens · Hereditary fructose intolerance is the diet-shifted twin with the same hepatic picture plus hypoglycemia, appearing at weaning · Direct hyperbilirubinemia in a well infant with acholic stools is biliary atresia, and the Kasai clock runs to about 60 days ⚠ · Girls with treated galactosemia still develop premature ovarian insufficiency ⚠, because the diet does not prevent it
Pairs with Part I Cholestasis & the LFT Patterns owns the adult conjugated-versus-unconjugated framework; this brief owns its neonatal form. Candidate twins — confirm: hereditary fructose intolerance, with the discriminator stored as a question: when did symptoms start relative to fruit or sucrose? And biliary atresia — is the infant sick or well, and are reducing substances present? Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the other positive newborn screen that turns on a direction: there the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect, here the enzyme and the organism do.
Transferable rule A positive newborn screen never names the disease because every option is on the panel, so the bilirubin fraction, the liver and the urine do the naming, and a febrile neonate is cultured and treated for sepsis in parallel with the metabolic answer rather than after it.
Class-vs-memberMaple syrup urine disease is the right class of screen-flagged inborn error but has no hepatomegaly and carries ketoacids rather than a reducing sugar.
Salient decoyThe positive screen sells cystic fibrosis, whose neonatal face is meconium ileus rather than fever with urinary sugar.
True-fact-wrong-slotSickle cell causes jaundice, but unconjugated and not at 10 days, because fetal hemoglobin protects the neonate.

Fecal Impaction & Overflow Diarrhea

The rectal exam is the diagnosis

Source vignette Pt — 77 yo F, 5 days without a bowel movement, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, empty rectal vault, prior laparotomy · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned adhesive small bowel obstruction, fecal impaction and sigmoid volvulus
The decision point

"Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault." That finding is the diagnosis — and it is incompatible with the usual competing answer: adhesive small bowel obstruction gives an empty rectum, a distended abdomen, and high-pitched or absent bowel sounds.

The detail that invites over-reading: last bowel movement 5 days ago, "characterized by loose stool." Constipation with loose stool feels contradictory — it's overflow diarrhea, liquid tracking around a hard impaction, and it's near-pathognomonic.

Stem findings → options ruled out
OptionThe sentence that kills it
AdhesionsFirm stool in the rectal vault (SBO empties the rectum); soft, undistended abdomen
Colon cancer"Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities"
DiverticulitisNo fever; diffuse, not focal LLQ, tenderness
Ischemic bowelNo hematochezia; no AF or atherosclerotic risk factors
VolvulusSoft abdomen without distension; no coffee-bean film
Two details most people skip Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic — it slows colonic transit and is the cause here, which is why the objective says "treatment of underlying causes." And "warm, dry skin" is the anticholinergic sign planted alongside the drug. Constipating culprits: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs, antihistamines, antipsychotics), opioids, verapamil, iron, calcium, aluminum antacids, ondansetron.
Management ladder — fecal impaction
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Enema (in-context: first-line)Fails to clear
2Manual disimpactionEnema unsuccessful
3Treat the cause — stop or reduce the oxybutynin; then maintenance PEG, fluids, mobilityAlways, after clearing
Scenario bank
  1. 77 yo F, 5 days without a BM, empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy → Adhesive small bowel obstruction → NG decompression + imaging
  2. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign → Sigmoid volvulus → endoscopic decompression
  3. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness → Diverticulitis → CT
  4. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia → Ischemic colitis
  5. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy → Colon cancer → colonoscopy
  6. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated → Stop the oxybutynin, start PEG
  7. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault → Disimpaction + methylnaltrexone or naloxegol
Where the rule breaks Impaction can sit distal to a second pathology — a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. What licenses stopping at impaction here is the normal colonoscopy 3 years ago plus absent weight loss and anemia. Change any of those and you relieve the impaction and investigate.
Pairs with Part I Constipation in a Child is the paediatric mirror — there the rectal vault is empty and an anal fissure closes the rectal route that is first-line here.
Transferable rule A switch requires new incompatibility, not new plausibility. Before changing an answer, ask whether the detail makes your current choice impossible — and check whether the stem contains an assassin for the option you're moving toward. Here it did, one sentence away from the finding already in hand.
Salient decoy

Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia

Choking on the first feed · UWorld · pass a tube before you order a picture

Source vignette Pt — 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned nasogastric tube placement, lateral neck radiography and echocardiography
The decision point

Formula mixed with saliva is the diagnosis. Milk that returns mixed with pooled secretions never reached a stomach — it filled a blind proximal pouch and overflowed. Add choking on the very first feed and coarse lungs from aspiration, and this is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

The question is then not what but what first, and the answer is the cheapest thing at the bedside: pass a nasogastric tube. It meets resistance at the pouch, and the film shows it coiled. The murmur, the maternal drug history and the absent prenatal care are all planted to sell an imaging or pharmacologic answer instead.

Defining criteria Type C — proximal pouch with a distal fistula, about 85% of cases (clinic ledger) · Gas in the abdomen — a distal fistula is present · Gasless abdomen — pure atresia with no distal fistula · H-type — no atresia, presenting months later with recurrent pneumonia
Neonatal choking and vomiting — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
EA with distal TEFChoking on the first feed, copious frothy secretions, polyhydramnios in uteroFormula mixed with saliva; tube will not pass
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaSevere distress at deliveryScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, shifted heart sounds
Congenital heart diseaseFeeding difficulty with cyanosisCyanosis and diaphoresis with feeds, no excess secretions
EpiglottitisFebrile stridor with droolingSchool-aged child, never a newborn
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisNonbilious projectile vomitingAge 3 to 6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, olive mass
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiencyGround-glass with air bronchograms, low lung volumes
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid useOnset at or beyond 24 hours, hypertonia and irritability
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border → Nasogastric tube placement → Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
  2. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance → Chest x-ray with the tube in place → A coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula
  3. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless → Esophageal atresia without a fistula → No tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach
  4. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram
  5. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair; evaluation for associated anomalies → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasound → VACTERL association
  6. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate → IV fluids and electrolyte repletion → Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects
  7. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas → Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids → Duodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram
  8. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes → Respiratory distress syndrome → CPAP, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises
  9. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone → Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in → Neonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails
  10. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair → NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suction → Keeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula
The newborn clock Age at presentation is a diagnostic instrument. Minutes to hours: TEF/EA, choanal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, Potter sequence. Beyond 24 hours: neonatal abstinence, sepsis, ductal-dependent lesions as the PDA closes, bilious vomiting and malrotation. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Months: H-type fistula, laryngomalacia. Every wrong option in this stem is a real disease placed at the wrong point on that clock.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · Diagnosis is made by the tube, not the scanner — resistance at roughly 9 to 11 cm (clinic ledger), confirmed on film · The abdominal gas pattern names the anatomic type before any endoscopy · VACTERL screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal ultrasound at minimum · A soft systolic murmur on day one is usually a closing ductus, not structural disease
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence is the mechanistic twin: amniotic fluid volume reads out fetal function in opposite directions. Cannot make urine gives oligohydramnios and Potter sequence; cannot swallow gives polyhydramnios and foregut or duodenal atresia. Store it as a question: which way did the fluid go? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn owns the trigger axis — cyanosis worse with feeding and better with crying is choanal atresia, not a fistula. Part I Multiple Anomalies in a Newborn holds VACTERL beside the syndromes it is mistaken for, and names what excludes each.
Transferable rule When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, the first question is anatomic, and the cheapest test of anatomy — does a tube reach the stomach? — comes before any picture or drug. The picture only confirms what the tube found, and every other option is a real disease placed at the wrong hour on the newborn clock.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated — for VACTERL, after the diagnosis, not before it.
True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours.
True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix.
Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.

Renal & Genitourinary 12 topics + 4 board-style

Two recurring lessons: normal values are eliminations, and a single discordant test component never overturns a convergent picture.

Pyelonephritis: Route & Disposition

The diagnosis is given; the question is where and how

The decision point

Fever + chills + dysuria + CVA tenderness hands you pyelonephritis. The real question is route and setting, and one line usually decides it: "only clear fluids for 2 days" means the patient cannot tolerate oral therapy.

Criteria for admission / IV therapy
  • Unable to tolerate oral intake
  • Hemodynamic instability or sepsis
  • Complicated anatomy: male sex, obstruction, stones, catheter, pregnancy
  • Failure of outpatient therapy, immunocompromise, extremes of age
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with fever and CVA tenderness, tolerating oral intake, no comorbidity → Outpatient oral therapy
  2. 28 yo F with pyelonephritis who is vomiting and cannot keep fluids down → Admit for IV antibiotics
  3. 28 yo F at 24 weeks of pregnancy with pyelonephritis → Admit for intravenous antibiotics — pregnancy alone warrants admission
  4. 28 yo F with dysuria and frequency, no fever and no CVA tenderness → Treat as cystitis with nitrofurantoin → nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis
  5. 28 yo F on appropriate antibiotics still febrile at 72 hours → CT for abscess or obstruction
  6. 28 yo F with pyelonephritis and a known resistant organism → Admit for IV therapy
  7. 9 mo F with fever to 39 C, fussiness and poor feeding; urinalysis shows positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase → Cefixime → a third-generation cephalosporin covers the gram-negative uropathogens
  8. Why trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and amoxicillin-clavulanate are no longer recommended as empiric therapy for paediatric urinary tract infection → Rising Escherichia coli resistance → local resistance patterns drive the empiric choice
  9. 9 mo F with a first febrile urinary tract infection, well-appearing and tolerating oral intake → Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolone cartilage toxicity restricts use to Pseudomonas
Two reading skills this stem teaches "Long-standing hypertension + BP 104/68" is NBME writing hypotensive without saying it — vitals must be read against the patient's baseline · a benign abdominal exam means no CT: imaging in pyelonephritis is reserved for failure to improve at 48–72 hours, suspected obstruction or stone, recurrence, or concern for emphysematous pyelonephritis in a diabetic.
Pairs with Part I Vesicoureteral Reflux owns what happens after the febrile UTI is treated and the imaging comes back. Part I Recurrent Urinary Infection in a Child owns the afebrile recurrences that never reach the kidney.
Transferable rule When the clinical diagnosis is sufficient and the patient is infected, treat — don't image. Uncomplicated version (healthy young woman tolerating PO, stable) → outpatient oral therapy.

BPH & Acute Urinary Retention

Reading a three-act chronology

The decision point

"Underlying cause" questions want the trunk of the causal tree, not a branch. Six months of hesitancy and dribbling → five days of frequency and incomplete emptying → one day of anuria with suprapubic pain. The retention, the UTI, and the creatinine of 3.4 all flow from prostatic obstruction.

Why 1+ blood means nothing Trace-to-1+ hematuria is expected with UTI, with bladder distension, and with BPH itself. Nephrolithiasis needs the pain syndrome — colicky flank pain radiating to the groin — and doesn't explain six months of hesitancy. A single nonspecific dipstick finding cannot outvote a six-month narrative.
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo M with 6 months of hesitancy, now anuric for a day with suprapubic fullness → Acute urinary retention from BPH → catheterize
  2. 72 yo M in retention; the question asks the underlying cause → Benign prostatic hyperplasia
  3. 72 yo M after catheter relief; first-line medical therapy → Alpha-blocker
  4. 72 yo M with a very large prostate seeking long-term volume reduction → Add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor
  5. 72 yo M with BPH started on oxybutynin for urgency, now in retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  6. 72 yo M in retention with a hard nodular prostate and PSA 40 → Prostate cancer → biopsy
The management sequel Acute retention → bladder catheterization first (suprapubic if the urethra is impassable) → treat the UTI → watch for post-obstructive diuresis → expect the creatinine to fall, proving the AKI was post-renal. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if confirmation is needed. Long-term: tamsulosin ± finasteride; TURP if refractory.
Transferable rule A single lab value should flip your answer only if it is incompatible with your diagnosis — not merely compatible with another one.
Treat-the-number

Diabetic Nephropathy Screening

Detection threshold, not accuracy

The decision point

"Most sensitive" asks for the lowest detection threshold. UACR detects 30–300 mg/g — the reversible window. Dipstick needs ~≥300 mg/day and is concentration-dependent. And early nephropathy causes hyperfiltration, so creatinine can be normal or low while glomeruli are being destroyed.

Defining criteria UACR window — detects 30–300 mg/g, the reversible stage · Dipstick threshold — ~≥300 mg/day, concentration-dependent · Early disease — hyperfiltration; creatinine normal or low while glomeruli are lost
Albuminuria screening schedule
PopulationStartFrequency
Type 2 diabetesAt diagnosis — silent hyperglycemia predates diagnosis by yearsAnnually
Type 1 diabetes5 years after diagnosisAnnually
Hypertension, CKD, SLE, sickle cell, HIV, nephrotoxic drugsAt diagnosisAnnually or by risk
Healthy asymptomatic adultDo not screen — USPSTF insufficient evidence—
Question verb → answer selected
Question asks…Answer
Most sensitive / screeningSpot urine albumin/creatinine ratio
Confirm an abnormal screen2 of 3 abnormal over 3–6 months — excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, CHF, hyperglycemia
Quantify total protein (non-albumin suspected)UPCR or 24-hour protein — dipstick and UACR miss light chains (myeloma: dipstick negative, SSA positive, UPEP shows M-spike)
Most accurate GFRMeasured clearance; cystatin C when creatinine is unreliable (amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders, cirrhosis)
Definitive / most accurate for causeRenal biopsy — but only when features are atypical
Most likely to slow progressionACE-I or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor (never ACE-I with ARB)
Scenario bank
  1. 56 yo M with type 2 diabetes diagnosed today; when does nephropathy screening start → At diagnosis
  2. 24 yo F with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16; when does screening start → 5 Years after diagnosis
  3. 56 yo M with type 2 diabetes; the most sensitive screening test → Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
  4. 56 yo M with a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio → Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio → confirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal over 3–6 months
  5. 56 yo M with confirmed albuminuria; what slows progression most → ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
  6. 56 yo M; the most accurate measurement of GFR → Inulin or iothalamate clearance
Biopsy triggers — "this isn't ordinary diabetic nephropathy" Absence of retinopathy · active sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts) · rapid GFR decline · nephrotic-range proteinuria too early · diabetes duration too short.
Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing "Microalbuminuria" → "UACR 85 mg/g" · "hyperfiltration" → "creatinine 0.7" in a diabetic · "Kimmelstiel-Wilson" → "nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy" · "transient albuminuria" → "he ran a 10K yesterday."
Transferable rule "Most sensitive" = lowest detection threshold. "Most specific / confirmatory" = hardest to fool. Normal creatinine never excludes early diabetic kidney disease.
Test-overrides-findings

Hematuria

Glomerular vs. non-glomerular

The decision point

When the urinalysis contains dysuria + leukocyte esterase + pyuria, hematuria is a feature of cystitis, not a separate finding requiring parallel workup. Treat the infection, then repeat the UA after antibiotics. If the blood doesn't clear, that's when imaging enters.

Nitrite is only ~50% sensitive It requires a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus, and Pseudomonas don't) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes UTI when LE, pyuria, and symptoms agree.
Glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria
GlomerularNon-glomerular
ColorBrown / tea / colaBright red, clots
SedimentRBC casts, dysmorphic RBCsNormal RBC morphology
ProteinPresentAbsent
CausesIgA nephropathy, PSGN, Alport, thin basement membrane, lupusUTI, stones, trauma, tumor, hypercalciuria, sickle trait, exercise
Scenario bank
  1. Hematuria 1–2 days after a URI, recurrent → IgA nephropathy → synpharyngitic, within 1 to 2 days of the sore throat
  2. Tea-colored urine + RBC casts + proteinuria + HTN, 2 weeks after sore throat → Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis → low C3, positive ASO
  3. Painless gross hematuria in an older smoker → Cystoscopy + CT urography
  4. Hematuria + sensorineural hearing loss + family history of renal failure → Alport syndrome → a type IV collagen defect
  5. Isolated microscopic hematuria in a well child, normal BP, no protein → Urine calcium/creatinine ratio (hypercalciuria is the most common cause)
  6. Sterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active teen → Chlamydia/gonorrhea NAAT (also: renal TB, interstitial nephritis, partially treated UTI, appendicitis)
  7. On cyclophosphamide → Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein → mesna + hydration; post-transplant → BK or adenovirus
Pairs with Part I Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child — the other half of this fork: protein without blood, and the one where a normotensive 3-year-old with periorbital edema is treated on presentation rather than biopsied. Store the discriminator as a question: is the urine showing red cells and casts, or protein alone?
Transferable rule When a stem gives a full lab panel, the diagnosis is in the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value. A discordant component is a sensitivity problem, not a veto.
Test-overrides-findings

Acute Scrotum & Scrotal Mass

Two separate trees, split by pain

The decision point

Timeline + location + infection signs. Torsion is sudden and maximal within minutes-to-hours; a 3-day escalating course with fever and dysuria and posterior tenderness is epididymitis — a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound and urology are torsion answers transplanted onto an epididymitis stem.

The acute scrotum — the differential
ConditionOnsetThe tellCremastericNext step
Testicular torsion EmergencySudden, minutesHigh-riding transverse testis, N/V, no feverAbsentEmergent urology — salvage window ~6 h
EpididymitisGradual, daysPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever; Prehn sign +IntactAntibiotics (clinical dx) + NAAT + UA
OrchitisDaysMumps history, unvaccinatedIntactSupportive
Torsion of appendix testisGradual, prepubertalBlue dot sign, superior poleIntactSupportive
Fournier gangrene EmergencyHoursToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic—Emergent debridement
Scrotal mass (painless tree)
FindingDiagnosis
Bag of worms, ↑ standing/Valsalva, ↓ supineVaricocele — ~90% left-sided (left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle)
Right-sided, sudden onset, or fails to decompress supineRetroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal imaging
Transilluminates, uniform, testis palpable withinHydrocele
Enlarges with Valsalva, reducible, doesn't transilluminateInguinal hernia
Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis, no transilluminationTumor → ultrasound + AFP/β-hCG/LDH → inguinal orchiectomy, never transscrotal biopsy
Testicular mass with gynecomastia, ↓ libido, or precocious puberty in a boy; markers normalLeydig cell tumor — a sex cord–stromal tumor secreting testosterone or estrogen. Reinke crystals on histology. Mostly benign; the hormonal syndrome is the tell, and AFP/β-hCG are negative
Testicular mass, heterogeneous with calcification and cystic areas on ultrasound; AFP and/or β-hCG elevatedTeratoma (nonseminomatous). In adults, malignant regardless of maturity; in prepubertal boys, benign — the one tumor whose behavior flips with age. Chemoresistant → resect residual masses after chemotherapy
Marker logic ties the mass table together AFP elevated → never a seminoma (yolk sac or embryonal/teratoma component) · β-hCG can rise in seminoma and nonseminoma — only AFP is exclusionary · both markers normal with a solid mass → pure seminoma or a sex cord–stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli), and the presence of a hormonal syndrome separates them · LDH tracks tumor burden, not histology · Sertoli cell tumor is the mirror twin of Leydig — also stromal, also usually benign, but typically hormonally silent.
Pearls Epididymitis treatment splits by age: <35 / sexually active → ceftriaxone + doxycycline; >35 / low STI risk → levofloxacin or TMP-SMX · varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility; testicular size discrepancy in an adolescent is the surgical indication · seminoma never makes AFP.
The two hard pairs
  • Varicocele vs. indirect inguinal hernia — both non-transilluminating, both enlarge with Valsalva. Separators: a hernia is reducible, feels like soft tissue or bowel, and you cannot palpate above it (it descends through the canal). A varicocele feels like worms, isn't reducible, and is confined to the scrotum.
  • Varicocele vs. spermatocele — both sit above and separate from the testis. Separators: the spermatocele transilluminates and does not change with position or Valsalva.
  • Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament in the upper thigh, in older women, and anatomically cannot reach the scrotum — high incarceration risk.
Varicocele mechanism ~90% left-sided: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle (± "nutcracker" compression between aorta and SMA), while the right drains obliquely into the IVC · subfertility comes from increased scrotal temperature impairing spermatogenesis; may cause ipsilateral atrophy · treatment: observation if asymptomatic → gonadal vein ligation or embolization for pain, >20% testicular volume discrepancy in adolescents, or abnormal semen analysis; scrotal support and NSAIDs for older men not seeking fertility. · A varicocele in a prepubertal child, right-sided, or persistent when supine is secondary until proven otherwise; in children think Wilms (with hypertension from renin secretion), in adults think RCC invading the renal vein
Scenario bank
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → Retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal CT
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → Hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → Indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → Ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal — it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → Spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → Refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → Femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → Testicular torsion → emergent surgery
  9. 4 yo M, painless soft scrotal mass superior to the right testicle that does not decompress supine, blood pressure 160/96 → Secondary varicocele from an abdominal mass → abdominal ultrasonography
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline in a scrotal pain stem is not laziness — that number is the torsion exclusion; confirmed-enough clinical infection → treat, don't image. And read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem: all anatomic processes → the question wants mechanism; all tests → next step in diagnosis; all drugs → treatment. The choice format tells you what kind of thinking is being graded.

Hypercalcemia Workup

PTH first, always

The decision point

Calcium high + phosphorus low = PTH-driven until proven otherwise. The first step in any confirmed hypercalcemia is PTH, because it splits the entire differential before anything else gets ordered.

  • PTH high or inappropriately normal → primary hyperparathyroidism (most likely) or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (separate with urine calcium)
  • PTH suppressed → then hunt: malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets), vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease, milk-alkali, thiazides, hyperthyroidism, immobilization
The Ca–Phos decoder ring Ca↑ / Phos↓ = PTH or PTHrP · Ca↑ / Phos↑ = vitamin D–mediated · Ca↓ / Phos↑ = renal failure or hypoparathyroidism · Ca↓ / Phos↓ = vitamin D deficiency. Symptoms: "stones, bones, groans, thrones, psychiatric overtones" — and polyuria with a dilute urine is hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and phosphorus 2.1, found incidentally → Check PTH first
  2. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and an elevated PTH → Primary hyperparathyroidism
  3. 58 yo F with calcium 13.4, suppressed PTH and weight loss → Malignancy → PTHrP and imaging
  4. 24 yo M with lifelong mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH and a urine calcium-creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01 → Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia → no surgery
  5. 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy → Granulomatous disease
  6. 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration → Isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
Normal labs that assassinate distractors A normal albumin means the calcium is truly elevated (no correction needed) · a specific gravity of 1.005 kills diabetes mellitus, because glucosuria drags SG up · low phosphorus argues against vitamin D excess, which raises both · enalapril rather than a thiazide removes the drug confounder deliberately.
Pairs with Part I Polyuria: Water or Solute owns the polyuria hypercalcaemia causes — an acquired, reversible resistance to vasopressin at the collecting duct, which corrects when the calcium does. Store the discriminator as a question: does the kidney concentrate after desmopressin?

Vesicoureteral Reflux

the grade decides both the treatment and the ending · board question · Did the VCUG show ureteral filling only, or dilation with blunted calices?

Source vignette Pt — 6 mo old after a first febrile urinary tract infection, left untreated · Imaging — voiding cystourethrogram shows ureteral dilation with blunted calices · Q — the expected long-term consequence; options spanned focal interstitial fibrosis from recurrent parenchymal infection, glomerular inflammation and acquired renal cysts
The decision point

The whole question is one phrase on the VCUG: dilation and blunting of the renal calices. Reflux that reaches only the ureter is mild and usually disappears on its own as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growth; reflux that has already deformed the calices is severe, and severe reflux untreated means recurrent febrile UTIs, bacteria in the parenchyma, an inflammatory response, ischemia, and focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis — renal scarring. Enough of it becomes chronic kidney disease, which in a child announces itself as secondary hypertension, proteinuria, and failure to thrive.

Defining criteria Vesicoureteral reflux — retrograde urine flow through a congenitally short intravesical ureter · Mild (grade I–II) — reflux into the ureter, with or without the kidney, and no renal damage · Severe (grade III–IV) — reflux into ureter and kidney with renal damage: dilated ureter, blunting of the calices, papillary damage · How each study contributes — ultrasound shows the hydronephrosis; the VCUG shows ureteral filling with or without a dilated collecting system, and is what assigns the grade
Pertinent positives & negatives Blunting of the renal calices — renal damage is already present; this single finding moves him from the resolving group to the scarring group · Dilation of the ureter and collecting system — grade III–IV territory, not I–II · First febrile UTI at 6 months — the presentation that earns imaging in the first place · Normal vital signs and examination — no hypertension, proteinuria or growth failure yet; the question asks about a trajectory, not today · "Mild" hydronephrosis — that adjective belongs to the ultrasound's degree of dilation, not to the reflux grade, which only the VCUG assigns
Classify first — vesicoureteral reflux
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence
Grade"dilation and blunting of the renal calices"Severe → prophylaxis ± surgery; observation alone is not an option
Primary vs. secondaryNo outlet obstruction, weak stream or neurogenic bladder describedPrimary reflux through a short intravesical ureter
Bladder and bowel functionNot yet applicable at 6 months ⚠︎In a toilet-trained child, screening and treating bladder–bowel dysfunction is part of management at every grade
Tier fingerprint done — the UTI has been treated, the ultrasound and the VCUG are both back, so no further-imaging option survives · normal — examination and vital signs, which is why nothing needs treating today · at stake — the grade, which is the only variable that changes the plan.
Management ladder — vesicoureteral reflux
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild (I–II)Observation, with or without prophylactic antibiotics; expect spontaneous resolution as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growthA breakthrough febrile UTI, or new renal damage on follow-up imaging
Severe (III–IV)Prophylactic antibiotics, with surgery as the next option; screen and treat bladder–bowel dysfunctionBreakthrough febrile UTIs despite prophylaxis, or progressive scarring → surgical correction ⚠︎
Established scarringLong-term surveillance of blood pressure, urinalysis for proteinuria, and growth ⚠︎Hypertension, proteinuria or declining function → chronic kidney disease care
Numbers that gate & exit ramps none are numeric here — the gate is categorical, mild versus severe, and it is read off the VCUG rather than calculated. · a boy with hydronephrosis and a weak urinary stream → outlet obstruction causing secondary reflux, a different pathway · urinary stasis → calcium stones · UTIs with urease-producing organisms → struvite stones.
Decision spine Was there a febrile UTI? — Yes → this is why imaging exists · What did the ultrasound do? — Found hydronephrosis — it detects, it does not grade · What did the VCUG show? — Ureter and calices, with blunting → severe · What does severe mean? — Recurrent infection and scarring, not spontaneous resolution · What is a scar, histologically? — Focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis — tubulointerstitial, not glomerular
Scenario bank
  1. 6-month-old after a first febrile UTI, VCUG shows ureteral dilation with blunted calices, left untreated → Focal interstitial fibrosis from recurrent parenchymal infection → Renal scarring progressing to chronic kidney disease
  2. 6-month-old, first febrile UTI, VCUG shows a dilated ureter with blunting of the calices → Prophylactic antibiotics → Severe reflux, with surgery as the next option
  3. 2-year-old, first febrile UTI, normal renal ultrasound, VCUG shows reflux into the ureter only → Observation with follow-up, expecting spontaneous resolution → Mild reflux
  4. 3-year-old on prophylaxis for grade IV reflux, now with a second breakthrough febrile UTI → Surgical correction of the reflux → Prophylaxis has failed
  5. 8-month-old boy with grade IV reflux, a weak urinary stream and a palpable bladder → Evaluate for bladder outlet obstruction → Secondary reflux behind posterior urethral valves
  6. 5-year-old with vesicoureteral reflux, chronic constipation and daytime wetting → Treat the bladder and bowel dysfunction → It is part of reflux management at every grade
  7. Child with severe reflux and established renal scarring; what to monitor long-term → Blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria → Together with growth
  8. 8-year-old with recurrent febrile UTIs since infancy, hypertension, proteinuria, poor growth and small scarred kidneys → Reflux nephropathy with chronic kidney disease → The endpoint prophylaxis prevents
  9. Why mild vesicoureteral reflux resolves without any intervention → The intravesical ureter lengthens as the child grows → Anatomy corrects itself
  10. Child with reflux and recurrent Proteus infections, now with a staghorn calculus → A struvite stone from urease-producing bacteria → Stasis alone would give calcium stones
Decoy note Two details make "no complications" feel safe: the mother reports no recurrence, and the examination is normal — both true, and both irrelevant to a question that says if untreated. The sharper decoy is the word mild, which the stem attaches to the hydronephrosis on ultrasound; a reader who carries that adjective across to the reflux answers a different patient's question. The grade lives on the VCUG, one sentence later.
Pearls Blunted calices mean severe reflux: recurrent infection scars the interstitium in wedges, and widespread scarring is chronic kidney disease. · Ultrasound finds the hydronephrosis; the VCUG assigns the grade — and only the grade predicts the ending. · Reflux scarring is tubulointerstitial: bacteria in the parenchyma → inflammation → ischemia → wedge-shaped fibrosis, with the glomeruli lost secondarily. · Widespread scarring shows up in a child as secondary hypertension, proteinuria, and failure to thrive — the pediatric face of chronic kidney disease. · Mild reflux resolves because the intravesical ureter lengthens as the child grows; the anatomy that caused it outgrows itself. · Reflux makes calcium stones through stasis and struvite stones through urease-producing organisms — never uric acid stones. · Bladder–bowel dysfunction is screened and treated alongside reflux at every grade; constipation is a modifiable part of the problem, not a coincidence.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence is the obstructive twin — the same VCUG, the same hydronephrosis, but reflux that is secondary to outlet obstruction rather than a short intravesical ureter. Store the discriminator as a question: is there a weak stream or a palpable bladder, and is the reflux the disease or its consequence? Candidate twin — confirm: a brief on the first febrile UTI in an infant and when to image does not exist yet; this brief begins after that decision has been made. Part I Recurrent Urinary Infection in a Child owns the lower-tract arm of the same complaint, where constipation rather than reflux is the risk factor.
Transferable rule When a question asks what happens if untreated, it is asking for the trajectory of the severity you were handed, not the disease's average — locate the grading finding before you pick a prognosis, and never let a severity adjective migrate from one study to another.
True-fact-wrong-slotInflammation of the renal glomerulus — That follows group A streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection; reflux injures the tubulointerstitium, and the glomerulus is a bystander
True-fact-wrong-slotDevelopment of renal cysts — Acquired cystic disease is a phenomenon of children on dialysis, not of reflux
Class-vs-memberObstruction from uric acid stones — The stones of reflux are calcium (stasis) and struvite (urease-producing organisms); uric acid stones come from overproduction, as in tumor lysis
Unchecked attributeNo long-term complications — That is the prognosis for mild reflux; the blunted calices already placed him in the severe group

Recurrent Urinary Infection in a Child

assign the tract, then name the risk factor · board question · Is this infection febrile or afebrile, and does the bladder empty?

Source vignette Pt — 4 yo F, third afebrile cystitis this year, functional constipation since starting day care, suprapubic tenderness and hard stool in the rectal vault · Q — the most likely explanation; options spanned urinary stasis, vesicoureteral reflux and inadequate treatment of the prior infection
The decision point

The stem is a lower-tract infection and says so four times: no fever, no vomiting, suprapubic tenderness, no back pain. That single classification does most of the elimination, because the anatomic causes of recurrent paediatric urinary infection — reflux above all — produce recurrent pyelonephritis rather than recurrent cystitis. What is left is a mechanical question about emptying, and the stem answers it explicitly: hard stool in the rectal vault in a child with functional constipation since day care. A chronically loaded rectum dilates, and the dilated rectum compresses the bladder and urethra so the bladder never empties; the residual urine is the culture medium, and E. coli ascends from the perineum into it. The management corollary is the part worth storing — treating the cystitis without treating the constipation guarantees a fourth episode, so long-term laxative therapy is part of the prescription.

Defining criteria Lower tract, cystitis — dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, afebrile, without flank or back pain · Upper tract, pyelonephritis — fever, flank or back pain, vomiting and an ill appearance; this is the pattern vesicoureteral reflux produces · Adequate therapy for a paediatric lower-tract infection — a short course, such as the 3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole given here · The interval that separates relapse from reinfection — a 6-week gap with symptom-free time between makes inadequate treatment of the prior episode unlikely
Pertinent positives & negatives Afebrile with suprapubic tenderness and no back pain — lower tract, and this is the sentence that kills the reflux option · Functional constipation dating to day-care entry — the stressor-driven withholding trigger, and the mechanism of the whole illness · Hard stool in the rectal vault with normal tone — a loaded, dilated rectum, while normal tone simultaneously argues against a neurologic cause and against anal trauma · Anal fissures at 12 and 2 o'clock — a complication of chronic constipation rather than evidence of injury; their position and the constipation history are the point · Normal genitalia — no injury, and combined with the fissures' explanation this is what makes abuse unlikely rather than merely unmentioned · Three cystitis episodes in a year, none febrile — recurrence confined to one tract; a reflux child would have had at least one febrile episode by now · Six weeks since a completed adequate course — an interval rather than a treatment failure · Otherwise unremarkable medical history — no other sites and no severe infections, so primary immunodeficiency has no foothold
Recurrent urinary infection in a child — the risk factors
Risk factorIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Urinary stasis from constipationA loaded rectum dilates, compresses bladder and urethra, prevents complete voiding, and the residual urine is colonised by ascending E. coliRecurrent afebrile cystitis in a constipated child, with hard stool in the vault and anal fissures— (the answer)
Vesicoureteral refluxA short intravesical ureter lets bladder urine reflux upward and seed the kidneyRecurrent febrile infection or pyelonephritis in an infant, hydronephrosis on ultrasound leading to a VCUGAfebrile, suprapubic, no flank pain — the wrong tract
Obstructive uropathy, posterior urethral valvesOutlet obstruction in a boy, with incomplete emptying at high pressuresMale infant, weak stream, palpable bladder, bilateral hydronephrosisFemale, normal stream, no distended bladder
Primary immunodeficiencyDefective clearance across sites and organismsSevere infections — pyelonephritis rather than cystitis — plus multiple infection types and failure to thriveSimple cystitis only, and a history otherwise unremarkable
Sexual abusePerineal trauma and inoculation; a real cause in children but rareGenital injury or bleeding, behavioural change, disclosureGenitalia normal, and the fissures are explained by constipation
Inadequate treatment of the prior episodeAn undertreated infection relapses with the same organismSymptoms never resolved, or recurrence within days of finishingA 6-week symptom-free gap after an adequate 3-day course
Management, in one line Management is a two-part prescription rather than a ladder: treat the infection, and treat the risk factor with long-term laxative therapy to soften stools, stop the withholding and let the dilated rectum return to normal size, which is what relieves the pressure on the bladder. Imaging is not the answer to this stem — a renal and bladder ultrasound belongs to the febrile urinary infection pathway, and a VCUG belongs downstream of that ⚠︎.
Decision spine Febrile or afebrile? — Afebrile, suprapubic, no back pain → lower tract · Does that kill the anatomic options? — Yes — reflux and obstruction produce upper-tract disease · Is this relapse or reinfection? — Six weeks, adequate course, symptom-free between → reinfection · Is anything else abnormal on examination? — Hard stool in the vault, anal fissures, a constipation history · What does a loaded rectum do to a bladder? — Compresses it, so it never empties
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo girl with her third afebrile cystitis this year, functional constipation since day care, suprapubic tenderness and hard stool in the rectal vault → Urinary stasis → Rectal dilation compresses the bladder
  2. 4 yo girl with constipation-associated recurrent cystitis, now treated for the acute infection; additional management → Long-term laxative therapy → Treating the underlying risk factor
  3. 4 yo girl with a second urinary tract infection, this time with temperature 39 C, vomiting and flank pain → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → Upper-tract disease changes the pathway
  4. 6-month-old boy with a febrile urinary tract infection whose renal ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis → Voiding cystourethrogram → Evaluating for vesicoureteral reflux
  5. 2-month-old boy with recurrent urinary tract infections, a weak urinary stream and a palpable bladder → Voiding cystourethrogram → Posterior urethral valves
  6. 5 yo girl with recurrent cystitis, soft daily stools, who reports holding her urine all day at school and performs holding maneuvers → Timed voiding with behavioral therapy → Dysfunctional voiding
  7. 5 yo girl with a urinary tract infection, genital bruising and vaginal bleeding, and a normal rectal examination → Evaluate for sexual abuse and involve child protective services → Genital injury is the discriminator
  8. 3 yo boy with two episodes of pyelonephritis, recurrent pneumonia, cutaneous abscesses and poor weight gain → Primary immunodeficiency → Severity plus multiple infection sites
  9. How chronic constipation produces recurrent bladder infection in a young child → The dilated rectum compresses the bladder and urethra, preventing complete voiding → Residual urine is colonized by ascending organisms
  10. 4 yo girl with recurrent cystitis and untreated constipation; which management will not prevent recurrence → Lengthening the antibiotic course → The risk factor is mechanical
Decoy note The anal fissures are the most cleverly placed detail in the stem, because they point at abuse and are simultaneously explained by the diagnosis. The stem also supplies the two facts that close the abuse question properly — normal genitalia and normal rectal tone — rather than leaving it to be dismissed by feel, which is how the exam signals which reading it wants. The other half of the decoy work is done by omission: the stem never says afebrile as a headline, it gives a temperature of 37.2, no fever, no back pain and suprapubic tenderness, and expects you to assemble them into a tract assignment yourself.
Pearls Afebrile recurrent cystitis in a constipated child is urinary stasis from a dilated rectum, and the lasting treatment is a laxative. · Tract before cause. Afebrile recurrent cystitis and recurrent febrile pyelonephritis have different differentials; reflux and obstruction live on the upper-tract side, and emptying problems live on the lower. · Constipation is the commonest modifiable risk factor for recurrent cystitis in a young child, and the mechanism is purely mechanical — a dilated rectum compressing the bladder. · Treating a urinary infection without treating the constipation is treating the episode instead of the disease; the laxative runs for months so the rectum can shrink ⚠︎. · Anal fissures are a complication of constipation, and their presence alongside normal genitalia argues against injury rather than for it. · Immunodeficiency shows up as severe and multi-site rather than as three simple cystitides; a child confined to one tract with one organism has a plumbing problem. · A recurrence weeks after a completed, appropriate course is reinfection rather than treatment failure — the interval is the discriminator, not the drug.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Vesicoureteral Reflux owns the upper-tract arm of this same complaint and already carries bladder–bowel dysfunction as part of reflux management at every grade; this brief is the case where the bowel is the whole diagnosis and there is no reflux to manage. Part II Pyelonephritis: Route & Disposition owns what happens once the infection is febrile, and Part I Constipation in a Child owns the upstream cycle whose urinary complication this is. Store the discriminator as a question: is this infection febrile or afebrile, and does the bladder empty?
Transferable rule A disease name strongly associated with a complaint will retrieve before the discriminator that governs it, and recently learned associations retrieve fastest of all. Convert every such association into a question — here, which tract? — because the stem usually answers the question before it offers the association. --- Batch 5, brief 03 · 2026-09-10.
Unchecked attributeVesicoureteral reflux — Reflux produces recurrent upper-tract disease; this child is afebrile with suprapubic tenderness and no back pain across three episodes
Salient decoySexual abuse — Genitalia are normal, and anal fissures are a common feature of chronic constipation, which the stem has already established
True-fact-wrong-slotInadequate treatment of prior infection — Three days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is adequate for a paediatric lower-tract infection, and a 6-week symptom-free gap means reinfection rather than relapse
Class-vs-memberPrimary immunodeficiency — Immunodeficiency presents with severe infections — pyelonephritis rather than cystitis — and with multiple types of infection; the history is otherwise unremarkable

Nocturnal Enuresis

Primary vs. secondary · both get a urinalysis

The decision point

Dry for ≥6 months and now wetting = secondary enuresis. Primary vs. secondary changes the differential — but both get a urinalysis first. One cheap test screens the entire organic differential, and a plausible psychosocial explanation (divorce, new sibling) never substitutes for excluding organic disease.

Defining criteria Secondary enuresis — previously dry ≥6 months, now wetting · First test, either type — urinalysis
Urinalysis findings → organic causes
UA findingDiagnosis
Leukocyte esterase, nitritesUTI — can present as new incontinence without dysuria in children
Glucosuria ± ketonesNew-onset type 1 diabetes — the can't-miss
Very low specific gravityDiabetes insipidus
Hematuria / proteinuriaCKD → metabolic panel, renal ultrasound
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo F dry for 2 years who is now wetting nightly → Secondary enuresis → urinalysis first
  2. 7 yo F with enuresis whose urinalysis shows glucosuria and ketones → New-onset diabetes mellitus → glucose and HbA1c
  3. 7 yo F with enuresis whose urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and nitrites → Urinary tract infection → culture and treat
  4. 7 yo F with enuresis and a very low urine specific gravity → Diabetes insipidus → water deprivation testing
  5. 5 yo M who has never been dry at night and is otherwise well → Primary enuresis — below the diagnostic age gate → reassurance
  6. 7 yo F with enuresis and a plausible psychosocial stressor at home → Obtain the urinalysis first
After a negative UA Address the stressor → behavioral (evening fluid restriction, timed voiding, no caffeine, voiding diary) → enuresis alarm (most effective long-term, but it is a conditioning device for primary enuresis) → desmopressin last, for sleepovers and camp, with high relapse and hyponatremia risk. Other secondary causes the stem will negate: constipation (very common), sexual abuse, OSA.
Pairs with Part I Polyuria: Water or Solute takes over once the very low specific gravity has pointed at diabetes insipidus — it owns the water deprivation test, what its result means, and the one child in whom it must not be done.
