Store the discriminator as a question: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?

Polyuria: Water or Solute

the urine osmolality sorts it before any hormone is named · UWorld · when the water deprivation test is indicated, and when it has already been answered

Source vignette Pt — 8 yo M, 2 months of excessive urination, drinking large volumes, irritable and restless; normal growth and milestones; no medications · Vitals — normal · Exam — physical and neurologic examination normal · Labs — Na 142, K 4.2, Cl 100, HCO₃ 24, BUN 30, creatinine 1.0, Ca 9.2, glucose 100 · Urine — specific gravity 1.001, no protein, blood, glucose or ketones; osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; 24-hour output 3.7 L · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned chest radiography, fractional excretion of sodium, brain MRI, an oral glucose tolerance test, renal ultrasonography and the water deprivation test
The decision point

Two numbers order this stem and neither of them is the one being asked about. Urine osmolality 120 is a water diuresis — the kidney is failing to concentrate, so solute diuresis and every test that chases it are out before any hormone is named. Then serum sodium 142, a normal value, is what makes the deprivation test necessary rather than redundant: a patient who drinks enough to hold his sodium normal has not yet shown whether the dilute urine is a failure to make or to heed vasopressin, or simply a kidney doing its job against a flood of water. Water deprivation is the manoeuvre that forces that distinction, by driving serum osmolality to the point where vasopressin secretion must be maximal and then asking what the urine did.

This one was answered quickly and correctly, so the lesson is not the key but the shape of the wrong options: the two imaging studies were not wrong tests, they were right tests in the wrong order — MRI localises an established deficiency, renal ultrasonography an established resistance, and both wait on a diagnosis this stem has not yet made.

Defining criteria Polyuria — urine output above 3 L/day in an adult, above 2 L/day/m² in a child · Dilute urine — urine osmolality under 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity under 1.006 · Concentrated urine — 600 mOsm/kg or above, meaning the kidney can concentrate and the diuresis is driven by solute · Deprivation endpoint — water withheld until serum sodium exceeds 145 and serum osmolality exceeds 295, the point at which vasopressin secretion should be maximal · Deprivation result — urine above 600 is primary polydipsia, urine still under 300 is an AVP disorder · Desmopressin result — urine osmolality rises in deficiency and stays low in resistance
FigureWhen water deprivation testing is indicatedshow

Redrawn from the published indications flowchart. Two deliberate changes: the concentrated-urine branch is labelled with what it means — solute diuresis — rather than only with what not to do, and the indicated branch carries its own interpretation, because the exam asks what the deprivation test showed about as often as it asks whether to order it.

Polyuria with dilute urine — the differentialand the two mimics that never need the test
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary polydipsiaDrinking drives the urine; psychiatric illness, or a drug that creates thirstSerum sodium low or low-normal; urine concentrates above 600 after deprivationNot excluded — this is one of the two the test is between
AVP deficiency (central DI)Impaired production or release: trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, hypophysitis, sarcoid or histiocytosis, a familial AVP mutation, pregnancyUrine stays dilute after deprivation, then rises with desmopressinNot excluded — the desmopressin step is what names it
AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)The kidney ignores the hormone: AVPR2 or AQP2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, severe hypokalaemia, lithium, chronic tubulointerstitial diseaseUrine stays dilute after desmopressin too; in a child, usually hereditaryNot excluded — complete resistance leaves the osmolality unchanged, partial raises it slightly
Solute (osmotic) diuresisGlucosuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or an osmotic diuretic such as mannitolPolyuria with a urine osmolality above 600; no deprivation test neededUrine osmolality 120, serum glucose 100, urine glucose negative
SIADHThe mirror image — water retained rather than lost; malignancy, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugsConcentrated urine with hyponatraemia, and no polyuriaDilute urine and a normal sodium — the opposite of the finding
Treatment, and the one child who must not be tested AVP deficiency — desmopressin in nearly all patients, oral, intranasal or parenteral; other agents are rarely needed · AVP resistance — remove the cause first (stop the lithium, correct the calcium and the potassium), then a thiazide with a low-sodium diet as first line; a low-protein diet cuts the solute load further; indomethacin is adjunct; amiloride is the one for lithium, because it blocks lithium entry into the collecting duct · Supervision — the deprivation test is performed in hospital in older children and adults, and is not performed in very young children, because the hypernatraemia it deliberately produces is dangerous in a child who cannot ask for water
Decision spine — solve the stem in 10 seconds

1. Is the urine dilute or concentrated? — 600 or above means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute, not for a hormone. 2. Is there glucose in the urine? — glucosuria explains the whole picture without one. 3. Is the sodium above 145 with osmolality above 295? — the AVP disorder is already proven; go straight to desmopressin. 4. Is the sodium frankly low? — polyuria with hyponatraemia is primary polydipsia and needs no deprivation test. 5. Is the sodium normal? — that is the one value that earns the test. 6. After deprivation, did desmopressin raise the urine osmolality? — yes is deficiency, so image the brain; no is resistance, so look at the kidney and the drug list.

Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localised
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatraemia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatraemia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatraemia needs no deprivation test
  9. Separating AVP deficiency from AVP resistance once the deprivation test has confirmed a disorder → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcaemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance; at the collecting duct
Pearls They re-ask this by moving the sodium: raise it above 145 and the test is redundant, drop it below normal and the diagnosis is already primary polydipsia — only a normal sodium buys the test · Serum vasopressin is not measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency — the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance — the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; the renaming changes nothing about what is scored · Hypothalamic injury kills the magnocellular cell bodies and the deficiency is permanent; injury below the infundibulum is usually transient, because those cell bodies survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase — it resolves with delivery and returns in the next pregnancy · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Nocturnal Enuresis already keys a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test — this brief is what happens after the test is ordered. Sellar and Suprasellar Masses owns the causes of AVP deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia Workup owns the commonest acquired resistance. Store the discriminator as a question: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium tells you not the diagnosis but whether you still need the test: a high sodium has already answered the question, a low sodium has answered it the other way, and a normal sodium is the only value that buys a water deprivation test.
Sequencing trapMRI of the brain is the right study once a deficiency is proven, and this stem has proven nothing yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography is the mirror error — it images the organ that is only implicated if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium measures perfusion, and nothing in this stem asks about perfusion.
Salient decoyChest radiography chases SIADH, which produces concentrated urine and hyponatraemia — both opposite to what is here.

NSAID Prerenal AKI in a Child

Gastroenteritis + ibuprofen · the labs assign the compartment

Source vignette Pt — 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, taking ibuprofen · Labs — BUN/creatinine ratio 32:1, specific gravity 1.028, bland urinalysis · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned isotonic fluids with stopping the ibuprofen, furosemide and renal ultrasonography
The decision point

In any AKI stem the laboratory data assign the injury compartment before the drug assigns the mechanism: BUN/Cr >20:1 + specific gravity >1.020 + bland sediment = prerenal — hypoperfused but intact kidneys, still concentrating. Ibuprofen's role is hemodynamic: hypovolemia makes GFR prostaglandin-dependent, and COX inhibition constricts the afferent arteriole. A drug named in the stem is a magnet for the drug-named option (interstitial nephritis) — the sediment and the 3-day timeline exclude it.

Defining criteria Prerenal pattern — BUN/Cr >20:1, specific gravity >1.020, bland urine sediment · ATN pattern — muddy brown casts, specific gravity ≈1.010, BUN/Cr <20:1 · Mechanism here — volume depletion makes GFR prostaglandin-dependent; NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole
Pediatric oliguria — cause by compartment
CauseIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Prerenal (NSAID + hypovolemia)vomiting/diarrhea; NSAID constricts the afferent arterioleBUN/Cr >20:1 + SG >1.020 + bland sediment
AINacute interstitial nephritisdrug hypersensitivity — NSAIDs after weeks, β-lactams, PPIsfever, rash, eosinophilia; WBCs/WBC casts
ATNacute tubular necrosisischemia or direct toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast)muddy brown casts; SG ≈1.010
HUS Can't missShiga toxin E coli, 5–10 days after bloody diarrheaschistocytes + thrombocytopenia + hematuria/proteinuria
Immune-complex GNPSGN, IgA nephropathypost-streptococcal (2–4 wk) or gross hematuria with URIhematuria + proteinuria ± low C3
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea on ibuprofen, BUN/Cr 32:1, SG 1.028, bland urinalysis → Isotonic fluids and stop the ibuprofen
  2. 5 yo F, bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pallor, petechiae, oliguria, schistocytes on smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents
  3. 68 yo F on naproxen for 3 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts → Acute interstitial nephritis → stop the NSAID
  4. 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 → Ischemic acute tubular necrosis
  5. 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 → Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids → the "triple whammy" of ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
  6. 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 → IgA nephropathy → timing with the URI and normal complement decide
  7. 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care
Pearls Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, angiotensin II constricts the efferent — NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors drop GFR from opposite ends, and NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic is the "triple whammy" · FENa <1% supports prerenal (unreliable after diuretics) · the AIN triad is present in a minority — WBC casts carry the diagnosis · PSGN vs IgA is timing plus complement: 2–4 weeks after with low C3 vs during the URI with normal C3.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia owns the smear-and-coags sort when the renal failure arrives with a falling platelet count.
Transferable rule Ratio → specific gravity → sediment, then and only then the drug. A fast answer on a stem carrying a full chemistry panel means the discriminating data were never read.
Salient decoyThe named drug pulls toward "drug-induced interstitial nephritis" — wrong timeline, wrong sediment.
True-fact-wrong-slotGastroenteritis cues HUS, which needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes, and an active sediment.

Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child

the pattern names the lesion, the age names the search · board question · Are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo M, one month of progressive facial puffiness, fatigue and decreased appetite; T 36.7, BP 110/70, HR 80; periorbital and pretibial oedema · Labs — creatinine 0.9, albumin 2.2; urinalysis 4+ protein with no red cells and no casts · Imaging — renal biopsy: diffuse granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops on immunofluorescence, subepithelial electron-dense deposits on electron microscopy — membranous nephropathy · Q — which additional study should be performed; options spanned antistreptolysin O titres, audiology evaluation, echocardiography, hepatitis B serologies and no additional workup
The decision point

The biopsy result is a premise, not a puzzle — the stem names the lesion for you. The question is what membranous nephropathy means in a 17-year-old, and it turns on one epidemiological fact: membranous nephropathy in adults is usually primary; in children it is usually secondary. So the diagnosis obliges a search for a cause, and the highest-yield one is hepatitis B, where circulating HBeAg–anti-HBeAg immune complexes deposit subepithelially and produce exactly this picture. Evaluating all patients with membranous nephropathy for hepatitis B is recommended; in a child it is close to mandatory.

Defining criteria Nephrotic syndrome — proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia; blood pressure and GFR usually normal, which is what separates it from nephritic disease · Membranous nephropathy, biopsy signature — subepithelial immune deposits with granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops; gradual podocyte damage, hence a subacute onset over weeks to a month · Primary versus secondary — adults usually primary, from autoantibodies to endogenous podocyte antigens; children rare and usually secondary, which is the gate this question turns on · The secondary-cause list — infection (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis), malignancy (solid tumours in adults), autoimmune disease (SLE, thyroiditis), drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine)
The child with proteinuria — the differentialnephrotic versus nephritic, then which lesion
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Membranous nephropathySubacute nephrotic syndrome; adult primary, child secondarySubepithelial deposits, granular IgG and C3 on capillary loops— (the diagnosis; the question is its cause)
Minimal change diseaseThe commonest childhood nephrotic syndromeAbrupt onset; normal light microscopy, podocyte effacement on EM onlySubacute course and a positive immunofluorescence
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis1–3 weeks after strep; nephriticHaematuria, hypertension, raised creatinine, low C3No red cells, normal BP, normal creatinine
Alport syndromeType IV collagen defect; X-linkedHaematuria plus sensorineural hearing loss; family historyNo haematuria; membranous is not associated with deafness
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosisNephrotic; African ancestry, HIV, obesitySegmental sclerosis on light microscopyBiopsy already names membranous
AmyloidosisNephrotic-range proteinuria in older adultsApple-green birefringence; restrictive cardiomyopathyBiopsy shows immune deposits, not amyloid; wrong age
Pertinent positives & negatives One month of gradual swelling — subacute; membranous accumulates deposits slowly, unlike minimal change disease, which presents abruptly · 4+ proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema — nephrotic, not nephritic · No red blood cells, no casts — excludes a nephritic process and with it post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and Alport syndrome · Blood pressure 110/70 with creatinine 0.9 — both normal, characteristic of membranous and against PSGN, where hypertension and a rising creatinine are the rule · Age 17 — the deciding attribute; primary membranous is an adult disease, so a paediatric case is secondary until proven otherwise · Biopsy already performed and diagnostic — the options that would establish a diagnosis are spent; only the aetiologic search remains
Decision spine Read the last sentence. — "Additional study" → the diagnosis is given · Nephrotic or nephritic? — Protein without cells or casts, normal BP and creatinine → nephrotic · Which lesion? — The stem already said: membranous · How old is the patient? — Seventeen → paediatric → secondary until proven otherwise · Run the secondary list. — Infection, malignancy, autoimmune, drugs · Which is on the option list? — Hepatitis B
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo M with 1 month of facial puffiness and oedema, 4+ proteinuria without red cells or casts, albumin 2.2, creatinine 0.9, BP 110/70; biopsy shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary loops with subepithelial deposits → Hepatitis B serologies → membranous nephropathy in a child is usually secondary
  2. 4 yo with abrupt onset periorbital oedema and 4+ proteinuria; light microscopy normal and electron microscopy shows podocyte foot-process effacement → Minimal change disease → empiric corticosteroids without biopsy
  3. 8 yo, 2 weeks after pharyngitis, with cola-coloured urine, BP 140/90, creatinine 1.6 and a low C3 → Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care and blood pressure control
  4. 12 yo boy with persistent microscopic haematuria and a family history of renal failure in maternal uncles → Audiology evaluation → Alport syndrome
  5. How chronic hepatitis B infection causes membranous nephropathy → HBeAg and anti-HBeAg immune complexes deposit in the subepithelial space → granular IgG and C3 along the capillary loops
  6. 58 yo with newly diagnosed membranous nephropathy and negative infectious and autoimmune serologies → Age-appropriate malignancy screening → solid tumours are the adult secondary association
  7. 17 yo with biopsy-proven membranous nephropathy whose infectious workup has not yet been sent → Concluding that no additional workup is needed → secondary causes predominate in children
  8. 66 yo with nephrotic syndrome, restrictive cardiomyopathy and apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining → Amyloidosis → echocardiography for cardiac involvement
The age is the gate Membranous nephropathy is a diagnosis in an adult and a question in a child. An adult with this biopsy is usually primary and the workup can be brief; a child with the identical biopsy has almost certainly got a cause, and finding it is the management. The same slide, read against the patient's age, produces two different next steps.
Pearls Nephrotic versus nephritic is settled on the urinalysis, not the protein — protein without red cells or casts, with a normal blood pressure and creatinine, is nephrotic · Subacute onset argues for membranous over minimal change, which arrives abruptly — deposits accumulate slowly, foot processes efface suddenly · Commit the location of the deposits — subepithelial is membranous, subendothelial is lupus nephritis, mesangial is IgA · "No additional workup" is almost never right when a secondary-cause list exists, and it is chosen most often by readers who have been thinking for a long time · Blood pressure and GFR are typically normal in membranous, and partial or complete remission is common with end-stage disease rare
Pairs with Part I Hematuria — glomerular vs non-glomerular, which owns the nephritic side of this fork and the Alport link. Store the discriminator as a question: are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?
Transferable rule When a stem hands you a biopsy diagnosis, it is not testing recognition — it is testing what the diagnosis obliges you to do next. Ask what the disease is associated with, and let the patient's age decide whether the association list is the answer or an afterthought.
Uniform-answer doubtNo additional workup — the biopsy names the lesion, not the cause; in a child the cause is the whole question.
True-fact-wrong-slotAntistreptolysin O — PSGN is nephritic, with haematuria, hypertension and a raised creatinine; strep is not associated with membranous.
True-fact-wrong-slotAudiology evaluation — deafness belongs to Alport, which presents with haematuria, not nephrotic-range protein.
Class-vs-memberEchocardiography — amyloidosis pairs nephrotic syndrome with cardiac disease, but the biopsy shows immune deposits and this is a teenager.
4 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Renal & Genitourinary

Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence

One lesion upstream of every finding · Aquifer · count the orphaned findings

Source vignette Pt — term newborn boy, respiratory distress, flat facies, clubfeet, distended abdomen with a suprapubic midline mass · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned posterior urethral valves, bilateral renal agenesis and congenital diaphragmatic hernia
The decision point

The stem hands you two independent clue-sets and the answer is the single lesion upstream of both. Flat facies, clubfeet and pulmonary hypoplasia mean fetal constraint and failed alveolar development, so oligohydramnios happened — that names the sequence, not the cause. Distended abdomen with a soft suprapubic midline mass in a male is a distended bladder, which names the cause.

In a newborn boy, bladder outlet obstruction is posterior urethral valves until proven otherwise. The two highest-drawing wrong options each explain one finding and orphan the rest: a diaphragmatic hernia explains the respiratory distress, a Wilms tumour explains the mass.

Defining criteria Oligohydramnios — amniotic fluid index at or below 5 cm, or a single deepest pocket under 2 cm · Potter sequence — the cascade downstream of oligohydramnios: pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, positional limb deformities · Sequence versus syndrome — one initiating defect producing a cascade, versus one cause producing independent anomalies · Why the lungs fail — fetal urine is the major source of amniotic fluid after about 16 weeks, so anything that stops urine output stops lung growth
The newborn with Potter sequence - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Posterior urethral valvesObstructing membrane in the posterior urethra, males onlyPotter sequence with a palpable suprapubic bladder; weak urinary stream
Bilateral renal agenesisNo kidneys, no urine, anhydramniosPotter sequence with no bladder to palpate and anuria
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney diseaseEnlarged echogenic kidneys, hepatic fibrosisBilateral flank masses with hepatomegaly
Preterm premature rupture of membranesFluid leaks out despite normal kidneysMaternal fluid leakage with a normal renal ultrasound
Prune belly syndromeDeficient abdominal wall musculatureWrinkled lax abdomen and bilateral undescended testes
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera herniate and crush the lungScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest
Duodenal atresiaBlocks fetal swallowing of fluidPolyhydramnios, the opposite direction; double bubble
Scenario bank
  1. Term newborn boy, respiratory distress, flat facies, clubfeet, distended abdomen with a suprapubic midline mass → Posterior urethral valves → bladder catheterization
  2. Newborn boy with Potter sequence and a distended bladder, most appropriate next step → Bladder catheterization to decompress, then VCUG → renal ultrasound cannot confirm the diagnosis
  3. Newborn, flat facies, clubfeet, severe respiratory distress, anuric at 48 h, no palpable bladder or kidneys → Bilateral renal agenesis
  4. Newborn, Potter facies, respiratory distress, bilateral flank masses, hepatomegaly → Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease → renal ultrasound
  5. Newborn at 32 wk, mother reports clear fluid leaking for 6 weeks, flat facies, clubfeet, respiratory distress, normal renal ultrasound → Preterm premature rupture of membranes
  6. Newborn girl with a distended bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis → Ureterocele → voiding cystourethrogram
  7. Newborn with a wrinkled, lax abdominal wall, bilateral undescended testes, and a dilated urinary tract → Prune belly syndrome
  8. Term newborn with severe distress at delivery, a scaphoid abdomen, heart sounds displaced to the right, bowel gas in the left hemithorax → Congenital diaphragmatic hernia → intubate and place a nasogastric tube
  9. Newborn with bilious vomiting, a double bubble on x-ray, and maternal polyhydramnios → Duodenal atresia
  10. 3 yo with a painless unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline, hematuria and hypertension → Wilms tumor → abdominal ultrasound
  11. 2 do M, no prenatal care, one wet diaper since birth, weight up 60 g from birth, abdomen distended, saturation 88% with diminished breath sounds and low lung volumes on chest film, urethral meatus intact → Renal and bladder ultrasound → ultrasound precedes the voiding cystourethrogram
  12. Newborn boy whose renal and bladder ultrasound shows a thick-walled distended bladder with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis → Voiding cystourethrogram → posterior urethral dilation confirms the diagnosis
  13. Newborn boy with posterior urethral valves and Potter sequence → Pulmonary hypoplasia → fetal urine makes the amniotic fluid that grows the lungs
  14. Fetus with duodenal atresia → Polyhydramnios → the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid; the mirror of the renal lesions
The order of operations Decompress before you image, image before you cut. Urethral catheter first, then voiding cystourethrogram — the confirmatory study, showing a dilated posterior urethra and a thick-walled trabeculated bladder. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Then VACTERL-style screening with echocardiography and renal ultrasound, and surgical valve ablation.
Pearls Fetal urine makes the lungs, which is why pulmonary hypoplasia rather than renal failure is the cause of death in Potter sequence · Posterior urethral valves is a male-only diagnosis; a newborn girl with the same picture has a ureterocele or urethral atresia · Sequence is not syndrome — one defect cascading, rather than independent anomalies from a shared cause · The neonatal renal mass differential is hydronephrosis first, then multicystic dysplastic kidney; the neonatal renal tumour is congenital mesoblastic nephroma, not Wilms · Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and Wilms does not
Pairs with Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula with Esophageal Atresia is the mechanistic twin — cannot make urine gives oligohydramnios, cannot swallow gives polyhydramnios. Also pairs with Part II Neonatal Respiratory Distress, where the fork is whether the lungs are structurally normal. Part I Vesicoureteral Reflux is the other end of the same imaging pathway — there the VCUG grades reflux, here it finds the obstructing valve.
The imaging sequence, and the weight clue Order — renal and bladder ultrasound first, then a voiding cystourethrogram if the ultrasound is abnormal, then cystoscopy to confirm and ablate; bladder drainage and electrolyte correction run alongside · Weight gain in the first 48 hours is abnormal — newborns lose weight, so a gaining newborn is retaining, and in a boy with a distended abdomen what he is retaining is urine
Transferable rule When a stem lists findings across three unrelated organ systems it is asking for the one lesion upstream of all of them, so name which findings your choice leaves unexplained and reject it if the count is above zero.
Class-vs-memberDiaphragmatic hernia and Wilms each explain the loudest finding and orphan the rest.
Trump-card inversionDuodenal atresia causes polyhydramnios, the opposite of what the clubfeet prove.
True-fact-wrong-slotTransient tachypnea is mild and self-limited, and cannot explain a mass or clubfeet.

Pyelonephritis: Naming the Organism

Nitrate reductase, not urease

Source vignette Pt — community-acquired urinary tract infection · Labs — urinalysis positive for nitrites · Q — the most likely causative organism; options spanned Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other enterics
The decision point

Positive nitrites in a community-acquired UTI. Nitrite requires nitrate reductase, which gram-negative enterics have and gram-positives don't — and among enterics, E. coli causes ~75–85% of community-acquired UTIs. Prevalence plus nitrite settles it in one step.

⚠︎ The bank's reasoning is wrong even though its answer is right The explanation states S. saprophyticus "is not a urease-splitting organism, so urinalysis would be unlikely to show positive nitrites." Two stacked errors: nitrites come from nitrate reductase, not urease, and S. saprophyticus is urease-positive. The conclusion holds — it is nitrite-negative — but because it lacks nitrate reductase. This is an error, not a currency update.
Urease vs nitrate reductaseenzyme → readout → organisms
EnzymeReactionReadoutOrganisms
Nitrate reductaseNitrate → nitritePositive nitritesE. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter · NOT S. saprophyticus, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas
UreaseUrea → ammonia → alkaline urinepH >7, struvite staghorn stonesProteus, Klebsiella, S. saprophyticus, Ureaplasma, H. pylori
Uropathogens & their tells
OrganismThe tell
E. coliMost common community-acquired; nitrite-positive; lactose-fermenting, green metallic sheen on EMB
Proteus mirabilisUrease-positive → alkaline urine, struvite stones; swarming motility; ammoniacal odor
KlebsiellaEncapsulated, mucoid; alcoholics and diabetics; more often nosocomial in UTI
S. saprophyticusYoung sexually active women; coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant; nitrite-negative
Enterococcus / PseudomonasCatheters, instrumentation, prior antibiotics; nitrite-negative
Citrobacter / Serratia / EnterobacterHospital-acquired — the stem must supply the exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo M with an indwelling catheter, fever and flank pain → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a catheter-associated UTI broadens beyond E coli to Enterococcus, Candida and Serratia
  2. 58 yo F, urine pH 8.5, staghorn calculus on CT → Proteus mirabilis
  3. 22 yo F, dysuria and frequency, LE-positive but nitrite-negative → Staphylococcus saprophyticus
  4. 26 yo F, dysuria with sterile pyuria, sexually active → Chlamydial urethritis → NAAT
  5. 64 yo M, diabetic, pyelonephritis with gas in the renal parenchyma → Emphysematous pyelonephritis → urgent urology
  6. 45 yo M, recurrent Proteus UTIs → Struvite stones → a urease-splitting organism alkalinizes the urine
  7. 72 yo M on appropriate antibiotics, still febrile at 72 h → CT for abscess or obstruction
The management half Male sex makes any UTI "complicated" by definition — that's why the stem is a man. Complicated means a longer course (7–14 days), a fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX rather than nitrofurantoin, and a lower threshold for imaging. BPH supplies the mechanism: incomplete emptying → stasis → ascending infection. Pairs with Part I Pyelonephritis & Disposition.
Boundary condition Nitrite sensitivity is only ~50% — a short bladder dwell time (frequent voiding, continuous catheter drainage) can give a false negative despite E. coli. A negative nitrite never excludes an enteric organism; a positive one strongly implies it.
Transferable rule When an option's exclusion rests on an enzyme, name which enzyme and which reaction. Urease and nitrate reductase get conflated constantly — including in vendor explanations — and the exam tests them as independent axes.

Incontinence & the Postvoid Residual

One number splits the differential

Source vignette Pt — woman with urinary leakage; no pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy or radiation · Labs — postvoid residual 800 mL · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned overflow, stress and urge incontinence and vesicovaginal fistula
The decision point

Postvoid residual 800 mL. Retention is overflow incontinence, and the PVR splits the entire differential before you weigh a single symptom.

Fistula isn't merely unsupported — it's mechanically impossible. A bladder draining continuously through a fistula cannot hold 800 mL. The stem kills it twice more: fistula requires pelvic surgery, obstetric injury, malignancy, or radiation (absent), and shows urine pooling in the vagina ("examination shows no abnormalities").

The bait: a positive cough stress test Normally that means stress incontinence — but a chronically overdistended bladder leaks with any rise in intra-abdominal pressure, so the test loses specificity once the PVR is high. A positive test that doesn't mean what it usually means is the same species as a negative test that doesn't exclude: context sets a test's operating characteristics.
Urinary incontinence types
TypeMechanismPresentationPVRTreatment
StressUrethral hypermobility / sphincter deficiencyLeaks with cough, sneeze, liftingLowPelvic floor → pessary → midurethral sling
Urge (OAB)Detrusor overactivitySudden urge then leakage, frequency, nocturiaLowBladder training → antimuscarinic or mirabegron → Botox
OverflowDetrusor underactivity or outlet obstructionHesitancy, weak stream, dribbling, recurrent UTIHIGHIntermittent catheterization; bethanechol; α-blocker if obstructive; stop anticholinergics
FunctionalCognitive or mobility barrierCan't reach the toilet; tract normalNormalScheduled toileting
FistulaAbnormal communicationContinuous leakage, vaginal urine poolingNormal/lowDye test, cystoscopy → repair
The causal chain & a drug pairing T1DM since age 6 → diabetic autonomic neuropathy → detrusor underactivity → retention → overflow leakage and the recurrent UTIs from stasis. Oxybutynin treats urge and would worsen overflow — the same drug that causes fecal impaction two systems over. Gut motility down, bladder emptying down: when it appears in an elderly or diabetic med list, check both.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F, leaks only when coughing, PVR 30, four vaginal deliveries → Stress incontinence → pelvic floor exercises first
  2. 68 yo F, sudden urge then leakage with nocturia, PVR 40 → Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity
  3. 72 yo M, hesitancy and weak stream, PVR 350, enlarged prostate → Overflow incontinence from outlet obstruction → α-blocker ± 5-α-reductase inhibitor
  4. 28 yo F, continuous leakage two weeks after a difficult delivery, vaginal urine pooling → Vesicovaginal fistula
  5. 84 yo F with dementia, wets before reaching the bathroom, tract normal → Functional incontinence
  6. 68 yo F on oxybutynin with rising PVR and retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  7. 45 yo F, urgency and frequency with dysuria, pyuria and nitrites → Urinary tract infection → not chronic incontinence
  8. 40 yo F with multiple sclerosis, mixed retention and urgency → Neurogenic bladder → urodynamics
  9. 32 yo F, T1DM, PVR 800 → Screen for autonomic neuropathy → gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia
Boundary conditions A high PVR establishes overflow is present, not that it's the only mechanism — mixed incontinence is common, and a positive cough test may reflect a real coexisting stress component. A PVR is only interpretable when measured after a normal void. ⚠︎ PVR thresholds (normal <50, abnormal >200) are memory-sourced; the 800 mL value and bethanechol are in-context.
Transferable rule When a stem gives a quantitative measure of organ function, check whether each candidate diagnosis is compatible with that number before weighing symptoms. An option the physiology forbids never needs a symptom argument.
Test-overrides-findings

Primary Monosymptomatic Enuresis: Management

Classify, then take the lowest unexhausted rung

Source vignette Pt — child with primary nocturnal enuresis, never having had a dry night, daytime-trained with no daytime symptoms; normal examination; nothing tried so far · Labs — urinalysis normal, glucose normal · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned reassurance with education and motivational therapy, an enuresis alarm and desmopressin
The decision point

Two classification calls decide this before any option is worth reading: primary ("never had a dry night") and monosymptomatic (daytime-trained, no daytime symptoms). With a normal exam, normal UA, and normal glucose this is maturational — and nothing has been tried yet. First rung: reassurance + education + motivational therapy.

Classification axes — enuresis
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence
Primary vs. secondary"never had a dry night"Maturational — no cause-hunt needed
Mono- vs. nonmonosymptomaticDaytime-trained ×2 yr, no daytime symptomsNo bladder diary, uroflow, or urology referral
Organic cause excluded?Normal UA, glucose 82, normal examEvery further-testing option is dead
Anything tried?NothingEvery escalation option is dead
Management ladder — primary monosymptomatic enuresis
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Education + reassurance + motivational therapy (reward effort and routine, not dry nights) · treat constipation first · void before bed · moderate evening fluids with generous morning intake3–6 months without improvement and the child/family is bothered
2Enuresis alarm — highest long-term cure, needs a motivated family, works over 2–3 months ⚠︎; continue until 14 consecutive dry nights · or desmopressin — rapid onset for camp/sleepovers, high relapse, hyponatremia riskFailure of both
3Oxybutynin if detrusor overactivity · imipramine rarely (cardiotoxic in overdose) · urology referral—
Within-tier fork & gating numbers Durable cure + motivated family → alarm; fast and event-driven → desmopressin. The exam tests this choice separately. Diagnostic gates: age ≥5 to diagnose · 6 months of prior dryness defines secondary · daytime symptoms define nonmonosymptomatic. Escalation gate: 3–6 months of failed tier 1. Age ≥5, the 6-month definition, and the 3–6 month trigger are in-context. The 14-dry-nights endpoint is the Cochrane definition of complete response (⚠︎ rendered here as a stopping rule).
Exit ramps Daytime symptoms → nonmono pathway (diary, uroflow; treat constipation — often curative) · recurrent UTIs → renal/bladder US ± VCUG · weak stream or dribbling in a boy → posterior urethral valves · sacral dimple, tuft, abnormal gait → spinal dysraphism → MRI · polyuria + polydipsia → DM/DI · growth failure or hypertension → renal disease · new onset after a stressor → screen for abuse.
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo F, 8 months of reward charts and voiding routine, family distressed → Enuresis alarm
  2. 6 yo F, sleepaway camp next week → Desmopressin → event-driven beats durable
  3. 7 yo F, dry ×1 year, now wetting → Secondary enuresis → urinalysis and cause-hunt
  4. 6 yo F with daytime urgency and squatting maneuvers → Nonmonosymptomatic enuresis → bladder diary, treat the constipation first
  5. 6 yo F, UA shows glucosuria → Workup for diabetes mellitus → not enuresis management
  6. 6 yo F on desmopressin with headache, vomiting, seizure → Hyponatremia → stop the drug, restrict fluids
  7. 7 yo M with weak stream and post-void dribbling → Posterior urethral valves → renal US + VCUG
  8. 4 yo M bedwetting, worried parents → Reassurance → below the diagnostic age gate of 5 years
  9. 6 yo F with a sacral tuft and brisk lower-extremity reflexes → Spinal MRI
Trap autopsy Desmopressin — skipped tier: correct tier-2 drug with zero months of tier 1 on the clock. Fluid restriction after 2 pm — wrong parameter: real intervention, wrong hour; evening moderation (~after 5 pm) with morning compensation is the advice, and 2 pm risks daytime dehydration. Renal US — phantom indication. Urine culture — redundant workup; UA already normal. Decoy: "three siblings dry by age 3" is parental-comparison bait — and a family history of enuresis actually supports the maturational diagnosis.
Paired pearls Desmopressin is an ADH (V2) analog — free-water retention is the mechanism of both its effect and its hyponatremic seizures. The alarm works by conditioning, which is why its cure survives discontinuation and desmopressin's doesn't. Imipramine kills in overdose via Na⁺-channel blockade → wide-QRS arrhythmias (treat with bicarbonate). Constipation impersonates bladder dysfunction — a distended rectum triggers detrusor overactivity.
Pairs with Part I Nocturnal Enuresis (secondary — dry ×1 year, now wetting → urinalysis). Same complaint, opposite classification, opposite answer. Store the discriminator: "Ever dry for 6 months?"
Transferable rule The stem's completed actions and elapsed time set the tier: a reported-normal workup kills every further-testing option, and an empty treatment history kills every escalation option. Classify, find the tier, then pick the lowest rung not yet exhausted.
Skipped tierWrong parameterMirror twin

Endocrine & Bone 10 topics + 2 board-style

Two-step algorithms dominate: TSH then RAIU, and PTH then everything else. Know which variable is broken before you titrate to it.

Thyroid Mimics & Discriminators

TSH first, then RAIU splits making from leaking

The decision point

TSH first: low TSH + high T4 = thyrotoxicosis; high TSH + low T4 = primary hypothyroidism; both low = central. Then RAIU splits thyrotoxicosis: high uptake = the gland is MAKING hormone; low uptake = leaking or exogenous, where antithyroid drugs are useless.

Thyroid disease — the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureKey labs / RAIUTreatment
Graves diseaseyoung woman; #1 hyperthyroidDiffuse goiter ± bruit; exophthalmos + pretibial myxedema — Graves ONLYTSI/TRAb +; diffuse ↑ uptakeMethimazole (PTU in 1st trimester), RAI, or surgery
Toxic multinodular goiterPlummer; elderly, longstanding goiterLumpy goiter; apathetic hyperthyroidism — new AFib, weight loss, depressionPatchy multifocal hot nodulesRAI or surgery. Autonomous nodules — not a thyroiditis
Toxic adenomaSingle autonomous noduleOne hot nodule, rest coldRAI or lobectomy. Hot nodules are almost never cancer
Subacute granulomatousde Quervain; post-viralPAINFUL, tender gland after a viral URI; pain to jaw/ear↑ESR; LOW RAIU; hyper → hypo → recoveryNSAIDs ± steroids. The only painful thyrotoxicosis
Painless / postpartum thyroiditisPainless small goiter; classically 2–6 mo postpartumTPO +, LOW RAIU, normal ESRβ-blocker only — nothing is being made
Hashimoto thyroiditis#1 hypothyroidFirm rubbery goiter; may have brief hashitoxicosisAnti-TPO; Hürthle cells, germinal centersLevothyroxine. Rapidly enlarging gland → B-cell lymphoma
Factitious thyrotoxicosisSupplements or healthcare access; NO goiterLOW RAIU + LOW thyroglobulinStop the hormone — Tg is high when a gland leaks
Riedel thyroiditisIgG4-relatedRock-hard, fixed, painless — mimics anaplastic carcinomaFibrosis, IgG4 plasma cellsSteroids/tamoxifen. Young + hard = Riedel; old = anaplastic
Thyroid storm EmergencyFever + tachyarrhythmia + delirium; precipitant: surgery, infection, iodine loadClinical diagnosis — don't wait for labsβ-blocker → PTU → iodine ≥1 h later → steroids (iodine first fuels synthesis)
Central hypothyroidismHypothyroid + other pituitary deficits; post-Sheehan, mass, apoplexyTSH low or normal WITH low T4Titrate to free T4, not TSH; screen cortisol first
Scenario bank
  1. 32 yo F with low TSH, high T4, a diffuse goiter with a bruit and proptosis → Graves disease → high radioiodine uptake
  2. 68 yo F with low TSH, a multinodular gland and patchy uptake → Toxic multinodular goiter
  3. 40 yo F with a painful tender thyroid after a viral illness, low uptake and high ESR → Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
  4. 30 yo F, 3 months postpartum, painless thyrotoxicosis with low uptake → Postpartum thyroiditis
  5. 45 yo F with high TSH, low T4, positive TPO antibodies and a firm goiter → Hashimoto thyroiditis → levothyroxine
  6. 28 yo F, thyrotoxic with low uptake and a suppressed thyroglobulin → Factitious thyrotoxicosis
  7. 55 yo F, thyrotoxic with fever 40, agitation and atrial fibrillation → Thyroid storm → beta-blocker, thionamide, then iodine
  8. 32 yo F with low TSH, high T4, a small nontender goiter and no eye signs → Radioactive iodine uptake → splits a gland making hormone from one leaking it
  9. 55 yo F with Graves disease, fever 40, delirium and atrial fibrillation the day after surgery → Beta-blocker → then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids
  10. 28 yo F with newly diagnosed Graves disease at 8 weeks of pregnancy → Propylthiouracil → PTU in the first trimester, methimazole after, radioactive iodine never
  11. 30 yo F, 3 months postpartum, with palpitations, a painless small goiter, positive TPO antibodies and low radioactive iodine uptake → Beta-blocker alone → nothing is being made, so antithyroid drugs are useless
Paired pearls Lid lag and stare = any thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic); proptosis + pretibial myxedema = Graves only · hot nodule ≈ never cancer; cold nodule → FNA · pregnancy: PTU first trimester, methimazole after, RAI never · nodule workup: TSH → low? uptake scan; normal or high? ultrasound → FNA.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the neonatal version, where the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect.

Levothyroxine Titration

The timing trick, and when it doesn't apply

The decision point

TSH lags dose changes by 6–8 weeks. A stem that specifies 8 weeks is telling you the TSH is now trustworthy — so a TSH of 9.5 means the dose is genuinely inadequate → increase it. When a stem conspicuously specifies a timeframe, it's telling you which rule applies, not testing whether you remember that a rule exists.

Defining criteria Recheck interval — TSH lags dose changes by 6–8 weeks; earlier values are untrustworthy · Subclinical hypothyroidism, treat if — TSH >10, TPO-positive, pregnant, or symptomatic · Pregnancy — requirement rises 30–50% immediately
The real trick set
  • Rechecked too soon (<6 wks after a change) → answer is "recheck in 6 weeks," not a dose change
  • TSH stays high despite escalating doses → adherence, then absorption: empty stomach; iron, calcium, PPIs, cholestyramine bind it; consider celiac disease
  • Pregnancy → requirement rises 30–50% immediately; increase as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
  • Elderly or CAD → start low, go slow (25–50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia
  • Central hypothyroidism → titrate to free T4; TSH is the broken variable
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal T4) → treat if TSH >10, TPO+, pregnant, or symptomatic
Scenario bank
  1. 44 yo F on levothyroxine for 8 weeks with a TSH of 9.5 → Increase the dose
  2. 44 yo F rechecked at 3 weeks with a TSH of 8 → Make no change — TSH lags 6 to 8 weeks behind the dose
  3. 44 yo F on levothyroxine with a TSH of 0.05 and palpitations → Decrease the dose
  4. 44 yo F on levothyroxine who is newly pregnant → Increase the dose by about 30% and recheck
  5. 44 yo F taking levothyroxine together with her calcium supplement → Separate them by 4 hours
  6. 78 yo F with coronary disease starting levothyroxine → Start low and titrate slowly
Pairs with Part I Levothyroxine in Pregnancy — the one setting where you adjust the dose before the TSH moves. Store the discriminator: "is she pregnant right now?"
Transferable rule Half-remembered gotchas are more dangerous than ignorance. Before applying a "trick," verify its trigger condition is actually in the stem. Sometimes the question really is that boring — and "this must be a trick" is itself the trick.

Gynecomastia vs. Male Breast Cancer

A known condition is a prior, not a verdict

The decision point

A unilateral, firm, progressive, nontender subareolar mass has only cancer adjectives. Klinefelter isn't the explanation — it's the risk factor (20–50× increased male breast cancer risk from a chronically elevated estrogen/androgen ratio). Image first, always.

Gynecomastia vs male breast cancer
GynecomastiaCancer
LateralityUsually bilateralUnilateral
PositionConcentric to the nippleEccentric, off-center
TextureRubbery, mobileFirm, fixed
TendernessOften tender earlyNontender
MarginsBlends into fatWell-defined or spiculated, ± calcifications
Skin / nippleNormalDimpling, retraction, ulceration, discharge
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a unilateral firm nontender subareolar mass and nipple retraction → Male breast cancer → mammography and biopsy
  2. 16 yo M with bilateral tender subareolar discs → Pubertal gynecomastia → reassurance
  3. 62 yo M with a breast mass and known Klinefelter syndrome → Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanation → biopsy anyway
  4. 55 yo M on spironolactone with bilateral tender gynecomastia → Drug-induced gynecomastia → change the agent
  5. 30 yo M with gynecomastia and a testicular mass → HCG-secreting germ cell tumor → ultrasound and tumor markers
  6. 62 yo M with soft symmetric fatty enlargement and no discrete mass → Pseudogynecomastia
Male breast cancer Risk factors: Klinefelter, BRCA2 (>BRCA1), family history, cirrhosis, obesity, chest radiation, exogenous estrogen · workup: mammography ± ultrasound → core biopsy · usually invasive ductal, >90% ER-positive → mastectomy + tamoxifen · every man with breast cancer gets genetic testing.
When it really is gynecomastia
  • Physiologic — three windows only: newborn, puberty (13–14, resolves in 1–2 yrs), elderly. Prepubertal gynecomastia is always pathologic.
  • Drugs (largest category): spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, finasteride, antipsychotics, digoxin, protease inhibitors, anabolic steroids, marijuana, alcohol
  • Cirrhosis · hyperthyroidism (↑SHBG → ↓free testosterone) · CKD · refeeding · hypogonadism
  • Tumors: hCG-secreting germ cell, Leydig/Sertoli, adrenal — gynecomastia + testicular mass → testicular ultrasound, hCG, AFP
Klinefelter 47,XXY; most common cause of primary hypogonadism and male infertility; tall with long limbs, small firm testes, sparse body hair; ↑FSH, ↑LH, ↓testosterone, ↑estradiol; seminiferous tubule hyalinization; also associated with mediastinal germ cell tumors, SLE, osteoporosis. Testosterone replacement does not restore fertility.
Transferable rule A known condition in the past medical history is a prior probability, not a verdict. If the lesion behaves differently than the known disease does, the known disease is the risk factor and something else is the diagnosis.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Hyperprolactinemia

Two-step inference, and a number that discriminates

The decision point

When a stem describes an illness and says the patient "remains on medication" without naming it, the question is a two-step inference: identify the drug class the illness requires, then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. Psychosis → antipsychotic → the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The number is the discriminator. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. A level of 70 assassinates the prolactinoma option without any imaging.

Mechanism & the antipsychotic ranking Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor; D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals like haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine, clozapine — which makes aripiprazole the answer to both "least likely to cause this" and "what should you switch to."
Hyperprolactinemia — causes by category
CategoryExamplesDiscriminator
PhysiologicPregnancy, nipple stimulation, stress, exercise, sleepPregnancy test first
DrugsAntipsychotics, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, SSRIs, opioids, estrogens, H2 blockersLevel 25–100
ProlactinomaMicro- or macroadenomaLevel >200; macroadenoma adds headache and bitemporal hemianopsia
Stalk effectAny sellar mass compressing the stalkModest elevation (<100) with a large mass on MRI
Hypothyroidism↑TRH stimulates lactotrophsTSH elevated
CKD, cirrhosisReduced clearance—
Workup order & two pituitary pearls Elevated prolactin → pregnancy test, TSH, medication review, renal function → only if all negative → MRI pituitary. Don't image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value — repeat with dilution. And prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically: dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine) are first-line even for macroadenomas because they shrink the tumor; surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.
Scenario bank
  1. Prolactin >200 with bitemporal hemianopsia → Macroprolactinoma → MRI → cabergoline
  2. Patient needs continued antipsychotic coverage → Switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine
  3. Prolactin 60 + TSH 25 + fatigue and cold intolerance → Hypothyroidism → levothyroxine
  4. Prolactin 45 on metoclopramide for gastroparesis → Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia
  5. Large sellar mass with prolactin only 45 → Stalk effect → a non-functioning mass, not a prolactinoma
  6. Huge pituitary mass with a normal-looking prolactin → Hook effect → dilute and repeat
  7. Amenorrhea + galactorrhea + negative pregnancy test → Prolactin and TSH before imaging
  8. Years of untreated hyperprolactinemia → Hypogonadism → infertility and osteoporosis
  9. Woman on an SSRI with new galactorrhea → Modest drug-induced elevation
Pairs with Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses owns the localization once the trophic-hormone pattern points at the region.
Transferable rule When a lab value has a well-known range that separates two candidate causes, the number is the discriminator, not the story.

Osteoporosis Screening

Verify each variable's direction

The decision point

DXA at age 65 for all women — or earlier if she has ≥1 risk factor (prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low BMI, chronic glucocorticoids). Run the risk-factor list before applying the age default. A patient with timely menopause and an empty list waits until 65.

⚠︎ Two ledgers. The rule above is the exam ledger and the operational shorthand. The USPSTF statement expresses the same idea quantitatively: screen before 65 when a FRAX-estimated 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk reaches that of a 65-year-old with no risk factors (~9.3%). The exam scores the risk-factor list; know FRAX for the clinic and for questions that hand you a percentage. Fully worked in the board-style brief DEXA: When Screening Starts Early.

The most common time-waster here: obesity is protective for osteoporosis, not a risk factor. The risk factor is low body weight (<58 kg / 127 lb) — higher weight increases bone density through mechanical loading and peripheral aromatization to estrogen.

Osteoporosis risk factors
NonmodifiableModifiable
Advanced age · postmenopausal · low body weight · White or Asian · malabsorption · hypercortisolism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism · RA · chronic liver or kidney diseaseSmoking · excess alcohol · sedentary lifestyle · glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, PPIs · vitamin D and calcium deficiency · estrogen deficiency (premature menopause, oophorectomy) · aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy
T-score vs Z-scorewhich scale, which patient, which cutoff
ScoreCompares toUse inCutoffs
T-scoreYoung healthy adult peakPostmenopausal women, men ≥50≥ −1.0 normal · −1.0 to −2.5 osteopenia · ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis
Z-scoreAge- and sex-matched peersPremenopausal women, men <50, children≤ −2.0 = below expected for age → hunt secondary causes
Diagnosis and treatment thresholds Osteoporosis can be diagnosed regardless of T-score by a fragility fracture of the hip or vertebra. Treat if: T ≤ −2.5, or prior hip/vertebral fragility fracture, or osteopenia plus FRAX ≥20% major osteoporotic or ≥3% hip.
Drug pearls Bisphosphonates first-line — upright with water, remain upright 30 min (esophagitis); long-term risks are osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture → drug holiday after ~5 yrs oral / 3 yrs IV if low risk · denosumab — rebound vertebral fractures if stopped abruptly, never simply discontinue · teriparatide/abaloparatide anabolic for very high risk · romosozumab carries a cardiovascular boxed warning · raloxifene lowers breast cancer risk but raises VTE · and the recycled one: correct vitamin D deficiency before starting a bisphosphonate or you precipitate hypocalcemia.
Scenario bank
  1. Same woman but weight 52 kg, smoker, mother fractured her hip → Run FRAX now → DXA if risk crosses threshold
  2. On prednisone 10 mg for 4 months → DXA now, regardless of age
  3. 68-year-old woman never screened → DXA now
  4. T-score −1.8 (osteopenia) → Run FRAX → treat if ≥20% major or ≥3% hip
  5. Premenopausal 32-year-old with a fragility fracture → Use the Z-score and work up secondary causes (celiac, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, eating disorder, amenorrhea)
  6. About to start alendronate → Check vitamin D and calcium first
  7. Thigh pain on long-term bisphosphonate → Atypical femoral fracture → imaging
  8. Man on androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer, or woman on an aromatase inhibitor → Screen with DXA
Transferable rule Before debating whether to screen early, verify each patient variable points the direction you assume it does. Obesity raises cardiovascular, endometrial, and OSA risk — and lowers osteoporosis risk. A variable's direction is disease-specific.
Salient decoy

Levothyroxine in Pregnancy

Hypothyroidism · the 30% rule · pregnancy-specific norms

The decision point

Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, and β-hCG (which shares an alpha subunit with TSH) stimulates the TSH receptor — so a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own. A patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate, so the answer is proactive: increase levothyroxine ~30% as soon as pregnancy is detected, even with a currently normal TSH. Waiting for the TSH to rise is the tested wrong move.

Defining criteria Dose rule — increase levothyroxine ~30% at the time pregnancy is detected · Monitoring — TSH every 4 weeks using pregnancy-specific norms; follow total T4 within pregnancy norms · Mechanism — estrogen raises TBG, more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor
Thyroid labs in normal first-trimester pregnancy
HormoneChangeInterpretation
Total T4IncreasedPhysiologic — TBG excess binds more hormone
Free T4Unchanged or mildly increasedThe value to trust
TSHDecreasedβ-hCG cross-reactivity — not hyperthyroidism
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F on a stable levothyroxine dose, positive home pregnancy test, TSH 1.8 → Increase the dose ~30% now → recheck TSH in 4 weeks
  2. 30 yo G1P0 at 9 weeks, asymptomatic, total T4 elevated, free T4 high-normal, TSH 0.3 → Normal pregnancy physiology → no treatment
  3. 31 yo F, hypothyroid, dose increased at 6 weeks; when to reassess → TSH in 4 weeks → pregnancy-specific norms
  4. 27 yo F with hypothyroidism taking liothyronine, planning pregnancy → Switch to levothyroxine before conception → T3 has a short half-life with wide level swings
  5. Mechanism: why does the levothyroxine requirement rise in pregnancy → Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulin → more hormone needed to saturate binding sites
Pearls Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment — the fetus depends on maternal T4 early · a low TSH with high total T4 in the first trimester is physiology, not Graves — free T4 decides · T3 (liothyronine) is never the pregnancy answer.
Pairs with Part I Levothyroxine Titration — same drug, opposite clock: outside pregnancy you wait 6–8 weeks for the TSH to be trustworthy; at conception you act before the TSH moves. Store the discriminator: "is she pregnant right now?"
Transferable rule When physiology predictably outruns a fixed drug dose, the exam rewards the pre-emptive adjustment — not the recheck-and-react answer that is correct in every other setting.
Treat-the-numberTSH 0.3 in early pregnancy invites antithyroid workup; β-hCG cross-reactivity is the explanation.
True-fact-wrong-slot"Recheck in 6–8 weeks" is the correct titration rule — placed in the one setting where acting first is right.

Congenital Hypothyroidism

read TSH direction and the neck to locate the defect · board question · is TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?

Source vignette Pt — 1 mo old, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since the first week, large tongue; no goiter described, maternal diet balanced with prenatal vitamins · Labs — TSH 110, T4 0.6 · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, panhypopituitarism and neonatal Graves disease
The decision point

Two stem facts close the question. TSH 110 with T4 0.6 puts the lesion below the pituitary — the feedback loop is intact and screaming, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright and neonatal Graves (which runs TSH-suppressed with high T4) is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins), which strips the two goitrous mechanisms — dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency — of their tell and leaves the default: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause; it explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

Defining criteria Primary congenital hypothyroidism — elevated TSH with low T4 (in-context: "increased TSH and decreased T4"); the diagnosis is made by newborn screening, not by symptoms · Prolonged (pathologic) neonatal jaundice — unconjugated jaundice persisting beyond age 2 weeks; it is the finding that converts a sleepy feeder into a thyroid workup
Pertinent positives & negatives TSH 110 with T4 0.6 — primary (glandular) failure; excludes panhypopituitarism and any central cause · Macroglossia + hoarse cry — mucopolysaccharide deposition in tongue and larynx; the specific soft-tissue signature of thyroid hormone deficiency, not of sepsis or a storage disease at this age · Direct bilirubin 0.7 of 8 — unconjugated; excludes biliary atresia and the cholestatic causes of the sick jaundiced neonate, and points at slowed gut motility plus reduced hepatic conjugating enzyme activity · No goiter described — argues against dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency, both of which enlarge the gland under TSH drive · Mother ate well and took prenatal vitamins; infant is formula-fed — iodine deficiency is off the table (formula is iodine-supplemented) · Normal tone with decreased activity — hypometabolism, not a neuromuscular disease; hypotonia may appear later and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis · Symptomatic at 1 month, not at birth — maternal T4 crossed the placenta and masked the deficit; timing is the concept's signature, not a distractor
Congenital hypothyroidism — locating the defect
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis/hypoplasia/ectopy)Failed formation or descent of the thyroid diverticulum from the pharyngeal floor along the thyroglossal duct; sporadic, no family historyHigh TSH, low T4, NO goiter, unremarkable maternal history; ectopic lingual tissue on scintigraphy— (the answer)
Dyshormonogenesis (thyroid peroxidase defect)Autosomal recessive enzyme block in organification; gland present but cannot make hormone, so TSH drive enlarges itGoiter in a hypothyroid newborn; consanguinity or affected sibling; deafness if Pendred ⚠︎No goiter, no family history; <15% of cases
Iodine deficiencyMaternal dietary lack in an endemic region; substrate, not machinery, is missing; goitrousMaternal diet/geography stated; goiter in mother and infantBalanced diet + prenatal vitamins; all formula contains iodine
Central (panhypopituitarism)Pituitary/hypothalamic failure; TSH is the deficient hormoneLOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4; midline defects (cleft lip/palate, single central incisor ⚠︎), micropenis, hypoglycemiaTSH 110 — the axis is intact and driving
Transplacental TSH-receptor stimulating antibodyMaternal Graves IgG crosses to the fetus → neonatal Graves, transient for weeks–months as antibody clears ⚠︎Low TSH, high T4, tachycardia, irritability, hyperphagia with poor weight gainDirection is inverted: TSH 110, T4 0.6, poor feeding and lethargy
Management, in one line Maternal TSH-receptor blocking antibody is the rare mirror of the last row — transient primary hypothyroidism with high TSH, indistinguishable from dysgenesis until it resolves ⚠︎.
Decision spine Is TSH high or low? — High → primary; the pituitary options are dead · Is T4 low? — Yes → hypothyroid, not a compensated or antibody-stimulated state · Is there a goiter? — No → not dyshormonogenesis, not iodine deficiency · Is there a maternal story? — Diet fine, no Graves → no acquired/transplacental cause · What's left is the default — dysgenesis, the most common cause; the home birth explains the delay in detection, not the disease
Scenario bank
  1. 3 wk M, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since week 1, large tongue; TSH 140, T4 0.5 → Start levothyroxine now → Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis
  2. 2 wk F with lethargy and poor feeding, firm anterior neck mass, older brother on levothyroxine, consanguineous parents; TSH 120, T4 0.4 → Dyshormonogenesis from a thyroid peroxidase defect → Levothyroxine; ultrasound shows an enlarged gland in place
  3. 5 d M with cleft palate, micropenis and fasting hypoglycemia; T4 low with TSH 0.8 → Central hypothyroidism from panhypopituitarism → Cortisol replacement before levothyroxine, then pituitary MRI
  4. 6 d F whose mother had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy; infant tachycardic, irritable, poor weight gain despite hyperphagia; TSH undetectable, T4 elevated → Start a beta blocker and methimazole → Neonatal Graves disease from transplacental TSH receptor stimulating antibody
  5. Newborn screen at 48 hours returns TSH 60 with low T4; the infant is asymptomatic and feeding well on examination → Start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging → Congenital hypothyroidism
  6. 3 wk M with poor feeding and prolonged jaundice, TSH 90 and T4 0.6, no palpable goiter; parents ask what caused it → Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide uptake scan → An absent or ectopic gland confirms dysgenesis
  7. 4 wk F starting levothyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism; the parent asks how to administer the crushed tablet → Mixing the dose into soy formula or an iron containing supplement → Crush and give in a small volume of water or breast milk
  8. 5 wk M with congenital hypothyroidism, total bilirubin 9 with direct 0.6, stools normally pigmented → Slowed gastrointestinal motility with reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugating enzyme activity → Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that resolves with levothyroxine
  9. 2 mo M diagnosed at 6 weeks and on levothyroxine for 4 weeks; TSH 45 with low normal free T4, parents confirm daily dosing → Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck in 4 weeks → Under replacement
  10. 3 mo F born where newborn screening is unavailable, never treated, now with developmental delay, poor linear growth and constipation; TSH 180, T4 0.3 → Start levothyroxine immediately → Untreated congenital hypothyroidism
Decoy note The home birth is the stem's most conspicuous detail and it is not a cause — it explains the missed newborn screen and therefore the unusual symptomatic presentation. The maternal diet sentence is a negative clue disguised as a positive one: it exists to kill option B. Primigravida, age 24, unremarkable family history are all inert here, though the absent family history does modestly argue against a recessive enzyme defect.
Pearls High TSH, low T4, no goiter is dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks-to-months, not at birth, is the fingerprint of congenital hypothyroidism — placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age earns a thyroid and a galactosemia thought; conjugated jaundice at any age earns a biliary one. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry equals mucopolysaccharide deposition — the exam's shorthand for hypothyroid soft tissue, distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia ⚠︎). · Treat on the screening result; imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks (in-context: no deficits when treatment begins in the neonatal period). · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn reroutes you to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem — dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. · In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified partner: The Sick Jaundiced Neonate with a Positive Screen — shared complaint (jaundiced newborn with an abnormal screen), discriminator as a question: is the hyperbilirubinemia conjugated, and is the infant ill or merely slow? Also pairs with Thyroid Mimics & Discriminators and Levothyroxine Titration, which own the adult version of the same TSH-direction logic and the dosing loop this brief only points at.
Transferable rule In any hormone-deficiency stem, the trophic hormone's direction locates the lesion — high TSH puts it in the gland, low TSH puts it in the pituitary — and once you are in the gland, the presence or absence of an organ (goiter or none) separates a machinery defect from a formation defect.
Class-vs-memberDefective thyroid peroxidase activity — Under 15% of cases and it almost always produces a goiter, which this exam does not describe; no family history in a recessive condition
True-fact-wrong-slotTransplacental TSH receptor–stimulating antibody — It causes neonatal Graves — suppressed TSH, high T4, tachycardia and hyperphagia; every value and symptom here is inverted
Salient decoyIodine deficiency, endemic goiter — That sentence excludes it: balanced diet plus prenatal vitamins, and all formula contains iodine
Test-overrides-findingsPanhypopituitarism — TSH 110 proves the pituitary is working; central disease gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH plus midline defects and micropenis

Inherited Tumor Syndromes

the visible lesion plus the organ pattern settles it · board question · What exactly is the retinal lesion, and what color is the skin patch?

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome
The decision point

The stem names the lesion for you: retinal hemangioblastoma, bilateral. That single identification closes the question, because no other option on the list produces one — NF1 gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules, MEN2B gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas, Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation, and Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor is the second half of the answer rather than a decoy: it reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion, and hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. The facial patch is what the question is actually testing — a single light brown macule is a normal café-au-lait spot, not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

Defining criteria The VHL testing gate — any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not · The café-au-lait gate — an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1; a few large macules with irregular borders, often segmental and respecting the midline, without freckling is McCune-Albright ⚠︎. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked · Patch color as a criterion — Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and belongs to a different family
Pertinent positives & negatives Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas — essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL and by itself triggers gene testing · Mother's adrenal tumor removed — pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern · A single light brown 4-cm patch — one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding; it is neither NF1's multiplicity nor Sturge-Weber's color · Age 16 with painless progressive blurring — VHL can present at any age but usually declares in early adulthood; vision falls from retinal edema and distortion · BP 110/72 and an otherwise normal examination — no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is precisely why surveillance exists
Inherited tumor syndromes — the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Von Hippel-LindauAutosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, CNS, adrenal medulla and kidneyRetinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma— (the answer)
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eyeMultiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; optic glioma and Lisch nodulesOne macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma
Sturge-Weber syndromeLeptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformationRed-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma ⚠︎The patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular
Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2BRET proto-oncogene; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomaConjunctival or corneal neuromas, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus ⚠︎Eye lesion is a hemangioblastoma; no thyroid disease
Li-Fraumeni syndromeAutosomal dominant TP53 loss; many tumor types across a young familySoft tissue sarcoma, early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma ⚠︎; no characteristic eye or skin lesionNo hemangioblastoma belongs to it
Other phakomatoses (tuberous sclerosis, NF2)Ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch, cardiac rhabdomyoma ⚠︎ · bilateral vestibular schwannomas ⚠︎The skin or the eighth nerve, not the retinaNeither lesion is present
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: confirm with VHL gene testing, then enter lifelong surveillance — retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI of brain and spine, MRI of abdomen — with resection of tumors as they appear and laser therapy as the preferred treatment for the retinal lesions (all in-context).
Decision spine Name the retinal lesion exactly. — Hemangioblastoma → VHL, and stop reading options · If it is a different eye lesion: — optic glioma or Lisch nodules → NF1; conjunctival neuromas → MEN2B; glaucoma with a choroidal malformation → Sturge-Weber · Read the skin patch's color. — Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine · Count the skin lesions. — One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 · Read the family's tumor for its organ. — Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS → VHL; adrenal medulla with thyroid → MEN2
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, a mother who had an adrenal tumor resected, and one light brown facial patch → Von Hippel-Lindau disease → The eye lesion names the syndrome
  2. 34 yo M with a solitary cerebellar hemangioblastoma and no family history of tumors → VHL gene testing → Testing follows the lesion, not the pedigree
  3. Newly confirmed von Hippel-Lindau disease; establishing surveillance → Retinal, adrenal, neuraxis and abdominal surveillance→ retinal examination, plasma metanephrines, MRI of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen; The four organs the syndrome occupies
  4. 22 yo F newly diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease, asked what it means for her 15-year-old brother → Offer him VHL gene testing now → each first-degree relative carries a 50% risk, and surveillance starts in childhood
  5. 40 yo M with von Hippel-Lindau disease and a 3 cm enhancing renal mass → Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy → Clear cell carcinoma, with more lesions expected
  6. 28 yo F with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, scheduled for resection → Alpha blockade started before any beta blockade → Unopposed alpha stimulation otherwise
  7. 4-month-old with a red-purple patch over the V1 distribution and a focal seizure → Brain MRI and ophthalmology referral→ for a leptomeningeal angioma and for glaucoma screening; Sturge-Weber syndrome
  8. 7-year-old with 8 cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and an optic glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1 → Multiplicity is the criterion, not presence
  9. 24-year-old with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of the lips and a marfanoid habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B → Neuromas rather than hemangioblastomas
  10. The molecular defect underlying von Hippel-Lindau disease → Loss of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3 → Autosomal dominant inheritance
  11. 9 year old with painless firm rubbery tongue nodules, marfanoid habitus and long fingers; the greatest threat to his life → Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2B — aggressive and early; prophylactic thyroidectomy often in infancy
