  12. Child with newly diagnosed MEN2B; what else must be evaluated → Plasma fractionated metanephrines → About half have phaeochromocytoma
  13. Adult with primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a gastrinoma → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 → No marfanoid habitus and no mucosal neuromas
  14. Patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, with a normal habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A → Parathyroid rather than neuromas separates 2A from 2B
  15. Child with perioral pigmented macules and recurrent intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Pigmented macules, not neuromas — the risk is polyps and cancer
  16. Adult with recurrent epistaxis and ruby mucosal papules that blanch with pressure → Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia → Telangiectasias blanch; neuromas do not
  17. Newborn with bilateral absence of the iris, hypospadias and an undescended left testis; the malignancy he is at risk for → Wilms tumour → WAGR — serial abdominal ultrasonography from infancy
  18. Newborn with aniridia and genitourinary anomalies; the underlying lesion → An 11p13 deletion → WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Range of developmental delay
  19. Why Wilms tumour in WAGR differs from isolated Wilms tumour → It is often bilateral and presents earlier → Isolated disease is usually unilateral at age 2 to 5
  20. Macrosomic newborn with macroglossia and hemihyperplasia at risk for embryonal tumours → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome → Overgrowth rather than aniridia
Decoy note Nearly two in five readers were captured by one sentence, and it is the skin sentence: the patch pulled 20% toward NF1 and 18% toward Sturge-Weber. Its actual content is a negative — a solitary café-au-lait macule is normal — so the stem's most conspicuous physical finding is the one that decides nothing. The mother's adrenal tumor is the opposite of a decoy: it is half the answer, supplying both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. And the normal blood pressure is inert for the diagnosis while quietly indicating that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.
Pearls Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. · A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma is a referral to genetics by itself — VHL testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. · Let the eye lesion name the syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL · optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 · conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B · choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. · Read a patch's color, not merely its presence: light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they belong to different syndromes. · VHL's organs are its surveillance list — retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla, kidney — which is why the follow-up is an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRIs. · Any pheochromocytoma in a young patient or with a family history is syndromic until proven otherwise: VHL, MEN2, NF1, or a hereditary paraganglioma gene ⚠︎. · Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Secondary Hypertension owns pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side — the same tumor reached from a different complaint. Store the discriminator as a question: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Candidate twin — confirm: a brief on the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set (NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber) does not exist yet; this brief wants it, and would hand off the non-tumor phakomatoses to it. Part I Precocious Puberty supplies the border and distribution attributes of the café-au-lait gate.
Transferable rule When a syndrome is identified by a visible lesion, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes while its identity is not — so name the tissue and the color before matching, and treat the most conspicuous physical finding as a candidate for being the one that decides nothing.
Unchecked attributeTwo café-au-lait macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and NF1’s six, so a reader carrying only a count rule lands on NF1 — the border, the segmental distribution and the absent freckling all say otherwise.
Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1 — One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome — The patch is the wrong kind: port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, this one is light brown and pigmented
True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome — TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma
Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B — Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has

Precocious Puberty

Central or peripheral, then read the skin · board question · which hormones are on board, and what does the skin look like?

Source vignette Pt — 6 yo F, breast budding and pubic hair, two large irregularly bordered hyperpigmented macules confined to the left chest and back without freckling, two long-bone fractures · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned McCune-Albright syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1 and an adrenal tumor
The decision point

The endocrine half of this stem does not discriminate — breast development plus pubic and axillary hair before age 8 establishes precocious puberty and stops there, because both central and peripheral causes produce it. What decides the question is everything that is not endocrine: two large macules with irregular contours confined to the left side, and two long-bone fractures in a 6-year-old. Those are the other two legs of a triad — peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia — and they name McCune-Albright syndrome, a somatic GNAS mutation causing constitutive G-protein activation, so the affected tissue secretes without waiting to be told. That is why the precocity is GnRH-independent, and why the same mutation can add thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome depending on which cell line carries it.

Defining criteria Precocious puberty — secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls or age 9 in boys · Central, GnRH-dependent — early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, so the whole axis turns on and puberty is consonant and progressive · Peripheral, GnRH-independent — premature sex-hormone secretion independent of GnRH, from gonad, adrenal or exogenous source · McCune-Albright triad — peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia presenting as recurrent fractures · The café-au-lait discriminators — NF1's macules are more numerous, at least six, with regular borders and axillary freckling; McCune-Albright's are few, large, irregularly bordered and often segmental, respecting the midline, without freckling (NF1 features in-context; the coast-of-Maine versus coast-of-California border naming and the segmental midline-respecting distribution are ⚠︎ memory-sourced)
Pertinent positives & negatives Breast budding and pubic hair together — oestrogen plus androgen, and an androgen-only source cannot produce the breast · No vaginal bleeding, headache, emesis or visual change — no mass effect, so the stem is pre-emptively excluding a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion · Two fractures at ages 4 and 5 — polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, because a healthy 6-year-old does not break long bones twice · Macules irregular in contour — the border is a criterion rather than a description, since NF1's are smooth-edged · Only two macules — below NF1's threshold of six and above the isolated-macule-is-normal bin, so the count falls between the two rules most readers carry · Confined to the left side — a segmental distribution, which is what a somatic mosaic mutation looks like on skin · No axillary freckling — stated as a negative specifically to retire NF1, whose cutaneous signature requires it · Family history unremarkable — consistent with a postzygotic somatic mutation, which is not inherited and carries no recurrence risk ⚠︎
Precocious puberty — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
McCune-Albright syndromeSomatic GNAS activating mutation, mosaic; autonomous hormone secretion from whichever tissue carries itPeripheral precocity with irregular unilateral café-au-lait macules and recurrent fractures; may add thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome— (the answer)
Adrenal tumourAutonomous adrenal androgen secretionIsolated premature adrenarche — pubic and axillary hair, acne, body odour, no breast development; rapid virilisationBreast budding is present, which androgens do not cause
Central precocious pubertyEarly axis activation, idiopathic in most girls or from a CNS lesionConsonant puberty with advanced bone age; LH rises on GnRH stimulation ⚠︎; MRI indicated in young children and most boys ⚠︎No skin or bone findings would be expected, and here both are present
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder; precocity via optic glioma at the hypothalamusAt least six café-au-lait macules with regular borders plus axillary freckling; Lisch nodules and long-bone dysplasiaTwo macules, irregular borders, and no freckling
Tuberous sclerosisNeurocutaneous hamartomas; precocity via brain hamartomaHypopigmented ash-leaf macules and shagreen patch, with seizures and cardiac rhabdomyoma ⚠︎The lesions are hyperpigmented rather than hypopigmented
Skin syndromes with no precocityPeutz-Jeghers: GI hamartomatous polyposis · Sturge-Weber: capillary-venous malformationPeutz-Jeghers: 1 to 5 mm perioral mucocutaneous macules · Sturge-Weber: red-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucomaNeither causes precocious puberty at all, and neither lesion matches
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in two sentences: central precocity is suppressed with a GnRH agonist, which works precisely because the axis is being driven from above ⚠︎, while peripheral precocity does not respond to a GnRH agonist and is treated by addressing the source — in McCune-Albright, aromatase inhibitors or oestrogen-receptor blockade ⚠︎. That inversion is the single most testable management point on the topic.
Decision spine Is this precocious puberty? — Secondary sexual characteristics before 8 in a girl, so yes · Which hormones? — Breast and hair, so oestrogen plus androgen, and an androgen-only source is out · Any mass-effect symptoms? — No headache, emesis or visual change, so the stem is closing the CNS door · What else is on the examination? — Macules and fractures, which are the discriminating data · Read the patch by its attributes. — Two, irregular, unilateral, no freckling — not NF1, not tuberous sclerosis, not Sturge-Weber
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo girl with breast budding and pubic hair, two large irregularly bordered hyperpigmented macules confined to the left chest and back without freckling, and two long-bone fractures at ages 4 and 5 → McCune-Albright syndrome → Peripheral precocity, irregular café-au-lait, fibrous dysplasia
  2. 6 yo girl with breast and pubic hair development, height crossing percentiles upward, advanced bone age and entirely normal skin → Measure basal LH with GnRH-stimulation testing if not diagnostic → Central precocious puberty
  3. 5 yo girl with confirmed central precocious puberty → Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain → Younger onset raises the risk of a CNS lesion
  4. 2 yo girl with isolated breast budding, no pubic hair, normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age → Reassurance and observation → Premature thelarche
  5. 7 yo girl with isolated pubic and axillary hair and body odor, no breast development, normal growth velocity → Reassurance with interval follow-up → Premature adrenarche
  6. 6 yo girl with pubic hair, clitoromegaly, severe acne and rapidly accelerating linear growth → Measure 17-hydroxyprogesterone → Virilization points at an adrenal source
  7. 7 yo boy with pubic hair and acne whose testes remain prepubertal in size → Evaluate for a peripheral androgen source → Bilateral testicular enlargement would indicate a central cause
  8. 4 yo girl with one large irregularly bordered macule, a femoral fracture, and biochemical thyrotoxicosis → McCune-Albright syndrome → Any endocrine organ carrying the mutation can be autonomous
  9. Distinguishing central from peripheral precocious puberty → LH response to GnRH stimulation → A rise indicates the axis is driving it
  10. Girl with McCune-Albright peripheral precocious puberty; which treatment will not be effective → GnRH agonist → The axis is not the driver
Decoy note The stem front-loads the endocrine complaint and buries the discriminators in the examination, which is what makes the wrong axis so easy to commit to. Note the two deliberate negatives: no headaches, emesis or visual disturbances closes the intracranial door before you open it, and no freckling is placed immediately after the macule description for one reason, to retire NF1 explicitly rather than by omission. The fracture history reads as incidental past medical history and is actually a third of the diagnosis; a stem that mentions two long-bone fractures in a preschooler is never making conversation.
Pearls Precocious puberty is a presenting complaint rather than a diagnosis: sort central from peripheral, then look outside the endocrine system for what names it. · Precocious puberty is a presenting complaint rather than a diagnosis. Sort central from peripheral, then look outside the endocrine system for what names it. · Breast tissue means oestrogen. An androgen-only source gives hair, acne and odour without breast development, and that single asymmetry eliminates a whole column of options. · Read a pigmented patch by four attributes: number, border, distribution and colour. NF1 is six or more, smooth-edged, with freckling; McCune-Albright is few, irregular and segmental; tuberous sclerosis is hypopigmented; Sturge-Weber is vascular red-purple. · A segmental lesion respecting the midline suggests somatic mosaicism, which is why McCune-Albright is not inherited and the family history is silent ⚠︎. · The GNAS mutation is organ-agnostic, so whichever tissue carries it secretes autonomously and thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome can replace or accompany the precocity. · GnRH agonists treat central precocity and do nothing for peripheral precocity — the inversion the exam likes, because the drug name sounds like it should work on anything hormonal ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Sexual Maturity Rating owns the staging framework and the timing gates and explicitly asked for this partner, and the discriminator between them is whether the stage is merely being described or is wrong for the age. Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes owns the café-au-lait gate from the tumour side, and this brief supplies the border and distribution attributes that gate is missing. Store the discriminator as a question: which hormones are on board, and what does the skin look like?
Transferable rule When every option is a named syndrome, the chief complaint is the thing they all share and therefore the thing that cannot decide — the answer lives in whichever physical finding only one syndrome produces. And a patch is described by four attributes for a reason: number, border, distribution and colour are each separately capable of eliminating a diagnosis. --- Batch 6, brief 03 · 2026-09-11.
Unchecked attributeAdrenal tumour — Adrenal tumours secrete androgens and produce isolated adrenarche; they cannot account for breast development
Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1 — Its macules are at least six, regular-bordered, with axillary freckling; this child has two, irregular, and the stem states no freckling
Class-vs-memberTuberous sclerosis — Its skin lesions are hypopigmented, and these are hyperpigmented
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome — The lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain rather than a pigmented macule, and it causes no precocious puberty
True-fact-wrong-slotPeutz-Jeghers syndrome — Those are 1 to 5 mm and perioral, not large truncal patches, and there is no precocious puberty

Marfanoid Habitus: Homocystinuria

Endocrine & Genetics · Marfanoid + stroke + ID = homocystinuria, not Marfan · lens direction confirms

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo F, sudden hemiparesis, developmental delay, fair skin, long thin limbs, decreased upper-to-lower segment ratio, joint hyperlaxity · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned homocystinuria, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and Marfan syndrome
The decision point

Three features separate homocystinuria from Marfan in a Marfanoid child: intellectual disability, thromboembolism (this child’s stroke), and downward lens dislocation (vs upward in Marfan). The fair complexion is a fourth clue — homocysteine interferes with melanin synthesis. Joint hyperlaxity occurs in both homocystinuria and EDS, but EDS does not produce a Marfanoid body habitus or stroke.

The miss: locking on joint hyperlaxity and skin hyperelasticity (the two features EDS and homocystinuria share) without asking what EDS does not explain: the Marfanoid proportions, the stroke, the developmental delay, and the fair complexion.

Defining criteria Homocystinuria — autosomal recessive, cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency; elevated homocysteine and methionine · Marfan vs homocystinuria — intellectual disability (homocystinuria) vs normal intellect (Marfan); thromboembolism (homocystinuria) vs aortic root dilation (Marfan); lens down (homocystinuria) vs lens up (Marfan) · Treatment — pyridoxine (B6), folate, B12 to lower homocysteine
The Marfanoid child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
HomocystinuriaAR, Marfanoid, ID, thrombosis, fair, lens downStroke or DVT in a Marfanoid child with intellectual disability—
Marfan syndromeAD, Marfanoid, aortic root dilation, lens up, normal IQTall + aortic dissection or lens up + normal intellectDevelopmental delay, stroke, fair skin
Ehlers-Danlos syndromeJoint hyperlaxity, skin hyperelasticity, easy bruisingJoint dislocations, tissue fragility, vascular ruptureNo Marfanoid habitus, no stroke from thrombosis
PhenylketonuriaAR, fair skin, ID, musty odor, eczemaFair + ID + musty odorNo Marfanoid habitus, no thrombosis
Fabry diseaseX-linked, angiokeratomas, neuropathy, corneal dystrophyBurning hands/feet, angiokeratomas, renal failureWrong habitus, no angiokeratomas
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo F with sudden hemiparesis, developmental delay, fair skin, long thin limbs, decreased upper-to-lower segment ratio, joint hyperlaxity → Homocystinuria → serum homocysteine and methionine levels
  2. 18 yo M, 195 cm tall, pectus excavatum, aortic root 4.8 cm, bilateral upward lens subluxation, normal IQ, no thrombosis history → Marfan syndrome → echocardiographic surveillance and beta-blocker
  3. 12 yo F with recurrent joint dislocations, velvety hyperextensible skin, easy bruising, normal height and proportions, normal intellect → Ehlers-Danlos syndrome → genetic testing for collagen defects
  4. Why patients with homocystinuria have fair skin and light hair → Excess homocysteine inhibits tyrosinase, reducing melanin production
  5. 8 yo M diagnosed with homocystinuria, elevated homocysteine → Pyridoxine with assessment for B6 responsiveness → first-line treatment
  6. 16 yo M with Marfanoid habitus and bilateral lens subluxation, the test that distinguishes homocystinuria from Marfan → Serum homocysteine level
  7. A child with confirmed homocystinuria, which of the following should be avoided → Nitrous oxide anesthesia → inactivates vitamin B12, worsening the metabolic block
Pearls Lens direction mnemonic — homocystinuria = down (the lens SINKs); Marfan = up and temporal · Homocystinuria thrombosis mechanism: homocysteine damages vascular endothelium and increases platelet adhesiveness — stroke, DVT, and PE can occur at any age · B6 responsiveness — divides management: B6-responsive (milder) do well on pyridoxine + folate + B12; B6-nonresponsive need dietary methionine restriction + betaine · Nitrous oxide — inactivates vitamin B12, contraindicated in homocystinuria · Both Marfan and homocystinuria cause ectopia lentis, but direction and cognition separate them
Pairs with Inherited Tumor Syndromes — shared domain: genetic syndromes with characteristic physical findings; discriminator: Marfanoid habitus vs café-au-lait macules.
Transferable rule When a Marfanoid child has any feature Marfan does not produce — intellectual disability, thrombosis, or fair complexion — the diagnosis is homocystinuria until proven otherwise, and the lens direction confirms it: down is homocystinuria, up is Marfan.
Salient decoyEDS tempts because joint hyperlaxity and skin hyperelasticity are shared features, but EDS does not produce Marfanoid habitus, stroke, or intellectual disability.
Mirror twinMarfan tempts because the Marfanoid habitus is the shared phenotype, but Marfan has normal intellect, no thrombosis, and lens dislocation is upward.

Endocrine & Bone

DEXA: When Screening Starts Early

Run the risk-factor list before applying the default

Source vignette Pt — postmenopausal woman with a prior wrist fragility fracture, a family history of hip fracture, 30 pack-years of smoking, and weight 50 kg · Q — the most appropriate screening step; options spanned DEXA now, FRAX now and DEXA at age 65
The decision point

Four screening risk factors — prior fragility fracture (wrist), family history of hip fracture, 30 pack-years, and low body weight (50 kg). Any one overrides the age-65 default → DEXA now.

This is a mirror twin, and the wrong answer is the twin's right answer. "DEXA at 65" is correct for the no-risk-factor version: 55 yo F, timely menopause, BMI 31, never smoked, no fractures.

⚠︎ Two ledgers on the early-screening trigger Exam ledger (bank, verbatim): DEXA "at age 65 years or earlier in those who have at least one risk factor — family history of hip fracture, prior fragility fracture, smoking history, low BMI, or use of corticosteroids."
Clinic ledger (USPSTF): under 65, screen when FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic risk ≥9.3%. The bank's version is the operational shorthand; the exam scores the shorthand.
Classification axes — DEXA timing
AxisThe settling sentenceConsequence
Risk-stratified?"sister… hip fracture" · "fracture of her right wrist in a fall" · "one pack daily for 30 years" · "50 kg"Age-65 default does not apply
Diagnosed?No DEXA performedAll pharmacotherapy is premature
Which bone fractured?Wrist, not hip or vertebraDoes not auto-diagnose osteoporosis → still needs DEXA
Lifestyle addressed?Physician already advised cessation, calcium, exerciseTier 1 is spent
Management ladder — osteoporosis screening & treatment
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Smoking cessation, calcium + vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall preventionAlways concurrent — never sufficient alone once a risk factor exists
2DEXAAge 65, or now with ≥1 risk factor
3BisphosphonateT ≤ −2.5 · or hip/vertebral fragility fracture · or T −1.0 to −2.5 with FRAX ≥20% major / ≥3% hip ⚠︎
Exit ramps Hip or vertebral fragility fracture → osteoporosis is diagnosed clinically → treat, don't just screen · chronic glucocorticoids → DEXA regardless of age · premenopausal or male <50 → Z-score and hunt secondary causes · aromatase inhibitor or ADT → screen · height loss or kyphosis → vertebral imaging.
Scenario bank
  1. 55 yo F, menopause at 50, BMI 31, never smoked, no fractures → DEXA at 65 → obesity is protective for bone
  2. 57 yo F with a vertebral compression fracture from standing height → Start a bisphosphonate now → osteoporosis is diagnosed clinically by the fragility fracture
  3. 48 yo F on prednisone 10 mg × 4 months → DEXA now, regardless of age
  4. 68 yo F, never screened → DEXA now
  5. 60 yo F, T-score −1.8 → Run FRAX → treat if ≥20% major or ≥3% hip
  6. 32 yo F with a fragility fracture → Use the Z-score; work up celiac, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, eating disorder
  7. 57 yo F starting alendronate → Check vitamin D and calcium first
  8. 72 yo M on androgen deprivation therapy → Screen with DEXA now
  9. 57 yo F, smoker, requesting HRT for bone protection → Avoid estrogen → smoking raises VTE risk, and HRT isn't first-line
Adversarial pass — one real hole The bank's list says "family history of hip fracture." FRAX asks specifically about a parental hip fracture, not a sibling's. It doesn't change this answer — three other factors qualify — but a stem whose only risk factor is a sibling fracture splits the ledgers. Parent counts everywhere; sibling counts on the exam.
Pairs with Part I Osteoporosis Screening. Store the discriminator as a question: "Does she have ≥1 risk factor — and did I actually count them?"
Transferable rule An age-based screening default is the answer only after the risk-factor list comes back empty. Run the list before applying the default.
Mirror twinSkipped tier

Diabetes: the Annual Care Bundle

Morbidity is not mortality

Source vignette Pt — 28 yo F, type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago, asymptomatic · Labs — A1c 6.1% · Q — the measure most likely to prevent disease-related morbidity; options spanned annual dilated eye examination, pneumococcal vaccination and monthly A1c measurement
The decision point

Morbidity ≠ death. Morbidity is disease burden — complications, disability. Mortality is death. They're paired precisely because they differ. "Prevent disease-related morbidity" in a diabetic means prevent the complications of diabetes, and the annual dilated eye exam catches the most common preventable one: retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced and the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.

Defining criteria A1c interval — every 3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; every 6 months when stable at goal · Pneumococcal vaccination — diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64
Outcome word → intervention selected
The stem asksIt meansIt selects
"prevent morbidity"Complications, disabilityScreening for the complication
"reduce mortality"DeathInterventions with survival data (COPD → LTOT)
"reduce hospitalization"AdmissionsThe driver of decompensation (CHF → BP control)
"most beneficial"Magnitude, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
The annual bundle Dilated eye exam annually · foot exam with monofilament annually · UACR + serum creatinine annually · blood pressure at every visit · lipids at least q5y · depression screening · weight and tobacco counseling.
⚠︎ Two problems with the vendor explanation 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It says vaccination "is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic" — but diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64. She is a candidate. E loses because vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes while the eye exam targets a diabetes-specific complication — not because she doesn't qualify.
2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals are ADA Standards of Care, not USPSTF.
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90–120 day RBC lifespan, so consecutive monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows. Intervals: q3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; q6 months if stable and at goal. At A1c 6.1% she's at goal → 6-month schedule, making monthly wrong by a factor of six.
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F, T2DM ×1 month, A1c 6.1%, asymptomatic → Annual dilated eye exam (plus foot exam, UACR)
  2. 28 yo F, T2DM at goal, asks about A1c frequency → Check the A1c every 6 months
  3. 28 yo F, T2DM, A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent → Check the A1c every 3 months
  4. 32 yo F, type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 → 5 Years after diagnosis → in type 2 diabetes screening starts at diagnosis
  5. 55 yo M, T2DM, question asks what reduces mortality → Smoking cessation, then BP and statin → not the eye exam
  6. 60 yo F, T2DM, UACR 85 mg/g → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor
  7. 45 yo M, T2DM, painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head → Neuropathic ulcer → off-loading + glycemic control
  8. 28 yo F with T2DM, due for vaccines; in addition to influenza → Pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is itself an ACIP indication at 19–64
Pairs with Part I Diabetic Nephropathy Screening — the renal limb of the same bundle. Store the discriminator: "Which outcome word is in the stem?"
Transferable rule Read the outcome noun before the options. Morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and benefit are four different targets, and a question can place the right intervention for the wrong target among the distractors.

Hematology 6 topics + 3 board-style

Anemia is sorted by the smear and the reticulocyte count before any name is reached; the drug, the platelet count and the direct antiglobulin test decide the rest.

Anemia with Thrombocytopenia

the smear, the Coombs and the coags name the process · board question · Are two cell lines down, is the smear sheared, and are the coagulation studies normal?

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo, bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric · Q — the expected laboratory value; options spanned a decreased platelet count, an increased serum haptoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test
The decision point

The stem hands you two legs of a three-legged syndrome and asks for the third. Scleral icterus with fatigue is hemolytic anemia; anuria for 24 hours with pedal edema is acute kidney injury; and the missing leg of hemolytic uremic syndrome is thrombocytopenia. The mechanism supplies it: Shiga toxin damages endothelium, platelets are consumed into microthrombi, and red cells are sheared as they pass — so the platelet count falls because of the same process that produces the schistocytes and the bilirubin. The bloody diarrhea a week ago, in a cluster of people who ate together and recovered, is the exposure that starts the clock.

Defining criteria HUS triad — microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury (rising BUN and creatinine) · Microangiopathic hemolysis — red cells sheared by platelet microthrombi, giving schistocytes, increased indirect bilirubin, and decreased haptoglobin · The preceding illness — Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae; bloody diarrhea first, with HUS appearing about a week later · Coombs in HUS — negative, because the red cells are destroyed mechanically rather than coated by antibody
Pertinent positives & negatives Bloody diarrhea one week ago — Shiga toxin colitis; the one-week latency between the diarrhea and the syndrome is the concept's signature · Shared meal with relatives who recovered — a point-source exposure that confirms the organism and explains nothing about the labs; most infected people never develop HUS ⚠︎ · Anuria for 24 hours with normal intake, plus 2+ pedal edema — acute kidney injury with volume overload, the third leg · Scleral icterus — indirect hyperbilirubinemia from hemolysis, the first leg · Fatigue and refusing to get out of bed — symptomatic anemia rather than ongoing volume loss; the diarrhea has resolved · No bruising or petechiae described — consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS is often not severe enough to bleed; its absence never argues against the diagnosis · No fever or neurologic change — argues away from the TTP end of the family and from sepsis-driven DIC ⚠︎
Anemia with thrombocytopenia — the differential
ProcessIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hemolytic uremic syndromeChild, Shiga toxin colitis, then endothelial injury with platelet microthrombi ~1 week laterBloody diarrhea → anemia + low platelets + AKI, normal coags, negative Coombs— (the answer)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpuraAdult; ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultralarge von Willebrand multimers ⚠︎Fever and neurologic changes without diarrhea; plasma exchange, not supportive care ⚠︎Age 7, preceding bloody diarrhea, no fever or neurologic findings
Disseminated intravascular coagulationA severely ill patient — sepsis, trauma, malignancy; consumption of factors as well as plateletsProlonged PT and aPTT with low fibrinogen ⚠︎ alongside the schistocytesPT is normal in HUS; no critical illness described
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG coats red cells; lupus, lymphoproliferative disease, or a drugDirect Coombs positive; spherocytes, not schistocytes; platelets and kidneys sparedRenal failure and edema, which antibody-mediated hemolysis does not cause
Isolated thrombocytopenia (immune)Low platelets alone after a viral illness; bruising and petechiae in a well childNormal hemoglobin and a normal smear — one cytopenia, not twoAnemia, jaundice and anuria are all present
Management, in one line Management is not this question's fork, so in one sentence: HUS is treated supportively — fluid and electrolyte management, transfusion, and dialysis when needed — with antibiotics and antimotility agents withheld in suspected Shiga toxin infection ⚠︎.
Decision spine How many cell lines are down? — Anemia plus a consumed platelet count → the microangiopathy family, not a single-lineage problem · Is the hemolysis mechanical or immune? — Schistocytes with a negative Coombs → mechanical shearing · Are the coagulation studies normal? — Yes → HUS or TTP, not DIC · Which organ, and what came first? — Kidney, after bloody diarrhea in a child → HUS · Now read each marker off the mechanism — haptoglobin consumed and falling, reticulocytes rising, indirect bilirubin rising, Coombs negative
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo with bloody diarrhea a week ago, now anuric and icteric; which laboratory value is expected → A decreased platelet count → The third leg of the HUS triad
  2. 5 yo on day 3 of bloody diarrhea, stool culture pending, well hydrated and making urine → Supportive care with fluids, withholding antibiotics → Antibiotics may increase Shiga toxin release
  3. 7 yo with hemolytic uremic syndrome, hemoglobin 6.2, urine output 10 mL/h, potassium 6.8 → Hemodialysis → Supportive care includes dialysis
  4. 42 yo F with fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets 15,000, normal PT and normal creatinine → Plasma exchange → Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  5. 42 yo F with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, platelets 12,000, no active bleeding → Platelet transfusion → It feeds the microthrombi
  6. 60 yo M with gram-negative sepsis, schistocytes, platelets 40,000, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis → Disseminated intravascular coagulation is secondary
  7. 9 yo F with 2 weeks of jaundice and fatigue, spherocytes on smear, direct Coombs positive, normal platelets and creatinine → Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia → Antibody-coated cells rather than sheared ones
  8. Child with brisk hemolysis; why the serum haptoglobin falls rather than rises → It binds free hemoglobin and the complex is cleared → Consumed, unlike the acute-phase reactants
  9. 6 yo with bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pale with hemoglobin 8 and platelets 60,000; confirming the mechanism → Peripheral blood smear for schistocytes → Mechanical hemolysis
  10. 5 yo, well appearing, petechiae 2 weeks after a viral illness, platelets 20,000, hemoglobin 12.8, otherwise normal smear → Immune thrombocytopenia → One cytopenia with no hemolysis
Decoy note The cookout and the recovered relatives are epidemiology, not pathophysiology — they confirm a point-source Shiga toxin exposure and settle no laboratory value. "Significant blood in his stool, which has since resolved" is the sharpest bait: it invites an iron-deficiency answer for bleeding that stopped days ago and was never chronic. And the absence of bruising or petechiae quietly tempts you away from the platelet answer, when consumptive thrombocytopenia in HUS frequently produces no bleeding at all.
Pearls Bloody diarrhea a week ago plus anuria and jaundice is HUS: schistocytes, low platelets, rising creatinine, and a negative Coombs. · Two cytopenias with schistocytes means mechanical destruction, and mechanical destruction means the Coombs is negative by definition — nothing is antibody-coated. · Haptoglobin is consumed in hemolysis while ferritin and other acute-phase reactants rise; a marker's direction follows from whether the process uses it up or the liver makes more of it. · Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis and fall in marrow failure — a falling reticulocyte count in a known hemolytic patient is aplastic crisis until proven otherwise ⚠︎. · Normal coagulation studies separate HUS and TTP from DIC; the kidney after bloody diarrhea in a child is HUS, the brain without diarrhea in an adult is TTP ⚠︎. · The two transfusions to withhold: platelets in TTP, which feed the microthrombi ⚠︎, and antibiotics in suspected Shiga toxin colitis, which may increase toxin release ⚠︎.
Pairs with Verified: Part II NSAID Prerenal AKI in a Child owns the acute-kidney-injury compartments and carries the HUS row from the renal side, and Part II Hereditary Spherocytosis owns the Coombs-negative hemolysis fork when the platelets and kidneys are normal. This brief owns the case where both cell lines fall together. Store the discriminator as a question: is a second cell line down, and is the smear sheared or spherocytic? Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis owns the other side of the platelet count, where hemolysis arrives with a normal platelet count and an antibody rather than a clot.
Transferable rule When a question asks which laboratory abnormality is "associated," it is testing the direction each marker moves under a stated mechanism, not whether you can name the marker — so derive direction from the mechanism (consumed or produced, mechanical or immune), and when the findings assemble a named syndrome, enumerate its triad rather than re-deriving each leg.
Unchecked attributeIncreased serum haptoglobin — The direction is inverted — haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed, so it falls in hemolysis
True-fact-wrong-slotPositive direct Coombs test — Coombs detects antibody-coated cells; HUS destroys red cells mechanically, so it is negative — and antibody hemolysis would not cause anuria and edema
Salient decoyDecreased ferritin level — The bleeding was acute and has resolved; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and rises with inflammation
Class-vs-memberIncreased PT — DIC also consumes clotting factors and needs a critically ill patient; in HUS the PT is normal
Unchecked attributeDecreased reticulocyte count — Reticulocytes rise in hemolysis; a falling count means the marrow has stopped, which is a different disease

Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis

exposure and latency name the mechanism · board question · Which drug was given, how long ago, and are the platelets and liver enzymes normal?

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo F with pneumonia, develops dark urine and abdominal pain one hour after intravenous ceftriaxone · Labs — hemoglobin 6.3, platelets normal, liver enzymes normal · Q — the most appropriate test; options spanned the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, a glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level and a serum fibrinogen level
The decision point

Three numbers close this, and none of them is the hemoglobin. Platelets 285,000 is normal, which kills disseminated intravascular coagulation and makes the fibrinogen pointless, because that is a consumptive process and cannot spare the platelet count. Alkaline phosphatase 66 with AST 42 and ALT 28 are all normal, which kills biliary obstruction and makes both abdominal images pointless; the bilirubin of 2.3 is therefore unconjugated, from red-cell breakdown rather than from a blocked duct. What is left is hemolysis, and the discrimination is between its two drug mechanisms — and here the stem is unusually generous, because it gives both discriminating attributes. The drug is a cephalosporin, which hemolyses by coating the erythrocyte as a hapten so IgG attaches and splenic macrophages destroy it. The latency is one hour, while oxidative hemolysis from G6PD deficiency arrives 2 to 4 days after exposure, and neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant in the first place. Immune hemolysis is diagnosed by detecting IgG or C3 on the red cell — the direct antiglobulin test.

Defining criteria Hapten mechanism — the drug binds the erythrocyte surface, IgG attaches to the drug-cell complex, and splenic macrophages destroy the coated cell, which is extravascular hemolysis; penicillins and cephalosporins do this · Immune-complex mechanism — the drug triggers immune complexes that fix complement for intravascular destruction · Onset — within hours to a few days of exposure for drug-induced immune hemolysis, and 2 to 4 days for G6PD oxidative hemolysis · The confirmatory test — the direct antiglobulin test, which detects IgG or C3 on the erythrocyte surface · Supporting laboratory pattern — raised indirect bilirubin, LDH and reticulocytes, low haptoglobin, and spherocytes on the smear · The commonest triggers — NSAIDs such as diclofenac, penicillins such as piperacillin, and cephalosporins such as ceftriaxone · The coagulation gate — a normal prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time alongside a normal platelet count exclude the consumptive causes and, with no trauma, exclude retroperitoneal hemorrhage as well
Pertinent positives & negatives Symptoms one hour after the first dose — the latency itself is diagnostic, because it is too fast for oxidative injury · Ceftriaxone — a named hapten-type trigger, and the single most important word in the stem · Platelets 285,000 — excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation and every consumptive microangiopathy, so the fibrinogen would be normal too · ALP 66, AST 42, ALT 28 — excludes biliary obstruction, and both imaging options die here rather than on clinical judgment · Total bilirubin 2.3 with normal liver enzymes — an unconjugated rise, which is a hemolysis pattern rather than a hepatobiliary one · Dark urine — hemoglobinuria or urobilinogen from hemolysis; in a child with normal liver tests this is red cells rather than bile · Mild upper abdominal tenderness — severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain, while biliary obstruction would hurt considerably more · Creatinine 0.9 — no renal failure, which argues against a microangiopathy and against massive intravascular hemolysis
Acute hemolysis in a hospitalized patient — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Drug-induced immune hemolytic anemiaA cephalosporin, penicillin or NSAID coats the red cell as a hapten, IgG binds, and the spleen clears itHemolysis within hours of the drug, normal platelets, positive direct antiglobulin test— (the answer)
G6PD deficiencyOxidant stress depletes glutathione; sulfonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, fava beans ⚠︎Hemolysis 2 to 4 days after an oxidant, bite cells and Heinz bodies, with a negative direct antiglobulin testOne hour, and neither drug is a typical oxidant
Mycoplasma cold agglutinin hemolysisAtypical pneumonia drives IgM against the I antigen, which fixes complement ⚠︎Direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 only, cold agglutinins, following the pneumonia by 1 to 2 weeks ⚠︎Onset one hour after the drug rather than weeks into the illness
Disseminated intravascular coagulation Can't missConsumptive coagulopathy from sepsis or shockSchistocytes, severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, prolonged coagulation timesPlatelets 285,000, which is normal
Biliary obstructionA stone or sludge blocks the ductSevere pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemiaALP 66, AST 42 and ALT 28 all normal, with mild pain
Acute hemolytic transfusion reactionABO incompatibility drives complement-mediated intravascular lysis ⚠︎Fever, back pain and dark urine minutes into a transfusionNo transfusion was given
Management, in one line Management is two sentences, because this stem asked only for the test: discontinue the offending drug, which usually resolves the hemolysis within hours to days, and transfuse if the anemia is severe, with glucocorticoids and IVIG reserved for severe cases.
Decision spine Is this hemolysis? — Anemia, unconjugated bilirubin, dark urine, normal liver enzymes → yes · Are the platelets normal? — 285,000 → the consumptive causes are gone, and so is the fibrinogen option · Are the liver enzymes normal? — Alkaline phosphatase and transaminases normal → both abdominal images are gone · Which drug, and how long ago? — Ceftriaxone, one hour → hapten rather than oxidant · What detects a hapten-driven process? — IgG on the red cell → the direct antiglobulin test
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo girl with pneumonia who develops dark urine, abdominal pain and hemoglobin 6.3 one hour after intravenous ceftriaxone, with normal platelets and normal liver enzymes → Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test → Immune-mediated hemolysis
  2. 5 yo girl with hemolysis after ceftriaxone whose direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG → Discontinue the ceftriaxone → Withdrawal resolves the hemolysis
  3. A 5-year-old girl with pneumonia develops immune hemolysis after intravenous ceftriaxone. Her hemoglobin falls to 4.5 g/dL with tachycardia, lethargy, and continued dark urine. → Transfuse and discontinue the offending drug → Severity gates transfusion
  4. 7 yo boy on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days with dark urine, bite cells and Heinz bodies on smear and a negative direct antiglobulin test → Stop the drug and measure glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase after recovery → Oxidative rather than immune hemolysis
  5. Child with known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency who needs antibiotic coverage for pneumonia; which agent to avoid → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole → Oxidant exposure precipitates hemolysis
  6. Adolescent 10 days into an atypical pneumonia who develops anemia and jaundice, with cold agglutinins and a direct antiglobulin test positive for C3 but not IgG → Mycoplasma-associated cold agglutinin hemolysis → IgM fixes complement on the red cell
  7. Child with drug-induced immune hemolysis whose drug was stopped 2 days ago, with a stable and rising hemoglobin and residual mild jaundice → Observation without glucocorticoids → Drug withdrawal is the treatment
  8. Hospitalized septic child with hemolysis, platelets 18,000, schistocytes on smear and a low fibrinogen → Treat the underlying sepsis with coagulation support → Consumptive coagulopathy
  9. Child 15 minutes into a packed red cell transfusion who develops fever, back pain and dark urine → Stop the transfusion immediately → Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction
  10. How cephalosporins and penicillins produce hemolytic anemia → The drug binds the erythrocyte surface as a hapten, IgG attaches, and splenic macrophages destroy the cell → Extravascular hemolysis
Decoy note The stem's abdominal findings do almost all of the misdirection. Upper abdominal discomfort, mild upper abdominal tenderness and a bilirubin of 2.3 assemble into a biliary picture for anyone who reads symptoms before chemistry, and two of the five options are abdominal imaging, which validates the impulse. But the actual reason for the pain is not the gallbladder: severe hemolysis causes abdominal or back pain from red-cell destruction in the vertebral bodies, liver and spleen. The other quiet detail is azithromycin, present to make you think of Mycoplasma and its cold agglutinins — a real cause of hemolysis in a child with pneumonia, and one that would give a C3-positive test rather than a negative one, so it still routes to the same answer.
Pearls Hemolysis within hours of a cephalosporin or penicillin is hapten-mediated and IgG-coated, so the direct antiglobulin test is what reveals it. · Latency is a diagnostic variable. Immune drug hemolysis arrives in hours, oxidative hemolysis in 2 to 4 days, and cold agglutinin hemolysis a week or two into the pneumonia that caused it ⚠︎. · Penicillins and cephalosporins hemolyse by hapten adsorption with IgG and splenic clearance — extravascular, spherocytes, positive direct antiglobulin test. · A normal platelet count excludes the consumptive causes. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and hemolytic uremic syndrome all destroy platelets, and drug-induced immune hemolysis does not touch them. · Normal alkaline phosphatase and transaminases with a raised bilirubin means hemolysis rather than obstruction — the enzymes separate the two, not the pain. · The direct antiglobulin test distinguishes what is stuck to the cell: IgG for warm and hapten-mediated disease, C3 for complement-fixing IgM such as cold agglutinins ⚠︎. · The treatment is stopping the drug; steroids and IVIG are for severe cases, and continuing the drug while treating the hemolysis is the error the bank tests.
Pairs with Verified: Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia owns the seam on the other side of the platelet count, where hemolysis arriving with thrombocytopenia means the smear and the coagulation studies name a different process. Part II Hereditary Spherocytosis owns the Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia that mirrors this brief's Coombs-positive one, and Part I Pediatric Community-Acquired Pneumonia carries the Mycoplasma cold-agglutinin association. Store the discriminator as a question: which drug, how many hours, and is the platelet count normal?
Transferable rule When two options are two mechanisms of the same syndrome, the stem has almost always supplied the attribute that separates them, usually an exposure and an interval, and the test you choose is downstream of the mechanism rather than of the syndrome. Spherocytes with a normal platelet count means an antibody; schistocytes with a low platelet count means a clot. --- Batch 5, brief 05 · 2026-09-10.
Unchecked attributeRetroperitoneal hemorrhage does cause back pain with acute anemia, but it follows trauma or a coagulopathy — a normal PT and aPTT with no injury retires it.
True-fact-wrong-slotAnaphylaxis to a beta-lactam is real, but it arrives within seconds to minutes with rash and edema, and it does not cause anemia.
Unchecked attributeGlucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level — Neither ceftriaxone nor azithromycin is a typical oxidant, and that hemolysis arrives 2 to 4 days after exposure rather than in one hour
True-fact-wrong-slotCT scan of the abdomen — Obstruction produces severe pain with raised alkaline phosphatase and transaminases, and all three are normal here
Sequencing trapLiver ultrasonography — The same failure as the CT, and it cannot explain a hemoglobin of 6.3
Unchecked attributeSerum fibrinogen level — That disease is consumptive and requires severe thrombocytopenia with prolonged coagulation times; platelets are 285,000

Hemoglobinuria: the Dipstick-Microscopy Mismatch

Hematology · heme-positive dipstick with no RBCs · the mismatch names the source

Source vignette Pt — 62 yo M with a mechanical mitral valve, dark urine · Labs — dipstick heme-positive with 1 RBC per high-power field, LDH 380, haptoglobin undetectable · Smear — schistocytes · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned intravascular hemolysis from the prosthetic valve, warfarin-related hematuria and infective endocarditis
The decision point

The urine dipstick detects the heme moiety — it cannot distinguish hemoglobin from myoglobin from intact red blood cells. When the dipstick is positive but the microscope shows 0–2 RBC/hpf, free hemoglobin or myoglobin is in the urine, not blood. This patient has a mechanical valve, schistocytes, elevated LDH, and low haptoglobin — textbook intravascular hemolysis — so the free pigment is hemoglobin released from sheared red cells passing through the prosthetic valve.

The miss: focusing on dark urine as gross hematuria rather than stopping at the mismatch. The dipstick said yes; the microscope said no. That contradiction is the entire question.

Defining criteria Dipstick-microscopy mismatch — heme-positive dipstick with ≤2 RBC/hpf on microscopy means free pigment, not bleeding · Hemoglobinuria clues — low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, schistocytes, indirect hyperbilirubinemia · Myoglobinuria clues — CK >10,000, muscle pain, recent crush/exertion/seizure
Heme-positive urine — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Mechanical valve hemolysisProsthetic valve, chronic mild hemolysis, dark urineDipstick+, no RBCs, schistocytes, low haptoglobin—
Anticoagulant hematuriaOn warfarin; dark/red urineRBCs present on microscopy0–2 RBC/hpf
RhabdomyolysisCrush injury, exertion, seizure; dark urineCK >10,000; also dipstick+/RBC−No muscle symptoms, no CK elevation
GlomerulonephritisProteinuria, dysmorphic RBCs, RBC castsRBCs and casts on microscopyNo RBCs, no casts
EndocarditisProsthetic valve + fever, new murmurFever, positive blood cultures, vegetationsAfebrile, no systemic infection
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a mechanical mitral valve, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 1 RBC per high-power field, LDH 380, haptoglobin undetectable, schistocytes on smear → Intravascular hemolysis from the prosthetic valve → monitor hemoglobin, supplement iron and folate
  2. 28 yo M found unconscious after a building collapse, dark brown urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 45,000 → Rhabdomyolysis → aggressive IV normal saline
  3. 45 yo F with dark urine and a heme-positive dipstick showing 0 RBCs on microscopy, the best test to distinguish hemoglobinuria from myoglobinuria → Serum creatine kinase
  4. 58 yo M with a mechanical aortic valve and worsening hemolytic anemia despite optimized anticoagulation, hemoglobin 7.2, reticulocytes 18% → Refer for valve replacement or repair → severe paravalvular hemolysis
  5. Why the dipstick is positive for blood when no red blood cells are seen on microscopy → The dipstick detects the heme moiety in free hemoglobin or myoglobin, not intact red blood cells
  6. 35 yo F with SLE, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts → Lupus nephritis → renal biopsy
  7. 24 yo M after a marathon, dark urine, heme-positive dipstick with 0 RBCs, CK 32,000, creatinine 2.4 → IV normal saline at 200 to 300 mL per hour → rhabdomyolysis with AKI
Pearls The dipstick-microscopy mismatch is the entire question: dipstick detects heme, not cells; positive dipstick + no RBCs = free pigment · Hemoglobin vs myoglobin — CK is the separator; CK >10,000 with muscle symptoms = myoglobin; normal CK with hemolysis markers = hemoglobin · Mild chronic hemolysis from a well-functioning mechanical valve is expected; worsening anemia or rising LDH suggests paravalvular leak → echo → possible reoperation · Schistocytes confirm mechanical fragmentation — they tie hemolysis to the valve rather than autoimmune or drug cause · Haptoglobin — consumed by binding free hemoglobin; most sensitive marker of intravascular hemolysis but also an acute-phase reactant (can be falsely normal during infection)
Pairs with Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis — shared finding: intravascular hemolysis with schistocytes; discriminator: is there a mechanical source?
Transferable rule When the dipstick says blood and the microscope says no, the question is not “where is the bleeding” but “where is the free pigment coming from” — and CK separates muscle from red cell, while the clinical context names the mechanism.
Unchecked attributeAnticoagulant hematuria tempts because the patient is on warfarin, but the RBC count on microscopy was not checked.
Salient decoyEndocarditis tempts because there is a prosthetic valve, but there is no fever or systemic infection.
Mirror twinRhabdomyolysis also causes dipstick+/RBC− mismatch, but there are no muscle symptoms and no CK elevation.

Microcytic Anemia: Iron First

Hematology · iron studies before electrophoresis · iron deficiency masks thalassemia

The decision point

Both iron deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia trait produce a low MCV. The reflex is to order hemoglobin electrophoresis, but iron deficiency lowers HbA2, the very marker electrophoresis uses to diagnose beta-thalassemia trait. If you run electrophoresis on an iron-deficient patient, a falsely normal HbA2 will mask coexisting thalassemia. The rule: iron studies first, correct the iron, then electrophoresis.

This is not a knowledge gap about the diseases; it is a sequencing rule about the tests.

Defining criteria Iron studies first — ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; iron deficiency must be corrected before electrophoresis is interpretable · HbA2 masking — iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 into the normal range · Beta-thalassemia trait HbA2 — elevated (>3.5%) only when iron stores are replete
Microcytic anemia — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellFirst test
Iron deficiency anemiaMenstrual loss, vegan/poor diet, GI bleed; low MCVLow ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin satIron studies
Beta-thalassemia minorMediterranean/Asian, lifelong mild anemia, target cellsElevated HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis (only when iron-replete)Iron studies first
Alpha-thalassemia minorSoutheast Asian/African, mild microcytic anemiaNormal electrophoresis; diagnosis by exclusion or gene testingIron studies → electrophoresis → gene analysis
Lead poisoningChild in old housing, developmental delay, abdominal painBasophilic stippling; elevated lead levelLead level
Anemia of chronic diseaseChronic infection, autoimmunity, malignancyLow iron, low TIBC (iron sequestered, not absent); ferritin normal/highIron studies
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, MCV 68, hemoglobin 9.2, the most appropriate initial test → Iron studies → iron deficiency must be assessed before electrophoresis is interpretable
  2. 15 yo F with confirmed iron deficiency anemia from heavy menses, hemoglobin 9.2, hemodynamically stable → Oral iron supplementation and reassess in 4 to 6 weeks
  3. 22 yo M of Mediterranean descent, MCV 64, hemoglobin 11.5, iron studies normal, HbA2 5.8% → Beta-thalassemia minor → genetic counseling
  4. Why hemoglobin electrophoresis can miss beta-thalassemia trait in an iron-deficient patient → Iron deficiency suppresses HbA2 production, normalizing a value that would otherwise be elevated
  5. 3 yo M in old housing with developmental delay, microcytic anemia, and basophilic stippling on smear → Lead poisoning → serum lead level and chelation if elevated
  6. 28 yo F of Southeast Asian descent, MCV 72, hemoglobin 11.0, normal iron studies, normal electrophoresis → Alpha-globin gene deletion analysis → alpha-thalassemia minor
  7. 18 yo F treated for iron deficiency with 3 months of oral iron, ferritin now 45, but MCV remains 66 and hemoglobin 10.8 → Hemoglobin electrophoresis → possible coexisting thalassemia trait
  8. 2 yo M, well-child visit, five 8-oz cups of whole cow milk daily, pale with tachycardia and a flow murmur, Hb 8, MCV 70, erythrocytes 3.1 million/uL, platelets and leukocytes normal → Elevated red cell distribution width → iron deficiency anemia
  9. 2 yo of Greek descent, MCV 65, Hb 10.2, erythrocytes 5.4 million/uL, RDW normal, ferritin and iron studies normal → Beta-thalassemia trait → a normal red cell count with a low MCV
  10. 2 yo M with Hb 8 and MCV 70 whose diet is cheese, yogurt and roughly 40 oz of whole cow milk daily → Limit cow milk below 24 oz per day and begin an empiric oral iron trial → iron deficiency from excessive milk intake
  11. Why the red cell distribution width rises in iron deficiency but stays normal in thalassemia trait → Iron available for erythropoiesis fluctuates, so cells are made at varying sizes → thalassemia produces uniformly small cells
  12. 16 yo F with heavy menses, a low MCV, a low erythrocyte count, an elevated RDW and a low ferritin → Iron deficiency anemia → oral iron
  13. 58 yo M with rheumatoid arthritis and a microcytic anemia; serum iron low, TIBC low, ferritin normal → Anemia of chronic disease → iron is sequestered, not absent
Pearls Iron studies → then electrophoresis — a sequencing rule, not a preference; the reason is biological: iron deficiency suppresses delta-globin chain production, lowering HbA2 into the normal range · Ferritin is the most specific single test for iron deficiency; TIBC and transferrin saturation add sensitivity when ferritin is borderline (ferritin is an acute-phase reactant) · Alpha-thalassemia minor has a normal electrophoresis — it is a diagnosis of exclusion or gene testing; the one microcytic anemia that electrophoresis cannot diagnose · The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) is a screening heuristic: <13 suggests thalassemia, >13 suggests IDA; it is not diagnostic and never the answer to “most appropriate test” · In a patient whose anemia does not correct with iron, the next question is whether there is a second cause — that is when electrophoresis earns its place
Pairs with Sickle Cell Trait versus Disease — shared tool: hemoglobin electrophoresis; discriminator: is the electrophoresis interpretable, or must iron be corrected first?
Telling them apart on the CBC alone RDW — elevated in iron deficiency because the iron available for erythropoiesis varies through the day, so cells are made at varying sizes; normal or low in thalassemia trait, where every cell is uniformly small · Erythrocyte count — low in iron deficiency because the marrow lacks substrate, but normal or elevated in thalassemia trait, which makes plenty of small cells · Mentzer index — MCV divided by RBC; over 13 favours iron deficiency and under 13 favours thalassemia trait · TIBC direction — elevated in iron deficiency as transferrin is upregulated, and low in anemia of chronic disease · MCHC — low in both iron deficiency and thalassemia, and elevated in hereditary spherocytosis from loss of membrane surface area · Cow milk threshold — over 24 oz per day after age 1 is the named risk factor, because milk is iron-poor, its calcium and caseinophosphopeptide block absorption, and volume displaces iron-rich food
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lab value and one disease suppresses the marker used to diagnose the other, the order of testing is not a preference — it is a dependency. Correct the confounder first, then run the definitive test.
Sequencing trapHemoglobin electrophoresis tempts because it “checks for thalassemia,” but iron deficiency makes it uninterpretable.
Class-vs-memberBone marrow biopsy tempts as the definitive heme test, but it is invasive and unnecessary when a dietary cause is obvious.

Hemophilia A Inhibitor

Hematology · refractory bleeding on replacement = alloantibodies · mixing study proves it

The decision point

A patient with known severe hemophilia A on factor VIII replacement has bleeding that does not respond to increased dosing. The aPTT is 112 seconds — massively prolonged despite daily infusions that should be correcting it. The infused factor VIII is being neutralized by alloantibodies. This is inhibitor development, occurring in ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A.

The aPTT at 112 on replacement therapy is the entire question: the intrinsic pathway is uncorrected despite receiving the missing factor. Platelets are 150K and PT is normal, eliminating every platelet and common-pathway option. The miss was a 47-minute doubt loop landing on platelet dysfunction — a knowledge gap compounded by exhaustive cycling.

Defining criteria Inhibitor development — alloantibodies (IgG) against infused factor VIII; ~25% of severe hemophilia A patients · Clinical clue — bleeding refractory to adequate factor replacement therapy · Lab clue — prolonged aPTT that does not correct on a mixing study · Bethesda assay — quantifies inhibitor titer; guides treatment (low <5 BU vs high ≥5 BU)
Refractory bleeding in a hemophiliac — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded by
Inhibitor developmentKnown hemophilia on replacement; increasing bleedsRefractory bleeding + prolonged aPTT on replacement + mixing study does not correct—
Acquired von Willebrand diseaseAutoimmune, lymphoproliferative; mucocutaneous bleedingMucosal bleeding; low vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactorHemarthrosis, not mucocutaneous
Fibrinogen dysfunctionDIC, liver failure; diffuse bleedingBoth PT and aPTT prolonged; low fibrinogenPT is normal
Heparin-induced thrombocytopeniaHeparin exposure; thrombosis + falling plateletsThrombocytopenia + thrombosis; 4T score, PF4 antibodyPlatelets 150K (normal)
Platelet dysfunctionUremia, ASA; mucocutaneous bleedingNormal coagulation studies + prolonged PFA-100aPTT 112; hemarthrosis, not petechiae
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo M with hemophilia A on prophylactic factor VIII, 5 days of right elbow swelling despite daily infusions, aPTT 112, PT normal, platelets normal → Inhibitor development → bypassing agent for acute bleed
  2. 12 yo M with hemophilia A and a known high-titer inhibitor (35 Bethesda units), acute hemarthrosis of the knee → Recombinant activated factor VII → bypasses factor VIII in the coagulation cascade
  3. 8 yo M with hemophilia A and a newly detected low-titer inhibitor (2 Bethesda units), long-term management → Immune tolerance induction with regular high-dose factor VIII → inhibitor eradication
  4. 10 yo M with hemophilia A on replacement therapy, recent increase in bleeding episodes, aPTT prolonged → Mixing study followed by Bethesda assay → confirm and quantify inhibitor
  5. Why a mixing study fails to correct the aPTT in a patient with a factor VIII inhibitor → The inhibitor is a time- and temperature-dependent antibody that neutralizes the normal factor VIII added in the mix
  6. 60 yo F with no bleeding history, new-onset large ecchymoses, aPTT 85, PT normal, mixing study does not correct after 2-hour incubation → Acquired hemophilia A → anti-factor VIII antibody titer
  7. 15 yo M with hemophilia A and inhibitor, life-threatening intracranial hemorrhage not responding to recombinant factor VIIa → Activated prothrombin complex concentrate → second-line bypassing agent
  8. 3 yo M with immediate right knee swelling after a fall, a large hip ecchymosis last week and scattered shin bruises; haemoglobin 13, platelets 187,000, leukocytes 8,500; radiograph shows a large effusion without fracture → Coagulation studies → haemarthrosis after minor trauma suggests a factor deficiency
  9. 4 yo M with recurrent haemarthroses; prothrombin time and platelet count are normal and the activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged → Factor VIII and factor IX activity levels → separates haemophilia A from B
  10. 3 yo M with suspected severe haemophilia presenting with haemarthrosis and easy bruising → Bone marrow biopsy → contraindicated in severe haemophilia because of bleeding risk
Pearls Mixing study — mix patient plasma 1:1 with normal plasma: if aPTT corrects → factor deficiency; if it does not correct → inhibitor; factor VIII inhibitor is time- and temperature-dependent (incubate at 37°C for 1–2 hours before reading) · Bethesda assay — low-titer (<5 BU) may respond to high-dose factor VIII; high-titer (≥5 BU) requires bypassing agents (rFVIIa or activated PCC) · Immune tolerance induction — repeated high-dose factor VIII to desensitize the immune system; the long-term eradication strategy · Acquired hemophilia A — the adult analogue: autoantibodies in a patient with no prior bleeding history, often autoimmune, malignancy, or postpartum · Hemarthrosis = factor problem; petechiae = platelet problem — this division answers most hematology stems before any lab is read
Pairs with Anemia with Thrombocytopenia — shared domain: coagulation workup; discriminator: aPTT correction on mixing.
Transferable rule When a patient on factor replacement therapy has bleeding that does not respond to dose escalation and the aPTT remains prolonged despite adequate dosing, the infused factor is being neutralized — and the mixing study is what proves it.
Unchecked attributePlatelet dysfunction tempts as a generic “bleeding” answer, but platelets are normal and the aPTT (not a platelet test) is the abnormal value.
True-fact-wrong-slotAcquired vWD can lower factor VIII, but presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, not hemarthrosis, and the patient already has a known factor deficiency.
Unchecked attributeFibrinogen dysfunction tempts as a coagulopathy, but the PT is normal — fibrinogen (common pathway) would prolong both.

Transfusion Reactions

timing and company decide, and most need nothing · board question · What are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo F with idiopathic aplastic anaemia, new petechiae and bruising over a week; during a platelet transfusion a chest rash spreads over the body · Labs — absolute neutrophil count 420, platelets 7,000 · Exam — T 37.2, BP 110/82, HR 90, RR 18, saturation 98%; oropharynx normal, lungs clear; diffuse urticarial rash on trunk and limbs plus pinpoint nonblanching macules and bruises at the extremities · Q — the best next step in evaluation of the reaction; options spanned culture of the product, direct Coombs test, no additional evaluation, peripheral smear and coagulation studies
The decision point

This is isolated urticaria in a haemodynamically stable patient, and the stem spends its last three sentences proving it: normal blood pressure, no wheeze, clear lungs, normal oropharynx, and improvement after an antihistamine with an hour of stable observation. That is an urticarial transfusion reaction — preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in the donated plasma, or the reverse. Management is exactly what already happened: stop, give an antihistamine, observe. The response is the diagnostic test, and the transfusion may be resumed without additional evaluation. There is nothing left to send.

Defining criteria Urticarial reaction — hives and itching only, onset hours into the transfusion, from preformed IgE against a soluble plasma allergen; stop, antihistamine, resume if otherwise asymptomatic, no workup · Anaphylactic reaction — onset seconds to minutes, from anti-IgA antibodies in an IgA-deficient recipient reacting to donor IgA; respiratory distress or wheeze, angioedema, hypotension; epinephrine, and washed products thereafter · Acute haemolytic reaction — ABO incompatibility from clerical error; fever, flank pain, hypotension, haemoglobinuria, direct Coombs positive · Transfusion-transmitted bacterial infection — fever, chills, hypotension, most common with platelets; culture both the recipient and the product
Transfusion reactions — timing, company and the movethe vitals sort them faster than the rash does
ReactionOnsetThe company it keepsWhat to do
UrticarialHoursHives and itching, nothing else; vitals normalStop, antihistamine, resume; no workup
