Acute haemolytic EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, flank pain, hypotension, dark urineStop; direct Coombs, smear, PT and PTT; supportive
Bacterial contamination EmergencyMinutes to hoursFever, rigors, hypotension; platelets most oftenCulture recipient and product; empiric antibiotics
Febrile non-haemolytic ⚠︎1–6 hFever and chills without haemolysisStop, antipyretic; leukoreduction prevents
TACO / TRALI ⚠︎Minutes to 6 hRespiratory distress — volume overload vs non-cardiogenic oedemaStop; supportive; the two split on volume status
Pertinent positives & negatives BP 110/82, HR 90, saturation 98% — haemodynamically stable; excludes anaphylaxis, haemolysis and sepsis in one line · Lungs clear, oropharynx normal — no bronchospasm, no angioedema; the two findings that would make this anaphylaxis · Afebrile at 37.2 — excludes both the febrile and the bacterial-contamination routes · Rash improved with diphenhydramine and stayed stable for an hour — the diagnostic confirmation; response is the test · Petechiae and bruises were present before the transfusion — they belong to a platelet count of 7,000 from aplastic anaemia, not to a new consumptive process · No flank pain, no dark urine — the haemolytic reaction's own findings are absent · It was a platelet transfusion — the product most associated with bacterial contamination, which is why culture is offered; with no fever the indication never opens
Decision spine What is the blood pressure and the saturation? — Normal → the dangerous reactions are out · Is there a fever? — No → not haemolytic, not bacterial, not febrile · Wheeze, angioedema or hypotension? — None → urticaria is isolated, so not anaphylaxis · How fast did it start? — Late, not in the first minutes → urticarial · Did it respond to the antihistamine? — Yes → that is the confirmation · So what is needed? — Nothing further; the transfusion may be resumed
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F with aplastic anaemia developing a diffuse urticarial rash late in a platelet transfusion; BP 110/82, saturation 98%, afebrile, lungs clear; rash improves after diphenhydramine and vitals stay stable for an hour → No additional evaluation is indicated → urticarial reaction; the transfusion may be resumed
  2. 30 yo who develops wheezing, facial angioedema and a blood pressure of 70/40 two minutes into a red cell transfusion → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylactic transfusion reaction
  3. Patient with selective IgA deficiency and a history of transfusion anaphylaxis who now requires red blood cells → Transfuse washed red blood cells → washing removes donor plasma IgA
  4. 45 yo who develops fever, flank pain, hypotension and dark urine 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion → Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction → ABO incompatibility from a clerical error
  5. 60 yo who develops fever to 39 C with rigors and hypotension 30 minutes into a platelet transfusion → Culture the recipient and the transfused product and start empiric antibiotics → bacterial contamination, most common with platelets
  6. The mechanism of an isolated urticarial transfusion reaction → Preformed IgE reacting against a soluble allergen in donor plasma → or donor IgE against a recipient allergen
  7. 12 yo with aplastic anaemia and platelets of 7,000 who develops hives during transfusion; pinpoint nonblanching macules were documented on her limbs before the transfusion began → Pre-existing thrombocytopenia → the petechiae are not part of the reaction
  8. IgA-deficient patient with prior transfusion anaphylaxis who urgently requires red blood cells → Standard unwashed packed red blood cells → residual donor plasma IgA triggers anaphylaxis
Decoy note The petechiae and ecchymoses are the trap and they do double duty — they look like a new haemorrhagic complication and they sit in the skin examination beside the urticaria, as though they arrived together. The stem says twice that they did not: she had bruising a week ago, and her platelet count is 7,000. A finding documented before the intervention cannot be a reaction to it.
Pearls The vitals sort transfusion reactions faster than the rash does — normal blood pressure, no fever and no hypoxia eliminate anaphylaxis, haemolysis, bacterial contamination and TRALI in one pass · Isolated urticaria is the one reaction you may transfuse through: stop, antihistamine, observe, resume the same unit · Timing separates the two allergic reactions — seconds to minutes with wheeze and hypotension is anaphylaxis; hours with hives alone is urticarial · Anaphylaxis to blood should make you think IgA deficiency, and the durable fix is washed products · Platelets carry the bacterial risk because they are stored at room temperature; fever and rigors during a platelet transfusion is the stem that earns cultures
Pairs with Part I The Immunoglobulin Panel, which owns selective IgA deficiency and already keys washed red cells — this brief approaches the same intersection from the transfusion side. Store the discriminator as a question: what are the vitals, and what else is on the skin besides hives?
Transferable rule When a stem narrates a treatment already given and then reports the response, the response is the diagnostic test — and the answer is usually that nothing further is needed. Read the last three sentences before ordering anything.
Redundant workupDirect Coombs test — answers "is this haemolysis?", already excluded by normal vitals, no fever, no flank pain and no dark urine.
Salient decoyPT and PTT — indicated only for haemolysis complicated by DIC; her bruising is thrombocytopenic and predates the transfusion.
Redundant workupPeripheral smear — would show schistocytes if microangiopathy were present; there is no haemolysis to look for.
Unchecked attributeCulture of the product — platelets do carry the bacterial risk, but culture requires fever, chills or hypotension; she is afebrile and stable.
3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Hematology

Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia

Pancytopenia with bone pain · UWorld and Aquifer · screen versus confirm

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, 2 weeks of fatigue, 1 week of leg pain, 1 day of fever with petechiae; pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy · Q — the most useful test; options spanned complete blood count with differential and smear, C-reactive protein and partial thromboplastin time
The decision point

Three findings together permit one disease: tri-lineage cytopenia, diaphyseal bone pain and diffuse nontender adenopathy with splenomegaly. That is marrow replacement, and marrow replacement is confirmed in the marrow.

But read the verb, because the same disease has two right answers. Most useful in making the diagnosis, or initial selects the complete blood count — cheap, fast, and enough to convert a vague illness into an oncologic emergency. Confirms, or diagnostic selects the bone marrow aspirate. The CBC makes you suspect leukemia; the marrow proves it.

Defining criteria Pancytopenia — reduction in all three lineages, the word that eliminates every single-lineage disease · ALL diagnostic gate — at least 20% lymphoblasts of marrow nucleated cells · M1, M2, M3 marrow — under 5%, 5 to 25%, over 25% blasts, a burden and response category rather than the diagnostic gate · Leukemic bone pain — diaphyseal or metaphyseal tenderness from marrow expansion, distinct from joint-line pain · Petechiae — a platelet problem, so PT and PTT are normal
The pale child with bone pain — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Acute lymphoblastic leukemiaPeak 2 to 5 yr; marrow replaced by lymphoblastsPancytopenia with diaphyseal pain and nontender adenopathy; counts go down
Sickle cell aplastic crisisParvovirus B19 arrests erythropoiesisIsolated anemia with reticulocytopenia; platelets and WBC normal
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent, prolonged fever and fatigueTender posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritisQuotidian fever, evanescent rashCounts go up — leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, ferritin high
Aplastic anemiaMarrow failure without infiltrationPancytopenia with an empty exam: no adenopathy, no organomegaly, no bone pain
Neuroblastoma Can't missUnder 5 yr; marrow metastases give identical cytopenia and bone painPeriorbital ecchymoses, proptosis, midline-crossing abdominal mass
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, well-appearing childIsolated thrombocytopenia with normal PT and PTT
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M with 2 wk of fatigue, 1 wk of leg pain and 1 day of fever with petechiae, pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy, most useful test → Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear → bone marrow confirms afterwards
  2. 5 yo M whose complete blood count shows hemoglobin 7, platelets 22,000 and WBC 3,100, confirmatory test → Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy → greater than 20% lymphoblasts
  3. 4 yo M, 3 wk fever, pallor, petechiae, nontender diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, midshaft femoral tenderness, WBC 2,800 and platelets 18,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy
  4. 4 yo M with fever, limp and pancytopenia in whom a colleague proposes empiric prednisone for presumed systemic JIA → Obtain bone marrow before any corticosteroid → steroids partially treat ALL and destroy the specimen
  5. 5 yo M with 4 wk of fatigue and pallor, pancytopenia, no adenopathy, no organomegaly and no bone pain → Aplastic anemia → bone marrow biopsy showing a hypocellular marrow
  6. 6 yo F, 5 wk of daily spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, WBC 24,000 and platelets 700,000 → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  7. 4 yo M with petechiae and bruising 2 wk after a viral illness, well-appearing and afebrile, platelets 12,000 with normal hemoglobin and WBC → Immune thrombocytopenia → observation
  8. 8 yo M with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin 4.2, reticulocytes 0.2%, normal platelets and WBC → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → transfuse and supportive care
  9. 3 yo M with fever, refusal to walk, pancytopenia, periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis, and an abdominal mass crossing the midline → Neuroblastoma → urine HVA and VMA
  10. 16 yo M, 3 wk fever, sore throat, tender posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes → Infectious mononucleosis → avoid contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
  11. 6 yo F with petechiae and gum bleeding, platelets 9,000, PT and PTT normal, otherwise well → No further coagulation testing is needed → petechiae are a platelet problem
  12. 5 yo M with pancytopenia and adenopathy in whom a normal white count on an earlier CBC is offered as reassurance → Accepting a normal white count as excluding leukemia → some ALL presents with under 1% circulating blasts
  13. 7 yo M, day 3 of ALL induction, potassium 6.8, phosphate 8.1, uric acid 14, calcium 6.8 and creatinine 2.1 → Tumor lysis syndrome → intravenous hydration and urate-lowering therapy
  14. 7 yo M on day 3 of ALL induction with rising potassium, phosphate and uric acid, a low calcium and a rising creatinine → IV hydration and urate-lowering therapy → tumor lysis syndrome
  15. 14 yo M with pancytopenia, marrow lymphoblasts and an anterior mediastinal mass on chest film → T-cell lineage → a mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL
Never steroids before the marrow Corticosteroids partially treat ALL, transiently improving the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Systemic JIA and ALL must be separated before treatment, not after. And a normal white count does not exclude ALL — the cytopenias carry the signal, not the blasts.
Pearls Leukemia lowers counts, systemic JIA raises them — ferritin, platelets and WBC all rise in sJIA · Neuroblastoma and ALL are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them · A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL, and a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL · Inflammatory markers monitor disease, they do not select between diagnoses that all raise them · Tumor lysis — potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury
Pairs with Part I Systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child — Master Table shares the presenting complaint. Store the discriminator as a question: are the counts up or down? Part I Benign Limb Pain in a Child owns the benign nocturnal limb pain whose normal examination excludes this diagnosis.
Transferable rule Sort laboratory options by what a result could change rather than by sophistication, because a test abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing and a test measuring an uninvolved compartment answers a question nobody asked.
Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalised adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered.
Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of haematologic test on the wrong compartment.

Hereditary Spherocytosis

Spherocytes with a negative Coombs · handoff · map the disease to its assay

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M, months of jaundice and splenomegaly; father affected · Labs — MCHC 38%, direct Coombs negative · Smear — spherocytes · Q — the most appropriate confirmatory test; options spanned eosin-5-maleimide binding, flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59, and hemoglobin electrophoresis
The decision point

The word doing the work is spherocytes: on a board smear they have exactly two owners, hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The negative Coombs settles that fork — antibody-coated cells are excluded, so the spherocytes are a membrane defect. MCHC 38% and the affected father corroborate; neither is the decider.

The last move is a mapping rather than a diagnosis. The options are tests, so name the disease and then name its assay: eosin-5-maleimide binding, with osmotic fragility as the older equivalent. Choosing CD55/CD59 is a stored-outcome error — Coombs-negative hemolysis retrieved as a conclusion rather than as a question, so the three findings that fail PNH here (normal white cells and platelets, spherocytes, an affected father) were never asked.

Defining criteria MCHC in HS — above 36%, because membrane loss dehydrates the cell and concentrates hemoglobin; the one common anemia in which MCHC is high · Confirmatory test — eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry showing reduced fluorescence, or increased osmotic fragility · The HS triad — Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly
Coombs-negative hemolysis in a child - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Hereditary spherocytosisAutosomal dominant ankyrin, spectrin or band 3 defect; extravascular splenic hemolysis, pigment stonesSpherocytes with a negative Coombs and MCHC above 36%
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG against red cells; lupus, CLL, methyldopa or penicillins; subacuteDirect Coombs positive — the only line separating it from HS
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuriaAcquired PIGA clone, complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, adultsHemolysis with cytopenias and thrombosis at odd sites, bland smear
G6PD deficiencyX-linked, episodic 2 to 3 days after an oxidantBite cells and Heinz bodies after a named trigger, MCHC normal
HemoglobinopathySickle or thalassemia, chronic inherited hemolysis with splenomegalyTarget cells or sickled forms with a low MCV
Production failureIron, B12 or folate deficiency, or marrow disease; pallor without jaundiceLow reticulocytes, with the MCV pointing the way
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M, months of jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, MCHC 38%, Coombs negative, father affected → Eosin-5-maleimide binding test → hereditary spherocytosis
  2. 24 yo F with lupus, 2 wk of fatigue and jaundice, spherocytes, direct Coombs positive → Prednisone → warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  3. 5 yo M with dark urine 3 days after TMP-SMX, bite cells and Heinz bodies, still actively hemolysing → Measuring G6PD activity during the acute episode → young surviving cells read falsely normal
  4. 30 yo M, dark morning urine, pancytopenia, new hepatic vein thrombosis, Coombs negative, bland smear → Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 → paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  5. 10 yo F with known hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 12 falling to 5 over a week, reticulocytes 0.1%, slapped-cheek rash at school → Transfusion → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  6. 14 yo M with hereditary spherocytosis and colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals → Right upper quadrant ultrasound → pigment gallstones
  7. 8 yo M, splenectomy a year ago for hereditary spherocytosis, temperature 39.5 C, ill-appearing → Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone now → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
  8. 18-hour-old newborn with jaundice, mother blood group O positive, infant A positive, spherocytes on smear, direct antiglobulin weakly positive → Phototherapy → ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
  9. 7 yo M with jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, Coombs negative and MCHC 37%, with no family history → Hereditary spherocytosis → a meaningful fraction are de novo or recessive
  10. 16 yo F with hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 8, fatigue limiting sport, gallstones on ultrasound, planned for splenectomy → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgery → moderate disease, splenectomy deferred to age 6 or older
Management, and what splenectomy does not fix Folic acid for chronic reticulocytosis, transfusion for aplastic or hemolytic crisis, and splenectomy for moderate to severe disease deferred until age 6 or older ⚠ and preceded by pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination, with cholecystectomy if pigment stones are present. Splenectomy stops the hemolysis but not the defect — spherocytes persist and Howell-Jolly bodies appear, and every post-splenectomy fever is treated as sepsis until proven otherwise.
Pearls Spherocytes have two owners, hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and the Coombs test is the entire discrimination; in a newborn add ABO incompatibility as a third · MCHC is the only red-cell index that rises in a common anemia, and RDW rises with it · HS is extravascular with indirect bilirubin, splenomegaly and pigment stones; PNH and severe G6PD hemolysis are intravascular with hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin and high LDH · A falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in any chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise · Do not assay G6PD during acute hemolysis, because the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal; repeat weeks later · A normal MCV does not exclude hemolysis, because a 10% reticulocytosis inflates it
Pairs with Candidate twin — confirm: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, sharing jaundice, anemia and spherocytes, with the discriminator stored as a question: is the direct Coombs positive? Second candidate: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria — are the white cells and platelets normal? Neither partner brief exists yet, so no reverse links are owed. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia is the seam: an isolated hemolytic anemia is one process, and a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia is another. Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis is the Coombs-positive mirror of this brief's Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia.
Transferable rule When the options are tests the question is still which disease, so name it from the smear plus one separating test and then map disease to assay, because when two diagnoses share a morphologic finding the answer is the test that separates them rather than the finding they share.
True-fact-wrong-slotPNH is the other famous Coombs-negative hemolysis, but it means cytopenias, a bland smear and acquired disease.
Salient decoyBoy with jaundice and hemolysis sells G6PD, which needs an oxidant trigger and is not passed father to son.
Class-vs-memberHemoglobinopathy is the right class of inherited red-cell disorder but gives targets or sickles, never spherocytes.

Sickle Cell Trait versus Disease

HbA exceeds HbS · UWorld · read the electrophoresis before the options

Source vignette Pt — 1 yo F, asymptomatic · Labs — hemoglobin electrophoresis HbA 60% and HbS 40%, normal complete blood count · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned sickle cell trait, sickle cell anemia and sickle-beta-plus thalassemia
The decision point

HbA 60% with HbS 40% and a stone-normal CBC is trait, not disease. Every wrong option — acute chest, dactylitis, stroke, osteomyelitis — is a genuine complication of sickle cell anemia, and none belongs to a carrier. Five of seven options die to one line of the lab panel.

Then a second layer catches those who did read it: the stem asks for the most common complication, not one that can occur. Splenic infarction is real in trait, at altitude, uncommonly. Painless hematuria is the common one, because the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic — the one microenvironment that polymerises HbS at the 40% a carrier has.

Defining criteria Trait — HbA about 60% exceeding HbS about 40%, with a completely normal CBC · Disease — HbA absent; any HbA at all excludes HbSS · Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia — HbA present but S exceeds A, with a low MCV · Newborn screen — FAS is trait, FS is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin predominates at birth
Hemoglobin electrophoresis — reading the pattern
ConditionElectrophoresis and CBCThe NBME tell
NormalHbA about 97%, A2 about 2.5%, F under 1%; normal CBC—
Sickle cell traitHbA about 60% over HbS about 40%; completely normal CBCA exceeds S, and there is no anemia
Sickle cell anemiaHbA 0%, HbS about 90%; anemia with reticulocytes 10 to 20%Absence of HbA is the finding
Hemoglobin SCHbA 0%, HbS about equal to HbC; milder anemiaRetinopathy and avascular necrosis out of proportion to the anemia
Sickle-beta-zero thalassemiaHbA 0%, HbS high, A2 elevated; low MCVLooks like SS but microcytic
Sickle-beta-plus thalassemiaHbA present but low, S exceeds A; low MCVHbA present yet S exceeds A, the sharpest mimic of trait
Scenario bank
  1. 1 yo F, HbA 60% and HbS 40%, normal CBC → Sickle cell trait → most common complication is painless hematuria
  2. 1 yo F with HbA 0% and HbS 90%, hemoglobin 7.5, reticulocytes 14% → Sickle cell anemia → penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination
  3. 20 yo M with sickle cell trait, nocturia and polyuria → Hyposthenuria → impaired urinary concentrating ability
  4. 22 yo M with sickle cell trait who collapses during military basic training → Exertional rhabdomyolysis
  5. 28 yo M with sickle cell trait and a renal mass → Renal medullary carcinoma
  6. 19 yo F with sickle cell trait and left upper quadrant pain after a high-altitude flight → Splenic infarction
  7. 26 yo F with sickle cell trait, pregnant, with dysuria → Urinary tract infection
  8. 9 mo M with painful swelling of the hands and feet and hemoglobin 7 → Dactylitis → often the first presentation of sickle cell disease
  9. 14 yo M with sickle cell disease, chest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate → Acute chest syndrome → transfusion and antibiotics
  10. 7 yo M with sickle cell disease and sudden hemiparesis → Ischemic stroke → exchange transfusion
  11. 6 yo M with sickle cell disease, sudden pallor and a reticulocyte count of 0.2% → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  12. 2 yo M with HbA 15%, HbS 70% and an MCV of 68 → Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia → HbA is present but S exceeds A
  13. Newborn screen reported as FAS → Sickle cell trait → counsel the parents, no treatment
  14. 26 yo F with trait whose partner also carries trait, asking about future children → 25% Disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffected
  15. 3 yo M with sickle cell anemia, fever 39.5, hypotension, tachycardia, leukocytosis with bandemia, the most likely organism → Streptococcus pneumoniae → empiric ceftriaxone
Why the kidney is the one organ trait touches The renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic — exactly the conditions that polymerise HbS at the 40% concentration a carrier has. Nowhere else in the body reproduces that microenvironment, which is why a carrier's spleen, lungs and bones are spared and the vasa recta are not.
Pearls In trait HbA always exceeds HbS, because alpha chains bind normal beta with higher affinity — memorise the inequality, not the numbers · HbF is 0% by 12 months, so a raised HbF later means hydroxyurea or a thalassemia · Renal medullary carcinoma is rare but nearly pathognomonic for trait · Trait carries a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death under extreme exertion, which is why it matters in athletes and recruits · Pneumococcus — #1 cause of sepsis in sickle cell despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes); Salmonella — #1 cause of osteomyelitis; the organism changes with the site: blood = pneumococcus, bone = Salmonella
Pairs with Part I Hematuria in Renal and GU should gain a sickle trait row; painless hematuria in a carrier is the commonest trait complication. Part I Chronic Dyspnea in Sickle Cell Disease owns the chronic pulmonary sequelae that follow the acute chest syndrome named here.
Transferable rule When a stem supplies a diagnostic lab panel that panel is the assassin, usually eliminating most options in one line, and family history is placed to make you skip it.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenic infarction is real in trait but uncommon, and the stem asks for the most common.
Mirror twinDactylitis is the disease version of the carrier stem.
Salient decoyThe affected sister sells the whole disease-complication list at once.

Infectious Disease 10 topics + 4 board-style

Screening thresholds, drug toxicities, and sequencing. Isolation precedes medication; aspiration precedes antibiotics.

Tuberculosis

Screen → sort → treat

The decision point

A positive test plus a normal CXR and no symptoms = latent TB → monotherapy. Positive test plus symptoms or an abnormal CXR = active TB → isolate first, then four drugs. No test distinguishes latent from active — the CXR and symptoms do.

PPD positivity thresholds by risk group
PPD is positive at…Group
≥5 mmHIV+ · recent TB contact · fibrotic changes on CXR · transplant, TNF-α inhibitor, prednisone ≥15 mg/day
≥10 mmHealthcare workers · immigrants <5 yrs from endemic areas · prisoners · homeless · IVDU · diabetes · CKD · children <4
≥15 mmNo risk factors
Test mechanics BCG-vaccinated → IGRA (unaffected by BCG) · anergy = false-negative PPD in HIV, steroids, sarcoid · PPD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
RIPE drug toxicities
RIPE drugToxicity
RifampinOrange secretions (benign — counsel, don't stop) · potent CYP inducer → OCP failure, warfarin; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy → give B6 · hepatitis · drug-induced lupus · sideroblastic anemia
PyrazinamideHyperuricemia / gout · hepatitis
EthambutolOptic neuritis — red-green vision lost first. "Eye-thambutol"
The costumes — how the same question keeps showing up
  1. Booster / two-step: HCW with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion → Treat as latent
  2. Window period: contact of an active case → PPD now and at 8–10 weeks → the only time "repeat later" is correct
  3. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (RA or IBD stem) → Screen for latent TB first
  4. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR → Airborne isolation → before any medication is started
Reference notes
  • HIV co-infection: PPD ≥5 mm = treat · TB drugs first, ART at 2–8 weeks (immediate risks IRIS) · rifabutin with protease inhibitors
  • Extrapulmonary: Pott (spine) · scrofula (cervical node) · meningitis (↑protein, ↓glucose, basilar) · sterile pyuria · miliary CXR · adrenal insufficiency
  • Location logic: primary = lower/mid lobe (Ghon complex); reactivation = apices (highest pO₂)
Treatment Latent: rifampin ×4 mo (preferred) · INH ×9 mo + B6 · INH + rifapentine weekly ×3 mo. Active: RIPE ×2 mo → INH + rifampin ×4 mo; reportable; DOT if nonadherent.
Sequencing trap

Bacterial Meningitis

The CSF 2×2

The decision point

The whole CSF grid collapses to a 2×2: cell type on one axis, glucose on the other.

CSF interpretation — the 2×2
Glucose LOWGlucose NORMAL
NeutrophilsBacterialEarly viral · parameningeal focus
LymphocytesTB · fungal (± partially treated bacterial)Viral
Organism by host
  • Neonate: GBS · E. coli (K1 capsule) · Listeria  |  Unvaccinated toddler: Hib
  • Teen / dorm / military: N. meningitidis  |  Adult (most common): S. pneumoniae
  • >50, pregnant, immunosuppressed: + Listeria → add ampicillin
  • VP shunt: S. epidermidis  |  Basilar skull fracture / CSF rhinorrhea: S. pneumoniae  |  HIV CD4 <100: Cryptococcus
Mechanism pearls Encapsulated organisms need opsonization — hit hardest in asplenia/sickle cell (lost filter), complement deficiency (lost MAC → recurrent Neisseria; screen with CH50), and cirrhosis (lost complement synthesis) · lipid A of LOS → TNF/IL-1 → shock, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen · Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O and spreads via ActA-driven host actin polymerization; intrinsic cephalosporin resistance · conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent response, which is why they work under age 2.
Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo M with fever and neck stiffness; CSF 3,000 neutrophils, glucose 25, protein 180 → Bacterial meningitis → dexamethasone with ceftriaxone and vancomycin
  2. 22 yo M with CSF 200 lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein → Viral meningitis
  3. 35 yo M with HIV; CSF lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein, basilar involvement → Tuberculous meningitis
  4. 22 yo M with suspected meningitis and papilledema on fundoscopy → CT head before lumbar puncture
  5. 22 yo M with suspected bacterial meningitis and a delayed CT scanner → Blood cultures and antibiotics before imaging
  6. 68 yo M with bacterial meningitis; what coverage must be added → Ampicillin for Listeria
  7. 8 yo M in summer, headache, fever, stiff neck, CSF with 200 WBCs and 85% lymphocytes, protein 60, glucose 55, Gram stain negative → Enteroviral meningitis → supportive care
  8. 5 yo F with fever and meningismus, CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein, well appearing → Supportive care and observation → viral meningitis
  9. The most common cause of aseptic meningitis in a child presenting during summer → Enterovirus → supportive care is sufficient
  10. 2 yo with fever, hypotension, lethargy and a purpuric rash on the legs; cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci → Serum fibrinogen → purpura signals disseminated intravascular coagulation
  11. When complement testing is indicated in a patient with meningococcal disease → After recovery, for recurrent or unusual-serogroup infection → terminal complement deficiency is C5 to C9, a predisposition rather than an acute study
  12. 1 year old with meningococcaemia who develops large purpuric lesions and sudden vasomotor collapse and dies; the autopsy finding → Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage → Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  13. Infant with fever, nuchal rigidity, spreading purpura and abrupt hypotension → Fulminant meningococcaemia → 10 to 20% of infected infants; mortality approaches 100%
  14. 16 yo M, 8 hours of abrupt high fever and sore throat with severe diffuse leg pain, says he has never felt this terrible; pale, nonexudative pharyngitis, supple neck, mottled tender legs; rapid strep and influenza negative; CBC and blood culture drawn → Lumbar puncture → early meningococcal disease; no seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise, so no CT first, and ceftriaxone does not wait
  15. Adolescent 10 hours into an abrupt febrile illness with severe leg pain, cold hands and feet and mottled skin, no rash yet → Meningococcemia → poor perfusion and severe myalgia arrive before the petechiae
Sequencing CT before LP only if: papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromise, depressed consciousness, age >60 — an open fontanelle in an infant generally removes the requirement, since it acts as a pop-off valve. Never delay antibiotics — draw cultures and treat. Empiric: vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin for Listeria); neonates get cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone (biliary sludging, bilirubin displacement). Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose — it blunts the cytokine burst from bacterial lysis.
Early meningococcal disease Onset — nonspecific fever, headache, vomiting, myalgia or sore throat, easily mistaken for a viral or streptococcal pharyngitis · Red flags — severe myalgia such as leg pain, poor perfusion with pallor, mottling or cold hands and feet, and the worst illness the patient has ever felt · Tempo — petechiae, meningeal signs and altered mental status follow within 12 to 24 hours · Workup — blood cultures and lumbar puncture, with ceftriaxone given without waiting for either · CT first only for — recent seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise · Complications — shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal haemorrhage · Prevention — droplet precautions and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
Follow-up facts Classic triad present in only 44% (van de Beek, NEJM 2004; n=696) · most common sequela is sensorineural hearing loss — check hearing in every survivor · prophylaxis: meningococcus → rifampin, cipro, or ceftriaxone; Hib → rifampin · eculizumab blocks C5 → mandatory meningococcal vaccination first.
Pairs with Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child owns the decision to obtain the fluid that this brief interprets.
Salient decoyHeterophile antibody test — mononucleosis gives exudate and posterior cervical nodes, not leg pain, mottling and a collapse measured in hours.
Salient decoyCT scan of the neck — deep neck infection brings trismus, uvular deviation or a bulging pharyngeal wall.
Salient decoyThroat culture for diphtheria — needs a gray, adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane.
Salient decoyHIV antigen/antibody test — acute HIV adds diffuse lymphadenopathy, rash and diarrhoea.

Vaccines in HIV

Live vaccines are CD4-gated, not banned

The decision point

The stored rule should be "HIV → check the CD4 count," not "HIV → no live vaccines." CD4 ≥200 permits varicella, MMR, and yellow fever (with caution). CD4 <200 contraindicates them. Never at any CD4: LAIV (use inactivated influenza), BCG, oral polio.

Defining criteria CD4 ≥200 — varicella, MMR, and yellow fever permitted (with caution) · CD4 <200 — live vaccines contraindicated · Never at any CD4 — LAIV, BCG, oral polio
Hepatitis B serology interpretation
HBsAganti-HBcanti-HBsInterpretation
−−−Susceptible → vaccinate
−−+Immune from vaccination
−++Immune from natural infection
++ (IgM)−Acute infection
++ (IgG)−Chronic infection
Scenario bank
  1. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 320, not immune to varicella → Give the varicella vaccine → permitted once CD4 is 200 or above
  2. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 120, not immune to measles → Withhold MMR until CD4 is 200 or above
  3. 30 yo M with HIV at any CD4 count, in influenza season → Inactivated influenza vaccine
  4. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 400, travelling to a yellow fever zone → Give yellow fever vaccine with caution
  5. 30 yo M with HIV asking about pneumococcal vaccination → Give pneumococcal vaccine regardless of CD4 count
  6. 30 yo M with HIV, CD4 90, asking about shingles vaccination → Recombinant zoster vaccine — non-live and permitted
HIV-specific additions to the adult schedule Meningococcal ACWY with boosters every 5 years (unique to HIV, asplenia, and complement deficiency — the opsonization club) · pneumococcal regardless of age · hepatitis A and B unless immune · HPV through 26 (consider to 45) · recombinant zoster from age 19 rather than waiting until 50 · influenza annually, inactivated.
Transferable rule Before rejecting a uniform option ("yes to all four"), you need a specific disqualifying criterion you can name — not a general sense that it's too easy.
Uniform-answer doubtMirror twin

DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution

Three false contraindications in one stem

The decision point

Separate contraindication (never give) from precaution (weigh risk vs. benefit) from neither. A brief self-limited seizure hours after a prior dose is technically a precaution — and precautions are overcome when benefit is high, as in an outbreak. Family history of epilepsy is in the "neither" bucket entirely.

DTaP — contraindications vs precautions
CategoryItems
Contraindication
(all pertussis-containing)		Anaphylaxis to the vaccine or a component · Encephalopathy (coma, decreased consciousness, prolonged seizures) within 7 days of a prior dose → give DT instead
Precaution
(defer or weigh)		Progressive/unstable neurologic disorder — infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy · seizure ≤3 days after a prior dose · temp ≥40.5 °C within 48 h · hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode within 48 h · inconsolable crying ≥3 h · Guillain-Barré within 6 weeks of prior tetanus toxoid · Arthus reaction · moderate-severe acute illness
Not a contraindicationFamily history of seizures or epilepsy · personal febrile seizure · mild illness · recent exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo M whose sibling had encephalopathy within 7 days of a pertussis dose; the patient himself had it → Contraindication — use DT
  2. 2 mo M with a brief self-limited seizure hours after a previous dose → Precaution — weigh risk against benefit
  3. 2 mo M with a family history of seizures → Not a contraindication
  4. 2 mo M with a mild febrile upper respiratory infection on the day of the visit → Not a contraindication — vaccinate
  5. 2 mo M with anaphylaxis after a previous dose → Contraindication
  6. 2 mo M with a temperature of 41 °C within 48 hours of a previous dose → Precaution
Standard pediatric immunizations by classwhich ones are live is the load-bearing fact
ClassVaccines
Live attenuatedRotavirus · measles · mumps · rubella · varicella — plus LAIV, BCG, oral polio and zoster
Inactivated (killed)Polio · hepatitis A · injectable influenza
ToxoidDiphtheria · tetanus
