The universal false-contraindication list Mild illness or low-grade fever · current antibiotic therapy · prematurity (vaccinate by chronologic age, full dose) · breastfeeding · family history of anything · recent exposure to an infectious disease · egg allergy (no longer a barrier to influenza vaccine) · penicillin allergy · pregnancy or immunosuppression in a household contact (exception: smallpox; avoid LAIV if a severely immunocompromised contact) · mild local reaction to a prior dose.
Schedule & timing DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months; 15–18 months; 4–6 years · Tdap at 11–12 and every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks · pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis only useful within 21 days · live vaccines same day or ≥28 days apart · after IVIG or blood products, defer MMR/varicella 3–11 months.
Transferable rule Vaccine questions are eligibility questions, and the stem's job is to make an ineligible-sounding history feel disqualifying. If you can't name the criterion, the answer is vaccinate.

Acute Cervicitis

Chlamydia & gonorrhea · treat before the test returns

The decision point

Mucopurulent cervical discharge + a friable cervix that bleeds on contact is a clinical diagnosis of cervicitis, most prevalent in women under 25. NAAT for both organisms is sent — and empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is given before results return, to interrupt transmission and prevent PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. The absence of cervical motion tenderness does not reassure: CMT marks ascent, and early or low-burden infection lacks it.

Defining criteria Clinical diagnosis — mucopurulent cervical discharge + friable cervix · Empiric regimen — ceftriaxone (covers N gonorrhoeae) + doxycycline (covers C trachomatis); azithromycin replaces doxycycline in pregnancy · Testing — NAAT for both organisms; treatment does not wait for it
Chlamydia & gonorrhea in women
AxisFindings
Risk factorsAge <25, high-risk sexual behavior
ManifestationsAsymptomatic most commonly; cervicitis, urethritis, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis)
DiagnosisNucleic acid amplification testing
TreatmentEmpiric ceftriaxone + doxycycline; confirmed chlamydia alone → doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy)
ComplicationsPID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility
Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo F, mucopurulent discharge, cervix bleeds on swab contact → Ceftriaxone + doxycycline now → empiric dual therapy precedes the NAAT result
  2. 24 yo G1 at 12 weeks with NAAT-confirmed chlamydia → Azithromycin → doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy
  3. 23 yo F with mucopurulent discharge, now uterine and adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness → Pelvic inflammatory disease → the infection has ascended
  4. 25 yo F, fever and uterine tenderness 3 days after vaginal delivery → Clindamycin plus gentamicin → polymicrobial ascent of vaginal flora, not an STI regimen
  5. 21 yo F, dysuria, leukocyte esterase positive but nitrite negative, mucopurulent cervical discharge on exam → Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitis → NAAT; the pelvic exam reframes the "UTI"
Pearls Azithromycin + doxycycline doubles atypical coverage and leaves N gonorrhoeae untreated — the classic wrong pairing · gonococcus is multidrug-resistant, including to sulfonamides — TMP-SMX never treats an STI syndrome · sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman (LE-positive, nitrite-negative) is chlamydia until the pelvic exam says otherwise · treat partners.
Transferable rule When a clinical diagnosis is sufficient and the sequelae are irreversible, the exam rewards treating at the visit — testing runs in parallel, never as a gate.
Class-vs-memberAzithromycin + doxycycline looks like dual therapy but both cover the same organism.
Test-overrides-findingsA negative nitrite cannot rule out infection that nitrite was never sensitive for — atypicals don't reduce nitrate.

The Immunoglobulin Panel

which antibody defect, and what it predicts · board question · Are B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

Source vignette Pt — toddler with ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile · Labs — IgM 450, IgG 250, IgA 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV
The decision point

The infection history only establishes that this is a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness — ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile clear that bar. The actual fork is decided by one line of the panel: IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. Every other option on the list requires IgM to be low (XLA, CVID), normal (selective IgA deficiency, Job), or accompanied by a non-immunologic finding this child does not have (Wiskott-Aldrich's microthrombocytopenia, HIV's inverted CD4/CD8). An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure — CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is the free confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40L deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) — the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or IgE; when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature — B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate — low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 — class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA and CVID (both require all isotypes low) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (ANC ≈1,350) — common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 — normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 — excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy — argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease — vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses; it also makes live vaccines a live safety question ⚠︎ · Lymphadenopathy — separates HIV from SCID: HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them
Antibody deficiencies — reading the isotype panel
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency)X-linked recessive boy, infancy; recurrent AOM/sinusitis/pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria, plus opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis) because the T-cell–APC limb is also brokenIgM high, IgG/IgA/IgE low, B cells normal — plus neutropenia— (the answer)
X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemiaBoy, infections begin ~6 months as maternal IgG wanes ⚠︎; recurrent sinopulmonary and enteroviral diseaseB cells absent/low with ALL isotypes low; scant tonsils and lymph nodes ⚠︎IgM 450 (high) with a normal lymphocyte compartment
Common variable immunodeficiencyAdolescent/young adult; sinopulmonary infections → bronchiectasis, plus autoimmunity, granulomas, and lymphoma risk ⚠︎All isotypes low with a NORMAL B-cell count; late onsetIgM 450 (high); age 14 months
Selective IgA deficiencyOften asymptomatic; otherwise recurrent respiratory/GI (giardiasis) or urogenital infection; anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products ⚠︎IgA alone low; IgG and IgM normalIgG 250 — the deficiency is not isolated
Syndromic defects with an Ig signature (Wiskott-Aldrich · Job/hyper-IgE)WAS: eczema + microthrombocytopenia + infection, X-linked. Job: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, pneumatoceles ⚠︎The non-immunologic finding makes the diagnosis, not the panel — small platelets; IgE markedly highPlatelets 260,000 and normal-sized; no eczema or abscess history
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia (HIV; protein-losing states ⚠︎)Opportunistic infection, diarrhea, failure to thriveInverted CD4/CD8 with leukopenia; IgG/IgA may be elevated from chronic stimulation while IgM is lowCD4/CD8 2.2, WBC 9,000
Management, in one line Management is not the fork this question tests, so in one sentence: replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes — immunoglobulin replacement for any low-IgG defect plus antibiotic prophylaxis (in-context; TMP-SMX as the agent is memory-sourced ⚠︎), no live vaccines ⚠︎, washed/IgA-depleted products instead of IVIG in selective IgA deficiency ⚠︎, and allogeneic HSCT as the only cure for CD40L deficiency ⚠︎.
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? — ICU pneumonia, perforated TMs, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? — Normal → XLA is out before you read another line · Is IgM high, normal, or low? — High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? — IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Any finding off the panel? — Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: — which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?
Scenario bank
  1. 11 mo M with newly diagnosed CD40 ligand deficiency, started on monthly immunoglobulin replacement → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis → Hyper-IgM syndrome
  2. 12 mo M with X-linked agammaglobulinemia on immunoglobulin replacement, presenting for the 12-month visit → Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine → X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  3. 23 yo F, sinopulmonary infections since age 16, bronchiectasis on CT, IgG/IgA/IgM all low, normal CD19+ B cells → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy → Common variable immunodeficiency
  4. 24 yo M with known selective IgA deficiency, upper GI bleed, hemoglobin 6.5, requires transfusion → Transfuse washed red blood cells → Selective IgA deficiency
  5. 9 yo M, recurrent nontender staphylococcal skin abscesses, chronic eczema, retained primary teeth, lung cyst after pneumonia, IgE 4,200 → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome → Antistaphylococcal prophylaxis and skin care
  6. 3 yo M, eczema, recurrent otitis media, bloody diarrhea, platelets 38,000 and small on smear → Refer for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  7. 18 mo M with hyper-IgM syndrome, 2 weeks of dry cough, hypoxemia, diffuse interstitial infiltrates, elevated LDH → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment
  8. 10 mo M, recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, IgG, IgA and IgM all markedly low → Flow cytometry for CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia if B cells are absent
  9. 4 yo M with CD40 ligand deficiency on immunoglobulin replacement, family asks how to reduce infection risk at home → Boiled or filtered drinking water → Cryptosporidium and sclerosing cholangitis
  10. 7 mo M, third otitis media, thriving, IgG mildly low with normal IgA and IgM, normal B cells, protective tetanus titers → Reassurance and repeat immunoglobulin levels → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
  11. 7 mo M with two otitis media episodes and prior bronchiolitis, growing at the 65th percentile, facial eczema, IgG low for age with normal IgA and IgM, normal leukocytes, and elevated tetanus- and diphtheria-specific IgG → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy → a normal vaccine response is the discriminator
  12. 7 mo M with transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, thriving, with two otitis media episodes → Observation with repeat immunoglobulin levels → it self-resolves by early childhood
  13. 4-month-old foster child with oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly → Perinatal HIV infection → HIV DNA PCR
  14. 3-month-old with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray, absent T cells on flow cytometry → Severe combined immunodeficiency → hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  15. 6-month-old born to a mother with unknown prenatal care, recurrent oral candidiasis, bilateral otitis media, CD4 count 180 → Perinatal HIV infection → start antiretroviral therapy
  16. 12 mo M, two prior pneumonias, chronic thrush, tympanostomy tubes, 2nd percentile height and weight, now intubated; lymphocytes 5%, CD3+ absent, CD19+ low, IgG 220, HIV antibody negative → Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation → the only definitive therapy in SCID
  17. 10 mo M with newly diagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency presenting for catch-up immunisations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines can cause fatal disseminated disease
Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are in-context expected — lymphocytosis accompanies active infection and, more usefully, confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which is what kills XLA. The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but actually support the answer: CD40L deficiency impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. "Vaccinations up to date" is not filler — it converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, which is an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure; absent B cells is XLA; all isotypes low with B cells present is CVID. · Read the panel in fixed order — B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE — and the disease names itself. Naming the disease first is how the wrong panel gets forced to fit. · The missing isotype predicts the organism: no opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae); a broken CD40L–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium ⚠︎. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion ⚠︎. · Any patient on immunoglobulin replacement or with a defective T-cell limb gets no live vaccines ⚠︎; and replacement IgG makes serologic testing uninterpretable afterward. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy — recheck, don't treat ⚠︎.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir — maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia — that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel — a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Verified: Part I Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infection (shared complaint: recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child; discriminator as a question: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy?). When the panel is normal, that brief owns the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does.
Transferable rule When recurrent sinopulmonary infection arrives with an immunoglobulin panel, the question is a pattern read, not a disease recalled: count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved — the preserved isotype names the block, and the missing ones name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeEczema plus recurrent infection is the Wiskott-Aldrich shape, but that syndrome requires small, low platelets — a normal count retires it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia — That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency — CVID needs IgM low as well, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection — Would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8; ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. Chronic HIV raises IgG/IgA and lowers IgM — the mirror image of this panel
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency — Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome — The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema

Tick-Borne Fever and Rash

treat the rickettsiosis before you prove it · UWorld · where the rash started, and what the platelets did

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, abdominal pain, body aches and headache with an unremarkable ED workup, now back with confusion and worse pain; lives by a lake surrounded by woods · Exam — T 39, BP 90/60, HR 120; new maculopapular rash on arms and legs, generalised abdominal tenderness without rebound, no neck stiffness, nonfocal neurologically · Labs — leukocytes 4,600, platelets 46,000, ALT 158, AST 202, creatinine 1.1 · Imaging — abdominal CT normal · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned amoxicillin, doxycycline, laparoscopy, prednisone, serum ceruloplasmin and stool ova and parasites
The decision point

Three to four days of undifferentiated fever, headache and myalgia followed by a rash on the extremities, in a child with wooded exposure, carrying the laboratory triad of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatremia — that is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and the management is empiric doxycycline started now. Diagnosis is made retrospectively by serology; the disease progresses to vascular collapse and death if you wait for it. The abdominal pain is not a second problem: severe abdominal pain is part of RMSF in children, and it is the specific reason this boy got a CT rather than an antibiotic on his first visit.

Defining criteria Rocky Mountain spotted fever — Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular organism transmitted by tick bite, peaking in summer; many patients never recall the bite, so its absence proves nothing · The rash — begins maculopapular on the wrists and ankles, spreads centrally, involves palms and soles, and evolves to petechiae · The laboratory triad — thrombocytopenia from intravascular platelet destruction, hyponatremia, and raised AST and ALT from hepatic endothelial injury · Treatment gate — doxycycline empirically on suspicion, in all patients including young children; staining risk is minimal over the 5 to 7 day course used ⚠︎
Pertinent positives & negatives Three days of nonspecific fever then a rash — the rickettsial tempo; the rash arrives late by design, which is why the first visit was unremarkable · Rash on arms and legs — extremity onset, spreading centrally · Platelets 46,000 with raised transaminases — the vascular-injury signature, belonging to no isolated abdominal process · Lives near woods — the exposure; no recalled bite is typical, not exculpatory · Severe abdominal pain with a normal CT — the paediatric RMSF mimic of appendicitis; the negative scan closes the surgical option rather than opening a new one · Confusion with a nonfocal examination and no neck stiffness — early encephalitic involvement, not meningitis · BP 90/60 with HR 120 — early vascular compromise, and the reason waiting is dangerous · No adenopathy, clear oropharynx — argues against the viral exanthems and mononucleosis
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Can't missSummer, wooded exposure; R. rickettsiiExtremity rash spreading centrally, palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases— (the answer)
Lyme diseaseSame season and habitat; Borrelia burgdorferiErythema migrans — a single expanding annular lesion with central clearingMaculopapular extremity rash; cytopenias and transaminitis atypical
Ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisSame tick exposure, similar prodromeSame labs, usually no rash; morulae in leukocytesA prominent rash is present
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, otherwise well childIsolated thrombocytopenia, normal liver, afebrileFever, rash, transaminitis and hypotension
Wilson diseaseGenetic copper transport defectKayser-Fleischer rings; hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease over monthsAn acute febrile illness with a rash over days
AmebiasisFever, abdominal pain, liver abscessBloody diarrhea; abscess on imagingCT normal, no diarrhea, rash unexplained
Decision spine How long has the fever run and when did the rash appear? — Three to four days, then rash, the rickettsial tempo · Where did the rash start? — Wrists and ankles, spreading inward · What did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do? — Low, low, high, the triad · Any outdoor or wooded exposure? — Yes, and a recalled bite is not required · Is there abdominal pain? — In a child that is part of the disease, not a second one · So when do you treat? — Now; serology is retrospective and untreated disease kills
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → staining risk is minimal with a 5 to 7 day course
  3. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  4. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Confirming the diagnosis in a child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
Decoy note Two details send you down abdominal and hepatic paths. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT is the classic paediatric RMSF presentation that gets children taken to theatre, and the stem shows the negative scan precisely so you stop pursuing it. Confusion pairs with transaminitis to suggest Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively — serology is for the chart, doxycycline is for the patient · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF — the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure — a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward — extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite means nothing — exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness — a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Part I Cellulitis & the Depth Ladder for the febrile-rash differential; Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis are the natural companions and are not yet written. Store the discriminator as a question: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, the diagnostic threshold collapses into the treatment threshold — treat on the clinical picture and let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; it is a reason to have already started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites — fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone — platelets of 46,000 invite ITP, but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin — correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin — liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy — the abdominal CT is already normal, so the ledger has answered the surgical question.

The Acutely Inflamed Cervical Node

acute and unilateral is bacterial · UWorld · tempo and laterality sort every neck node

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, lump on the right neck noticed yesterday, today red, painful and larger; cough, rhinorrhea and low-grade fever a week ago, resolved; family reunion in eastern Arkansas with several cousins also coryzal · Exam — T 38.6, HR 98; 5 cm tender, warm, poorly mobile anterior cervical node with overlying erythema; no hepatosplenomegaly · Q — the most appropriate treatment; options spanned azithromycin, cefdinir, clindamycin, itraconazole, oseltamivir and supportive care only
The decision point

Two axes settle this: tempo and laterality. A node that appeared yesterday and is bigger, red and tender today is acute; a single inflamed node on one side is unilateral. Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis in a child under five is a bacterial infection of the node itself, and the organisms are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, with anaerobes when there is periodontal disease. Empiric therapy has to cover gram-positives including MRSA plus anaerobes, and among the offered agents only clindamycin does all three. The preceding viral illness is not the cause — it is the portal, and it has already resolved.

Defining criteria Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis — child under 5; a 3 to 6 cm node, markedly tender, warm and erythematous, with or without fever; the child is usually well-appearing and the diagnosis is clinical · Empiric coverage required — S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes, and anaerobes, which is clindamycin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reasonable where community MRSA is low, a first-generation cephalosporin where periodontal disease is unlikely · Suppuration — fluctuance on examination signals abscess and adds incision and drainage · Observation gate — supportive care alone is defensible only in an afebrile child with minimal tenderness and minimal enlargement
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset yesterday, larger today — acute; excludes cat-scratch disease and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, both chronic and slowly enlarging · Unilateral — a node infection, not reactive adenopathy, which is bilateral · Tender, warm, erythematous — inflammatory; mycobacterial nodes are nontender and violaceous · T 38.6 — opens the antibiotic gate that observation would otherwise satisfy · 5 cm — large enough to risk suppuration; size is part of the treatment gate · Poorly mobile with overlying erythema — tethering from inflammation; malignancy is painless and not erythematous · URI a week ago, now resolved — the portal of entry, not the active illness · No hepatosplenomegaly or diffuse adenopathy — excludes disseminated histoplasmosis and mononucleosis
The inflamed cervical node — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Acute bacterial lymphadenitisUnder 5, after a URI; S. aureus and S. pyogenesAcute, unilateral, tender, warm, erythematous, with or without fever— (the answer)
Cat-scratch diseaseKitten scratch or bite 1 to 2 weeks earlier; BartonellaChronic, slowly enlarging node with a papule at the inoculation siteOnset yesterday; no animal exposure
Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisAlso under 5, indolent courseChronic, violaceous, nontender; treated by excision ⚠︎Acute, tender, erythematous and febrile
Reactive viral adenopathyConcurrent URI or influenzaBilateral, small, mobile, mildly tenderUnilateral and 5 cm; the URI has resolved
Disseminated histoplasmosisMississippi and Ohio River ValleysPulmonary disease with mediastinal adenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly with diffuse adenopathyIsolated neck node; no organomegaly or lung findings
Decision spine Acute or chronic? — Days means bacterial; weeks means Bartonella or mycobacterial · Unilateral or bilateral? — Unilateral is a node infection; bilateral is reactive · Tender and erythematous, or violaceous and painless? — Tender means pyogenic · Febrile? Large? — Both means antibiotics, not observation · Fluctuant? — If yes, drain as well · Which agent covers S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes? — Clindamycin
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier → Clindamycin → covers MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes
  2. 4 yo with a 2 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema → Supportive care with reassessment → observation is appropriate below the treatment gate
  3. 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema → Incision and drainage with continued antibiotics → suppuration has developed
  4. 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where a kitten scratched him → Cat-scratch disease → azithromycin
  5. 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well → Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis → surgical excision
  6. 3 yo with acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community with high MRSA prevalence → Cefdinir → no coverage of Staphylococcus aureus or anaerobes
  7. 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy → Disseminated histoplasmosis → itraconazole
  8. 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes → Reactive viral adenopathy → supportive care
  9. 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash → Staphylococcus aureus → With Streptococcus pyogenes — acute, unilateral, suppurative
  10. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries → Anaerobic oral flora → Prevotella and relatives follow periodontal disease
  11. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit → Francisella tularensis → The exposure names the organism
  12. Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days → Acute viral adenitis → Bilateral and acute points at adenovirus and its relatives
  13. 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 → Acute bacterial lymphadenitis → empiric clindamycin
Decoy note The geography is the trap and it is precisely placed: eastern Arkansas is genuinely endemic for histoplasmosis, and the stem puts it in the same sentence as the sick contacts so it reads as an exposure history. It is neither — the cousins explain the resolved URI, and the location explains nothing, because histoplasmosis does not present as a single hot node.
Pearls Tempo and laterality sort neck nodes before anything else — acute and unilateral is bacterial, chronic and unilateral is Bartonella or mycobacterial, acute and bilateral is viral · Clindamycin is the answer because of its spectrum, not its class — a cephalosporin that misses staphylococci fails even though the class sounds right · Violaceous and nontender is mycobacterial, and its treatment is surgical excision rather than antibiotics ⚠︎ · Fluctuance changes the plan, not the drug — it adds drainage · A resolved URI a week earlier is a portal of entry, not a competing diagnosis; a concurrent URI would point at reactive adenopathy instead
Pairs with Part I Pediatric Upper Respiratory Infection, which owns the reactive-adenopathy end of this spectrum and the exudative pharyngitis fork. Store the discriminator as a question: how fast did it appear, and is it one node or many?
Transferable rule When every option is a drug, the question is spectrum, not diagnosis — name the organisms you must cover, then find the single agent that covers all of them. And a geographic detail earns its place only when the syndrome matches the endemic disease, not merely the map.
Unchecked attributeSupportive care only — the observation gate requires an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; this is 38.6 with a 5 cm inflamed node at risk of abscess.
Unchecked attributeAzithromycin — correct for cat-scratch and part of mycobacterial therapy, but both are chronic and indolent; this appeared yesterday.
Class-vs-memberCefdinir — covers S. pyogenes but not S. aureus or anaerobes, and the two are clinically indistinguishable here.
Salient decoyItraconazole — eastern Arkansas is histoplasmosis country, but histoplasmosis presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease, not an isolated hot node.
True-fact-wrong-slotOseltamivir — influenza adenopathy is bilateral and accompanies active respiratory symptoms, which have resolved.

Oral Vesicles in a Child

the location names the virus · UWorld · front of the mouth or back

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam — scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with grey shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q — the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

Two features settle this and both are anatomical. First, the lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate, which removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis at a stroke, since adenovirus, EBV and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate and none produces oral vesicles. Second, and this is the whole question, the lesions are posterior — soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars — with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, lives in the back of the mouth; herpetic gingivostomatitis lives in the front, with red swollen gums. The stem spares exactly the structures HSV would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina — coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with grey vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis — HSV-1; 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate — excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved — the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared — a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash — separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described — a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks — age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly — nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior grey vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash— (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? — Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? — Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? — Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? — No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? — Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? — Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and grey shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with grey vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; grey vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie — one attribute decides the entire question, and both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does — same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · shedding continues in stool for weeks after recovery ⚠︎, so hand hygiene rather than exclusion is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Pediatric Upper Respiratory Infection, which owns the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief owns what happens when the lesions are vesicular instead. Store the discriminator as a question: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back?
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where before you ask what — and treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus — oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus — a common cause of paediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes — exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus — exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

Recurrent Abscesses and Granulomas

the organism list is the diagnosis · board question · Are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?

Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, 3 days of fever, cough and irritability; perirectal abscess drained at 9 months; T 38.9, bilateral lower-lobe crackles · Imaging — bilateral pneumonia on chest film; after 3 days of antibiotics still febrile, CT shows a small left effusion with paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy · Labs — lymph node and lung biopsy shows granuloma formation; culture grows Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia · Q — the mechanism responsible; options spanned decreased immunoglobulin production, decreased superoxide production, defective opsonization, impaired clearing of airway secretions and impaired neutrophil chemotaxis
The decision point

Two findings name the defect and neither is the pneumonia. Granulomas on biopsy and a Burkholderia cepacia culture together point at one disease: chronic granulomatous disease, a disorder of NADPH oxidase, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms. The enzyme drives the neutrophil respiratory burst, so its loss means decreased superoxide production — phagocytes migrate normally and ingest normally, but have impaired intracellular killing. The organism list follows directly: neutrophils can borrow hydrogen peroxide made by the pathogen itself, so susceptibility particularly involves characteristic catalase-positive organisms that destroy their own peroxide; this is not an exclusive organism list. The granulomas are the same defect seen histologically: phagocytes arrive but clear pathogens poorly, contributing to granuloma formation.

Defining criteria Chronic granulomatous disease — NADPH oxidase disorder, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms; impaired respiratory burst and reduced reactive oxygen species, so intracellular killing is impaired · The organism pattern — particular susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because catalase degrades the pathogen's own hydrogen peroxide and denies the neutrophil a borrowed oxidant: S aureus, B cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus · Sites — lungs, skin, liver and lymph nodes; perirectal abscess is characteristic, with diffuse granulomas in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts · Diagnosis — measure neutrophil superoxide production: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry preferred, nitroblue tetrazolium the older equivalent · Treatment — prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma; haematopoietic cell transplant is curative
Recurrent infection — reading the mechanismwhich defect, by organism and by histology
MechanismDiseaseThe NBME tellExcluded here by
↓ superoxide productionChronic granulomatous diseaseCatalase-positive organisms + granulomas + abscesses (perirectal, liver)— (the answer)
Impaired airway clearanceCystic fibrosisNasal polyps, clubbing, steatorrhoea; also gets B cepaciaNo granulomas; infections confined to the sinopulmonary tract
↓ immunoglobulin productionX-linked agammaglobulinaemiaEncapsulated organisms; all isotypes low, absent B cellsNo granulomas, no abscesses, wrong organism
Defective opsonisationComplement (C3) deficiencyEncapsulated organisms, recurrent pyogenic infectionSame — and B cepacia is not the pattern
Impaired neutrophil chemotaxisLeukocyte adhesion deficiencyDelayed umbilical cord separation, infections without pus, marked leukocytosisPus was present (abscess drained); no granulomas
Pertinent positives & negatives Granulomas on biopsy — the most specific finding; excludes CF, XLA, complement deficiency and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, none of which form them · Burkholderia cepacia — catalase-positive, and shared with cystic fibrosis, which is exactly why it is not sufficient alone · Perirectal abscess at 9 months — extrapulmonary abscess; CF does not do this, and it is the finding that separates the two · Persistent fever after 3 days of appropriate antibiotics — killing is defective, not coverage · Hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy — node involvement, part of the CGD site pattern · Male, age 2 — consistent with the common X-linked form presenting in early childhood; autosomal recessive forms also occur · Normal ear, nose and throat examination — no chronic rhinosinusitis, arguing further against CF
Decision spine Are there granulomas? — Yes → CGD, essentially alone among the immunodeficiencies · What grew? — A catalase-positive organism → confirms · Where are the infections? — Lung and perirectal → extrapulmonary, so not CF · Was there pus? — Yes → chemotaxis and adhesion intact, so not leukocyte adhesion deficiency · What is the mechanism of that defect? — NADPH oxidase → decreased superoxide · How is it confirmed? — Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia → Decreased superoxide production → NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
  2. 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging → Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry → measures the neutrophil respiratory burst
  3. Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? → Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxide → the neutrophil cannot borrow the pathogen's oxidant
  4. 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections → TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxis → bacterial, fungal and immunomodulatory cover
  5. 5 yo with chronic granulomatous disease and repeated life-threatening infections despite full prophylaxis → Haematopoietic cell transplantation → the only curative therapy
  6. Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a leukocyte count of 38,000 → Leukocyte adhesion deficiency → impaired chemotaxis and adhesion
  7. 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhoea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas → Cystic fibrosis → sweat chloride testing
  8. 9 mo M with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, all immunoglobulin isotypes low and absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinaemia → immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  9. 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, a perirectal abscess drained in infancy and granulomas on biopsy → Chronic granulomatous disease → confirm with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
The organism is never the discriminator here Burkholderia cepacia belongs to two diseases — cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease — so it identifies neither alone. Granulomas and extrapulmonary abscesses are what split them, and a perirectal abscess in an infant is the single most specific line in a CGD stem. It sits in the past medical history, where it is easy to skim.
Pearls Granulomas plus abscesses plus a catalase-positive organism is CGD, and no other immunodeficiency assembles that trio · Catalase-positive is a mechanism, not a list — the neutrophil can use the organism's own peroxide, helping explain susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive organisms; other organisms are not excluded · Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry has replaced nitroblue tetrazolium as the preferred test; both measure the same respiratory burst · CGD prophylaxis is three drugs — antibacterial, antifungal and interferon gamma — and transplant is the only cure · Phagocytes in CGD migrate and ingest normally; the failure is intracellular killing, which is why pus forms and chemotaxis-defect diseases look different
Pairs with Part I The Immunoglobulin Panel, which owns the antibody deficiencies and now has a phagocyte counterpart — the two together cover the immunodeficiency option list. Store the discriminator as a question: are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?
Transferable rule When an organism belongs to two diseases, it cannot be the discriminator — find the finding that belongs to only one. Here the shared organism is B cepacia and the private findings are the granuloma and the perirectal abscess.
Unchecked attributeImpaired clearing of airway secretions — cystic fibrosis makes no granulomas, and its infections stay sinopulmonary; a perirectal abscess is outside its territory.
Class-vs-memberDefective opsonization — complement deficiency gives encapsulated-organism infection without granulomas.
Class-vs-memberImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis — leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives pus-free infections with delayed cord separation; pus was drained here.
True-fact-wrong-slotDecreased immunoglobulin production — XLA gives encapsulated sinopulmonary infection; no granulomas, wrong organism.

Infectious Disease

Peritonsillar Abscess and the Deep Neck Spaces

Trismus with a deviated uvula · UWorld · no imaging needed

Source vignette Pt — 14 yo M, a week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis
The decision point

A week of worsening unilateral sore throat with trismus, a muffled voice and a uvula deviated away from the swelling is a peritonsillar abscess, and it is a clinical diagnosis. Imaging answers a question that has already been answered — the next step is needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

The deep neck spaces sort by age and by what the child cannot do. Trismus and uvular deviation are peritonsillar; pain on neck extension with a bulging posterior wall is retropharyngeal; tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx is epiglottitis.

Defining criteria Peritonsillar abscess — trismus, muffled hot-potato voice, uvula deviated to the contralateral side, unilateral tonsillar bulge · Retropharyngeal abscess — pain on neck extension, bulging posterior pharyngeal wall, typically under 5 years · Epiglottitis — toxic, tripoding, drooling, stridor, with a deceptively normal oropharynx
The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Peritonsillar abscessAdolescent or young adult, days of worsening unilateral painTrismus with uvular deviation; no imaging required
Retropharyngeal abscessUnder 5 years, often after a pharyngeal infectionPain on neck extension, bulging posterior wall; CT neck with contrast
EpiglottitisUnvaccinated child, hours not daysTripoding with stridor and a normal pharynx; secure the airway in theatre
Infectious mononucleosisBilateral exudates, posterior cervical nodesSplenomegaly; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
Ludwig anginaDental source, floor of mouthTongue elevation and submental induration; airway first
Lemierre syndrome Can't missAfter oropharyngeal infectionPersistent fever with nodular lung opacities; internal jugular thrombophlebitis
Scenario bank
  1. 14 yo M, week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left → Peritonsillar abscess → no imaging - needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics
  2. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess, what must the antibiotics cover → Group A Streptococcus and respiratory anaerobes
  3. 4 yo M, fever and drooling with pain on neck extension and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall → Retropharyngeal abscess → CT neck with contrast
  4. 5 yo M, unvaccinated, toxic and tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  5. 17 yo F back from camp, bilateral exudative tonsils, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Infectious mononucleosis → heterophile antibody, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
  6. 14 yo M whose drained abscess is followed by persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain and nodular lung opacities → Lemierre syndrome → contrast CT and anaerobic coverage
  7. 50 yo M with a dental infection, floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation → Ludwig angina → airway first
  8. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling where phlegmon versus abscess is uncertain → Intraoral ultrasound
  9. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling who develops new neck swelling and torticollis → Parapharyngeal extension → CT neck with contrast
  10. 14 yo M with a third peritonsillar abscess this year → Tonsillectomy
  11. 6 yo F with bilateral exudates, no trismus, no uvular deviation, positive rapid strep → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → penicillin or amoxicillin
Airway before anything In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis the airway is the emergency and examination can precipitate obstruction — do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating theatre. Recurrent peritonsillar abscess, three or more in a year, earns tonsillectomy.
Pearls Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound only helps when phlegmon versus abscess is genuinely uncertain · Retropharyngeal abscess hurts on extension; meningitis hurts on flexion · Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis produces a florid morbilliform rash · Lemierre syndrome is Fusobacterium necrophorum with septic pulmonary emboli after an oropharyngeal infection
Pairs with Part I Pediatric Upper Respiratory Infection covers the uncomplicated end of this spectrum; the discriminator as a question is whether anything is unilateral.
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, the imaging option is almost always the wrong next step, because the picture cannot change what you already know and costs time the airway may not have.
Sequencing trapImaging before drainage in a clinically obvious abscess.
Mirror twinRetropharyngeal abscess is the younger child's version, separated by extension versus trismus.

The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source

Paradoxical irritability · Aquifer · every stem negative is an eliminated source

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo M, fever 39.5 C, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up · Labs — WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils; urine dipstick negative on a concentrated specimen · Q — the most appropriate test; options spanned lumbar puncture, abdominal ultrasonography and stool PCR
The decision point

One sentence in the physical examination is the whole question: he is calm when left alone and screams when picked up. That is paradoxical irritability — handling stretches inflamed meninges, so being comforted makes an infant worse. It is the meningeal sign of infancy, and it exists because nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months.

Everything else in the stem is a negative that closes an alternative source. No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch. A negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite in urine concentrated to a specific gravity of 1.030 closes the urinary branch — concentration is what makes the negative trustworthy. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, the answer is the lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Paradoxical irritability — quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved · Fever without a source — documented fever with no localising findings after history and examination · Dipstick sensitivity — leukocyte esterase about 83%, nitrite about 53%; both negative in concentrated urine is genuinely reassuring
The toxic febrile infant — where is the source
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Bacterial meningitisAny age; infants show no neck signsParadoxical irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry
Intussusception6 to 36 months, ileocolic, often post-viralParoxysmal crying with pain-free intervals, sausage mass, currant-jelly stool
Urinary tract infectionThe commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infantsPositive leukocyte esterase or nitrite with pyuria
Bacterial gastroenteritisHigh fever with crampingBloody or mucoid stools, many per day, sick contacts
Viral respiratory infectionCough, congestion, coryzaRhinorrhea and cough, both explicitly absent here
Occult bacteremia or pneumoniaFever with leukocytosis, no localising signTachypnea with hypoxia or focal crackles, not fever-driven tachypnea alone
Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo M, fever 39.5, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up, WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils, urine dipstick negative in concentrated urine → Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture → bacterial meningitis
  2. 9 mo M with paroxysmal crying and legs drawn up, calm between episodes, lethargic, sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception
  3. 8 mo F, fever 39.2, no localising findings, urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase → Urine culture and empiric antibiotics → urinary tract infection
  4. 6 mo M with suspected meningitis in whom lumbar puncture will be delayed an hour → Give empiric antibiotics now and perform the lumbar puncture after → a sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable trade
  5. 3 wk old F with a temperature of 38.4 C, well-appearing, with no identified source → Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics → under 28 days, well appearance does not reassure
  6. 10 mo M with fever, irritability, a bulging anterior fontanelle and a high-pitched cry → Bacterial meningitis → neuroimaging only if focal signs are present
  7. 7 mo M with 3 days of fever to 39 C, then defervescence followed by a blanching rose-pink truncal rash → Roseola infantum → human herpesvirus 6, no testing needed
  8. 12 mo F with suspected meningitis, papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit → Head CT before lumbar puncture → antibiotics first, then CT, then LP
  9. 8 mo M with fever, petechiae and hypotension → Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture → treat first, tap after
Sequence and its exceptions Head CT precedes lumbar puncture only for focal deficits, papilledema, altered consciousness or immunocompromise — and antibiotics precede the CT, not the other way round. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended: the fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so tap without imaging first. Under 28 days a well appearance does not reassure: full evaluation, admission and empiric antibiotics regardless. Empiric coverage beyond the neonatal period is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; neonates get ampicillin plus cefotaxime or gentamicin to cover Listeria.
Pearls Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski are unreliable in infants; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry · A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out — nitrite is insensitive because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction · Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localising findings · Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis owns the CSF grid, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Store the link as a question: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child owns what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Part II Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics owns the afebrile neonate whose lab is the only sign; store the discriminator: is the infant febrile, or is the WBC the decider?
Transferable rule When the options are tests, name the disease first and let the test follow, and in a febrile infant do it by elimination, because every negative the stem supplies is an eliminated source and the diagnosis is whatever survives.
Mirror twinIntussusception is the other inconsolable-infant diagnosis, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals.
Class-vs-memberUrine culture is the right class of test on the wrong fluid.
Salient decoyThree loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 with 83% neutrophils.

Congenital CMV and the TORCH Discriminations

Periventricular calcifications · UWorld · organism first, then its signature sequela

Source vignette Pt — 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly · Imaging — periventricular calcifications · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital cytomegalovirus, congenital toxoplasmosis and congenital rubella
The decision point

Two steps, and the second is where most people fall off: identify the organism, then jump to its signature sequela. The question never asks which infection.

The organism is settled by one word — periventricular. Calcifications hugging the ventricular margin are CMV; scattered through the parenchyma they are toxoplasmosis. The indoor cat exists to sell toxoplasmosis, and it is compatible with congenital CMV rather than incompatible with it.

Defining criteria Periventricular calcifications — CMV · Diffuse parenchymal calcifications — toxoplasmosis, with chorioretinitis · Subcortical calcifications with arthrogryposis — Zika · Diagnostic window — urine or saliva PCR within the first 3 weeks of life, after which congenital and perinatal acquisition cannot be separated
Congenital infection — the differential
InfectionIllness scriptThe NBME tell
CMVMost common congenital infection; hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephalyPeriventricular calcifications with microcephaly; sequela is sensorineural hearing loss
ToxoplasmosisCat litter, undercooked meatDiffuse parenchymal calcifications and chorioretinitis; sequela is obstructive hydrocephalus
RubellaUnvaccinated motherCataracts and a continuous machine-like PDA murmur
SyphilisUntreated maternal infectionSnuffles, palm-and-sole rash, periostitis; no CNS calcifications
HSV Can't missIntrapartum acquisitionDays 5 to 21, vesicles, seizures, temporal lobe
ZikaMaternal travelSevere microcephaly with subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis
Parvovirus B19Maternal febrile illness with arthralgia; risk highest before 20 weeksHydrops fetalis or fetal loss; congenital anomalies are rare in survivors
Listeria monocytogenes Can't missNonspecific maternal febrile illness, often foodborneSevere neonatal sepsis with disseminated abscesses in liver, spleen, lung, kidney and brain
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly, periventricular calcifications → Congenital CMV → valganciclovir
  2. 2 mo F with symptomatic congenital CMV, greatest long-term risk → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. Newborn with diffuse parenchymal calcifications, chorioretinitis and ventriculomegaly → Congenital toxoplasmosis
  4. Newborn with cataracts and a continuous machine-like murmur → Congenital rubella
  5. Newborn with snuffles, a palm-and-sole rash and long-bone periostitis → Congenital syphilis → penicillin
  6. 7 yo with notched incisors, saddle nose and interstitial keratitis → Late congenital syphilis
  7. Neonate on day 10 with vesicles, seizures and temporal-lobe changes → Neonatal HSV → intravenous acyclovir
  8. Newborn with severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis after maternal travel → Congenital Zika
  9. Newborn with suspected congenital CMV, how to confirm the diagnosis → Urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks of life
  10. Newborn with a positive saliva CMV PCR → Confirm with urine PCR → saliva gives false positives
  11. Newborn with symptomatic congenital CMV, treatment duration → 6 Months of valganciclovir
  12. Newborn with congenital CMV who passes the newborn hearing screen → Serial audiology through childhood → the loss is often late-onset
  13. Infant with congenital CMV and enlarged ventricles → Hydrocephalus ex vacuo → parenchymal volume loss
  14. 2-day-old, failed hearing screen bilaterally, absent red reflex, continuous murmur at the left second interspace, hepatosplenomegaly, growth below the 5th percentile, mother with a first-trimester febrile illness and arthralgia → Congenital rubella syndrome → hearing loss, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus
  15. Why the first trimester is rubella's dangerous window → Transplacental infection during organogenesis → spontaneous abortion or congenital rubella syndrome
  16. Newborn with suspected congenital rubella syndrome; establishing the diagnosis → Infant rubella IgM serology → serology rather than PCR, because the PCR window belongs to cytomegalovirus
  17. Pregnant woman with fever and arthralgia at 16 weeks whose fetus develops ascites, effusions and skin edema → Parvovirus B19 with hydrops fetalis → anomalies are rare in survivors
Why getting this right may not mean you read it right Rubella also causes sensorineural hearing loss, so a reader who misidentified the organism as rubella could still have landed on the correct sequela. Getting this question right does not prove you read the calcification pattern.
The rubella triad Sensorineural hearing loss — a failed newborn hearing screen · Cataracts — an absent red reflex, or leukocoria · Patent ductus arteriosus — a continuous machine-like murmur at the left second interspace · Plus — growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and a purpuric blueberry-muffin rash · Maternal arthralgia after a febrile illness in pregnancy has two owners — rubella gives organ malformation from first-trimester organogenesis, parvovirus B19 gives hydrops and no malformation
Pearls CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss · Only about 10% are symptomatic at birth, and that group carries up to 50% hearing-loss risk untreated · Six months of valganciclovir beats six weeks — 8% versus 13% hearing worsening at one year · Hearing loss is progressive and can be late-onset, so passing the newborn screen does not discharge the child from audiology · CMV — ventricles enlarge ex vacuo from volume loss · Toxoplasmosis — ventricles enlarge from obstruction
Pairs with Part I Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis carries the childhood sensorineural causes and should gain the congenital CMV row. Part I Cerebral Palsy and the MRI Pattern reads the same films forward — the calcification pattern and the white-matter injury each name a different cause.
Transferable rule When a stem gives a syndrome and asks for its complication, there are two independent failure points, and exposure history is placed to attack the first one, so anatomic distribution beats exposure history every time both are offered.
Unchecked attributeCytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis both follow a mild maternal flu-like illness, but neither produces cataracts or a cardiac defect — the maternal history is shared and the fetal organ pattern is what separates them.
Salient decoyThe indoor cat sells toxoplasmosis but is compatible with CMV.
True-fact-wrong-slotRubella has real cataracts, but no periventricular calcifications.

Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics

Afebrile neonate with leukopenia · board question · the WBC decides when the temperature does not

Source vignette Pt — 3 do F, irritable and refusing feeds, HR 180, normothermic · Labs — WBC 3,000, glucose normal · Q — the most appropriate pharmacotherapy; options spanned ampicillin plus gentamicin, intravenous dextrose and morphine sulfate
The decision point

The stem strips away fever and gives you an afebrile 3-day-old with irritability, feeding refusal, and tachycardia. Everything in the behavioral pattern is shared by NAS, hypoglycemia, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis. The single value that separates sepsis from all three is WBC 3,000 — leukopenia. NAS produces tremor with a normal WBC; hypoglycemia is excluded by a normal glucose; thyrotoxicosis requires a maternal Graves history. Leukopenia in a neonate reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis. The empiric regimen is ampicillin plus gentamicin — ampicillin for GBS and Listeria, gentamicin for gram-negative coverage.

You answered correctly in under two minutes.

Defining criteria Early-onset neonatal sepsis — onset within 72 hours; organisms from the maternal genital tract (GBS, E. coli, Listeria) · Late-onset neonatal sepsis — onset 72 hours to 90 days; nosocomial organisms join (coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus) · Neonatal empiric coverage — ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime); ceftriaxone is avoided because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and causes biliary sludging
The irritable neonate — what decides the diagnosisleukopenia separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Neonatal sepsis Can't missDay 0–7, maternal GBS or chorioamnionitis; subtle — poor feeding, temp instability, apnea, tachycardiaLeukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift; the neonate who “doesn’t look right”— (the answer)
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid use, onset 24–72 hHigh-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing, hyperactive Moro; normal WBCNo maternal drug history; leukopenia
Neonatal hypoglycemiaIDM, LGA, SGA, pretermJitteriness, lethargy, seizures; glucose <40–45Glucose normal
Neonatal thyrotoxicosisMaternal Graves diseaseTachycardia, irritability, exophthalmos, goiterNo maternal thyroid history; leukopenia
Inborn error of metabolismPoor feeding after protein or galactose, day 2–5Metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, specific dietary triggerNo metabolic derangement described
Scenario bank
  1. 3 do F, irritable, refusing feeds, HR 180, normothermic, WBC 3,000, glucose normal → Ampicillin and gentamicin → early-onset neonatal sepsis
  2. 2 do M, jittery, high-pitched cry, sneezing, hyperactive Moro reflex, maternal heroin use, WBC 12,000, glucose normal → Neonatal abstinence syndrome → supportive care, consider morphine if severe
  3. 1 do F, jittery, lethargic, glucose 28, mother with gestational diabetes → Intravenous dextrose infusion → neonatal hypoglycemia
  4. 4 do F, tachycardia, tremor, poor weight gain, exophthalmos, maternal Graves disease → Neonatal thyrotoxicosis → propranolol and methimazole
  5. 5 do M with confirmed neonatal sepsis; which antibiotic to avoid → Ceftriaxone → displaces bilirubin from albumin and causes biliary sludging
  6. 6 hr old M born to mother with chorioamnionitis, grunting with nasal flaring, HR 170 → Blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → early-onset GBS sepsis
  7. Most common organism causing early-onset neonatal sepsis in a term infant → Group B Streptococcus → intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
  8. 21 do M, fever 38.8, irritability, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle → Lumbar puncture with blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → late-onset neonatal meningitis
Age-based empiric regimens Neonate (0–28 days): ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime) — covers GBS, E. coli, Listeria · Infant >28 days: ceftriaxone plus vancomycin — the neonatal organisms recede and ceftriaxone’s biliary risk becomes acceptable · Never ceftriaxone in a neonate: it displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract. The under-28-day rule also means a well appearance does not reassure — full evaluation, admission, and empiric antibiotics regardless of clinical impression.
Pearls Neonates with sepsis may be afebrile or hypothermic — fever is unreliable in the first month, and leukopenia is more ominous than leukocytosis because it signals marrow exhaustion · Early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract: GBS, E. coli (K1 capsule), Listeria · Late-onset organisms add nosocomial flora: coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Candida in VLBW infants · GBS prophylaxis (intrapartum penicillin) reduced early-onset GBS disease but did not change E. coli rates — E. coli now predominates among preterm and VLBW neonates · 5% weight loss at day 3 is physiologic (up to 7–10% in breastfed newborns) and decides nothing
Pairs with Part II The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source owns the source-identification algorithm and the under-28-day rule; store the discriminator as a question: is the neonate febrile, or is the lab the only sign? Part I Bacterial Meningitis owns the CSF grid and the neonatal organism-by-host list.
Transferable rule In a neonate, the absence of fever does not exclude sepsis — the lab decides when the temperature does not, and leukopenia in a newborn is sepsis until proven otherwise. When the stem strips away fever and maternal drug history, the WBC is the decider, not the behavioral pattern.
Salient decoyIrritability and poor feeding pattern-match to NAS or hypoglycemia; leukopenia belongs to neither.
Class-vs-memberCeftriaxone and vancomycin is the right class of empiric coverage at the wrong age — neonates get ampicillin plus gentamicin.
True-fact-wrong-slotPropranolol genuinely treats neonatal thyrotoxicosis, but thyrotoxicosis does not produce leukopenia.

Neurology & HEENT 12 topics + 3 board-style

Three questions triage every red eye. Two tuning forks triage every hearing loss.

Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis

Rinne and Weber before anything else

The decision point

Conductive loss: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, Rinne shows BC > AC in that ear. Sensorineural: Weber lateralizes away, Rinne stays AC > BC bilaterally. A conductive loss with a normal otoscopic exam in a young adult is otosclerosis.

Otosclerosis pathophysiology A genetic bone-remodeling disorder of the otic capsule at the fissula ante fenestram — an otospongiotic (hypervascular, resorptive) phase followed by a sclerotic phase that fixes the stapes footplate. Autosomal dominant with ~40% penetrance, onset in the 20s–40s, female 2:1 — so family history is often absent. Estrogen and progesterone accelerate it, which is why it is classically unmasked in pregnancy. Measles virus RNA has been found in otosclerotic foci.
Exam & audiogram Paracusis of Willis — hears better in noisy environments · Carhart notch — dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, an artifact of ossicular fixation · Schwartze sign — reddish blush from hypervascularity · treatment: amplification or stapedectomy · van der Hoeve syndrome = osteogenesis imperfecta + otosclerosis + blue sclerae (both type I collagen disorders).
Scenario bank
  1. 35 yo F with progressive conductive loss, Weber lateralizing to the affected ear, normal drum → Otosclerosis
  2. 35 yo F with Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear and Rinne AC over BC bilaterally → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. 35 yo F with conductive loss, foul discharge and a retraction pocket → Cholesteatoma
  4. 68 yo M with symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss and poor speech discrimination → Presbycusis
  5. 45 yo F with unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus and imbalance → Vestibular schwannoma → MRI
  6. 50 yo M with sudden unilateral sensorineural loss over hours → Sudden sensorineural hearing loss → urgent corticosteroids
  7. 5 yo M, progressive hearing difficulty over a year, born small for gestational age at 36 weeks, Weber lateralises to the unaffected ear with air conduction better than bone conduction bilaterally → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → delayed-onset sensorineural hearing loss
  8. 3 yo F with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, an older brother in hearing aids since infancy, normal development → Connexin 26 mutation → the commonest cause of hereditary sensorineural loss
  9. The most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss in children → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → often asymptomatic at birth, with hearing loss that may be delayed
The sensorineural mimics Aminoglycosides cause sensorineural loss (hair cell damage), never conductive · Ménière = episodic vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus · presbycusis = gradual, high-frequency, elderly · vestibular schwannoma = unilateral SNHL + tinnitus → MRI. All have normal otoscopy — the tuning forks separate them from otosclerosis.
Pairs with Part I Cholesteatoma and Chronic Ear Drainage expands the cholesteatoma line of this brief into its own topic.

The Red Eye

Three questions triage all of it

The decision point

1. Is visual acuity affected? 2. Is there true deep pain (not gritty or itchy)? 3. Is the pupil, cornea, or globe abnormal? Any "yes" means this is not simple conjunctivitis and the answer moves toward urgent ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis types
TypeDiscriminatorTreatment
Viral (adenovirus)Watery, follicular tarsal conjunctiva, preauricular node, URI prodromeSupportive — cool compresses, artificial tears
BacterialPurulent, lids stuck shut on waking, papillaryErythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim
Contact lens wearerAny red eye → think PseudomonasFluoroquinolone; remove lens; urgent ophtho if infiltrate
AllergicITCHING is the hallmark; bilateral, cobblestone papillaeOlopatadine, ketotifen
Gonococcal EmergencyHyperacute (<24 h), copious purulence — can perforate the corneaIM ceftriaxone + irrigation + urgent ophtho
ChlamydialChronic >3 weeks, follicular, sexually active adultOral azithromycin/doxycycline + treat partners
The can't-miss red eyes
DiagnosisThe tellAnswer
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere pain, halos, vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil, hard globe; triggered by dark rooms or anticholinergicsTimolol + apraclonidine + pilocarpine + IV acetazolamide → laser peripheral iridotomy
HSV keratitisDendritic ulcer on fluorescein, ↓ corneal sensationTopical trifluridine or oral acyclovir — never steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicusV1 vesicles + Hutchinson signOral antivirals + ophtho
Anterior uveitisCiliary flush, cell and flare, consensual photophobia; HLA-B27, JIA, sarcoidTopical steroid + cycloplegic — the one place prednisolone is right
ScleritisBoring pain that wakes from sleep, does not blanch with phenylephrine; RA, GPASystemic NSAIDs/steroids
