EpiscleritisSectoral, minimal pain, blanches with phenylephrineSupportive
EndophthalmitisPost-op or post-injection, pain + ↓VA + hypopyonIntravitreal antibiotics — emergency
Orbital cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegiaCT orbits + IV antibiotics (preseptal has none of those)
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo M with bilateral watery red eyes, a preauricular node, recent URI and normal vision → Viral conjunctivitis → supportive care
  2. 24 yo M contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate → Bacterial keratitis → urgent ophthalmology, never patch
  3. 62 yo F with severe pain, halos, a mid-dilated fixed pupil and vomiting → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → topical agents plus acetazolamide
  4. 24 yo M with a dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining → HSV keratitis → topical antiviral, never steroids
  5. 30 yo M with ankylosing spondylitis, photophobia, ciliary flush and anterior chamber cells → Anterior uveitis → topical steroid plus cycloplegic
  6. 55 yo F with rheumatoid arthritis and severe boring eye pain that wakes her at night → Scleritis
  7. Newborn with purulent conjunctivitis on day 3 of life → Gonococcal conjunctivitis → parenteral ceftriaxone
  8. 9 yo M with bilateral eye itching, watery discharge, cobblestone papillae under the upper eyelids, nasal congestion each spring → Allergic conjunctivitis → olopatadine or ketotifen drops
  9. 5 yo F, 3 days of photophobia with lids crusted shut on waking, diffuse bulbar and palpebral erythema, mucopurulent discharge, acuity unchanged → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Mucopurulent discharge with normal acuity
  10. School-age child with mucopurulent conjunctivitis and no contact lens use; the likeliest organism → Haemophilus influenzae → With S pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis
  11. Child with an undifferentiated red eye and mucopurulent discharge; which is contraindicated before slit-lamp examination → Topical corticosteroid drops → Steroid on an unrecognised HSV keratitis worsens it
Neonatal conjunctivitis — a pure timing question Day 0–1 chemical · day 2–5 gonococcal → IM/IV ceftriaxone + irrigation · day 5–14 chlamydial → oral erythromycin (counsel on pyloric stenosis) · day 6–14 HSV → IV acyclovir. Birth prophylaxis (erythromycin ointment) prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial disease.
The steroid rule Topical steroids are the answer in uveitis and scleritis, and the catastrophe in HSV keratitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and undifferentiated red eye. If you cannot name the diagnosis with certainty, steroids are never the answer.

Headache Types & Cluster Headache

Migraine · cluster · tension · the autonomic tell

Source vignette Pt — 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis and rhinorrhea · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia and acute angle-closure glaucoma
The decision point

Acute unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs — ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection — is a cluster headache, and the autonomic column is what decides the stem. Attacks wake the patient from sleep, peak fast, last ~90 minutes, and recur several times daily for weeks before remitting. Acute treatment is 100% oxygen; sumatriptan aborts attacks but is second-line (slower onset, side effects). Vision stays intact — vision change or a fixed mid-dilated pupil moves the diagnosis to angle-closure glaucoma.

Defining criteria Cluster attack — excruciating periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs, often nocturnal onset · Pattern — several attacks daily for 6–8 weeks, then remission lasting months to years · Abortive — 100% oxygen first-line; sumatriptan second · Prophylaxis — verapamil
Headache types — the differential
MigraineClusterTension
SexF > MM > FF > M
OnsetVariableDuring sleep, similar timing dailyUnder stress
LocationOften unilateralBehind one eyeBand-like, bilateral
CharacterPulsatile, throbbingExcruciating, sharp, steadyDull, tight, persistent
Duration4–72 h15–180 min30 min to months
AssociatedPhotophobia, phonophobia, nausea, ± auraIpsilateral autonomic signs — tearing, ptosis, miosis, rhinorrhea, flushingPericranial muscle tenderness
Scenario bank
  1. 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis, and rhinorrhea → Cluster headache → abort with 100% oxygen
  2. 27 yo M with cluster headaches recurring nightly for 3 weeks; best prophylaxis → Verapamil
  3. 24 yo F, 8 hours of unilateral throbbing pain with nausea and photophobia, prior similar episodes → Migraine → NSAID or triptan early
  4. 35 yo F under work stress, band-like bilateral head tightness with neck muscle tenderness, normal exam → Tension headache
  5. 55 yo M, seconds-long electric shocks over the cheek and jaw triggered by chewing and brushing → Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine
  6. 63 yo F, acute eye pain with halos around lights, decreased vision, fixed mid-dilated pupil → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → pressure-lowering drops, then laser iridotomy
Pearls Autonomic signs are nearly universal in cluster — their absence should force a second look · agitation during the attack is a cluster tell (migraineurs lie still) · rhinorrhea plus facial pain baits the sinusitis answer, but sinusitis pain is not episodic and brings congestion and fever, not ptosis · trigeminal neuralgia lasts seconds, cluster lasts an hour and a half.
Pairs with Part I Headache in a Child: What Earns Imaging owns the pediatric red-flag gate that runs before this type differential.
Transferable rule Headache stems are solved on two axes — duration and company: seconds = neuralgia, minutes-to-hours with autonomic signs = cluster, hours-to-days with nausea/photophobia = migraine. Match the clock before the character of the pain.
Salient decoyRhinorrhea suggests sinusitis; the episodic pattern and autonomic bundle decide otherwise.
Class-vs-memberSumatriptan genuinely aborts cluster — but oxygen is the keyed first-line abortive.

Sellar and Suprasellar Masses

endocrine signs localize the tumor, imaging confirms it · board question · Does the endocrine axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and is the chiasm involved?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo F, 6 months of morning headaches, height crossed the 75th to the 10th percentile with weight at the 60th, Tanner 1, papilledema · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned MRI of the brain with contrast, a hand radiograph for bone age and noncontrast head CT
The decision point

Every option names a compartment, so the question is localization and the neurologic examination is deliberately clean — no dysmetria, no gait abnormality, no focal weakness, no skin findings. What is left are three endocrine facts: linear growth arrested at age 11 while weight held, Tanner 1 at 13, and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrest of puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed; and multiple axes failing together points at the stalk, not the gland. Add a headache with disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus and the mass is midline and suprasellar — cystic and calcified on MRI, a craniopharyngioma from Rathke pouch remnants.

Defining criteria Growth failure — downward crossing of height percentiles after a previously stable channel (50th to 5th between ages 11 and 13 here), with weight preserved. Pituitary or hypothalamic causes lose height before weight; nutritional and gastrointestinal causes lose weight before height ⚠︎ · Pubertal delay — the vendor's gate is no breast development by age 12 in girls; the threshold conventionally taught is age 13 ⚠︎ (clinic ledger). Tanner 1 at 13 clears either gate, so the discrepancy does not change this answer — but note which figure you are being scored on · Stalk pattern vs gland pattern — multiple anterior axes down plus posterior failure (diabetes insipidus) localizes to the stalk; a single hypersecreting axis with intact others localizes to the gland (in-context: stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly manifesting as growth failure from TSH or GH deficiency)
Pertinent positives & negatives Height 50th → 5th, weight 75th and steady — endocrine growth failure; excludes malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, and undernutrition, which cost weight first · Tanner 1 at 13 — gonadotropin deficiency; a second failed axis, which converts "short child" into "hypopituitary child." · Optic disc edema with a supple neck and no fever — raised intracranial pressure without meningitis; here from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle · Normal finger-nose-finger and normal gait — excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma, the posterior fossa option · Normal skin — excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists · No focal deficit, no fever — excludes brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever · Headaches for a year before worsening — a slow-growing lesion; craniopharyngiomas are subtle for years before diagnosis
The sellar/suprasellar mass — the differential
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
CraniopharyngiomaRathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; bimodal peaks at 5–14 and 50–75; years of subtle symptomsCystic and calcified suprasellar mass; growth failure + pubertal delay + bitemporal hemianopsia— (the answer)
Suprasellar germinoma — can't missAdolescent, often male; midline germ cell tumor of the suprasellar or pineal regionDiabetes insipidus arrives first, before the anterior axes; non-calcified; CSF/serum β-hCG or AFP elevated; radiosensitiveNo polyuria or polydipsia; the anterior axes failed first
Prolactinoma / pituitary adenomaAdolescent or adult with galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic featuresIntrasellar, non-calcified; one axis hypersecreting with the others intactTwo axes down, no galactorrhea, and the mass would not obstruct CSF flow (partner brief owns this)
Optic pathway gliomaYoung child, often NF1; pilocytic astrocytoma of the chiasm or nerveCafé-au-lait macules and axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with normal appetite)Normal skin, normal pupils, and weight preserved
Rathke cleft cystSame embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headacheProgressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure is too much disease for a simple cyst
Langerhans cell histiocytosisYoung child; infiltrates the stalkCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk, plus lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rashNormal skin, no polyuria, no bone pain
Management, in one line The sequencing lesson this stem contains is one line and the bank carries it: once the mass is found, glucocorticoid replacement goes in before levothyroxine — thyroid hormone raises metabolic demand and can precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency ⚠︎ — and desmopressin, not fluid restriction, answers the post-operative hypotonic polyuria.
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? — No → this is not a hemispheric or posterior fossa question · Plot the growth chart. — Height falling, weight holding → endocrine · Count failed axes. — Growth and puberty → panhypopituitarism → the stalk · Is there posterior pituitary failure? — Polyuria present → germinoma or histiocytosis climb the list. Absent here · Is there raised pressure or a field cut? — Papilledema, bitemporal hemianopsia → the mass is midline and suprasellar, and the MRI descriptor is calcified and cystic
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F, 6 months of morning headaches, height crossed 75th to 10th percentile with weight at 60th, Tanner 1, papilledema → MRI of the brain with contrast → Suspected suprasellar mass
  2. 9 yo M, MRI shows a cystic calcified suprasellar mass, resection planned → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → Craniopharyngioma
  3. 14 yo M, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia, urine osmolality 90, non-calcified suprasellar mass, CSF beta-hCG elevated → Suprasellar germinoma → Radiation therapy
  4. 10 yo F, POD 1 from suprasellar tumor resection, urine output 350 mL/h, serum Na 152, urine osmolality 85 → Desmopressin → Central diabetes insipidus
  5. 8 yo M with a new suprasellar mass, BP 84/50, Na 128, glucose 52 → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → Adrenal crisis
  6. 15 yo F, amenorrhea and galactorrhea, normal growth, Tanner 4, MRI shows a 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification → Prolactinoma → Cabergoline
  7. 6 yo M, declining vision with nystagmus, cafe-au-lait macules and axillary freckling, thin despite a good appetite → MRI of the brain and orbits → Optic pathway glioma in NF1
  8. 11 yo F with a known suprasellar mass, now vomiting with a depressed level of consciousness, dilated lateral and third ventricles → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → Obstructive hydrocephalus
  9. 10 yo M, 1 year after resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma, currently asymptomatic → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → Lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance
  10. 13 yo F with a suprasellar mass and loss of both temporal visual fields → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → Bitemporal hemianopsia
Decoy note The one-year duration is not a reassurance signal — it is the classic tempo of a slow-growing suprasellar tumor. The normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise — calcified and cystic names craniopharyngioma. · Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging. A height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it is the one finding a normal neurologic examination cannot conceal. · Height lost with weight preserved is endocrine; weight lost before height is nutritional or gastrointestinal. The diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma is the exception that proves it — emaciation with a normal appetite ⚠︎. · Diabetes insipidus first, anterior axes later shifts the list from craniopharyngioma to germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis; send CSF and serum β-hCG and AFP before you assume the calcified answer. · Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism ⚠︎, and expect the post-operative sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled. · Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly — height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty. It does not produce papilledema. Check TSH and free T4, and let the disc edema break the tie.
Pairs with its mirror twin, Headache in a Child: What Earns Imaging. Same complaint — a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches — with the red-flag gate answered in opposite directions. Store the discriminator as a question: is anything abnormal outside the headache history — the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Posterior Fossa Localization owns the other compartment: when the abnormality is on the neurologic examination rather than the growth chart, the mass is in the posterior fossa, not the sella. Hyperprolactinemia owns the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Part I Polyuria: Water or Solute owns the step before this one — whether the polyuria is water or solute, and whether the deprivation test is still owed.
Transferable rule When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic — a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they arrive years before the field cut and the papilledema.
True-fact-wrong-slotSubependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles — Tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis; the stem states the skin examination is normal, and TSC does not arrest linear growth
Class-vs-memberTumor in the cerebellar vermis — Vermian tumors present with truncal ataxia and dysmetria; this examination is explicitly clean, and they do not touch the pituitary
Sequencing trapParietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim — Abscess is acute, febrile, and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection
Salient decoyEnhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal — Acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence

Headache in a Child: What Earns Imaging

what licenses neuroimaging, and what does not · board question · Is anything abnormal outside the headache history — the examination, the fundus, the growth chart, the vitals?

Source vignette Pt — 10 yo M, 1 year of bilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and vomiting, relieved by sleep, normal examination · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned reassurance with a trigger diary and early-dose ibuprofen, MRI of the brain and daily topiramate prophylaxis
The decision point

The fork is a threshold, not a differential: this headache is already diagnosable — unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worsened by activity, with nausea and vomiting, in an adolescent girl with a two-year history of the same thing — so the only question is whether anything in the stem crosses the imaging gate. Three features are offered as if they do, and none of them does: vomiting is a diagnostic criterion of migraine, not a pressure sign; the disability ("could not finish her homework") measures severity, which no guideline images for; and the increase in frequency is a change in rate, not in character (in-context: the headaches "have the same characteristics," remain monthly, and the change tracks the arrival of regular menses since menarche). The examination is normal, including the pupils, and no papilledema is described. No additional testing (in-context: imaging is reserved for an abnormal neurologic examination, signs of raised intracranial pressure, or a dramatic change in headache characteristics).

Defining criteria Indications for neuroimaging in pediatric headache — — (1) abnormal neurologic examination findings, such as weakness or ataxia; (2) signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as papilledema; (3) a dramatic change in headache characteristics. None is present here · Not an indication — — a modest rise in frequency when the headaches keep the same character, remain relatively infrequent, and have a physiologic explanation for the change · Migraine, diagnostic features — — pulsatile, unilateral (may be bilateral in children), hours to days; photophobia and phonophobia; nausea or vomiting; ± aura; normal neurologic examination. Formal criteria add ≥5 prior attacks lasting 2–72 hours in patients under 18 (4–72 in adults); beyond 72 hours is status migrainosus (ICHD-3)
Pertinent positives & negatives Two years of similar headaches — recurrent and stereotyped; excludes "first and worst," which is the thunderclap gate · Vomited twice — a migraine criterion; it becomes a pressure sign only when it is morning vomiting, projectile, or paired with papilledema · Pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal — closes indication (1) and, in the absence of described disc edema, indication (2) · Menarche at 12, now regular cycles — the physiologic explanation for the change in rate; a change with a cause is not an unexplained change · Afebrile, alert and oriented — excludes meningitis, and with it the lumbar puncture option · Began after a sleepover — sleep deprivation is a named migraine trigger, not evidence of ingestion
Classify first — headache in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Examination and fundus normal?"Pupils equal and reactive... remainder of neurologic examination normal"; no papilledemaCloses both of the first two imaging indications, and the IIH branch with them (in-context: papilledema would be expected)
Character or only rate?"Similar headaches over the past 2 years"; "every other month… now monthly," same featuresRecurrent, not first-and-worst; a rate change only, which does not meet "dramatic change in characteristics"
Explanation for the change?"Menarche at age 12; menstrual periods now regular"A physiologic cause is identified, so the change is accounted for
Systemic signs?"Temperature 37 C," alert, normal vitalsNo infection, no toxidrome
Tier fingerprint done — nothing but intermittent acetaminophen · failed — 2 years of attacks with inadequate abortive dosing and timing, the actual unmet need · bothered — missed schoolwork, which licenses better treatment, not more testing.
Management ladder — headache in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Clinical diagnosis; trigger diary (sleep, meals, menses, screens); sleep-hygiene and hydration counseling; no laboratory or imagingAny red-flag gate is breached, or attacks recur despite trigger control
2Abortive therapy at first symptom, at full weight-based dose — ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rest in a dark quiet room, antiemetic if vomiting blocks oral dosingAn early, adequately dosed NSAID fails on 2 consecutive attacks ⚠︎
3Triptan for refractory attacks, then daily prevention (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate ⚠︎) if attacks reach ≥4 headache days per month ⚠︎Reassess prevention at 2–3 months ⚠︎
Exit / de-escalationMedication-overuse headache — withdraw the offending analgesicSimple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans/combination analgesics on ≥10 days/month ⚠︎
Numbers that gate & exit ramps diagnostic — up to 3 days per attack; ≥5 prior attacks of 2–72 hours ⚠︎. Escalation — 2 adequately dosed failures ⚠︎, ≥4 headache days/month ⚠︎, and the overuse thresholds above ⚠︎. Exam versus clinic ledger: the exam keys the preventive rung, though pediatric trials found amitriptyline and topiramate no better than placebo ⚠︎ — do not let that change the keyed rung. · Papilledema → MRI (venography if otherwise normal ⚠︎), then LP with an opening pressure → idiopathic intracranial hypertension. · Fever with meningismus → lumbar puncture; thunderclap → noncontrast CT, then LP if negative ⚠︎. · Wakes from sleep, worse on waking or with Valsalva → MRI, however migrainous the rest sounds. · Focal deficit or ataxia → Posterior Fossa Localization; falling height percentile or arrested puberty → MRI with sellar views → "The sellar/suprasellar mass." · Household all symptomatic → carboxyhemoglobin; immunocompromised, shunted, or anticoagulated → image, full stop.
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination normal, including the fundus? — Yes → the strongest two indications are closed · First and worst, or recurrent and familiar? — Recurrent → no urgent pathway · Did the character change, or only the rate? — Rate only → not a dramatic change · Is there a physiologic explanation for the change? — Menarche and regular cycles → yes · Any systemic signal — fever, altered sensorium, abnormal vitals, growth failure? — None → the answer is a diagnosis and a treatment plan, not a test
Scenario bank
  1. 10 yo M, 1 year of bilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and vomiting, relieved by sleep, normal examination → Reassurance, trigger diary, and early-dose ibuprofen → Pediatric migraine
  2. 13 yo F with 2 years of migraines, now with papilledema and vomiting on waking → MRI of the brain → Suspected intracranial mass
  3. 16 yo F, obese, daily headache with pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema, MRI of the brain normal → Lumbar puncture with opening pressure → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
  4. 15 yo M, sudden headache maximal within seconds while lifting weights, worst of his life, normal examination → Noncontrast CT of the head → Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage
  5. 4 yo M, 12 h of headache with T 39.2, nuchal rigidity, irritable, no focal deficit or papilledema → Lumbar puncture → Bacterial meningitis
  6. 8 yo F, 6 months of headaches with a normal neurologic examination, height crossed from 50th to 5th percentile with weight held → MRI of the brain with sellar views → Suprasellar mass
  7. 12 yo M with morning headaches and nausea on winter weekdays; mother and brother affected, all better away from home → Carboxyhemoglobin level → Carbon monoxide exposure
  8. 6 yo F, frontal headaches only on school afternoons, squints at the board, normal neurologic examination → Ophthalmologic examination with refraction → Uncorrected refractive error
  9. 13 yo F, 3 years of episodic headaches now monthly and predictable in the 2 days before each period, unchanged in character → Menstrual migraine → Trigger counseling and timed NSAIDs
  10. 15 yo M using ibuprofen or acetaminophen on 20 days per month for a headache that is now daily and dull → Continuing the daily as-needed analgesic → Medication-overuse headache
Decoy note "Awakened from sleep" is the finding that would flip this stem — and it is not here; do not import it from the twin. The homework detail measures disability, which sets the treatment tier and never the imaging threshold, and the near-doubling of frequency is real but explained.
Pearls Frequency changes earn an explanation; character changes, examination findings, and pressure signs earn a scan. · Reassurance is defensible only when you can name the criteria you cleared. "No additional testing" is rejected far more often for feeling too easy than for a stated disqualifying finding — uniform-answer doubt, and it costs points on every shelf. · Change in rate ≠ change in character. Ask what changed; if the answer is only "more often," look for the physiologic cause (menarche, a new schedule, a new medication) before you look at the brain. · MRI for chronic and progressive; CT for acute and hemorrhagic. Getting the threshold right and the modality wrong still scores zero. · Boundary: nocturnal awakening, morning vomiting, and headache worsened by Valsalva are pressure signs even when the rest is textbook migraine — they override the phenotype. · Migraine onset and change in frequency cluster around menarche; the same estrogen link makes menstrual migraine the commonest "my headaches got worse this year" story in an adolescent.
Pairs with its mirror twin, Sellar and Suprasellar Masses. Same complaint, same age and sex, opposite side of the gate: there, the headache came with papilledema, a height percentile crossing, and Tanner 1; here it comes with a normal examination and an explained change in frequency. Store the discriminator as a question, never as an outcome: is anything abnormal outside the headache history — the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination? Headache Types & Cluster Headache owns the type differential once imaging has been excluded; Low Back Pain: Red Flags is the same gating logic in a different region — the pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does.
Transferable rule An imaging threshold is crossed by findings, not by suffering: the examination, the fundus, the tempo of change in character, and the systemic signs decide, while frequency, duration, and disability decide only the treatment tier. When a pattern changes and you can name why, you have explained the change — not discovered a red flag.
Mirror twinCT scan of the head — The gate is examination findings, pressure signs, or a change in character — none present; and even where imaging is indicated for a chronic pediatric headache the modality is MRI, so the option fails twice
Salient decoyUrine toxicology screen — Toxic ingestion presents with altered sensorium, pupillary abnormality, respiratory depression, or seizure; she is alert with reactive pupils, and the sleepover is a sleep-deprivation trigger
Sequencing trapSerum electrolyte measurement — Two episodes in a well-hydrated, alert adolescent change no management decision; the ledger already answers the question electrolytes would ask
True-fact-wrong-slotLumbar puncture — She is afebrile with a normal examination, and IIH would show papilledema; LP before imaging in a patient with pressure signs is also out of order

Cholesteatoma and Chronic Ear Drainage

the mass behind an intact drum · board question · Is the drum intact, is the mass on it, and is the loss conductive?

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, a month of purulent ear drainage unimproved by topical and oral antibiotics; intact immobile tympanic membrane with a superior retraction pocket and a pearly white mass, conductive hearing loss; cleft palate, prior effusions and tympanostomy tubes · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cholesteatoma, acute otitis media with perforation and otitis externa
The decision point

Three examination findings close this before any option is read. The drum is intact, so the drainage is not coming through a perforation, which is what otitis media with discharge requires. The drum is immobile with a superior retraction pocket containing a pearly white mass, so the lesion is of the tympanic membrane rather than of the canal, which removes otitis externa and a foreign body. And the loss is conductive, so the ossicles are the problem rather than the nerve, which removes the schwannoma. The history explains why: cleft palate, chronic middle-ear effusions and tympanostomy tubes are the three named risk factors, all of them mechanisms for the chronic middle-ear disease that pulls a retraction pocket into the attic. That pocket traps desquamated epithelium, keratin accumulates, and the mass erodes toward the ossicles — a cholesteatoma, treated by surgical excision.

Defining criteria Cholesteatoma — a benign growth of squamous epithelium with accumulation of keratin debris within the middle ear; most cases are acquired and unilateral · Pathogenesis — chronic middle-ear disease creates a retraction pocket, an invagination of the tympanic membrane, which traps epithelium and debris · The two consequences it is tested on — chronic otorrhea when the trapped debris becomes infected, and conductive hearing loss when growth reaches the ossicles · Risk factors — recurrent acute otitis media, chronic middle-ear effusion, tympanostomy tube placement, and cleft palate through its association with middle-ear disease · Examination — a pearly white mass or a visible retraction pocket with draining debris behind an intact drum, placed in the anterosuperior quadrant in-context. The two locations are not in conflict — they name different entities: congenital disease sits behind an intact drum (classically anterosuperior, though surgical series find it variable), while acquired disease arises from pars flaccida or posterosuperior retraction. Read the drum first, then the quadrant
Pertinent positives & negatives Drainage for a month, unimproved on topical and oral antibiotics — the antibiotic-refractory gate; infection alone would have moved · Tympanic membrane intact — excludes acute otitis media with perforation, which is what produces discharge in that disease · Immobile on insufflation — the drum is tethered by the retraction pocket, and there is middle-ear disease behind it · Superior retraction with a pearly white mass — the lesion is on the drum rather than in the canal, and this finding is specific · Conductive hearing loss — ossicular involvement; a sensorineural loss would point at the nerve and a different disease entirely · Cleft palate, prior effusions, prior tympanostomy tubes — the three risk factors stacked, and the reason this child rather than another · No pain and no fever — argues against acute otitis media and against otitis externa, both of which hurt · No dizziness with a normal gait — no labyrinthine fistula yet, and their absence is what makes this elective rather than urgent ⚠︎
Chronic ear drainage — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
CholesteatomaChronic middle-ear disease creates a retraction pocket that traps squamous epithelium and keratin, expanding toward the ossiclesPearly white mass behind an intact drum with painless refractory otorrhea and conductive loss— (the answer)
Acute otitis media with perforationMiddle-ear infection under pressure ruptures the drum and drainsBulging, erythematous or perforated drum, with pain and fever preceding the dischargeDrum intact, non-bulging, uninflamed, painless
Otitis externaCanal maceration and inflammation, usually infectious, classically in swimmersTragal tenderness with a swollen tender canal, responding to topical dropsFailed appropriate topical therapy, and the mass is on the drum
Necrotising otitis externa Can't missPseudomonas osteomyelitis of the skull base in diabetics and the immunocompromised ⚠︎Severe pain with granulation tissue at the bony–cartilaginous junction and cranial neuropathiesA child, painless, without granulation tissue
Foreign body in the canalOften asymptomatic, but may cause pain, discharge and decreased hearingObject visible in the canal, with abrasions from prior removal attemptsThe mass is within the drum rather than the canal, and there were no removal attempts
Vestibular schwannomaCerebellopontine angle tumour compressing the cochlear nerve; NF2 in the youngSensorineural loss with tinnitus, adult onset, NF2 stigmataConductive loss, no tinnitus, age 5, no NF2 findings
Management, in one line Management is one sentence, because this stem asked only for the process: cholesteatoma is treated by surgical excision, and no further topical or oral antibiotic will resolve it — antibiotics treat the superinfected debris rather than the epithelium generating it.
Decision spine Is the drum intact? — Yes → the discharge is not coming through a perforation, so acute otitis media is out · Where is the mass? — On the drum in a retraction pocket → not the canal, so otitis externa and foreign body are out · Which kind of hearing loss? — Conductive → ossicles rather than nerve, so the schwannoma is out · Did adequate antibiotics fail? — A month of topical and oral therapy → this is not primarily an infection · Do the options name diseases or processes? — Processes → translate the diagnosis into epithelium and keratin, then pick
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo boy with a month of purulent ear drainage unimproved by topical and oral antibiotics, an intact immobile tympanic membrane with a superior retraction pocket and a pearly white mass, and conductive hearing loss → Cholesteatoma → Trapped squamous epithelium and keratin debris
  2. 5 yo boy with cholesteatoma of the right middle ear and conductive hearing loss; definitive management → Surgical excision → Antibiotics do not remove the epithelium
  3. Child with a known cholesteatoma who develops acute unilateral facial droop on the affected side → Urgent imaging and surgical referral → Facial nerve erosion
  4. Child with a cholesteatoma who develops vertigo when pressure is applied to the external auditory canal → Urgent surgical referral → Labyrinthine fistula
  5. 3 yo with 2 days of fever and ear pain, a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane, now with sudden drainage and relief of pain → Oral antibiotic therapy → Acute otitis media with perforation
  6. 12 yo competitive swimmer with ear pain, tenderness on tragal traction, a macerated erythematous canal and a normal tympanic membrane → Topical antibiotic drops → Otitis externa; water exposure is the risk factor, and the drum is what sorts the risk lists
  7. 68 yo man with diabetes, severe otalgia, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal and a new facial nerve palsy → Computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy → Necrotizing otitis externa
  8. 4 yo with unilateral conductive hearing loss and a white mass behind an intact tympanic membrane, with no history of ear infection, effusion or tube placement → Congenital cholesteatoma → No retraction pocket was required
  9. Why a cholesteatoma produces conductive rather than sensorineural hearing loss → The expanding keratin mass erodes and immobilizes the ossicular chain → Sound never reaches an intact cochlea
  10. 5 yo with a cholesteatoma and persistent malodorous drainage; which management will not resolve the condition → Another course of topical and oral antibiotics → It treats the superinfection rather than the lesion
Decoy note The single most misleading word in the stem is purulent. It licenses an infectious reading for a month, and that is exploited: the drainage is real, and it is the cholesteatoma's trapped debris becoming superinfected, which is why antibiotics produce partial, temporary, unsatisfying responses. Note also what the stem tells you about three years ago — tubes removed, audiometry normal. That is not background colour, it establishes that the conductive loss is new, which converts chronic ear problems into something has changed. The absence of dizziness and the normal gait are not filler either: they confirm that no labyrinthine complication has occurred yet, which is why the question asks what is responsible rather than what to do first.
Pearls A retraction pocket traps keratin and squamous epithelium behind an intact drum, causing painless otorrhea and conductive loss; treatment is surgical excision. · Discharge through an intact drum is not otitis media; middle-ear infection drains only through a perforation, so an intact drum with otorrhea means the source is the drum itself or the canal. · A cholesteatoma is not a tumour and not an infection — it is skin in the wrong place, growing and shedding keratin, which is why the treatment is surgical and antibiotics only quiet the smell. · The risk-factor triad is recurrent acute otitis media, chronic effusion, and tympanostomy tubes, and cleft palate multiplies all three through eustachian tube dysfunction. · Conductive loss localises to the ossicles, so a cholesteatoma that has grown far enough to be heard is far enough to be eroding. · The complications worth recognising are erosion into neighbours — facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula with vertigo on canal pressure, and intracranial extension ⚠︎ — each converting an elective operation into an urgent one. · A white mass behind an intact drum in a child with no history of ear disease at all is congenital, which needs no retraction pocket to explain it ⚠︎.
The drum sorts the risk factors External canal risks — water exposure, trauma from swabs or ear candling, foreign material such as hearing aids and headphones, and dermatologic conditions such as eczema · Middle ear risks, which are not canal risks — sick contacts, incomplete immunization, tobacco smoke exposure, prior tympanostomy tubes and recurrent acute otitis media · Why water does it — it strips antibacterial cerumen, raises the canal pH, macerates the skin barrier and introduces organisms, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa grows in water · The boundary — the tympanic membrane separates the two compartments, which is why a middle-ear risk factor transfers no risk to the canal
Pairs with Verified: Part I Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis owns the tuning-fork sort that assigns any hearing loss to conductive or sensorineural and currently carries this disease as a single bank line; this brief is that line's expansion. Part II Sinusitis with Intracranial Extension is the same logic in the neighbouring air-filled space, where a chronic infection of a bony cavity is dangerous because of what it erodes into. Store the discriminator as a question: is the drum intact, and is the mass on it or in the canal?
Transferable rule When an option list describes processes rather than diseases, the item is testing whether you know the pathology behind the name, so translate your diagnosis into its mechanism before scanning or you will match on the clinical noise instead. And a discharge that fails adequate antibiotics is telling you the drainage is a symptom of something structural rather than the disease itself. --- Batch 5, brief 04 · 2026-09-10.
Salient decoyAcute middle ear effusion with tympanic membrane inflammation — That disease requires a bulging or inflamed drum, and drainage in it implies perforation; this drum is intact, non-bulging and uninflamed
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic foreign body impaction with canal abrasion — The mass is within the tympanic membrane rather than the canal, and there were no prior removal attempts to abrade anything
Class-vs-memberExternal ear canal epithelial maceration and inflammation — Appropriate topical therapy failed, and a discrete mass on the drum is not a canal finding
Unchecked attributeSchwannoma formation with cochlear nerve injury — Schwannomas give sensorineural loss with tinnitus, occur in adulthood, and would need NF2 stigmata in a child

Seizure with Fever in a Child

the age window and the intracranial signs decide whether it is benign · board question · Is this child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Source vignette Pt — 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge
The decision point

Febrile seizure is not available here, and the reason is the first line of the stem: 10 weeks old. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years, and a child outside that window with fever and a seizure is a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently reach the same answer — a full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure, and drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. The supple neck is not reassurance, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants, which is why the fontanelle and the tone are what you read instead. The answer is lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Simple febrile seizure — age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging · Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture — age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease · Additional considerations for tapping — current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history · The open-fontanelle exemption — signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head CT first
Pertinent positives & negatives Age 10 weeks — outside the febrile-seizure window entirely, and this alone forecloses discharge · Full anterior fontanelle — a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image · Fontanelle open — the pop-off valve, and the reason CT is not needed first · Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure — a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, which is prolonged altered mental status and its own indication · Weak suck and decreased tone — altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation · Neck supple — excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable under about 12 to 18 months ⚠︎ · Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped — removes the benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes, and removes EEG, since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent · Skin normal — no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation, but the tap is already earned by four other findings · Vaccinations up to date — removes the incomplete-immunization consideration without removing the indication
Seizure with fever in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bacterial meningitis Can't missAny age, and infants localise poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signsSeizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with CSF culture deciding— (the answer to pursue)
Simple febrile seizureViral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal childAge 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examinationAge 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle
Complex febrile seizureThe same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hoursFocal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence in the same illness, earning EEG and often imaging ⚠︎The seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes
Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't missNeonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningealProlonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes with red cells ⚠︎Not excluded — it is found by the same tap, and acyclovir is added ⚠︎
Meningococcemia Can't missN. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensationPetechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tapSkin examination normal, normotensive
Abusive head trauma Can't missInfant with subdural collections, and may be afebrileSeizure with a bulging fontanelle, retinal hemorrhages and no fever, with unexplained irritability ⚠︎Fever 39.3 with a viral prodrome — but this is the case where imaging is the answer
Decision spine How old? — Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is dead · Is she seizing now? — No, it stopped in 4 minutes → the benzodiazepine is dead · Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? — No → EEG is dead · Any sign of intracranial infection? — Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes · Does she need a CT first? — The fontanelle is open → no, so tap her
Scenario bank
  1. 10-week-old girl with fever, vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsiness persisting an hour later, an open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck and decreased tone → Lumbar puncture → Age outside the window plus signs of intracranial infection
  2. 18-month-old boy with temperature 39.1 C and a single 3-minute generalized seizure who is alert with a normal examination 20 minutes later → Reassurance and discharge → Simple febrile seizure
  3. 2-year-old girl with fever who is still convulsing 8 minutes after the seizure began → Intravenous lorazepam → Duration gates the benzodiazepine
  4. 3-year-old boy with fever, a generalized seizure, a spreading petechial rash and hypotension → Give empiric intravenous antibiotics immediately and perform the lumbar puncture afterward → Meningococcemia
  5. 12-month-old girl with fever and a seizure who has papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit, with a closed anterior fontanelle → Antibiotics, then head CT, then lumbar puncture → The imaging exception
  6. 6-week-old boy, afebrile, with a seizure, a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy → Neuroimaging → Abusive head trauma
  7. 4-year-old boy having his third seizure of this febrile illness, this one left-sided and lasting 20 minutes → Electroencephalography → Complex febrile seizure
  8. 2-year-old with fever, seizure and persistently altered mental status whose cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells → Herpes simplex encephalitis → Add acyclovir to empiric therapy
  9. Why an open anterior fontanelle removes the usual requirement for head CT before lumbar puncture → It acts as a pop-off valve that decompresses rising intracranial pressure, limiting herniation risk → The anatomy suspends the rule
  10. Infant with fever, petechiae and hypotension in whom the lumbar puncture will be delayed; which action is inappropriate → Delaying antibiotics until the lumbar puncture is completed → Treat first, tap after
  11. 2 yo M, 2 days of rhinorrhea, fever 39.2 C this morning, a 3-minute generalized seizure, sleepy and confused when paramedics arrived, now alert and playful with a normal examination; uncle has epilepsy; immunizations current → Reassurance and discharge home → simple febrile seizure; the postictal drowsiness has resolved and an uncle's epilepsy changes nothing
  12. Parents of a 2 yo after a first simple febrile seizure ask what to expect → About 30% have another; epilepsy risk stays near 1% → antipyretics do not prevent the next one
  13. 2 yo back to baseline after a brief generalized febrile seizure, but with 2 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhea and dry mucous membranes → Serum electrolytes and glucose → hypoglycemia or hyponatremia can provoke a seizure
  14. 11-month-old back to baseline after a first simple febrile seizure, with no pneumococcal or Hib vaccine doses → Lumbar puncture → incomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap
Decoy note The supple neck is the most reassuring-sounding finding in the stem and it means nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants, which is precisely why the criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. Notice also that the stem builds a careful negative examination — normal tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin — which reads as no source found and quietly strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it: when every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. And the up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list without touching the four indications already present.
Counselling, and what each test is for Recurrence — about 30% have another febrile seizure · Epilepsy — risk slightly raised, about 1% overall · Antipyretics — treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure · Course — resolves by school age, with no effect on development · Risk factors — fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunisation, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy · Timing — usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear · Brain imaging — focal neurologic signs · EEG — recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure · Admission — not back to neurologic baseline · Electrolytes and glucose — vomiting or diarrhoea, since hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia can provoke a seizure · Lumbar puncture — also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunisation, or when already on antibiotics
Pearls Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, is a lumbar puncture — and an open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years, and it is the fastest disqualifier on the topic — check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, which is why infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child, and why the CT-before-tap rule generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication; when that happens, ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants do not have neck signs — read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead, because a supple neck excludes nothing under about 18 months ⚠︎. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is not a long febrile seizure, it is altered mental status, and it earns a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension the order inverts: antibiotics first, tap after, because a sterilised Gram stain is an acceptable price.
Pairs with Verified: Part II The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source owns the workup when there is no seizure and stops at the decision to tap; this brief owns what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis owns the CSF grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Store the discriminator as a question: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
Transferable rule A benign diagnosis defined by an age range is disqualified by the age before it is disqualified by anything else, so check the gate before weighing the findings. And when a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent — if the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply. --- Batch 5, brief 07 · 2026-09-10.
True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging — The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary
Mirror twinReassurance and discharge — Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it
Salient decoyElectroencephalography — EEG is for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam — Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing

Cerebral Palsy and the MRI Pattern

the MRI pattern names the cause · board question · What does the MRI actually describe, and are the findings unilateral or global?

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo, born at 31 weeks, left-sided spasticity · Imaging — MRI shows white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity, transplacental Toxoplasma infection and inherited thrombophilia with perinatal stroke
The decision point

Every option is a candidate cause, so the question is which one produces this lesion — and the lesion is described for you. White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia: ischemia and necrosis in the poorly perfused zone beside the ventricles, and the signature injury of prematurity. The examination confirms the rest independently: increased tone, 3+ reflexes and ankle clonus on the left only, with a right-sided lesion, is spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury — and a congenital infection produces global deficits, not one-sided spasticity.

Defining criteria Cerebral palsy — nonprogressive motor dysfunction caused by a neurologic injury; the etiology is often multifactorial and may never be identified · Periventricular leukomalacia — ischemia and necrosis of the poorly perfused white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, seen as white matter injury on MRI; premature infants are at greatest risk, and their friable germinal matrix vessels also predispose to intraventricular hemorrhage · Early signs that should raise suspicion — motor delay (not rolling by 4 months corrected), early hand preference before age 1, persistent neonatal reflexes (tonic neck beyond 6 months), abnormal tone · The tone evolution — infants may be hypotonic initially, with spasticity developing over time, accompanied by hyperreflexia and often clonus
Pertinent positives & negatives White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle — periventricular leukomalacia; this single descriptor selects prematurity and excludes every other option's imaging signature · Born at 31 weeks — the commonest setting for cerebral palsy; premature infants carry the greatest risk · Left-sided findings with a right-sided lesion — spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury; intrauterine infection produces global, not one-sided, deficits · Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, sustained clonus — upper motor neuron; excludes spinal dysraphism, where lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased · Early hand preference at 7 months — abnormal before age 1, and one of the earliest signs · Not rolling over — motor delay, judged against corrected age in a 31-weeker · Head circumference at the 50th percentile — no microcephaly, which argues further against congenital infection · Babinski present bilaterally — normal at this age ⚠︎; the asymmetry of tone and reflexes is the finding, not the plantar response · Veterinary office, inconsistent prenatal care — a constructed toxoplasmosis story that the MRI descriptor refutes
Cerebral palsy — the MRI pattern names the cause
EtiologyIllness scriptThe NBME tell — imagingExcluded here by
Prematurity / low birth weightIschemia in the watershed white matter beside the ventricles; friable germinal matrix vesselsPeriventricular leukomalacia; intraventricular hemorrhage— (the answer)
Hypoxic-ischemic injuryPerinatal asphyxia in a term infant; low Apgars, encephalopathy, seizuresWatershed injury; basal ganglia and thalamic lesionsBorn preterm; no depressed Apgars or neonatal encephalopathy described
Perinatal stroke (± inherited thrombophilia)Arterial infarct around the time of birth; hemiplegia emerging in infancyInfarct in a vascular distribution, most often the middle cerebral arteryThe lesion is periventricular white matter, not a territory
Intrauterine infectionCMV, toxoplasmosis; transplacental transmissionIntracranial calcifications; microcephaly; global deficitsPeriventricular white matter injury, normocephaly, unilateral findings
Neural tube defect (folate deficiency)Spinal dysraphismA spinal lesion — and the examination is lower motor neuron: decreased lower-extremity tone and reflexesHypertonia with hyperreflexia and clonus
Magnesium sulfate exposureGiven to the mother for preterm laborTransient neonatal hypotonia only; no long-lasting effectFindings at 7 months, and they are hypertonic
Management, in one line Management is not the fork this stem tests, so in one sentence: cerebral palsy is managed supportively and lifelong — early intervention and physical therapy, tone management, and surveillance of hips, feeding and growth, seizures, vision and hearing ⚠︎ — with no treatment that reverses the static injury itself.
Decision spine Upper or lower motor neuron? — Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, clonus → upper · Unilateral or global? — Left side only → a single-sided lesion, so global insults drop out · What does the MRI actually say? — Periventricular white matter → leukomalacia · What produces that pattern? — Prematurity — and the stem gives you 31 weeks · Does any exposure in the history produce it? — No: infection calcifies, thrombophilia infarcts a territory, magnesium is transient, folate affects the spine
Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo born at 31 weeks with left-sided spasticity and MRI showing white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle → Ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity → Periventricular leukomalacia
  2. Term infant with Apgars 2 and 4, neonatal encephalopathy and seizures; MRI shows watershed and basal ganglia lesions → Hypoxic-ischemic injury → The term-infant pattern
  3. 4 mo term infant with new left arm weakness; MRI shows infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory → Evaluate for perinatal stroke risk factors including thrombophilia → A vascular distribution, not leukomalacia
  4. Newborn with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss and petechiae → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → Calcifications rather than white matter injury
  5. 7 mo infant with early hand preference and asymmetric tone, growing normally → Refer for brain MRI and early intervention therapy → Suspected cerebral palsy
  6. 3 yo with spastic diplegia, toe-walking and tight hamstrings, ambulating with difficulty → Physical therapy with orthoses and focal tone management → The commonest cerebral palsy subtype
  7. 7 mo infant born at 31 weeks who is not yet rolling; parents ask whether she is delayed → Assess milestones against her corrected age of about 5 months → Correct the age before judging delay
  8. 6 mo infant with decreased lower-extremity tone, absent reflexes and a sacral dimple → Spinal imaging → Closed spinal dysraphism
  9. 4 yo with known cerebral palsy who has lost independent ambulation over 6 months → Attributing the regression to the cerebral palsy → Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive
  10. 5 yo with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy at a routine health maintenance visit → Hip surveillance imaging with feeding, growth, vision, hearing and seizure review → The comorbidities of a static injury
Decoy note The veterinary office is the most deliberately constructed detail in this stem: an occupation chosen to evoke cat litter, reinforced one clause later by inconsistent prenatal care, and refuted one sentence later by the MRI. Three maternal drugs are named and only one is an option — and the antenatal corticosteroids actually lowered this infant's risk rather than raising it. The bilateral Babinski is a normal finding at 7 months ⚠︎ and is there to be over-read; the asymmetry of tone and reflexes is what matters.
Pearls White matter injury beside the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia, and prematurity is what causes it. · The imaging pattern maps to the insult: periventricular white matter → prematurity · watershed or basal ganglia → hypoxic-ischemic injury · a vascular territory → perinatal stroke · calcifications → congenital infection. · Distribution names the subtype: both legs is spastic diplegia, the commonest; one side is spastic hemiplegia, and it should match a unilateral lesion. · Hand preference before age 1 is abnormal, and it is often the earliest sign a parent reports. · Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive — losing an acquired milestone is a different disease and reopens the workup ⚠︎. · Infants with cerebral palsy may begin hypotonic and become spastic later, so normal early tone never excludes it. · Magnesium sulfate given before preterm birth is neuroprotective and reduces cerebral palsy risk ⚠︎ — the exact opposite of what its appearance in the option list implies.
Pairs with Verified: Part II Prematurity Follow-Up and Corrected Age owns periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular hemorrhage as prematurity outcomes and the corrected-age arithmetic this brief leans on; Part II Congenital CMV and the TORCH Discriminations owns the calcification pattern and the global-deficit picture that the toxoplasmosis distractor belongs to; Part II Tethered Cord and Closed Spinal Dysraphism owns the upper-versus-lower motor neuron examination that separates a brain lesion from a spinal one. Store the discriminator as a question: what does the imaging actually describe, and are the deficits one-sided or global?
Transferable rule An exposure in the history suggests; a described imaging pattern decides. When a stem supplies both, read the imaging sentence first — the exposure was written to build a story, and the pattern is the only line capable of ending it.
Salient decoyTransplacental Toxoplasma gondii — Congenital infection produces intracranial calcifications and global deficits; this MRI describes periventricular white matter and the findings are strictly one-sided, in a normocephalic infant
True-fact-wrong-slotLack of maternal folic acid — Folate deficiency causes neural tube defects, in which lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased — the opposite of this examination
Unchecked attributeMaternal magnesium sulfate — It causes transient hypotonia in the immediate newborn period, not lasting spasticity at 7 months
Class-vs-memberInherited thrombophilia — Stroke shows an infarct in a vascular distribution, usually the middle cerebral artery, not periventricular leukomalacia

Sinusitis with Intracranial Extension

A normal neuro exam is a low-sensitivity test

Source vignette Pt — child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging
The decision point

The stem builds acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (double worsening), then layers on intracranial extension flags: focal headache, early-morning vomiting (ICP rises in recumbency), and drowsiness. That converts an oral-antibiotic problem into an urgent imaging problem.

"Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess — frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. And when raised ICP is suspected, image before LP.

Sinusitis complications — features → next step
ComplicationFeaturesNext step
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitisEyelid swelling; normal EOM, normal vision, no proptosisOral antibiotics
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuityCT orbits + IV antibiotics
Pott puffy tumorFrontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess — doughy forehead swellingCT/MRI + IV antibiotics + surgery
Brain abscess EmergencyFocal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficitCT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage
MeningitisDiffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobiaImage first if ICP signs, then LP
Cavernous sinus thrombosisCN III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterallyMRI/MRV + IV antibiotics
Signs of raised ICP & abscess essentials Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) · papilledema · altered mental status · late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on DWI separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.
Scenario bank
  1. Eyelid swelling but normal EOM and vision → Preseptal cellulitis → oral antibiotics
  2. Proptosis and painful eye movement → Orbital cellulitis → CT orbits + IV antibiotics
  3. Doughy swelling over the forehead → Pott puffy tumor → imaging + IV antibiotics + drainage
  4. CN VI palsy with proptosis becoming bilateral → Cavernous sinus thrombosis → MRV
  5. Fever + nuchal rigidity with no ICP signs → Lumbar puncture without prior CT
  6. A child has rhinosinusitis with a double-worsening course, focal headache, and 12 days of symptoms. The neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no vomiting or drowsiness. → Uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with CD4 <100 → Toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma → multiple basal ganglia lesions favour toxoplasmosis
  8. Child with morning headache and vomiting plus ataxia, no infection → Posterior fossa tumor → same ICP syndrome, non-infectious cause
  9. Adult with a ring-enhancing lesion and recent dental infection → Brain abscess by contiguous spread
Transferable rule A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive — morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness — symptoms of raised ICP outrank a reassuring exam.
Test-overrides-findingsSequencing trap

VP Shunt Complications

Neurology · shunt in situ changes the entire ICP workup · image first, never LP

The decision point

A child with a VP shunt presents with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and hypertension — four signs of increased intracranial pressure. The diagnostic reflex for raised ICP is neuroimaging, and the specific concern is shunt malfunction causing recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus. CT of the head is the first step — it shows whether the ventricles have re-dilated.

The miss: choosing LP. LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus — the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space can cause transtentorial herniation. In a shunt patient, CSF is obtained by tapping the shunt reservoir, never by lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Signs of increased ICP in children — headache, vomiting (especially morning), irritability, lethargy, hypertension with bradycardia (Cushing response), papilledema, sunset sign, bulging fontanelle · Shunt malfunction — any ICP sign in a patient with a VP shunt · VP shunt tap — CSF is obtained percutaneously from the shunt reservoir, not by lumbar puncture
Management ladder — VP shunt with raised ICPCT first, shunt tap for CSF
TierInterventionEscalate when
1CT head: compare ventricle size to baselineVentricles enlarged → shunt malfunction confirmed
2Shunt series (skull, chest, abdomen x-rays): trace catheter for disconnection, migration, kinkingDiscontinuity or migration visible
3Shunt tap (percutaneous reservoir aspiration): cell count, Gram stain, culture; measure opening pressureElevated pressure → obstruction; elevated WBC or positive culture → infection
4Surgical shunt revision or externalizationClinical deterioration despite medical management
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo F with a VP shunt, 24 hours of vomiting, irritability and lethargy, BP 125/75, afebrile → CT scan of the head → evaluate for shunt malfunction
  2. 6 yo M with a VP shunt, CT showing dilated ventricles compared to baseline → Shunt series radiographs to evaluate catheter integrity → shunt malfunction confirmed
  3. 3 yo M with a VP shunt placed 3 months ago, fever 38.8, irritability, CT showing stable ventricles → Shunt tap for CSF cell count, Gram stain and culture → possible shunt infection despite normal ventricles
  4. 5 yo F with a VP shunt, CT showing dilated ventricles and shunt series showing catheter discontinuity at the neck → Urgent neurosurgical shunt revision → shunt malfunction from catheter fracture
  5. Why lumbar puncture is contraindicated in a child with a VP shunt and signs of increased intracranial pressure → Obstructive hydrocephalus creates a pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar space, risking transtentorial herniation
  6. 2 yo M with a VP shunt placed 2 weeks ago, low-grade fever, poor feeding, CSF from shunt tap showing 250 WBCs with 80% neutrophils and positive Gram stain for cocci in clusters → Shunt infection with Staphylococcus epidermidis → externalize shunt and start IV vancomycin
  7. 8 yo F with a VP shunt, acute headache and vomiting, CT shows slit ventricles with no change from prior → Evaluate for slit ventricle syndrome or alternate causes of headache → slit ventricle syndrome
Exit ramps Normal CT + fever → still tap the shunt (ventriculitis) · Normal CT + no fever + no recent surgery → GI, metabolic, or other cause · Peritoneal signs → distal catheter complication (pseudocyst, peritonitis)
Pearls S. epidermidis — most common shunt infection organism; a skin commensal that colonizes the hardware; S. aureus second; Gram-negatives in neonates · The shunt series is three plain films (skull, chest, abdomen) that trace the catheter from ventricle to peritoneum — looking for fracture, disconnection, or migration · Slit ventricle syndrome — chronic overdrainage collapses the ventricles, causing intermittent obstruction and headache with small or normal ventricles on CT · Shunt infection risk is highest in the first 6 months after placement or revision · The open fontanelle in infants acts as a pressure pop-off valve — papilledema and Cushing response may be absent; instead look for bulging fontanelle and increasing head circumference
Pairs with Posterior Fossa Localization — shared finding: raised ICP and hydrocephalus; discriminator: is a shunt present?
Transferable rule A VP shunt changes the entire workup for raised intracranial pressure — imaging replaces LP as the first move, the shunt reservoir replaces the lumbar space as the CSF source, and the catheter itself becomes a suspect that must be traced on plain films.
Sequencing trapLP tempts as the standard workup for altered mental status, but it is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus — herniation risk.
Sequencing trapEmpiric antibiotics tempt when infection is the concern, but the patient is afebrile, and antibiotics should follow culture (shunt tap), not precede it.
True-fact-wrong-slotIV acetazolamide decreases CSF production but treats idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not obstructive hydrocephalus from shunt failure.

Night Blindness

the fundus names the cause · UWorld · pale disc or cupped disc, and is the front of the eye normal

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive difficulty seeing at night while driving, with a near-collision; strict vegan eating a variety of plant products · Exam — visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; lashes, conjunctivae and cornea unremarkable; pupils equal and reactive, extraocular muscles intact, red reflex equal; midperipheral visual field defect both eyes · Fundus — optic disc pallor, attenuation of retinal vessels and focal areas of discoloration, bilateral · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned cataract, open-angle glaucoma, retinal detachment, retinitis pigmentosa and vitamin A deficiency
The decision point

Night blindness has a short differential and the fundus settles it in one look. Optic disc pallor with attenuated retinal vessels and patchy pigmentary change is the triad of retinitis pigmentosa — rods degenerate first, and rods are densest in the midperiphery and responsible for dim-light vision, which is why the first symptom is night blindness and the first field defect is midperipheral. Acuity stays 20/20 until cones go late. Every competing option is excluded by a finding the examiner deliberately printed: a normal red reflex and 20/20 vision close cataract, a pale rather than cupped disc closes glaucoma, a two-month progressive course with no tear closes detachment, and normal cornea and conjunctivae close vitamin A deficiency, whose ocular disease is xerophthalmia.

Defining criteria Retinitis pigmentosa, funduscopic triad — retinal vessel attenuation from reduced metabolic demand, waxy optic disc pallor from nerve gliosis and atrophy, and abnormal retinal pigmentation in a bone-spicule pattern, which is a late finding · Symptom sequence — night blindness first, then progressive midperipheral field loss, then decreased acuity late when cones are involved; onset from age 10 into adulthood · Xerophthalmia — the mimic's gate: dryness of the cornea and conjunctivae with night blindness, which is what vitamin A deficiency looks like in the eye · Glaucomatous disc — an increased cup-to-disc ratio; the retinitis pigmentosa disc is pale and not cupped
Pertinent positives & negatives Two months, progressive — a degeneration, not an event; excludes retinal detachment · Visual acuity 20/20 — cones intact, so early disease, and inconsistent with cataract · Red reflex equal bilaterally — no lens opacity, closing cataract independently · Cornea and conjunctivae unremarkable — no xerophthalmia, closing vitamin A deficiency on examination rather than on diet · Midperipheral field defect — the rod-dense zone, the signature distribution of early disease · Optic disc pallor, not cupping — the single most efficient discriminator in the stem · Vessel attenuation with focal discoloration — the pigmentary retinopathy itself · Age 17 — open-angle glaucoma is a disease of late adulthood
Night blindness — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Retinitis pigmentosaInherited photoreceptor degeneration, rods first; most legally blind by 40Disc pallor plus vessel attenuation plus bone-spicule pigment; night blindness then midperipheral field loss— (the answer)
Vitamin A deficiencyMalabsorption, restrictive diet or povertyXerophthalmia — dry cornea and conjunctivae, Bitot spots, corneal ulcerationCornea and conjunctivae normal; varied plant diet
Open-angle glaucomaPainless gradual peripheral field loss in late adulthoodIncreased cup-to-disc ratio with raised intraocular pressureAge 17, and the disc is pale rather than cupped
Retinal detachment Can't missAcute; myopia, trauma or prior surgeryFloaters, flashes, a curtain; tear or elevation on fundusTwo-month progressive course, no tear or elevation
CataractAge, steroids, diabetes; glare from headlights at nightDecreased acuity plus diminished red reflex plus lens opacity20/20 acuity with an equal red reflex
Management, in one line Refer for formal visual fields and electroretinography with genetic counselling; treatment slows rather than reverses and most patients are legally blind by age 40, so the deliverable is prognosis, low-vision support and family screening — not a cure.
Decision spine Is the acuity normal? — Yes, so the problem is not the lens or the macula · Is the red reflex intact? — Yes, so cataract is out · Acute or progressive? — Two months and worsening, so not a detachment · Pale disc or cupped disc? — Pale means retinitis pigmentosa, not glaucoma · Is the front of the eye normal? — Yes, so no xerophthalmia and not vitamin A · Where is the field defect? — Midperipheral, which is the rods
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive night blindness, visual acuity 20/20, midperipheral field defect both eyes, funduscopy shows optic disc pallor with attenuated vessels and focal pigmentary change, cornea and conjunctivae normal → Retinitis pigmentosa → rods degenerate before cones
  2. 4 yo recently resettled refugee with night blindness, dry conjunctivae with Bitot spots and corneal xerosis → Vitamin A deficiency → oral vitamin A supplementation
  3. 17 yo F with night blindness, midperipheral field loss and a fundus showing disc pallor with vessel attenuation → Electroretinography with formal visual fields and genetic counselling → confirming retinitis pigmentosa
  4. 68 yo M with painless gradual peripheral field loss, intraocular pressure 26 and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8 → Open-angle glaucoma → topical prostaglandin analogue
  5. 55 yo M with sudden floaters and flashes followed by a curtain across the temporal field → Same-day ophthalmology referral → retinal detachment
  6. 72 yo F troubled by glare from oncoming headlights at night, visual acuity 20/60, diminished red reflex → Cataract → lens opacification
  7. Why night blindness is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa → Rod photoreceptors degenerate before cones → rods serve dim-light vision and the midperiphery
  8. Newly diagnosed 17 yo with retinitis pigmentosa asks what should be done for her 12 yo brother → Ophthalmologic examination with genetic counselling for first-degree relatives → most cases are inherited
Decoy note Strict vegan is the whole trap, and it is placed before any examination finding so it frames everything that follows. The counter-detail — eats a variety of plant products — is in the same sentence and is doing the opposite work. When a stem gives you a risk factor and then immediately qualifies it, the qualifier is the instruction.
