Dermatology & Wounds

Scabies

A close contact with the same rash outranks morphology

Source vignette Pt — 63 yo M, itchy web-space papules; roommate has the identical rash · Q — the most appropriate treatment; options spanned permethrin, topical triamcinolone and a single dose of oral ivermectin
The decision point

A roommate with the identical itchy rash makes this transmissible by prolonged skin contact — that single fact eliminates contact dermatitis, drug eruption, and every non-communicable itch. Add the distribution and the timeline and nothing else fits. Treatment: permethrin 5%.

Stem findings & their diagnostic weight
FindingWhy it matters
Severe itchMost pruritic common dermatosis; classically worse at night
Hands/wrists → other hand → waistlineTextbook map: finger web spaces, flexor wrists, axillae, belt line, periumbilical, genitals. Spares head and neck in adults
"Spots turned into scabs"Excoriations, not vesicular crusts
Roommate moved in a few weeks agoMatches the 3–6 week incubation on first infestation — a sensitization delay, not a replication delay
Trap autopsy Oral acyclovir — zoster is dermatomal, unilateral, painful, doesn't migrate hand→hand→waist, and doesn't infect a roommate. Oral cephalexin — "no crusting or spreading erythema" exists solely to kill this; impetigo means honey-colored crust. Oral prednisone / topical triamcinolone — both treat the itch, not the mite, and steroids produce scabies incognito: a masked, worsening infestation. The pruritus is a type IV hypersensitivity to mite antigen; suppressing the response doesn't touch the organism.
Treatment specifics that get tested separately Permethrin 5%, neck-down (whole body in infants), left on 8–14 hours, repeated in 1 week — the first application doesn't kill eggs · treat all household and close contacts simultaneously, symptomatic or not · wash bedding and clothing hot, or bag 72 hours · oral ivermectin (200 mcg/kg, repeat day 8) for crusted scabies, outbreaks, or adherence problems — avoid in pregnancy and under 15 kg.
The pearl that generates its own question Post-scabetic pruritus persists 2–4 weeks after successful treatment — the leading reason therapy is thought to have failed. That's when triamcinolone and antihistamines become correct: after the mite is dead, not instead of killing it.
Scenario bank
  1. 63 yo M, web-space papules, roommate with the same rash → Permethrin ×2 a week apart, treat contacts, launder linens
  2. 63 yo M, still itching 3 weeks after permethrin, no new burrows → Post-scabetic pruritus → topical steroid, not re-treatment
  3. 78 yo M in a nursing home, thick hyperkeratotic plaques, minimal itch, immunosuppressed → Crusted (Norwegian) scabies → oral ivermectin + topical, contact isolation
  4. 6 mo F, itchy vesicles on palms, soles, scalp, face → Infantile scabies → apply including the head
  5. 28 yo M, new apartment, itchy welts on exposed skin in linear clusters, no web-space lesions → Bedbugs
  6. 63 yo M with honey-colored crust and surrounding erythema → Impetiginized scabies → permethrin plus cephalexin
  7. 34 yo pregnant woman with scabies → Permethrin is safe; avoid ivermectin
  8. 63 yo M whose rash returns at 6 weeks → Contacts untreated, or the second application skipped
Transferable rule A close contact with the same condition outranks morphology — it converts the differential to transmissible causes before you interpret a single lesion. And when the loudest symptom is itch, check whether the offered drug kills the cause or only the sensation.

Obstetrics & Gynecology 10 topics + 3 board-style

Interval arithmetic and eligibility rules. The physiologic state of the patient decides which explanations are even permitted.

Vaccines & Timing in Pregnancy

Which one is due today?

The decision point

These stems stack several things the patient will eventually need, so the question is really "which one is due today?" — and the deciding variable is a date, a gestational age, or a serology, not a symptom. In the classic version the answer is signaled by "mid-September" in the first sentence: influenza vaccine, given as soon as it becomes available, in any trimester.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhat kills it
Anti-D immunoglobulinShe is Rh-negative with a negative screenTiming — routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks
MMRShe is non-immune to rubellaLive — contraindicated; give immediately postpartum
TdapIndicated in every pregnancyTiming — but as an optimization, not a gate. 27–36 weeks maximizes transplacental IgG transfer; Tdap is safe at any gestational age and is given off-window for wound prophylaxis or an outbreak. See Tdap in Pregnancy at 10 Weeks
Varicella vaccineRecent exposureLive — contraindicated, and she is already immune
VZIGExposure + pregnancy is the classic PEP settingVaricella IgG positive = immune; PEP is for the non-immune

Two killed by timing, two by live-vaccine status, one by serology. Each distractor fails for a different reason — you eliminate them on their own terms rather than comparing them.

Vaccines in pregnancyroutine / high-risk / contraindicated
Recommended for allIf high-riskContraindicated
Inactivated influenza (any trimester) · Tdap every pregnancy, 27–36 wk · COVID-19 · maternal RSV (32–36 wk) · anti-D at 28 wkHepatitis A, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, VZIG if exposed AND non-immuneMMR · varicella · LAIV · zoster · BCG · oral polio — all live. HPV is not live but is deferred
Rh immunoglobulin timing 28 weeks routinely · within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive · any sensitizing event (vaginal bleeding, spontaneous or threatened abortion, ectopic, molar pregnancy, amniocentesis/CVS, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma) · and the trap — a positive antibody screen means she is already alloimmunized, so anti-D is useless and you switch to titers and MCA Doppler.
Varicella in pregnancy Non-immune + exposed → VZIG within 10 days (ideally 96 hours) · maternal varicella → varicella pneumonia, high mortality → IV acyclovir · congenital varicella syndrome at 8–20 weeks: limb hypoplasia, cicatricial dermatomal scarring, chorioretinitis, cataracts · neonatal varicella if maternal rash occurs 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → VZIG to the newborn.
Scenario bank
  1. A pregnant patient with recent varicella exposure has a negative varicella IgG. → VZIG within 10 days
  2. Same patient at 28 weeks → Anti-D immunoglobulin
  3. Same patient at 30 weeks → Tdap
  4. Same patient postpartum → MMR → safe while breastfeeding
  5. Rh-negative with vaginal bleeding at 14 weeks → Anti-D now, regardless of gestational age
  6. Rh-negative with a positive antibody screen → Antibody titers with serial MCA Dopplers → she is already alloimmunized, and anti-D cannot undo it
  7. Varicella rash with dyspnea in pregnancy → Varicella pneumonia → IV acyclovir
  8. Maternal rash 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → VZIG to the neonate
  9. MMR inadvertently given during pregnancy → Counsel and reassure; not an indication for termination
  10. Pregnant patient asks about HPV vaccine → Defer to postpartum
Transferable rule When several choices are all things this patient will eventually need, scan for the number — date, gestational age, titer — before weighing the indications.

Cervical Cancer Screening

Intervals, abnormal results, special populations

The decision point

Each negative test starts its own clock, the test type sets the length, and you're due when your longest valid coverage expires. Negative cytology = 3 years of coverage from that date. Negative HPV-containing test = 5 years.

Cervical screening schedule
Age / situationTestInterval
<21None — regardless of sexual debut, partners, or vaccination—
21–29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30–65Primary HPV alone (preferred, clinician- or self-collected)Every 5 years
30–65 alternativesCytology alone · or co-testing3 years · 5 years
>65Stop if adequate prior screening and no CIN2+ in 25 years—
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F whose cytology was negative 2 years ago → Return in 1 year
  2. 34 yo F whose co-test was negative 3 years ago → Return in 2 years — the 5-year clock governs
  3. 34 yo F with negative cytology and HPV 16 positive → Colposcopy
  4. 26 yo F with ASC-US and a negative reflex HPV → Resume routine screening
  5. 34 yo F with HSIL on cytology → Colposcopy, or immediate excision
  6. 34 yo F with AGC on cytology → Colposcopy with endocervical and endometrial sampling
⚠︎ Primary HPV start age — the ledgers split Exam ledger (USPSTF, what the bank scores): primary HPV testing begins at age 30; 21–29 is cytology alone.
Clinic ledger (ACS 2020): primary HPV begins at age 25, every 5 years, preferred — which removes the 25–29 cytology block entirely.
Answer 30 on the exam. The age-21 floor is identical in both and is not in dispute — see Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor.
Abnormal result management by age
ResultAge ≥25Age 21–24
ASC-USReflex HPV: positive → colposcopyRepeat cytology in 1 year
LSILColposcopy if HPV+ or unknownRepeat cytology in 1 year
ASC-HColposcopy regardlessColposcopy
HSILColposcopy or immediate excision (see-and-treat LEEP)Colposcopy only
AGCColposcopy + ECC, plus endometrial biopsy if ≥35 or AUBSame
Cytology negative, HPV 16/18+Colposcopy now—
Colposcopy outcomes SCJ not fully visualized → endocervical curettage · CIN1 → observe · CIN2 → treat (observation acceptable if fertility-desiring) · CIN3 → treat · adenocarcinoma in situ → cold knife conization (LEEP fragments margins) · invasive cancer → staging, not LEEP · post-treatment surveillance for 25 years.
Special populations HIV — start within 1 year of sexual debut (the one exception to "never before 21"); cytology annually ×3 then q3y; never stop at 65 · total hysterectomy for benign disease → stop · cervix retained → continue · hysterectomy for CIN2+ → vaginal cuff cytology 25 years · HPV-vaccinated → same intervals · pregnant → colposcopy safe, ECC and endometrial biopsy contraindicated, defer CIN2/3 treatment to postpartum.
Two decoys A female partner does not lower risk — HPV transmits between women and screening is identical. Obesity is a real endometrial risk factor but does not trigger endometrial biopsy without AUB.

Postmenopausal Bleeding

One line decides it

The decision point

"No menstrual period for over a year" makes her postmenopausal, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Amount and duration are irrelevant; a single episode of spotting counts. ~90% of endometrial cancer presents this way; ~9–10% of PMB is cancer.

Postmenopausal bleeding workup
StepFindingAction
Endometrial evaluation — TVUS or EMBStripe ≤4 mmNo further workup unless bleeding recurs
Stripe >4 mmEndometrial biopsy
On tamoxifenBiopsy regardless — the threshold doesn't apply
Biopsy insufficient or bleeding recurs—Hysteroscopy with D&C
Results → management Hyperplasia without atypia → progestin (oral or LNG-IUD) · atypical hyperplasia / EIN → hysterectomy (up to 40% harbor concurrent carcinoma) · carcinoma → surgical staging with TAH-BSO + nodal assessment. Risk factors are unopposed estrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen, granulosa cell tumor, Lynch syndrome. Combined OCPs and multiparity are protective.
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with no period for 18 months, now spotting → Endometrial cancer until proven otherwise → transvaginal ultrasound or biopsy
  2. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding and an endometrial stripe of 3 mm → Atrophic endometrium → a stripe of 4 mm or less is reassuring
  3. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding and an endometrial stripe of 8 mm → Endometrial biopsy
  4. 58 yo F with an insufficient biopsy sample and continued bleeding → Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage
  5. 58 yo F with postmenopausal bleeding while taking tamoxifen → Proceed with full evaluation regardless → tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk
  6. 58 yo F with light postmenopausal bleeding lasting only one day → Evaluate with endometrial sampling → amount and duration are irrelevant
The two traps in one stem Fibroids cause bleeding in premenopausal women; after menopause they involute. Atrophy is the most common cause of PMB (~60%) — but it is a diagnosis of exclusion, so "pale vagina with minimal rugation" does not license reassurance. And a progestin IUD is contraindicated in undiagnosed bleeding.
Pairs with Part I Familial Adenomatous Polyposis holds the hereditary colon cancer differential in which Lynch syndrome — the endometrial-cancer pedigree — is the polyp-poor row. Store the discriminator as a question: is there an endometrial cancer in the family?
Transferable rule When a stem offers a familiar benign explanation, check whether the patient is still in the physiologic state where that explanation applies.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Ectopic Pregnancy

Location questions need imaging, not numbers

The decision point

Pregnancy is already confirmed by the urine test. The question is no longer "is she pregnant?" but "where is the pregnancy?" — and only one tool answers a location question: transvaginal ultrasound. A single serum β-hCG localizes nothing.

Defining criteria Methotrexate eligibility — unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Unstable ectopic — hypotension, rebound, or shoulder pain → emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy
Where β-hCG actually belongs
  1. Symptomatic + positive pregnancy test → Transvaginal ultrasound now
  2. Intrauterine pregnancy seen → Stop the workup → heterotopic pregnancy is rare outside IVF
  3. Adnexal mass or free fluid → Ectopic pregnancy → treat
  4. TVUS indeterminate → Check the β-hCG against the discriminatory zone → above 1,500 to 2,000 with an empty uterus is a presumed ectopic, and below it serial hCG q48h (a normal IUP doubles; ectopic rises <35–50%; miscarriage falls)
Stability picks the branch Hypotensive, rebound, or shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) → skip everything, emergent laparoscopy/laparotomy. Stable ectopic workup = image; unstable = operate — the same logic as PE.
Pearls Biggest acquired risk factor is prior PID (tubal scarring); also prior ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD in place, smoking (impairs ciliary transport) · half of ectopics have no palpable adnexal mass · methotrexate if unruptured, hCG <5,000, <3.5 cm, no fetal cardiac activity, reliable follow-up · Rh-negative mother with any bleeding in pregnancy → RhoGAM.
Transferable rule When two tests both seem reasonable, choose the one whose result forks the management tree. A single hCG changes nothing tonight; the ultrasound changes everything.

HPV Vaccination & Series Rules

A two-lock door

The decision point

Two independent facts: (1) age at first dose sets the series length — under 15 → 2 doses; ≥15 → 3 doses (immunocompromised → 3 regardless. (2) Never restart a vaccine series — delayed doses are simply given late. Minimum intervals matter; maximum intervals don't exist.

Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F receiving her first HPV dose → Two doses
  2. 17 yo M receiving his first HPV dose → Three doses
  3. 13 yo M with HIV receiving his first dose → Three doses regardless of age
  4. 15 yo F who received one dose 14 months ago → Continue the series — never restart
  5. 28 yo F asking about catch-up vaccination → Shared decision-making through age 45
  6. 12 yo F who had dose one at age 11 and dose two 4 months later → Repeat the second dose → doses less than 5 months apart do not count
Bankable rules "Do not restart, do not repeat" applies to every vaccine series — a gap just means resume where you left off · catch-up HPV vaccination is recommended through age 26, with shared decision-making 27–45 · sexual activity, prior HPV exposure, and abnormal Pap results do not change the recommendation — vaccinate anyway, because it still protects against strains not yet acquired.
Transferable rule When a guideline stem includes lifestyle color, ask whether it actually changes the algorithm. Usually it's there precisely because it doesn't.
Salient decoy

Adolescent Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

Reassurance needs a benign cause AND an acceptable consequence

The decision point

Anovulatory cycles from an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis are genuinely normal in the first 1–2 years after menarche — which is why most people choose reassurance. But reassurance requires two things: a benign cause and an acceptable consequence. Anemia is a consequence. The physiology being normal doesn't make the outcome acceptable.

Mechanism: immature axis → no LH surge → anovulation → no corpus luteum → no progesterone → unopposed estrogen drives continuous proliferation with no secretory differentiation → the lining outgrows its blood supply and sheds unpredictably. Progesterone converts proliferative to secretory endometrium and produces organized withdrawal bleeding.

Defining criteria Normal adolescent cycle — length 21–45 days (adults 24–38), duration ≤7 days, ≤3–6 products/day · Reassurance requires — a benign cause AND an acceptable consequence; anemia is not an acceptable consequence
The detail most people skip "Nonpainful." Ovulatory cycles are crampy — painless heavy irregular bleeding is the anovulatory signature. Normal adolescent parameters: cycle length 21–45 days (adults 24–38), duration ≤7 days, ≤3–6 products/day.
Adolescent AUB — clue → diagnosis → workup
ClueDiagnosisWorkup
Irregular, heavy, painless, within 2 yrs of menarcheAnovulation from an immature axisClinical
Heavy since the very first period, bruising, epistaxis, family historyvon Willebrand disease — up to 20% of adolescents with heavy mensesvWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII — PT/aPTT are often normal and do not exclude it
Hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricansPCOSAndrogens, glucose
GalactorrheaProlactinomaProlactin → MRI
Weight loss, athlete, low BMIFunctional hypothalamic amenorrheaFemale athlete triad
Any sexually active patientPregnancyPregnancy test before anything else
Scenario bank
  1. An adolescent with clinically diagnosed anovulatory bleeding within 2 years of menarche has a hemoglobin of 13 and is not bothered by the bleeding. → Reassurance + menstrual calendar
  2. Heavy since menarche + easy bruising + family history → Von Willebrand panel (normal PT/aPTT doesn't rule it out)
  3. Hirsutism, acne, BMI 34, acanthosis → Polycystic ovary syndrome → androgens + combined OCP
  4. Hemodynamically unstable acute heavy bleeding → Admit for intravenous conjugated estrogen → with a high-dose OCP taper, tranexamic acid and transfusion
  5. Galactorrhea + amenorrhea → Prolactin → pituitary MRI
  6. Sexually active → Pregnancy test first → always, before anything else
  7. Athlete with weight loss and amenorrhea → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea
  8. Wants a non-hormonal option for heavy bleeding → Tranexamic acid
  9. Adolescent with obesity and prolonged anovulation not responding to medical therapy → Endometrial biopsy → now reasonable after failed medical therapy
  10. Woman ≥45 with AUB → Endometrial biopsy regardless of ultrasound findings
The IUD pairing The copper IUD makes menses heavier and longer — contraindicated in heavy bleeding with anemia. The levonorgestrel IUD makes them lighter and is a legitimate treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.
Transferable rule "This is physiologically normal for her age" answers the diagnosis, not the management. Before choosing reassurance, check whether the stem gave you a consequence — anemia, growth failure, functional impairment. A consequence converts a normal variant into something you treat.
Uniform-answer doubt

Contraception & DMPA

A pregnancy test precedes every contraceptive decision

The decision point

When two explanations produce identical symptoms, test for the one that changes management and can't be missed. DMPA side effects — breast soreness, weight gain, fatigue, amenorrhea — are indistinguishable from early pregnancy. And the arithmetic assassin: DMPA is due every 13 weeks; her last injection was 4 months ago, so she has been uncovered.

The structural rule: a pregnancy test precedes every contraception decision, every amenorrhea workup, and absolutely every IUD placement — inserting an IUD into an established intrauterine pregnancy can disrupt it.

Defining criteria DMPA dosing window — every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · Return to fertility — delayed up to 10 months · Before any contraceptive decision — a pregnancy test
DMPA facts Suppresses GnRH → no LH surge → no ovulation; thickens cervical mucus · every 13 weeks with a ~2-week grace period · irregular bleeding early, then amenorrhea in ~50% at 1 year · weight gain from appetite stimulation · reversible loss of bone mineral density (boxed warning) · the unique one: delayed return to fertility up to 10 months · no estrogen, so safe in smokers ≥35, migraine with aura, VTE history, and immediately postpartum.
Contraception rules by situation
SituationRule
Smoker ≥35Avoid estrogen (WHO category 4) → progestin-only, IUD, implant
Migraine with auraAvoid estrogen — stroke risk
VTE history, uncontrolled HTN, SLE with antiphospholipid antibodiesAvoid estrogen
<21 days postpartum (or <42 if breastfeeding / VTE risk)Avoid estrogen; progestin-only and IUD are fine
Heavy menstrual bleedingLNG-IUD — copper makes bleeding worse
Emergency contraceptionCopper IUD most effective (up to 5 days); ulipristal > levonorgestrel, especially if BMI >30
Enzyme-inducing antiepilepticsCOC and implant efficacy drops → DMPA or IUD
Wants pregnancy soonAvoid DMPA
Secondary amenorrhea framework Defined as no menses >3 months with previously regular cycles (or >6 months if previously irregular). Pregnancy test first, then TSH, prolactin, FSH. FSH high → primary ovarian insufficiency · FSH low/normal → hypothalamic or pituitary · prolactin high → prolactinoma, dopamine blockers, or hypothyroidism · no withdrawal bleed even to estrogen + progesterone after a D&C → Asherman syndrome.
Scenario bank
  1. Negative pregnancy test → Offer any method she prefers → copper IUD, combined pill or implant
  2. Positive test → Prenatal care; DMPA exposure is not teratogenic
  3. A patient requesting contraception wants to conceive within a year. → DMPA → fertility return takes up to 10 months
  4. 38-year-old smoker requesting contraception → A progestin-only method or an IUD → not an estrogen-containing method
  5. Migraine with aura → No estrogen-containing method
  6. Needs emergency contraception 4 days after unprotected sex → Copper IUD → or ulipristal
  7. On DMPA 3 years, concerned about bone density → Counsel that loss is reversible, ensure calcium and vitamin D, consider alternatives
  8. Amenorrhea 4 months with a negative pregnancy test → TSH, prolactin, FSH
  9. Amenorrhea after a D&C → Asherman syndrome
  10. Exclusively breastfeeding, <6 months postpartum, amenorrheic → Lactational amenorrhea method requires all three; formula-feeding voids it
Transferable rule When a stem offers a plausible drug-effect explanation for symptoms that overlap a can't-miss diagnosis, the drug effect is a diagnosis of exclusion — especially when a date in the stem shows the drug wasn't actually working.

Uterine Fibroids

Treat consequences, not findings

The decision point

Fibroid size does not drive treatment — symptoms do. Stems front-load "markedly enlarged," "multiple," "intramural and pedunculated" to make impressive anatomy feel like it demands action, then explicitly negate every symptom domain. Asymptomatic fibroids get observation.

Findings audit — benign or consequential?
FindingConsequence?Answer
Benign rash (miliaria)No, but a removable causeRemove the cause
Normal anovulation (adolescent AUB)Yes — anemiaTreat
Impressive fibroid anatomyNoneReassure and observe
Indications for treating fibroids — the entire question
  • Heavy or prolonged menses, especially with anemia
  • Bulk symptoms — pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, hydronephrosis
  • Pelvic pain or dyspareunia
  • Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss (submucosal)
  • Rapid growth, or any growth after menopause → leiomyosarcoma concern
Location determines the symptom Submucosal → heavy bleeding and infertility (most symptomatic despite often being smallest) · intramural → bleeding and bulk · subserosal / pedunculated → pressure, and can torse · cervical → obstruction. Fibroids are estrogen- and progesterone-dependent, so they regress after menopause — which is why they can never explain postmenopausal bleeding.
The enlarged uterus — the differential
Enlarged uterusUterusThe tell
LeiomyomaIrregular, firm, lumpy, mobileHeavy menses; regresses after menopause
AdenomyosisGlobular, symmetric, boggy, tenderSevere dysmenorrhea; MRI shows a thickened junctional zone
PregnancySymmetric, softAmenorrhea → β-hCG
Endometrial cancerNormal or enlargedPostmenopausal bleeding → biopsy
LeiomyosarcomaRapidly enlarging, especially postmenopausalDoes not arise from a leiomyoma; avoid morcellation
Scenario bank
  1. Menorrhagia with hemoglobin 9 → Levonorgestrel IUD → first-line medical therapy
  2. Hydronephrosis on imaging → Surgical management → hydronephrosis makes it symptomatic
  3. Submucosal fibroid with recurrent pregnancy loss → Hysteroscopic myomectomy
  4. Large fibroid with anemia before planned surgery → GnRH agonist short-term (osteoporosis risk beyond 6 months; use add-back)
  5. Globular tender uterus with severe dysmenorrhea → Adenomyosis → LNG-IUD or hysterectomy
  6. Postmenopausal rapidly enlarging uterine mass → Leiomyosarcoma → work it up without morcellation
  7. Heavy bleeding, declines hormones, wants to preserve fertility → Tranexamic acid
  8. Completed childbearing, severe symptoms, failed medical therapy → Hysterectomy → the definitive option
  9. Pedunculated subserosal fibroid with acute severe pain → Torsion or degeneration of the fibroid → imaging
A detail that was bait in one stem and signal in another A same-sex relationship appeared in the cervical cancer stem as a decoy (implying low risk — wrong, screening is identical). Here it functions as valid reasoning: low pregnancy risk means the contraceptive benefit of a COC or IUD doesn't offset their risks. Details aren't inherently bait or signal — what the detail is being asked to decide determines which it is.
Transferable rule Treat consequences, not findings. Anatomic impressiveness on a CT report is not clinical significance — it's treat-the-number in imaging clothing.
Treat-the-number

Teratogenic Exposures

the malformation pattern names the drug · board question · Which single malformation belongs to only one agent?

Source vignette Pt — newborn male, growth restricted at 2.5 kg at 38 weeks, mother 29 with no prenatal care, forceps delivery for fetal heart rate abnormalities, Apgars 6 and 8 · Exam — microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate, and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges · Q — which maternal history would be found; options spanned alcohol use, cocaine use, lisinopril use, phenytoin use and untreated syphilis
The decision point

Two findings do the work, and they are the two that alcohol does not cause. Cleft palate and distal phalangeal hypoplasia together are fetal hydantoin syndrome — in utero exposure to a folate-antagonising antiepileptic, classically phenytoin, which crosses the placenta and produces low fetal folate with high oxidative metabolites. The wide anterior fontanelle and microcephaly complete it. Fetal alcohol syndrome shares the microcephaly and the midface hypoplasia but has no association with clefting, and its signature is a smooth philtrum with a thin vermilion border and short palpebral fissures — none of which is described.

Defining criteria Critical periods — 0–2 weeks all-or-none (death or no effect); 3–8 weeks organogenesis, the structural-malformation window; beyond 8 weeks growth restriction, CNS and functional deficits rather than structural defects · Fetal hydantoin syndrome — microcephaly, wide anterior fontanelle, cleft lip and palate, distal digit and nail hypoplasia, cardiac defects, neural tube defects · Fetal alcohol syndrome — smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures, midface hypoplasia, microcephaly, and no clefting · Antiepileptic management — switch to a lower-risk agent such as levetiracetam 6 months before conception, 4 mg folic acid from 3 months before conception, and make no changes after conception; screen with alpha-fetoprotein and anatomy ultrasonography
Teratogenic medications — drug to signaturethe malformation that belongs to only one agent
DrugSignature defect
PhenytoinDistal digit and nail hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate, wide fontanelle, microcephaly, cardiac, neural tube defects
ValproateNeural tube defects — the highest-risk antiepileptic
CarbamazepineNeural tube defects, less than valproate
TopiramateOral clefts, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental effects
PhenobarbitalCardiac, orofacial and urogenital malformations
IsotretinoinMicrotia and small ears, microcephaly, cleft palate, cardiac, thymic hypoplasia, hydrocephalus
MethotrexateLimb and craniofacial defects, cranial ossification defects, neural tube defects, abortion
ACE inhibitors / ARBsRenal dysgenesis → oligohydramnios → Potter sequence, growth restriction
WarfarinNasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia; fetal haemorrhage later
LithiumEbstein anomaly
MethimazoleAplasia cutis, oesophageal atresia, facial anomalies
TetracyclinesTooth discolouration, inhibited long-bone growth
FluoroquinolonesCartilage and bone toxicity
DiethylstilbestrolClear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, uterine malformation
ThalidomidePhocomelia
Pertinent positives & negatives Cleft palate — present in hydantoin and absent in fetal alcohol syndrome; the single most discriminating finding in the stem · Hypoplasia of the distal phalanges — near-specific for antiepileptic exposure · Wide anterior fontanelle — part of the hydantoin pattern, and easy to skim · Symmetric growth restriction with microcephaly — shared by alcohol, phenytoin, isotretinoin and cocaine, so it discriminates nothing · No smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border or short palpebral fissures — the fetal alcohol facial triad is absent · No prenatal care — explains why a maternal medication history was never taken; it is the setup, not a finding · No snuffles, hepatomegaly or maculopapular rash — congenital syphilis is excluded on its own features
Decision spine Is there a structural malformation? — Yes → exposure fell in the 3–8 week window · List the findings that only one agent causes. — Cleft palate and distal digit hypoplasia · Which agent owns both? — Phenytoin · Check the nearest mimic. — Alcohol shares the microcephaly but never the cleft · Is there an alternative explanation for the growth restriction? — It is nonspecific and belongs to every option · What would have prevented it? — Pre-conception switch plus 4 mg folate
Scenario bank
  1. Newborn male, growth restricted at 38 weeks to a mother with no prenatal care, with microcephaly, a wide anterior fontanelle, cleft palate and hypoplasia of the distal phalanges → Maternal phenytoin use → fetal hydantoin syndrome
  2. Child with a smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, short palpebral fissures and midface hypoplasia with microcephaly, and no cleft lip or palate → Fetal alcohol syndrome → alcohol is not associated with clefting
  3. Newborn with severe oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, flat facies and positional limb deformities; the mother took an antihypertensive throughout pregnancy → Maternal ACE inhibitor use → renal dysgenesis causing Potter sequence
  4. Newborn with Ebstein anomaly on echocardiography whose mother is treated for bipolar disorder → Maternal lithium use → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve
  5. Newborn with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses on radiograph; the mother has a mechanical mitral valve → Maternal warfarin use in the first trimester → low molecular weight heparin should have been substituted
  6. 26 yo on valproate for epilepsy who hopes to conceive in about a year → Switch to levetiracetam now and begin 4 mg folic acid → change the regimen before conception, not after
  7. 28 yo on carbamazepine who presents newly pregnant at 9 weeks gestation → Switching to a different antiepileptic now → organogenesis is largely complete and overlapping agents doubles exposure
  8. 22 yo about to start isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne → Two negative pregnancy tests 19 or more days apart with two forms of contraception → iPLEDGE risk-management requirements
Anticoagulation in pregnancy, in one line Low molecular weight heparin and unfractionated heparin have no fetal effects; warfarin is teratogenic to bone and cartilage. So mechanical valve patients take LMWH in the first trimester, warfarin in the second and third, and unfractionated heparin near delivery — the whole logic being that heparins do not cross the placenta and warfarin does.
Pearls Cleft plus distal digit hypoplasia is phenytoin; alcohol takes the philtrum and the palpebral fissures, phenytoin takes the palate and the fingertips · Timing predicts the kind of damage — before 2 weeks all-or-none, 3–8 weeks structure, after 8 weeks growth and brain · Change antiepileptics before conception, never after; once pregnancy is recognised organogenesis is mostly done, and switching adds seizure risk plus a second teratogen · Valproate is the worst antiepileptic and levetiracetam the usual substitute · Oligohydramnios with Potter sequence should raise ACE inhibitors as well as renal agenesis — same cascade, different first cause · Lithium → Ebstein anomaly is the one psychiatric-drug-to-cardiac-lesion pairing worth memorising outright
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence, which owns the oligohydramnios cascade this brief reaches from the drug side, and Part I Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease, which owns Ebstein anomaly. Store the discriminator as a question: which single malformation does only one drug on the roster cause?
Transferable rule Teratogen questions are a matching exercise with a fixed roster — so the work is finding the one malformation that belongs to only one agent, and ignoring the shared features that every option can produce.
Unchecked attributeAlcohol use — shares microcephaly and growth restriction, but has no association with cleft lip or palate, and none of the facial triad is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotCocaine use — causes preterm delivery, abruption and growth restriction, but no congenital defects.
Class-vs-memberLisinopril — a named teratogen, but it produces renal failure and Potter sequence, not clefting or digit hypoplasia.
True-fact-wrong-slotUntreated syphilis — symptomatic cases show snuffles, hepatomegaly and a maculopapular rash, none present here.

Primary Amenorrhea

uterus present or absent, then read the FSH · board question · Is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?

Source vignette Pt — 15 yo, no menses, distressed at looking younger than peers; no headache or visual change; mother and grandmother menarche at 13; height below the 3rd percentile, weight 20th · Exam — no breast development, normal external genitalia, Tanner 2 pubic hair; urine beta-hCG negative · Imaging — pelvic ultrasonography shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries · Labs — FSH 60 (normal under 40), LH 52 (normal 5–25) · Q — the next step in management, then the underlying cause; options spanned hormone measurements, imaging, karyotype and reassurance
The decision point

Primary amenorrhea is no menarche by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by 13 without them. The first step is pelvic ultrasonography, and the reason is architectural: the obstruction can sit anywhere along hypothalamus → pituitary → ovary → uterus → vagina, and imaging is the only test that answers the anatomical half of that chain in one move. Every hormonal test is interpretable only once you know whether there is a uterus. Then the algorithm forks twice. Uterus present → read the FSH: high FSH with high LH is primary ovarian insufficiency, and with short stature that is Turner syndrome — gonadal dysgenesis from loss of an X, giving streak ovaries and absent oestrogen, while intact adrenals still produce pubic hair. Uterus absent → read the pubic hair: present means the androgen receptor works, so 46,XX Müllerian agenesis; absent means it does not, so 46,XY complete androgen insensitivity.

Defining criteria Primary amenorrhea — no menarche by age 15 with secondary sexual characteristics, or by age 13 without them · First step — pelvic ultrasonography, to establish whether a uterus is present before any hormone is measured · Uterus present, FSH high — primary ovarian insufficiency; with short stature, Turner syndrome (45,X on karyotype, FISH if mosaicism is suspected) · Uterus present, FSH low or inappropriately normal — central: MRI for a hypothalamic or pituitary lesion, or GnRH deficiency, Cushing syndrome, functional hypothalamic amenorrhea · Uterus absent — serum testosterone: female-range with normal pubic hair is Müllerian agenesis (46,XX); male-range with absent pubic and axillary hair is complete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)
Primary amenorrhea — the two-step algorithmanatomy first, then the gonadotropins
StepFindingConclusion
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus presentGo to the FSH
1. Pelvic ultrasoundUterus absentGo to the testosterone and the pubic hair
2a. FSH high± short staturePrimary ovarian insufficiency → karyotype → Turner if 45,X
2a. FSH low or normal± anosmia, weight loss, athlete, cushingoidCentral: MRI, or functional, Kallmann or Cushing
2b. Testosterone female-rangePubic hair presentMüllerian agenesis (46,XX) → evaluate the renal tract
2b. Testosterone male-rangePubic hair absentComplete androgen insensitivity (46,XY)
Pertinent positives & negatives Height below the 3rd percentile — the Turner giveaway; almost all patients develop short stature, often the only feature besides amenorrhea · No breast development with Tanner 2 pubic hair — oestrogen absent, adrenal androgens intact; the dissociation that points at the ovary rather than the axis · FSH 60 and LH 52 — loss of oestrogen negative feedback; hypergonadotropic hypogonadism · Prepubertal uterus with small ovaries — streak gonads; the uterus is present but was never stimulated · No headache or visual change — argues against a sellar mass, which is the central branch · Normal external genitalia — the genital tubercle is unaffected in every diagnosis on this list · Negative beta-hCG — pregnancy excluded before anything else, as it must be
Decision spine Is the definition met? — No menarche by 13 without secondary characteristics → yes · What is the first test? — Pelvic ultrasound; anatomy before hormones · Is there a uterus? — Yes → read the FSH · Is the FSH high or low? — High → the ovary failed, not the brain · Is she short? — Below the 3rd percentile → Turner · What confirms it? — Karyotype showing 45,X, with FISH for mosaicism if normal
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with no menarche, no breast development, Tanner 2 pubic hair, height below the 3rd percentile, normal external genitalia and a negative urine beta-hCG → Pelvic ultrasonography → establish the anatomy before measuring hormones
  2. 14 yo with primary amenorrhea and no secondary sexual characteristics in whom ultrasonography has confirmed a uterus → FSH level measurement → it separates central (low or normal) from peripheral (high) causes
  3. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, no breast development and short stature; ultrasound shows a prepubertal uterus with small ovaries and FSH is 60 with LH 52 → Turner syndrome → 45,X on karyotype
  4. 16 yo distance runner with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast and pubic hair, normal external genitalia; ultrasound shows normal ovaries and no uterus → Müllerian agenesis → failure of paramesonephric duct development
  5. 16 yo with primary amenorrhea, Tanner 4 breast development, absent pubic and axillary hair, tall stature and no uterus on ultrasound → Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome → 46,XY with male-range testosterone
  6. 15 yo with primary amenorrhea, a uterus on ultrasound, FSH 3 and LH 2, normal weight and normal sense of smell → MRI of the brain → a low FSH points centrally
  7. 16 yo newly diagnosed with Müllerian agenesis → Renal ultrasonography → renal tract anomalies are commonly associated
  8. 17 yo gymnast training twice daily with a BMI of 16, primary amenorrhea, a uterus present, and low FSH and LH → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea → energy deficit suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis
  9. Why girls with Turner syndrome develop pubic hair but no breast development → Adrenarche is intact while ovarian oestrogen production fails → the adrenal glands are unaffected by loss of an X chromosome
Right test, wrong time Most wrong options here are correct tests offered one step too early. A 17-hydroxyprogesterone, a testosterone, a karyotype and an MRI are each the right move in some branch of this algorithm — and every one of them is uninterpretable until the ultrasound has said whether there is a uterus. Reassurance is the other trap: it is right for a girl under 15 who has secondary sexual characteristics, and wrong here because the definition is already met and her height is below the 3rd percentile.
Pearls Ultrasound first, always — every hormone in this workup is uninterpretable until you know whether there is a uterus · Uterus present → FSH. Uterus absent → pubic hair. Two questions, in that order, resolve almost every primary amenorrhea stem · High FSH means the ovary failed; low FSH means the brain is quiet — the gonadotropins tell you which end of the axis to investigate · Turner patients have pubic hair, because adrenarche is adrenal and the adrenals are normal; hair without breasts names the ovary as the failure · Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity both present with an absent uterus and split on hair · Müllerian agenesis obliges a renal ultrasound — the ducts develop alongside the urinary tract, so anomalies travel together · An athlete with amenorrhea can still have a structural cause; functional hypothalamic amenorrhea never explains missing anatomy
Pairs with Part I Adolescent Abnormal Uterine Bleeding, which owns the opposite complaint on the same axis — too much bleeding rather than none — and shares the immature-axis physiology. Part II Sexual Maturity Rating owns the staging vocabulary this brief uses throughout. Store the discriminator as a question: is there a uterus, and if so is the FSH high or low?
Transferable rule When a workup has an anatomical branch and a hormonal branch, image first — a hormone measured before you know the anatomy produces a number you cannot interpret, and most of the wrong answers in these stems are correct tests offered one step too early.
Sequencing trap17-hydroxyprogesterone — real in the amenorrhea workup for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, but indicated only once a uterus is confirmed and with suggestive features.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance and observation — the definition is already met, and height below the 3rd percentile is itself a finding.
Unchecked attributeAndrogen insensitivity — requires an absent uterus; she has one.
Mirror twinDevelopmental failure of the urogenital sinus — produces a vaginal dimple with a uterus present, the mirror image of Müllerian agenesis.
Salient decoyAbnormal GnRH pulsatility — twice-daily training is a real risk factor, but central causes give low gonadotropins and cannot remove a uterus.

Obstetrics & Gynecology

Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

Treat on the exam finding, not the culture · Aquifer · the threshold is low by design

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo F, sudden pelvic pain, T 39 C, cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, no adnexal mass · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned starting empiric antibiotics now, obtaining pelvic ultrasonography first and awaiting nucleic acid amplification results
The decision point

The stem has already met the diagnostic threshold. PID is a presumptive clinical diagnosis, and the gate is deliberately low: a sexually active young woman with pelvic pain, no other identified cause, and any one of cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. She has cervical motion tenderness, and the purulent discharge plus fever above 38.3 C are supporting criteria.

The threshold sits there because treatment prevents the sequelae and delay causes them. Managing the alternatives — ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian cyst, torsion — is not impaired by starting antimicrobials. There is no diagnostic penalty for treating early and a permanent one for treating late: infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain.

Defining criteria Minimum criteria — pelvic or lower abdominal pain with no other identified cause plus at least one of cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness · Additional criteria — temperature above 38.3 C, mucopurulent cervical discharge or friability, abundant WBCs on saline microscopy, raised ESR or CRP, documented gonococcal or chlamydial infection · Negative predictor — normal cervical discharge with no WBCs on wet prep makes PID unlikely
Acute pelvic pain in a young woman - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Pelvic inflammatory diseaseAscending gonococcal, chlamydial or vaginal-flora infectionCervical motion tenderness with mucopurulent discharge
Ectopic pregnancy Can't missAmenorrhea then unilateral painPositive hCG with an empty uterus; a pregnancy test is always mandatory
Tubo-ovarian abscessA complication of PID rather than a separate diseasePalpable or sonographic adnexal mass; admit
Ovarian torsionSudden severe unilateral pain with an ovarian massNausea and vomiting, usually afebrile, absent Doppler flow
AppendicitisPeriumbilical pain migratingMcBurney point tenderness, no cervical findings
PyelonephritisAscending urinary infectionCostovertebral angle tenderness with pyuria
Management ladder — pelvic inflammatory disease
TierInterventionEscalate when
PresumptiveStart empiric antibiotics as soon as the clinical diagnosis is madeAny hospitalisation criterion below
OutpatientCeftriaxone 500 mg IM once, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 daysNo improvement within 72 hours means admit and reconsider the diagnosis
InpatientCeftriaxone 1 g IV daily with doxycycline and metronidazole, or cefoxitin or cefotetan with doxycyclineTubo-ovarian abscess failing medical therapy means drainage
TransitionOral doxycycline and metronidazole after 24 to 48 hours of improvement, completing 14 days—
Follow-upRetest for gonorrhea and chlamydia at 3 months—
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, sudden pelvic pain, T 39 C, cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, no adnexal mass → Start empiric antibiotics now → PID is a presumptive clinical diagnosis
  2. 19 yo F meeting PID criteria with a 6 cm tubo-ovarian abscess on ultrasound → Admit for intravenous antibiotics → drainage if no response
  3. 22 yo F meeting PID criteria with a positive pregnancy test and an intrauterine gestation → Hospitalize for intravenous antibiotics → doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy
  4. 24 yo F meeting PID criteria with a copper intrauterine device in place → Treat and leave the device in place → reconsider removal only if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours
  5. 18 yo F on outpatient PID therapy with no clinical improvement at 72 hours → Admit for intravenous therapy and reassess the diagnosis → consider diagnostic laparoscopy
  6. 20 yo F diagnosed with PID whose last sexual intercourse was 3 weeks ago → Evaluate and presumptively treat partners from the last 60 days → for chlamydia and gonorrhea regardless of her results
  7. 17 yo F with pelvic inflammatory disease and new right upper quadrant pleuritic pain → Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome → perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions
  8. 16 yo F with sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain, vomiting, an adnexal mass and no fever → Ovarian torsion → Doppler ultrasound then laparoscopy
  9. 17 yo F newly diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease, what else to test for → HIV and syphilis → plus gonorrhea and chlamydia, retesting at 3 months
When to admit Surgical emergency cannot be excluded, tubo-ovarian abscess, pregnancy, severe illness or vomiting or temperature above 38.5 C, inability to tolerate oral therapy, or no response to oral therapy. Adolescence is not itself a criterion — the same thresholds apply as for adults. All contraceptive methods can be continued during treatment, and an intrauterine device does not need removal.
Pearls The low threshold is the guideline, not a shortcut — clinical diagnosis carries a positive predictive value of only 65 to 90% for salpingitis, and that is accepted deliberately · Only about half of acute PID has a positive gonorrhea or chlamydia test, so a negative test never excludes it · Metronidazole joined the routine regimen in 2021 for anaerobic coverage; older item banks may key ceftriaxone plus doxycycline alone · Quinolones are no longer recommended because of gonococcal resistance · Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is PID that reached the liver capsule, with right upper quadrant pleuritic pain
Pairs with Part I Ectopic Pregnancy is the mandatory partner: both present as acute pelvic pain in a reproductive-age woman, and the fork is settled by one test. Store the discriminator as a question: what is the pregnancy test?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is defined as presumptive and clinical, the arrival of its confirmatory test is documentation rather than management, so ask what the pending test could change today and treat if the answer is nothing.
Sequencing trapUltrasound is normal in uncomplicated PID and delays the only intervention that prevents sequelae.
Class-vs-memberUrine culture is the right class of test on the wrong compartment.
True-fact-wrong-slotContraception is appropriate care but is prevention, not treatment of an established infection.

Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor

An eligibility gate, not a risk calculation

Source vignette Pt — 20 yo F, sexual debut at 15, five lifetime partners, inconsistent condom use · Q — the most appropriate screening step; options spanned no screening until 21, cytology now and co-testing now
The decision point

A 20-year-old is below the screening floor. Sexual debut at 15, five partners, inconsistent condoms — every one of those raises HPV exposure and none of them lowers the starting age. The answer is no cytology; screening begins at 21.

The rule is deliberately risk-blind. HPV in adolescents is near-universal and clears in ~90% within 2 years; progression to cancer takes a decade-plus. Screening early finds transient infection and produces excisional procedures (LEEP) that raise preterm-birth risk in women who were never going to develop cancer. That's why cervical cancer under 21 is rare — and why screening her would harm without benefit.

Cervical screening — age gates
AgeScreen withInterval
<21Do not screen — regardless of sexual history, partners, or STI history—
21–29Cytology aloneEvery 3 years
30–65Cytology q3y · co-testing q5y · primary HPV q5y3 or 5 years
>65Stop if adequate prior negative screening and no CIN2+ in 25 years—
⚠︎ Primary HPV start age — the ledgers split Exam ledger (bank/USPSTF): primary HPV testing from age 30.
Clinic ledger (ACS 2020): primary HPV from age 25, q5y, preferred.
Answer 30 on the exam. Know 25 exists so a clinic attending's answer doesn't unseat you.
Exit ramps — where the age floor genuinely moves HIV infection → screen at diagnosis (or within 1 year of sexual debut if younger), then annually × 3, then q3y — this is the one exception that beats age 21 · other immunocompromise (transplant, chronic steroids) → same accelerated schedule · in-utero DES exposure → annual · prior CIN2+ → surveillance q3y for 25 years, including past 65 · hysterectomy with cervix removed for benign disease → stop entirely; cervix retained (supracervical) → keep screening · vaccinated → schedule unchanged.
Scenario bank
  1. 20 yo F, debut at 15, five partners → No screening → begin at 21
  2. 18 yo F newly diagnosed with HIV → Screen now, then annually × 3
  3. 21 yo F, virgin, never sexually active → Screen anyway; the recommendation is age-based, not activity-based
  4. 24 yo F with ASC-US cytology → Reflex HPV; if negative, resume routine
  5. 28 yo F, normal cytology 2 years ago → Return in 1 year → every 3 years from the last test
  6. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV positive, not 16 or 18 → Repeat co-test in 1 year
  7. 33 yo F, cytology negative / HPV 16 positive → Colposcopy → genotype escalates
  8. 67 yo F, three consecutive negatives, no CIN history → Stop screening
  9. 67 yo F with CIN2 treated 10 years ago → Keep screening → the 25-year clock overrides age 65
  10. 42 yo F, hysterectomy for fibroids, cervix removed → Stop · hysterectomy for cervical cancer → continue vaginal cuff cytology
  11. 20 yo F with visible cervical lesion or postcoital bleeding → Biopsy the lesion → that's diagnostic, not screening
Trap autopsy The stem's entire risk paragraph is a salient decoy constructed to make "no screening" feel negligent. Colposcopy is the sequencing trap — it's for an abnormal result, and she has no result. HPV vaccination counseling is a true-fact-wrong-slot: she's 20, catch-up runs through 26, so it's genuinely indicated — just not what the question asked.
Pairs with Part I Cervical Cancer Screening (interval mechanics when cytology and co-testing fall out of sync) and HPV Vaccination & Series Rules. Store the discriminator: "Is she eligible yet?" — asked before "is she at risk?"
Transferable rule Screening guidelines are population rules with age gates. Individual risk factors adjust intensity within the eligible window; they rarely move the floor. Check eligibility before you calculate risk.
Salient decoySequencing trapTrue-fact-wrong-slot

Tdap in Pregnancy at 10 Weeks

A window that optimizes, not a gate that excludes

Source vignette Pt — 26 yo F at 10 weeks gestation, asking which vaccines she needs · Q — the most appropriate immunization plan; options spanned Tdap in the third trimester, Tdap today and deferring Tdap to postpartum
The decision point

She is 10 weeks pregnant and asks about vaccines. Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, but the antibody transfer that protects the newborn is maximized when it's given at 27–36 weeks, preferably early in that window. So at 10 weeks the answer is administer Tdap in the third trimester — schedule it, don't decline it.

Correction to an earlier framing in this document The Part I pregnancy-vaccine brief listed Tdap's trap as "Timing — 27–36 weeks," which reads like an eligibility gate. It isn't. Tdap is safe at any gestational age, and if a pregnant woman has a wound requiring tetanus prophylaxis, or is caught in a pertussis outbreak, you give it then. 27–36 weeks is an optimization of transplacental IgG transfer, not a permission window. Gate vs. optimization is exactly the distinction NBME builds a question on.
Vaccine rules in pregnancy
VaccineIn pregnancyThe tell
TdapEvery pregnancy, ideally 27–36 weeksRepeat each pregnancy even if given last year — it's for this fetus
Influenza (IM, inactivated)Any trimester during seasonNo timing window — 10 weeks in flu season → give today
RSV (RSVpreF, Abrysvo)32–36 weeks, seasonalMaternal vaccine or infant nirsevimab — generally not both
COVID-19Recommended, any trimester—
MMR · VaricellaContraindicated — livePostpartum, before discharge; non-immune rubella is a classic stem
Live attenuated influenza (nasal)ContraindicatedThe class-vs-member trap: "influenza vaccine" is right, that influenza vaccine is wrong
HPVDefer to postpartumNot teratogenic — deferred for lack of data
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F at 10 weeks asking about vaccines → Tdap in the third trimester (+ influenza now if in season)
  2. 26 yo F at 30 weeks, Tdap in a prior pregnancy 2 years ago → Give Tdap again
  3. 26 yo F at 12 weeks in October → Inactivated influenza vaccine today → no window
  4. 26 yo F at 14 weeks with a dirty puncture wound, last Td 12 years ago → Tdap now → the window doesn't apply to prophylaxis
  5. 26 yo F at 34 weeks in November, no RSV vaccine → RSVpreF now → or plan nirsevimab for the infant
  6. 26 yo F, rubella non-immune on prenatal labs → MMR postpartum before discharge → not during pregnancy
  7. 26 yo F who received MMR then discovered she's pregnant → Counsel and monitor; not an indication for termination
  8. 26 yo F at 10 weeks, offered the nasal influenza vaccine → Give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine → the nasal formulation is live
  9. Household members and the partner of a newborn, no prior Tdap → Vaccinate them at least 2 weeks before contact → cocooning
  10. 26 yo F postpartum, breastfeeding → All vaccines including live ones are permitted
Paired pearls Maternal Tdap is for the infant, who can't be vaccinated until 2 months — the deadliest pertussis window is the first 3 months · antibody transfer needs ~2 weeks to develop and time to cross, which is what makes late-third-trimester dosing suboptimal and preterm delivery the reason to dose at 27, not 36 · breastfeeding lifts every restriction; pregnancy is the constraint, lactation is not.
Pairs with Part I Vaccines & Timing in Pregnancy — this brief supersedes its Tdap timing row. Store the discriminator: "Is this window a gate or an optimization?"
Transferable rule When a recommendation carries a time window, ask what the window protects. If it optimizes an effect (antibody transfer), you can move outside it when the indication changes. If it defines eligibility (age 21 for cytology), you cannot.
Class-vs-memberSequencing trap

Preventive Medicine & Ethics 5 topics + 2 board-style

Ranking questions and eligibility questions. Capacity determines the reporting path.

Ranking Preventive Interventions

"Most beneficial" is a magnitude question

Source vignette Pt — 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia · Q — the intervention that most reduces mortality; options spanned smoking cessation, a statin and lisinopril
The decision point

When every option is guideline-supported, the question is asking you to rank by magnitude of benefit. Nothing beats quitting a pack a day: smoking cessation reduces all-cause mortality more than any drug on the list, cuts CV risk substantially within 1–2 years, and approaches never-smoker risk over ~15 years.

Ranking preventive interventions — why each loses
ChoiceLegitimate claimWhy it loses
Smoking cessation—Largest mortality benefit of any intervention
LisinoprilDiabetic + HTN → ACE-I preferred, especially with albuminuriaBP only mildly elevated, no proteinuria — real but smaller
StatinDiabetic 40–75 → indicated regardless of LDLTrue indication, but ~25% relative risk reduction — cessation dwarfs it
↑ HCTZBP above goalMarginal, and worsens glucose and lipids in a diabetic
↑ MetforminA1c above targetGlycemic control reduces microvascular complications; weak macrovascular effect (UKPDS)
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo M smoker with hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidemia; which most reduces mortality → Smoking cessation
  2. 58 yo M who has already quit; which intervention is next → A statin
  3. 58 yo M asking how soon quitting helps → Cardiovascular risk falls within 1 to 2 years
  4. 58 yo M ready to quit within the month → Varenicline plus behavioural support
  5. 58 yo M who is not ready to quit → Motivational interviewing
  6. 58 yo M with 30 pack-years who quit 5 years ago → Annual low-dose CT screening
The hierarchy to bank For macrovascular outcomes: smoking cessation > BP control > statin > glycemic control. If smoking cessation is an option and the patient smokes, it wins — unless the question is scoped to a specific organ ("risk of nephropathy progression" → ACE-I/BP; "microvascular complications" → A1c). Lifestyle answers are traps when vague ("recommend exercise") and winners when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).
Treat-the-number

Lipid Screening & Vaccine Eligibility by Condition

Where the exam answer and the current guideline diverge

The decision point

USPSTF retired its standalone lipid-screening recommendation. Lipid measurement now lives inside the statin primary-prevention recommendation: adults 40–75 get lipids as part of periodic 10-year ASCVD risk assessment. Under 40 and in children, the evidence is rated insufficient.

Scenario bank
  1. 48 yo M asking when his lipids should be checked → As part of periodic 10-year risk assessment, ages 40 to 75
  2. 48 yo M with cirrhosis; which additional vaccines → Pneumococcal, hepatitis A and hepatitis B
  3. 48 yo M after splenectomy → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib
  4. 48 yo M starting eculizumab → Meningococcal vaccination is mandatory
  5. 48 yo M receiving a cochlear implant → Pneumococcal vaccination
  6. 26 yo F who is pregnant, asking which vaccines she needs → Tdap and inactivated influenza
The legacy numbers question banks still use Men ≥35 screen · women ≥45 at increased risk · ages 20–35 (men) and 20–45 (women) only with risk factors (diabetes, HTN, smoking, obesity, premature family history). Conventional interval: every ~5 years; ACC/AHA says 4–6 years from age 20. AAP — not USPSTF — recommends universal pediatric lipid screening once at 9–11 and again at 17–21.
Adult vaccine special populations — the recycled core
ConditionExtra vaccinesWhy
Chronic liver disease / cirrhosisPneumococcal, Hep A, Hep BThe liver makes complement — cirrhosis means lost opsonins; portosystemic shunting bypasses Kupffer cells; hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver is fulminant
Asplenia / splenectomy / sickle cellPneumococcal + Hib + meningococcalLost filter — encapsulated organisms need splenic clearance
Complement deficiency / eculizumabMeningococcalC5–C9 kills Neisseria
CSF leak / cochlear implantPneumococcalDirect meningeal access
PregnancyTdap every pregnancy (27–36 wk), inactivated influenzaNo live vaccines — MMR, varicella, LAIV
Transferable rule When a stem shows you an enlarged organ, ask what the enlargement means hemodynamically before pattern-matching to its absence. A congested spleen is not an absent spleen — cirrhosis loses opsonins, asplenia loses the filter, and the vaccine lists differ accordingly.

Preoperative Thresholds

Numbers that gate procedures

The decision point

Preop questions test which numbers actually gate which procedures. If the value clears the threshold, the answer is almost always proceed — NBME rewards restraint.

Platelet count thresholds
Platelet countMeaning
<10,000Spontaneous bleeding risk → prophylactic transfusion even if asymptomatic
<50,000Transfuse only for active bleeding or before surgery/invasive procedures
≥50,000Adequate for nearly all surgery, including dental extraction and central lines
≥100,000Reserved for neurosurgery and posterior eye surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 8,000 before elective surgery → Prophylactic platelet transfusion
  2. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 60,000 before a minor procedure → Proceed without transfusion
  3. 60 yo M with a platelet count of 40,000 before major surgery → Transfuse to at least 50,000
  4. 60 yo M needing neurosurgery with a platelet count of 80,000 → Transfuse to at least 100,000
  5. 28 yo F with ITP, platelets 8,000 and petechiae, no surgery planned → Corticosteroids or IVIG → transfused platelets are consumed too
  6. 60 yo M with platelet clumping on the smear and a reported count of 40,000 → Pseudothrombocytopenia → repeat in a citrate tube
Variants Petechiae with a count of 8,000 in a healthy young woman → ITP → steroids/IVIG, not transfusion (transfused platelets get consumed too) · heparin day 5–10 with a 50% drop → HIT → stop heparin, start argatroban, never transfuse · clumps on the smear → pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA → repeat in a citrate tube — the one time "recheck the count" is correct · DDAVP is for qualitative defects (von Willebrand disease, mild hemophilia A, uremic platelet dysfunction), not for a low count.

Elder Abuse & Mandated Reporting

Capacity determines the path

The decision point

Reasonable suspicion → report to Adult Protective Services. You do not need proof, and you do not investigate first. Confounders like warfarin (easy bruising) and dementia (unreliable historian) are real and irrelevant to the decision — APS investigates; you don't adjudicate.

Scenario bank
  1. 82 yo F with bruises in multiple stages of healing and a vague mechanism → Report now, on suspicion alone → proof is not required, and confirming it is not the physician's job
  2. 82 yo F on warfarin with easy bruising and an implausible history → Report to Adult Protective Services → anticoagulation explains bruising, not the implausible history; suspicion alone obligates the report
  3. 82 yo F with dementia who denies abuse while her caregiver is present → Interview her alone
  4. 34 yo F disclosing intimate partner violence, fully competent, who declines reporting → Support and safety planning, respecting her autonomy
  5. 6 yo M with a spiral femur fracture and an inconsistent history → Mandatory report to child protective services
  6. 82 yo F with suspected abuse; who investigates → Adult Protective Services → the physician reports suspicion; APS investigates
The findings that build suspicion Bruises in multiple stages of healing (the single most tested physical finding, as in child abuse) · implausible or vague mechanism · caregiver who cannot explain the injuries · patient who becomes uncomfortable and minimizes when asked alone · risk profile: dementia, dependency, caregiver stress. Interview technique matters and can itself be the answer: separate the patient from the caregiver, ask direct nonjudgmental questions, don't confront the suspected abuser.
Reporting pathways
SituationPath
Elder / dependent adult abuseAPS — report on suspicion, mandated in most states
Child abuseCPS — report on suspicion, no parental consent needed
Intimate partner violence in a competent adultNOT reportable without consent in most states → safety assessment, safety plan, resources, document
Gunshot / stab wounds, certain infectionsReportable regardless
The asymmetry rule Capacity determines the path. Children and cognitively impaired elders get reported over anyone's objection; a competent adult experiencing IPV gets support and autonomy. And "document and re-ask at the next visit" is never the answer once abuse is on the table — it sends a dependent patient back into the home you suspect.

The Vegan Diet

Unprocessed & unfortified · what must be supplemented

Source vignette Pt — 24 yo F on a strict unprocessed vegan diet taking no supplements · Q — the supplement required; options spanned vitamin B12, folic acid and protein supplementation
The decision point

The stem's deciding words are "unprocessed" and "no supplements." A well-planned vegan diet meets most needs — the exam's fork is which nutrients cannot come from unfortified plants: B12 always, vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only ~half the requirement, less in northern latitudes), and calcium (plant sources are oxalate-bound). Iron and zinc join the list for children and menstruating women. The planted wrong answers are folate and protein — abundant in legumes, greens, and grains.

Vegan diet — nutrient risk profile
CategoryContent
Common deficienciesVitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium
At-risk groupsIron, zinc — children (growth) and menstruating women
Not deficientFolate (greens, legumes, fruit); protein and essential amino acids in balanced diets
BenefitsLower glucose and cholesterol; reduced cardiovascular risk
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo F on a strict unprocessed vegan diet, no supplements; the required supplement → Vitamin B12 → no unfortified plant source exists
  2. 26 yo M vegan in a northern state, diffuse bone aches and proximal weakness → Vitamin D deficiency → skin synthesis covers only about half the requirement
  3. 15 yo F vegan with heavy menses, pallor and microcytic anemia → Iron deficiency → supplement; menstruating vegans are an at-risk group
  4. 30 yo F vegan, macrocytic anemia with loss of vibratory sense → Vitamin B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration; folate deficiency has no neurologic signs
  5. 2 yo child raised on the family's unprocessed vegan diet; beyond B12 and vitamin D, supplement → Iron and zinc → rapid growth raises requirements
Pearls Plant calcium (spinach) is oxalate-bound and poorly absorbed · B12 deficiency = macrocytosis plus dorsal-column signs; folate deficiency = macrocytosis alone · non-heme iron absorbs poorly — pair it with vitamin C · balanced vegan diets supply complete protein; "protein deficiency" is bait.
Transferable rule Diet questions are solved by sourcing, not by lists: ask where each nutrient physically comes from — a nutrient with no unfortified plant source must be supplemented, and a nutrient plants are rich in is the distractor.
True-fact-wrong-slotFolate matters in pregnancy stems — planted here where vegan diets are folate-rich.
Uniform-answer doubt"A well-planned vegan diet is nutritionally adequate" feels too permissive but is the credited frame — except for B12.
2 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Preventive Medicine & Ethics

Adolescent Immunization and the Age Platform

Platform, series complete, season · Aquifer · a date buried in line one is data

Source vignette Pt — 11 yo F, up to date on vaccines at age 9, seen in June for a pre-participation evaluation, healthy, no travel · Q — the most appropriate vaccine today; options spanned Tdap, influenza and measles-mumps-rubella
The decision point

Age 11 is the adolescent immunization platform, and it is the only age gate any option here satisfies. She was up to date at 9, so every infant and early-childhood series is finished — hepatitis B, MMR and pneumococcal conjugate. Tdap is the one vaccine whose scheduled slot is now.

Influenza is the trap, and it is a timing trap rather than an eligibility one. She is due for influenza vaccine every year, just not in June: the target window is September or October, and July and August are explicitly discouraged for single-dose recipients because immunity wanes before influenza peaks from December through February.

Defining criteria Adolescent platform at 11 to 12 years — Tdap, HPV and MenACWY come due together · Influenza timing — offer in September or October; avoid July and August for anyone needing a single dose · Catch-up principle — every encounter is a vaccination opportunity, including a sports physical
Each option and the gate it fails
VaccineWhen it is actually givenWhy not at this visit
TdapSingle dose at 11 to 12 years— it is the answer
InfluenzaAnnually, ideally September to OctoberIt is June, and July to August is discouraged
MMR12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 yearsSeries complete before age 9
Pneumococcal conjugateInfant series at 2, 4, 6 and 12 to 15 monthsComplete; no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old
Hepatitis BBirth, 1 to 2 months, 6 to 18 monthsSeries complete in infancy
Scenario bank
  1. 11 yo F, up to date on vaccines at age 9, seen in June for a pre-participation evaluation, healthy, no travel → Tdap → adolescent platform at 11 to 12 years
  2. 11 yo F receiving Tdap today, what else is due at the same visit → HPV and MenACWY → the full 11 to 12 year platform
  3. 16 yo M who received MenACWY at age 11 → MenACWY booster dose → MenB by shared decision-making at 16 to 23
  4. 11 yo F, up to date, seen in early October for a pre-participation evaluation → Give Tdap and influenza vaccine at this visit → both are due now
  5. 15 yo F who has never received HPV vaccine → Begin the HPV series today → catch-up is recommended through age 26
  6. 11 yo M with functional asplenia from sickle cell disease, otherwise up to date → MenACWY as a two-dose primary series, plus MenB → asplenia changes the schedule
  7. 11 yo F newly arrived from abroad with no written immunization records → Vaccinate as though unimmunized → written records only
  8. 11 yo F with rhinorrhea and a temperature of 37.8 C, otherwise well → Vaccinate today → mild illness is not a contraindication
  9. Why influenza vaccine is deferred in June for a child who needs only one dose → Immunity wanes before influenza peaks in December to February → target September or October
A live divergence worth knowing As of January 2026 the CDC schedule specifies one HPV dose at 11 to 12 while the AAP recommends two doses at 9 to 12. The classic keyed answer on retired exam items remains two doses if initiated before 15 and three if at 15 or older or immunocompromised, so expect the exam ledger to lag the clinic ledger here. Dose-count mechanics live in the HPV brief.
Pearls The 11 to 12 platform is three vaccines: Tdap, HPV and MenACWY, and boards test it by offering one among decoys or asking what else is due · MenACWY gets a booster at 16 when the risk period begins; MenB is separate at 16 to 23 by shared decision-making · Asplenia, complement deficiency and eculizumab convert MenACWY into a two-dose primary series with lifelong boosters · Mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics and breastfeeding are not contraindications · Undocumented means unvaccinated — verbal report does not count
Pairs with Part I HPV Vaccination & Series Rules owns the series rules and Part I DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution owns pertussis contraindication versus precaution. Store the link as a question: is this an age-platform question or a series-mechanics question?
Transferable rule When every option is a real vaccine the question is an eligibility gate, and there are only three gates — age platform, series already complete, and season — so check them in that order.
Treat-the-numberTwo years since the last visit baits an interval calculation for a series with no remaining doses.
True-fact-wrong-slotPneumococcal and hepatitis B recommendations feel unsettled enough that something seems owed.

Adolescent Confidentiality

Ask what would have to be true to break it

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, well, discloses weekend marijuana use during the confidential portion of the visit · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned confidential counseling with CRAFFT screening, informing his parents and ordering a urine drug screen
The decision point

A minor discloses substance use during a confidential interview. The answer is keep it confidential and counsel him directly — because substance use is a confidential service in essentially every state, and nothing in the stem triggers an exception. Confidentiality here isn't a courtesy; it's the mechanism that makes honest disclosure possible at all, and adolescents who don't expect it don't disclose.

The right move is procedural, not just permissive: set the frame before he talks ("what you tell me stays between us, unless someone's safety is at risk"), then use the disclosure — screen with CRAFFT, deliver brief counseling, and encourage him to tell his parents himself. Encouraging voluntary disclosure is not the same as disclosing.

Defining criteria Suicidal or homicidal intent — harm to self or others; break confidentiality · Physical or sexual abuse — including statutory abuse by partner age; break confidentiality and report · Imminent danger — specific and serious; imminence is the word that decides · Not an exception — vagueness, a parent asking, an embarrassing diagnosis, or risky behavior that is not imminently lethal
Adolescent confidentiality — what is protected
Confidential without parental consent
STI diagnosis and treatment (all 50 states)
Contraception
Pregnancy care (abortion varies — many states require notification or consent)
Substance use evaluation and treatment
Mental health services (age and state vary)
Emancipated / mature minors: married, military, parenting, self-supporting, court-declared → consent as adults
Trap autopsy "Inform his parents" — the trump-card inversion: parental authority feels like the higher principle, and for most care it is, but the confidential-services carve-outs exist precisely to override it. "Tell him you can't promise confidentiality" — true-sounding and destructive; the correct framing is conditional, naming the specific exceptions, not a blanket refusal. "Refer to a substance-use program" — a sequencing trap: escalation before you've screened severity; occasional use gets brief counseling, not a program. "Order a urine drug screen" — he already told you. Testing to confirm a disclosure is redundant, and a non-consented screen is its own ethics violation.
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well → Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents
  2. 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself → Break confidentiality — safety exception
  3. 16 yo M who drives after drinking → Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the driving → escalate only if he describes an imminent plan to drive impaired
  4. 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told → Provide it confidentially
  5. 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old → Report it → the age gap converts this to statutory abuse
  6. 17 yo M with chlamydia → Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality
  7. 17 yo F, married, needs surgery → She is emancipated and consents herself
  8. 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed → Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home
  9. 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed → Parental consent required → surgical care is not a confidential service
  10. 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks → Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first
  11. 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance → Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point
Paired pearls Set the frame before the disclosure, not after — retroactive confidentiality doesn't exist · CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble) is the validated adolescent screen; ≥2 is positive · emergency care never waits for consent · "encourage him to tell his parents" is almost always in the correct answer — it preserves confidentiality and the family relationship.
Pairs with Elder Abuse & Mandated Reporting above — same axis, opposite direction. There, impaired capacity forces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential service forces silence over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older.
Transferable rule Confidentiality questions are exception-list questions. Don't weigh how serious the behavior sounds — ask whether it satisfies a named exception (harm to self, harm to others, abuse). If it doesn't, confidentiality holds no matter how alarming the disclosure.
